Taiwan’s BizLink teams up with AMS-Osram on AI data center links
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:24:40 UTC
20:24:40 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — BizLink Holding Inc. is tapping the growing convergence of optical and copper connectivity to advance interconnect technology for AI data centers.
The connectivity solutions provider announced Monday that it is partnering with Austria-based optical and sensor solutions provider AMS-Osram. BizLink will contribute its optical expertise and high-volume production capabilities, while AMS-Osram will provide its laser technology, according to UDN and LTN.
The cooperation comes as AI systems scale up, requiring reliable interconnect solutions that balance power consumption, latency, and density. The companies said their architecture addresses these requirements by spreading data across many parallel, lower-speed channels instead of sending large amounts of data through fewer, more complex high-speed channels.
The companies hope to bring the architecture into mass production. They have already built key components of the system, including a two-dimensional array of individually controlled tiny lasers that operate at 850 nanometers to transmit data, along with BizLink’s fiber-to-fiber connectors and optical packaging.
As AI data centers expand and connectivity speeds increase, both copper and optical technologies are expected to play important roles. Copper connections can continue handling shorter links within a rack, while light-based optical links are increasingly used for longer distances between racks.
The industry therefore expects AI data center connectivity to rely on the complementary use of the two technologies rather than a complete shift from copper to optical, according to LTN.

Xinhua News Agency: China just announced President Xi’s state visit to the United States. Could you please share more information about the schedule and China’s expectation for China-U.S. relations?
Guo Jiakun: At the invitation of President Donald J. Trump, President Xi Jinping will soon pay a state visit to the United States. During his visit, President Xi will have in-depth exchange of views with President Trump on major issues concerning bilateral ties and world peace and development.
Head-of-state diplomacy plays an irreplaceable role in providing strategic guidance to China-U.S. relations. The exchange of visits by the two presidents within the span of half a year will mark a milestone of historic significance. China will work with the United States to enrich the dimensions of the China-U.S. constructive relationship of strategic stability, strengthen dialogue and cooperation, and properly manage differences, so as to deliver greater benefits to our two peoples and further contribute to world peace, stability and prosperity.
China News Agency: On the fifth anniversary of the Global Development Initiative (GDI) put forward by President Xi Jinping, could you update us on the implementation of the initiative over the past five years? Is China considering hosting events on the initiative on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly?
Guo Jiakun: Five years ago today, President Xi Jinping put forward the GDI at the general debate of the 76th session of the UN General Assembly. Focusing on development, a timeless theme for humanity, the initiative pools together international efforts to put development high on the global macro policy agenda, aims to expedite the implementation of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and has injected strong impetus into revitalizing global development. The initiative has received extensive recognition from the international community.
Over the past five years, under the guidance of President Xi Jinping and with the joint effort of various parties, fruitful outcomes have been made in implementing the GDI. The GDI has turned from a Chinese proposal into a global consensus, with people-centered development philosophy enjoying increasing popularity. The GDI has played a greater role in driving global development by real actions. Under the framework of the initiative, more than US$23 billion have been mobilized, and more than 2,000 cooperation projects have been carried out. In particular, practical cooperation under the framework of the Global Development and South-South Cooperation Fund has yielded fruitful outcomes in 70 plus countries, benefiting more than 40 million people. The GDI has developed better cooperation architecture across various sectors, laying the groundwork for advancing international development cooperation as well as realizing UN Sustainable Development Goals.
The general debate of the 81st session of the General Assembly starts tomorrow. On the sidelines of the general debate, China will host a High-Level Dialogue on the Fifth Anniversary of the Global Development Initiative at the UN headquarters in New York on September 25. We look forward to working with the broader UN membership to take stock of the achievements and useful experiences over the past five years, share development opportunities, explore cooperation on development, facilitate the implementation of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and build a community with a shared future for humanity.
The New York Times: A U.S. official said last week at a briefing that China has not fully resumed rare earth deliveries despite agreeing to do so at previous summits of the two leaders. What is China’s position?
Guo Jiakun: I’d refer you to competent authorities for the specific question. China is committed to keeping the global industrial and supply chains of critical minerals safe and stable. China and the United States should jointly implement the important common understandings reached between the two presidents and maintain the steady growth momentum of China-U.S. economic and trade ties.
Shenzhen TV: Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson stated on September 18 that Russia had sent a note of protest to the Japanese side regarding the deployment of Typhon missile systems on Kyushu Island. The Kremlin considers the deployment unacceptable and demanded that the Japanese side fully recognize the results of WWII and abandon its remilitarization policy. China also recently sent a note to the Japanese side to express its concerns. Can you confirm that and share more details on that?
Guo Jiakun: The deployment of Typhon missile system, a strategic offensive weapon, is yet another example of Japan’s accelerated remilitarization. Such move will only push up the risk of military confrontation and arms race, threaten strategic balance and regional stability, and harm the legitimate security interests of neighboring countries. The international community is on high alert, with people from multiple Asian countries voicing their opposition to the deployment. China has also lodged strong protests against Japan through diplomatic channels on multiple occasions, and has recently sent a diplomatic note to Japan to reiterate China’s solemn position.
On the occasion of the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trials, China urges Japan to do serious soul-searching on its history of aggression, face up to the call from regional countries, and stop advancing its remilitarization agenda.
Reuters: The New Zealand Defence Force said today that two of its naval ships have transited the Taiwan Strait. The New Zealand PM called this a routine activity and said he was not expecting any backlash from China. Does China have any comment on this event?
Guo Jiakun: China’s position on foreign military vessels’ transit through the Taiwan Strait is consistent.
Beijing Youth Daily: According to preliminary results, the United Russia Party is leading in Russia’s State Duma elections held from September 18 to 20. What’s China’s comment?
Guo Jiakun: China extends congratulations over the smooth conclusion of the Russian State Duma elections. The elections are a major event on Russia’s political calendar. The results of the elections represent the will of the Russian people. As a friendly neighbor and comprehensive strategic partner of coordination for a new era, China firmly supports the Russian people’s independent choice and stands ready to continue working with the Russian side to act on the important common understandings between the two presidents to make fresh progress and bring bilateral relations to new heights.
The New York Times: Is China amenable to an extension of the November 10 deadline for expanded restrictions on rare earth exports, and if so, for how long?
Guo Jiakun: I’d refer you to competent authorities.
China Daily: It’s reported that a terrorist attack on a police facility in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on September 18 caused heavy casualties. Does China have a comment?
Guo Jiakun: China strongly condemns this attack. We mourn for the loss of lives and extend sincere sympathies to the injured and the bereaved families.
Terrorism is a common enemy of humanity. Fighting terrorism is in the shared interests of all countries. China will continue its steadfast support for Pakistan’s counter-terrorism efforts. We call on all countries to join forces in tackling the threat of terrorism and safeguard global security and stability.
The New York Times: China’s restrictions this year on rare earth exports to Japan have affected American supply chains. Will this also be discussed at the summit later this week in Washington?
Guo Jiakun: I’ve just shared relevant information on the summit.
On the rare earth exports restriction you mentioned, in accordance with laws and regulations, China prohibits the export of all dual-use items to Japanese military users and for Japan’s military use, and any export that could help enhance Japan’s military capabilities. The aim is to thwart Japan’s remilitarization and attempt to possess nuclear weapons. China’s position of keeping the global industrial and supply chains of critical minerals safe and stable has not changed. All parties have the responsibility to play a constructive role to this end.
The New York Times: Do you have any further details regarding what progress may have been made in the conversations in New York City between Vice Premier He Lifeng and Treasury Secretary Bessent?
Guo Jiakun: The Chinese side has released a readout, which you may refer to. I have no further information to offer.
The New York Times: CNN reported at the end of last week that the U.S. military had been falsely responding to an AI report that a Chinese vessel was moving military components to the Middle East. Do you have any comment on this?
Guo Jiakun: I am not aware of what you mentioned.

Tens of thousands of German auto workers protest to save jobs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:18:00 UTC
20:18:00 KST

Tens of thousands of German auto workers protest to save jobs
FRANKFURT – German automotive workers held nationwide protests on Sept 21, calling for government and management action to protect jobs and factories as the car industry hits crisis point.
Growing Chinese competition, compounded by weak domestic demand and US tariffs, has thrown the German car industry into crisis.
Volkswagen plans to cut 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade, the biggest ever restructuring in global automotive history. Mercedes-Benz and BMW are also downsizing.
Tens of thousands of people were expected to take part in the protests, which the IG Metall union said would take place at more than 280 sites across Germany.
Speaking at VW’s iconic Wolfsburg factory, the largest in the world by floor area, IG Metall leader and VW supervisory board member Christiane Benner said: “Things have really hit the fan.”
“Companies like VW, BMW, Audi, Bosch, Mercedes and Porsche were synonymous with fantastic cars and high quality,” she said.
“Now, management is driving the industry at full throttle into a brick wall.”
Many blame the industry’s woes on the management for starting too late with the transition to electric vehicles and being too slow to invest in software.
Others point to Chinese government support for its domestic carmakers which many in Europe say has unfairly led to overcapacity in the global car industry.
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said last week he would press for the European Union to further protect the continent’s carmakers from Chinese competitors, saying it was important to not be “naive”.
Speaking on Sept 21, Benner called on the government to make energy cheaper, provide financial help for suppliers who need to retool and promote domestic production with “Made in EU” rules.
“Colleagues in these tumultous times need to be able to count on the protection of comprehensive welfare and industrial policy,” she said.
Painful truths
Speaking after Benner, Daniela Cavallo, head of VW’s works council, told workers some “painful” truths.
“Europe’s automotive industry will be remade,” she said. “Long-established carmakers will fall by the wayside. Others will have to merge.”
“The battle over how to share the burden has already begun,” she added. “The question is not what we as employees will be asked to take, but rather how we collectively can distribute sacrifices fairly among ourselves.”
Wolfgang Schroeder, a political scientist at the University of Kassel who researches labour relations, told AFP that the protests were a sign of “real fear over the future of the industry”.
“A nationwide action that is not related to pay negotiations or to specific disputes with companies but to a whole sector and its problems, that’s rather new,” he said. AFP

NEW YORK, September 21. /TASS/. Qatar has lost around 17% of its liquefied natural gas (LNG) export revenue due to Iranian attacks and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Qatar Central Bank Governor Bandar bin Mohammed bin Saoud Al Thani said.
"We have been impacted by the situation [the conflict in the Middle East - TASS] and as you know, 17% of our [LNG export] revenue has been wiped out," he said in an interview with Bloomberg.

Around 25% of global oil trade and about 20% of global LNG trade passes through the strait. The US administration subsequently effectively signaled an end to the large-scale use of military force against Iran and a shift toward attempting to economically strangle the country through sanctions.

Two athletes, a world of hope as refugee team makes Asian Games debut
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:17:30 CST
20:17:30 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- For Hunaidi Talal Hassan, reaching the Asian Games is a dream years in the making. "For us, this is not just a competition, it is a dream we have worked towards all our lives," the 18-year-old told a press conference on Monday. "We always had hope. And today we are here living that dream."
Hassan and fellow taekwondo athlete Muhammed Mahmoud Jasem make up the first refugee team to participate in the Asian Games. Both are from Syria and now live in Jordan. At Aichi-Nagoya 2026, they bring ambitions for the competition ahead, along with stories of how sport helped them see a future when one had seemed out of reach.
Hassan took up taekwondo at nine. The sport, she says, has changed many things in her life for the better. Being at the Games is a source of happiness and pride, made all the more meaningful by the difficulties she has faced.
"We faced many challenges, but we kept going and never gave up on our dreams," she said.
Jasem began practicing taekwondo at 14. For him, its importance has long extended beyond training and competition.
"This sport means a lot to me. It was my only hope," he said.
Living in a refugee camp, Jasem had struggled to imagine what lay ahead. Taekwondo gave him reason to believe a better life was possible. He kept training, and years of effort brought him to the Asian Games, where representing refugee athletes is both an honor and a responsibility.
"I'm not just participating in a regular competition. I'm carrying a story with me. I hope it will be a success story," he said.
Both athletes want to do well. They also want people to understand the journeys that brought them here. Speaking through an interpreter, they thanked their coaches, families and others whose support and belief had helped them reach the Games.
Introducing the pair, Olympic Council of Asia Deputy Director General Vinod Kumar Tiwari emphasized that they had earned their places through training and sacrifice, just like every other competitor.
Their presence also carries a wider meaning, he said. For people forced to leave their homes, sport can offer purpose, belonging and hope.
Beyond competition, both athletes also spoke about their experience at the opening ceremony. Through an interpreter, they expressed pride in attending as members of the first refugee team at an Asian Games.
Shiva Keshavan, vice chair of the OCA Athletes Committee, had met them at the athletes' accommodation and spoken with them again before the press conference. They had told him about the people they encountered and the athletes they met while entering the opening ceremony.
For Keshavan, those encounters are part of what sport makes possible.
"They are part of a family. We welcome them with open arms," he said. "The human connections, the bonds that they will make here will last a lifetime."
The questions on Monday also looked beyond the Games: how could the opportunities opened up in Nagoya be sustained once the competition was over?
OCA officials said they would discuss the athletes' needs with them and build on the training support already in place in Jordan. Tiwari expressed hope that refugee team would continue to take part in future Asian Games, drawing on the IOC's experience.
Speaking after the press conference, Mohammad Tayyab Ikram, president of the International Hockey Federation and chair of the OCA Coordination Committee for the 2026 Asian Games, said plans included reaching athletes in more locations and providing access to suitable training facilities.
National Olympic committees and international federations would work together to assess athletes' backgrounds, sporting ability and eligibility, he said. Helping them establish stable lives and continue their sporting careers was particularly important.
Ikram also said he expected the number of refugee athletes participating in the Games to increase. ■

COLOMBO, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka Police will introduce on-site drug-testing kits within the next two to three months as part of efforts to curb driving under the influence of narcotics, Inspector General of Police Priyantha Weerasooriya said on Monday.
Weerasooriya said police had observed a shift in the causes of serious road accidents, with narcotics use becoming an increasing concern. A recent pilot operation targeting buses found that more than 5 percent of drivers tested had been under the influence of narcotics, he said.
At present, suspected drug-impaired drivers must be referred for medical testing, unlike alcohol cases, which can often be detected at the scene. Police have made drug testing mandatory for drivers involved in serious accidents, Weerasooriya said.
He said alcohol and drug use, reckless driving, speeding and traffic violations remained major causes of fatal accidents.
Sri Lanka has recorded 1,849 fatal accidents so far in 2026. Compared with the same period last year, fatal accidents have increased by eight and deaths by 16, he said. ■

Feature: Zhu Yuling begins new table tennis chapter after eight-year Asian Games absence
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:17:06 CST
20:17:06 KST

by sportswriters Sun Zhe and Huang Haoran
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- For Zhu Yuling, the table tennis arena at the Asian Games felt both familiar and unfamiliar.
She had been here before, winning the women's team gold medal with China at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta. But eight years later, Zhu returned to the continental championships in a different jersey, representing Macao, China.
And in her first match at the Aichi-Nagoya Games, Zhu found herself across the table from her former teammates as her team faced China, the dominant force in women's table tennis, in the group stage.
"I was still very nervous in my first match," Zhu said. "Standing on the court at a continental multi-sport event, the feeling was very hard to describe."
Her first opponent could hardly have made the moment more emotional: Wang Manyu, the current women's singles world No. 1.
Zhu, 31, also once the world's top-ranked women's singles player herself, took the first two games 11-9, 11-9. Wang fought back to win the third 11-7, but Zhu closed out the match 13-11 in the fourth.
Later, Zhu faced another former teammate, Sun Yingsha, losing 3-0 as China eventually won 3-1. But her performance had already won warm applause from the crowd.
"My condition was even better than I had imagined," Zhu said. "Before the match, I went to my coach and told him I wanted to play first and face the strongest opponent. I wanted to find out where I was at and also fight for the chance to play the second match. In fact, I did it."
For Zhu, simply being there was already a victory.
Eight years ago she was a key member of China's team that won gold in Jakarta. She was then pushing toward the Tokyo Olympics, seemingly on a clear path at the highest level of the sport.
Then her life took an unexpected turn.
In August 2020, Zhu was diagnosed with a fibroadenoma, a non-cancerous breast lump. More than a year later, after undergoing surgery, she was forced to put down her paddle. She missed the Olympics, left China's national team and gradually disappeared from the spotlight.
But Zhu did not remain defined by what she had lost.
In 2022, Zhu began pursuing a doctorate in management at the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, researching career transitions among elite athletes, a subject closely tied to her own experience. She later joined Tianjin University as a physical education teacher.
Another chapter began in February 2024, when Zhu obtained Macao residency through the Macao Special Administrative Region government's talent recruitment program and began representing Macao, China in international competition.
Zhu was starting her second career in table tennis virtually from zero, while juggling classes to teach, a doctoral dissertation to finish, and training sessions and tournaments to prepare for.
Yet less than a year after returning to the international table tennis circuit, she had climbed back into the world's top 10.
Now, at the Asian Games, she has a new goal.
Macao, China opened its second women's team match with a 3-1 victory over Nepal on Monday.
"My goal is to create the best result in Macao's history," Zhu said. "This is very significant for us. We hope that, through our own efforts, we can inspire more young people in Macao."
After watching Zhu fight for every point against China, her Macao teammate Leung On Na broke down in tears.
"Seeing her fight for every single ball, I was really moved," Leung said.
For Zhu, however, this is not a story of hardship, but of gratitude for having another chance to compete.
"I think my life has been quite smooth," she said. "Although I am no longer at the top of the pyramid, being able to stand on the court itself means that, for me, I have already overcome myself." ■

Australian vaccine platform targets emerging mosquito-borne disease threats
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:17:01 CST
20:17:01 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- An Australian vaccine platform demonstrated in animals could soon become a "plug-and-play" system to rapidly adapt to future mosquito-borne disease threats in humans, researchers said.
Building on more than a decade of work, University of Queensland (UQ) researchers have developed the ISVac platform, which uses a mosquito-specific virus genetically engineered to generate virus particles that are non-infectious to humans or animals, according to a UQ statement released Monday.
The particles have been used as vaccines against Japanese encephalitis virus in pigs and West Nile virus in crocodiles, said UQ Associate Professor Jody Peters.
"This next stage is a huge leap forward, developing a potential new tool to protect humans against emerging mosquito-borne diseases," Peters said.
"With the changing climate there's been an expansion of where mosquitoes are thriving, and it is pushing mosquito-borne diseases into new regions," she said, adding that Japanese encephalitis, which can cause severe neurological illness, lifelong disability and death, was not seen in Australia until 2022.
If successful, the platform could support the development of vaccines against other mosquito-borne diseases, including dengue, Zika, yellow fever and West Nile virus, the researchers said. ■

Sri Lanka records highest educated youth unemployment in regional IMF comparison
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:17:01 CST
20:17:01 KST

COLOMBO, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka has recorded the highest unemployment rate among young people with advanced education in a group of Asian economies examined by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), local news outlet Newswire reported Monday.
According to a chart published in the September 2026 edition of the IMF's "Finance & Development" magazine, based on 2025, or the latest available data, about 43 percent of Sri Lankans aged 15 to 24 with post-secondary education are unemployed. The figure is the highest among the economies compared, ahead of India at about 42 percent and Bangladesh at about 36 percent.
The data showed that youth unemployment across Asia is often substantially higher among those with advanced education than among the general population. The pattern is particularly pronounced in South Asia.
The findings point to a problem extending beyond the availability of jobs, with graduates increasingly facing a mismatch between their qualifications and the skills demanded by employers. Similar pressures have been reported across Asian economies, although the scale differs considerably between countries.
Technological change could further complicate the situation. The IMF noted that artificial intelligence has the potential to improve productivity and economic growth, but could also increase labor-market pressure on young workers if adoption advances faster than skills development. ■

Asian Games | Feature: Lee Hyun-jung powers South Korea to gold after years chasing NBA dream
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:16:53 CST
20:16:53 KST

by sportswriters Li Bowen, Cao Yibo, Yue Chenxing
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- The final buzzer sounded and the scoreboard read 67-57. South Korea's players poured off the bench and crumpled into one another at midcourt. Lee Hyun-jung stood among his teammates, and the tears came before he could stop them.
"I always seem to cry when I win a championship. The feeling of winning is so wonderful, and I think that is why the tears came. I also know how hard my teammates fought for this gold medal," Lee said after the game.
Lee had played nearly the entire final against host Japan, shooting 8 for 12 from the floor and 5 of 8 from three-point range. He finished with 27 points, 18 rebounds, three assists the whole game.
The teams were tied 28-28 at the break. In the fourth quarter, Lee kept rising to hit, stretched the lead to 13 and snuffed out Japan's last run. South Korea had its first Asian Games men's basketball gold in 12 years.
"I'm unbelievably happy. More than anything, I'm extremely grateful to my teammates," Lee said afterward.
The medal carried weight beyond the podium. South Korea's conscription law requires able-bodied men to serve roughly 18 months in the military. Winning a gold medal at an Asian Games is one of the few ways of achieving an exemption. At 25, Lee had played this final with his career clock on the line. 18 months away from top-level competition would have ruined any chance he has left of reaching the NBA.
That is a dream he has chased for years.
Born on October 23, 2000, in Seongnam, Lee grew up inside a basketball-playing family. His mother, Sung Jung-a, took a silver medal while representing South Korea at the 1984 Olympic Games. His father, Lee Yoon-hwan, played semi-professionally before becoming a high school athletic director and coach. His older sister, Lee Ri-na, played for South Korea's under-16 national team.
Lee did not take the red carpet laid out at home. He moved alone at 17 to the NBA Global Academy in Canberra, Australia, played for the BA Centre of Excellence and learned English at Lake Ginninderra Secondary College. From there he committed to Davidson, the small North Carolina school where Steph Curry played, choosing the Wildcats over an offer from Washington State.
At Davidson, Lee became the fourth South Korean to reach NCAA Division I. He averaged 8.4 points as a reserve freshman in 2019-20 and made the Atlantic 10 all-rookie team. As a sophomore he started every game and became the first player in program history to shoot at least 50 percent overall, 40 percent from three and 90 percent from the free throw line in the same season. As a junior he averaged 15.8 points and 6.0 rebounds, scored a career-high 32 against Charlotte and was named first-team All-Atlantic 10.
Then came the fall. A foot injury kept him from the NBA scouting combine. A prospect once viewed as a late second-round talent went undrafted in 2022.
He kept going. He joined the Santa Cruz Warriors of the G League in February 2023, averaged 5.5 points in 12 games and played for the Philadelphia 76ers in that year's Summer League. When it did not lead to a roster spot, he signed with the Illawarra Hawks of Australia's National Basketball League and helped them win the 2025 NBL championship.
That July, Lee signed with the Nagasaki Velca in Japan's B. League. He helped the team win that year's championship and was named MVP, making him the first South Korean to earn that honor in the B. League.
This summer he returned to the NBA circuit for his third Summer League, this time with the San Antonio Spurs, and the Portland Trail Blazers later gave him an Exhibit 10 training-camp deal.
Lee thought of his national team coach, Nikolajs Mazurs, while he wept on the Nagoya floor. The coach, alone in a foreign country, reminded him of his own younger self, the teenager who had left for Canberra with no support staff, no family nearby, no guarantee.
Mazurs arrived under anything but certainty. The 45-year-old Latvian was hired in December 2025. Before the Asian Games, South Korea had lost more games than it had won under him, including two straight warm-up defeats to Japan, and doubt followed the team into the tournament.
"A lot of people said that it would be difficult for us to win the gold medal," Lee said. "But under our coach's system, we worked hard to become more coordinated as a team. We did not allow ourselves to become discouraged by outside opinions. I think the fact that we stayed focused on one another and developed our chemistry led to this result."
"Despite everything, he did not become discouraged. He adapted well to us, and we managed to win the gold medal together. I am extremely grateful to him, and maybe thinking about the coach was one of the main reasons I cried so much," Lee added.
South Korea did not win this with Lee alone. Lee Jung-hyun added 14 points and seven assists beside him. Much of Lee's work was more than his three-pointers, 18 rebounds, many snatched over Japan's bigger frontcourt for second shots. A wing who built his reputation as a shooter had played like a center on the glass when it mattered most.
"I kept thinking the same thing: if I had an opportunity, I would take the shot, and I had to run one more step and make one more effort for my teammates. That was all I was thinking about," Lee said. ■

This year's World Cleanup Day (WCD) focuses on reducing food waste and raising awareness; the movement originated in Estonia as the Teeme ära! Campaign back in 2008.
From its humble beginnings, Teeme ära! ("Let's do it!") has grown into a global initiative. Since 2018, more than 139 million people from 211 countries and territories have taken part in WCD events, collecting over 870,000 tonnes of waste in the process.
The UN General Assembly officially designated September 20 as World Cleanup Day in 2023, and the movement's global headquarters, the NGO Let's Do It World, is still based in Estonia.
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) noted WCD's growth and importance. "This is not merely a clean-up campaign. It is an initiative that strengthens community cooperation, builds trust, and helps keep our planet sustainable," he said. He added that the movement is centered on the responsibility each person bears for their surroundings, with a goal of engaging at least 5 per cent of the population of every country taking part.
Minister: Russia must be held accountable for the €150 billion environmental damage it caused in Ukraine
Tsahkna also noted WCD serves as a reminder that the environment is often a silent victim of war, including in Russia's ongoing occupation of Ukrainian territories.
"Through its war of aggression, Russia has caused an estimated €150 billion in environmental damage in Ukraine," he said. "The aggressor is using nature as a strategic weapon. In recent months, Russia has increasingly targeted civilian infrastructure, bombing fuel depots, railways, and ports. The resulting pollution, contamination, and fires are causing severe damage to Ukraine's natural environment, water resources, air quality, and ecosystems," the minister went on via a press release.
"Agriculture has suffered particularly heavily. Bombing, artillery fire, and destroyed military equipment have contaminated agricultural land, one of Ukraine's most important economic resources, with toxic substances and heavy metals. Their impact on crops and ecosystems will be felt for decades. The deliberate destruction of the environment is a crime, and Russia must be held accountable."
Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, the war has generated an estimated 311 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions in Ukraine, while approximately 30 per cent of Ukraine's territory is contaminated by landmines and unexploded ordnance. The cost of clearing the country of mines alone is estimated at US$38 billion.

====================================================================================================

Spain and Türkiye: Five centuries of evolving ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:13:24 UTC
20:13:24 KST

For centuries, Turks and Spaniards imagined each other, long before they ever truly met.
In 16th- and 17th-century Spain, "the Turk" appeared in paintings, plays, festivals, sermons, and battle accounts. The Ottoman Empire was then one of the great powers of the Mediterranean and also one of the main rivals of the Spanish monarchy.
Across the sea, however, Spain generally occupied a less constant place in Ottoman concerns.
This contradiction (imagining the other a lot and knowing little about them) was a recurring theme at a congress held in Istanbul to commemorate the Spanish-Ottoman Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1782.
For two days, Spanish and Turkish historians reconstructed a relationship more complex and nuanced than the simple story of rivalry, peace, and subsequent reconciliation.
Because Spain and Türkiye have been meeting for five centuries. What has changed is the way they do it.
From its earliest centuries, the Ottoman Empire held a prominent place in the Spanish imagination.
Both powers vied for control of the Mediterranean Sea; corsairs linked to the Ottoman regencies in North Africa, such as Algiers and Tunis, raided the Iberian coasts, and thousands of people directly experienced war or captivity.
The Battle of Lepanto in 1571, a historic naval confrontation in which the prominent writer Miguel de Cervantes , author of Don Quixote, participated, left an indelible mark on the geopolitics of the time and ended up becoming the great symbol of that rivalry.
But in those times, “the Turk” was much more than a military adversary. He appeared in plays, romances, celebrations, and paintings.
A project led by art historian Ivan Rega Castro on the construction of the Turkish imaginary analyses precisely how these representations adapted to the needs of each era.
In Hispanic painting of the 16th and 17th centuries, his presence was relatively discreet but constant, extending even to the monarchy's American territories.
Over time, moreover, the Turk became a recognisable image of the “enemy”: he could appear as a defeated captive, a fearsome warrior, or even as a ridiculed figure, and was even used anachronistically to represent conflicts that occurred centuries before the Ottoman expansion.
The problem is that those images could be much more intense than the actual knowledge of the other person.
Even enemies negotiated
The image of the Turk as a great Mediterranean adversary did not prevent Spaniards and Ottomans from talking to each other when necessary.
By the end of the 16th century, after decades of conflict, both empires began to seek ways to reduce a rivalry that was becoming increasingly costly.
No permanent embassies existed between Madrid and Istanbul, but emissaries, intermediaries, merchants, and agents carried messages between the courts.
Diplomatic contacts, secret negotiations, and even projects aimed at achieving a more lasting peace existed.
During the Istanbul congress, historian and expert on the early modern Ottoman period Evrim Turkcelik succinctly summarised the situation with the phrase: “Negotiating without normalisation”.
This helps us understand a reality often lost when history is reduced to the Battle of Lepanto and the Mediterranean Wars. Spain and the Ottoman Empire could be at war at one time and, at the same time, maintain open channels of communication.
Furthermore, the Mediterranean in the 16th and 17th centuries was not divided into two completely isolated worlds.
Goods and news circulated through its ports, but so did freed captives, converts to Islam, interpreters, merchants, and religious figures.
The border separated, but it also connected.
This coexistence of rivalry and diplomatic interaction also explains why the treaty signed in 1782 did not emerge from nothing.
Rather, it was the decisive step from occasional diplomacy, dependent on intermediaries and specific circumstances, to a much more stable relationship.
The big change came at the end of the 18th century, when the period marked by the Battle of Lepanto and the great naval and military rivalry was behind us, and both powers had new priorities.
Spain was looking more and more towards the Atlantic and America, while the Ottoman Empire had to face, among other challenges, the advance of the Russian Empire towards the Black Sea and southeastern Europe.
In 1782, they signed a Treaty of Peace, Friendship, and Commerce in Istanbul, ratified the following year. Rather than ushering in a sudden friendship, the agreement transformed the former adversary into a stable partner.
As historian Elsa Medina Iglesias summarised during the congress, it was the convergence of “two reasons of state”.
From then on, the relationship no longer relied solely on occasional envoys and paved the way for more regular legations, consulates, and commercial contacts.
From political to cultural rapprochement
The next major change came in the 20th century. After the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, the Republic of Türkiye was proclaimed in 1923 under the leadership of Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, and just a year later, Spain signed a Treaty of Friendship with the new state.
A prime example of that era was Yahya Kemal Beyatli, one of the great Turkish poets of the 20th century and author of Dance in Andalusia, who arrived in Madrid in 1929 as a diplomat and the first plenipotentiary minister of the new Republic in Spain.
He perfectly encapsulates how culture and diplomacy were beginning to intertwine in a relationship very different from that of previous centuries.
For decades, however, the relationship remained relatively discreet. A genuine rapprochement began to become more visible in the 1980s and 90s.
Spain had emerged from a 40-year dictatorship and joined NATO and the then European Economic Community.
Meanwhile, Türkiye, a member of the transatlantic alliance since 1952, was also strengthening its ties with Europe. Official visits became more frequent, and both governments began to maintain a more regular political relationship.
One of the clearest symbols of this new era was the Alliance of Civilisations.
Proposed in 2004 by the then Spanish prime minister, Jose Luis Rodriguez Zapatero (2004-2011), and co-sponsored by Türkiye under the government of Recep Tayyip Erdogan, the initiative stemmed from a simple idea: in an increasingly interdependent world, the security, development, and prosperity of some societies could not be understood in isolation from others.
Based on this premise, it sought to generate a common political will to combat prejudice, misperceptions, and polarisation, especially between Western and Muslim societies.
The United Nations formally incorporated it in 2005.
It is difficult to find an image further removed from Lepanto: Spain and Türkiye presenting themselves together, not as representatives of civilisations destined to clash, but as promoters of dialogue between them.
Today, the relationship between Spain and Türkiye is no longer built solely on governments and embassies.
It is an increasingly broad and diverse relationship, encompassing businesses, universities, tourists, students, and books, and it promises to continue deepening as exchanges between the two societies grow.
In 2025, trade between the two countries exceeded $20.5 billion, a record figure.
That same year, more than 452,000 Spaniards travelled to Türkiye. Istanbul, Cappadocia, and the Aegean coast are now increasingly popular tourist destinations for Spaniards.
Contact between the two countries is thus beginning to extend beyond diplomatic summits.
Cultural ties have also strengthened. The Cervantes Institute has operated in Istanbul since 2001, and the Yunus Emre Institute has had a branch in Madrid since 2018.
Both serve as spaces to promote their respective languages and cultures through courses, cultural activities, and meetings that bring the two societies closer beyond official relations.
Added to this is a growing circulation of books and ideas: Turkish authors such as Orhan Pamuk , Zulfu Livaneli , and Ahmet Hamdi Tanpinar can now be read in Spanish, bringing themes such as Istanbul, memory, modernisation, and the tensions between tradition and change closer to Spanish-speaking audiences.
At the same time, Spanish works continue to find new readers in Turkish.
History has not simply been a leap from enmity to friendship. The process was more complex and gradual: Spaniards and Ottoman Turks first imagined each other, then learned to negotiate, later built permanent relationships, and finally began to get to know each other more directly.
The Mediterranean Sea, which separated the worlds of Philip II in the 16th century and the Ottoman sultans, remains in the same place. The distance between its two shores, however, seems to be shrinking.
(This article was first published on TRT Español)

Feature: A Maowusu reunion rooted in American’s kindness, forged by Chinese farmer’s grit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:11:17 UTC
20:11:17 KST

HOHHOT, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) — For more than a quarter of a century, a retired American teacher and a Chinese woman fighting desertification have lived on opposite sides of the Pacific, bound together by old photos, a newspaper and a forest. On Sunday, they finally met again, face to face.
As Ronald Sakolsky descended an escalator at an airport in Ordos, north China’s Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, he wiped tears from his eyes with his right hand while clutching a bouquet in his left.
At the bottom stood Yin Yuzhen, a woman who has spent over four decades wringing green life from the Maowusu, the fourth-largest sandy area in China. The short ride down the escalator was the last stretch before their long-awaited embrace, 26 years after their first in-person meeting.
Their friendship began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China’s Henan Province — more than 11,000 kilometers from his home in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, under a teachers’ exchange program between the two countries.
One ordinary evening, a television program caught his eye. On the screen was Yin, planting trees to help hold back the advancing sands of the Maowusu sandy land.
Stretching across parts of Inner Mongolia, Shaanxi and Ningxia, the Maowusu has been one of the front lines in China’s fight against desertification in the north: an effort launched in 1978 and slated to continue through 2050.
But for Yin, the fight against the sand was not an abstract national effort. In those years, a night of strong winds could leave the doorway of their dugout sealed by sand. There was grit in the food, dirt in the water, and little else in sight but miles of shifting yellow stretching in every direction.
By 1999, Yin had planted trees across some 30,000 mu (about 2,000 hectares) of barren land — an area equivalent to around 2,800 standard soccer pitches.
“I was so touched that I started to cry,” Sakolsky recalled, thinking back to that evening. “I honestly cannot tell you why. Something just happened to me. I just felt like I needed to help.”
Over the next two months, he contacted more than a dozen organizations across the United States. A Boston-based charity agreed to provide a grant of 5,000 U.S. dollars.
At the time, the donation was a staggering sum for Yin — enough to build a house, cover the costs of raising her children, and give her family a very different life. Yet, Yin spent it all on saplings, keeping only a single banknote as a memento.
In May 2000, Sakolsky took a train from Luoyang, Henan, and then switched to another vehicle, jolting all the way into the sandy land to see the saplings with his own eyes.
He later described the landscape as desolate: “No roads, no trees, no houses. We were just driving over one dune after another.”
Then he spotted Yin. “She popped out of a hole,” Sakolsky said. The two couldn’t speak each other’s language, and they relied entirely on gestures and smiles to communicate. Yin showed Sakolsky how to plant.
To Sakolsky, the saplings looked so fragile that he thought they might never grow much higher than his knees. Deep down, he could not see how this patch of sand could ever become a forest. He told her so plainly: “This is impossible.”
That night, Yin and her husband invited him to their home for dinner, and made him a steaming bowl of noodles.
“Delicious,” Sakolsky recalled.
Sakolsky went home months later, and they lost touch. Across the Pacific, he kept telling his students about the Chinese woman who was trying to turn a desert green. In China, whenever Yin met an American, she would pull out an old photograph of Sakolsky and ask if they knew how she could get in touch with him.
RECONNECTED ONLINE
Year after year, her search went nowhere, until a video and a social media post achieved what years of searching had not.
In May this year, Yin stood before the forest she had spent decades growing, holding up the old dollar bill — the one she had saved from the money Sakolsky had raised. She looked into the camera and said: “Mr. Sakolsky, if you see this video, I invite you to come back to China and see the forest that grew from the money you sent us.”
The appeal quickly went viral online. Within hours, messages began reaching Sakolsky in the form of emails and texts from strangers telling him that a Chinese woman was looking for him. Less than 26 hours after Yin posted the video, they found him. The two then reconnected online.
This was followed by photographs and videos. For the first time, Sakolsky saw what had become of the saplings he had once thought too small to make much difference: a forest of more than 50,000 trees.
“Amazing. Absolutely amazing,” he said.
A DREAM FULFILLED
Upon arriving in Beijing early this past Sunday, Sakolsky received mooncakes sent by Yin, a traditional Chinese symbol of reunion, and tomatoes grown in the sandy land. He flew to Ordos that afternoon.
“This is a dream come true from a lady who is the hero of the story,” he told media gathered around them at the local airport.
“I never thought I would see her again,” Sakolsky said. For him, this visit brought home the power of a culture that lives by its promises. Yin had vowed that the saplings would take root and grow, and that one day he could come back to see them for himself.
Today, including the trees funded by Sakolsky’s efforts, Yin and her family have planted trees across 70,000 mu, an area roughly the size of 6,500 standard soccer pitches. Poplars, oriental arborvitaes, spruce and Mongolian Scots pines now rustle in the wind as birds chirp.
Official figures show that about 85 percent of the Maowusu has been restored. Between 2021 and 2025, China accounted for roughly one-quarter of the world’s increase in green vegetation and managed to rehabilitate approximately 152 million mu of sandified land.
When he raised the money in 1999, he expected nothing in return, Sakolsky said.
“You can’t give something and then expect something back,” he told Xinhua. “I raised that money because I wanted to thank China, and I wanted to help her make China a little more beautiful. That’s all.”
On Monday afternoon, Sakolsky walked through a carpet of fallen leaves as Yin led him to a tall, sturdy poplar, more than 10 meters high, in a grove named in his honor.
He could hardly believe it. This was the tree he and Yin had planted together 26 years ago. Back then, the sapling had been no thicker than a finger, swaying in the wind as if it might be swallowed by the sand at any moment.
Yin handed him a shovel. “Let’s plant another one.”
The two bent down together. Yin steadied the sapling as Sakolsky pressed soil around its roots — his hands trembling slightly but his movements steady.
“I planted a friendship tree in Inner Mongolia,” Sakolsky said.
FRIENDSHIP FOR GENERATIONS
To welcome Sakolsky, more than a dozen members of Yin’s family had come from different places to be there for the meeting. Red chili peppers hung by the doorway and small pumpkins lined the walls, while the courtyard had been swept clean.
“I asked my children to come back because I hope the friendship between our two families will last for generations,” Yin said. “I want my children and grandchildren to remember it.”
For Sakolsky, the reunion with Yin and her family is about more than a forest. It is a reminder that no act of kindness, no matter how small, is ever wasted. Given time, a small act can take root, spread and grow into something no one could have imagined.
The story of Sakolsky and Yin adds another thread to the long history of goodwill between the people of China and the United States — from the American volunteer pilots who fought alongside Chinese forces during World War II to the historic visit of a U.S. table tennis team to China in 1971 and, more recently, the Philadelphia Orchestra’s decades of performances in the country.
During his stay in China from Aug. 23 to Sept. 1, Sakolsky will also take part in China-U.S. teacher exchanges and return to Henan, where he will meet teachers and students at the school where he once taught, among other activities.
The retired history teacher believes that while people may look different and come from different cultures, underneath it all, everyone bleeds red.
“Whether you’re Chinese or American, we all love our families, we all love life, and we all love the Earth,” he said.
Americans and Chinese need to “focus on our similarities and not on our differences,” he once noted. He hopes that when the trip is over, the message can reach people around the world: Chinese and American people “can work together and make a peaceful world.”
“I see where the United States and China can work together,” said Sakolsky. “So I will not quit. She never quit. ‘Quit’ is not in her vocabulary. Together, it works.”

Houthis push for control of Yemen highlands as Trump reported to have called off airstrikes

Houthis push for control of Yemen highlands as Trump reported to have called off air strikes
- Houthis are advancing to seize strategic highlands in Yemen, aiming to cut off Saudi-backed areas from the Red Sea coast, despite Saudi air strikes and US hesitance to intervene.
- US President Trump reportedly called off planned air strikes on Houthis last minute, increasing tensions and complicating Saudi Arabia's efforts to control the conflict.
- The conflict threatens global oil supplies by risking closure of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait; Saudi Arabia reroutes oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, raising fuel prices worldwide.
AI generated
DUBAI – Houthi fighters were pushing to seize strategic heights in Yemen on Sept 21 to cut off the Red Sea coast from remaining areas held by Saudi-backed forces, after a report that US President Donald Trump had called off US strikes on the group at the last minute.
A lightning advance by the Iran-backed group in September has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theatre and further threatened global energy supplies.
Washington has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to join the fight in Yemen. The Houthis said on Sept 19 that they had fired on Riyadh, where loud booms were followed by columns of smoke visible near the airport.
Saudi Arabia has not commented on the first apparent strikes on the capital since the escalation began.
The New York Times reported that the Trump administration had prepared on Sept 20 to launch air strikes against the Houthis after fresh pleas from the Saudi Crown Prince. But the newspaper said Trump called off the air strikes at the last minute, even as troops were loading bombs onto aircraft.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report and the US military’s Central Command did not respond to an e-mail seeking comment.
Fighting in highlands
The Houthis, who have controlled Yemen’s capital since 2014, seized the country’s Red Sea coast in September in a lightning advance that routed forces of an internationally recognised Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia and based in the south.
Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on the fighters’ positions in the highlands, according to the Houthis. But the air power advantage has so far done little to slow the advance of the fighters as Saudi-backed government forces have melted away.
According to the United Nations, nearly 700 people have been killed and thousands injured in the flare-up in fighting. More than 120,000 Yemenis have fled homes within Yemen, and thousands more have fled by boat across the Red Sea to Africa.
Five Yemeni military sources told Reuters the Houthis were now seeking to seize strategic heights, known as the Kahboub Mountains, in two provinces, Taiz and Lahij, which separate the Red Sea coast from the government-held south.
Fighting has centred on the outskirts of the remote mountain Al-Wazi’iyah district in Taiz province, and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast between the mouth of the Red Sea that the fighters captured last week and the government’s base in Aden.
The Houthis aim to secure the rear of their forces around the Bab al-Mandab Strait leading into the Red Sea by taking control of the heights, which would allow them to open new fronts, according to the sources. That would help protect exposed positions the Houthis captured during their advance around Dhubab on the Red Sea and on Perim Island in the strait.
Saudi oil exports
The surge in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis creates a new dilemma for Trump, under pressure to help defend Washington’s close Saudi allies but anxious not to further expand the deeply unpopular war he launched in February against Iran.
The United States bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire with the group and has kept out of the conflict since.
The Houthis’ newfound control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait risks cutting off the main alternative route that Saudi Arabia has used for oil exports that bypass disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia has responded by increasing shipments through Hormuz, where a small number of tankers are increasingly shuttling back and forth to bring out oil with their transponders off, charging record fees of as much as a quarter of the value of the cargo to brave the wartime risk. They then transfer the oil to other ships in the Indian Ocean, bound for customers in Asia or elsewhere.
Satellite data shows Saudi exports through Hormuz reaching 2.9 million barrels per day in recent days, up from just 700,000 in August, partially making up for a halt to Saudi loadings at its Red Sea port of Yanbu.
That has helped put a cap on the global price of crude oil, which has retreated closer to US$100 a barrel after approaching US$110 last week. But consumers and industry are still paying record prices for refined fuels.
The US retail price of diesel, politically sensitive for Trump with midterm elections in six weeks, hit another all-time high on Sept 21 above US$6.51 a gallon. It was around US$3.75 before Trump launched the war alongside Israel in February.
In the latest reported attack in Hormuz, Britain’s UKMTO maritime security agency said a ship sailing into the strait had been hit with a projectile, causing minor injuries to crew.
Diplomacy in the wider conflict has largely been stalled since a June interim agreement between the United States and Iran collapsed within weeks. Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to fly on Sept 22 to New York to attend the UN General Assembly, the first such visit since Trump launched Operation Epic Fury against his country alongside Israel in February. EU Fails to Agree on Putin Sanctions Renewal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:07:00 UTC
20:07:00 KST

EU ambassadors failed again on Monday to agree on renewing individual sanctions against Russia, leaving restrictions on Russian President Vladimir Putin and thousands of other people and entities unresolved shortly before they expire.
The EU’s Committee of Permanent Representatives, known as Coreper, discussed the renewal on Monday morning but reached no decision, European Pravda reported, citing EU diplomatic sources.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Coreper did not decide on extending the sanctions. The next meeting is scheduled after lunch,” one diplomat said.
A second meeting was expected later on Monday. The current short-term extension of the sanctions is due to expire on Tuesday.
France and Slovakia seek delistings
EU countries normally renew the individual sanctions every six months. However, on Sept. 14, they extended the restrictions for only seven days after failing to resolve objections raised by France and Slovakia.
The two countries reportedly want Russian oligarchs removed from the sanctions list before approving a longer extension.
European Pravda previously reported that France was seeking the removal of billionaire Alisher Usmanov. During earlier negotiations in March, Slovakia pushed for the removal of Usmanov and Alfa Bank co-founder Mikhail Fridman.
Any decision to extend or amend the sanctions requires unanimous approval from all 27 EU member states. An objection from one government can therefore block the renewal of the entire list.
Kremlin Says No Progress in Ukraine Peace Talks
The unresolved extension covers sanctions against Putin, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, former Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych and other senior officials, military commanders, lawmakers, businesspeople, and entities accused of supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine.
What the sanctions cover
The EU sanctions regime applies to nearly 3,000 individuals and entities associated with Russia’s aggression, occupation of Ukrainian territory, and efforts to undermine Ukraine’s sovereignty and independence.
The measures include asset freezes and travel bans. EU citizens and companies are also prohibited from making funds or other economic resources available to sanctioned people and organizations.
The bloc introduced the regime in 2014 following Russia’s occupation and illegal annexation of Crimea. It was significantly expanded after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The dispute concerns individual listings and is separate from the EU’s broader sectoral restrictions on the Russian economy, which have their own renewal timetable.
The EU also adopted its 21st sanctions package in July, targeting additional vessels in Russia’s shadow fleet, financial institutions, and businesses supporting Moscow’s war effort.
EU diplomats were expected to make another attempt to resolve the disagreement later Monday. Without unanimous approval, the individual sanctions could lapse when the temporary extension expires.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico to sue over White House ban
MS NOW, CNN and Politico said they were suing the Trump Administration to protect their First Amendment rights after president Donald Trump’s announcement that he would ban them from the White House’s building grounds.
The three news outlets said they had notified the government that they were filing their lawsuit in the US District Court for the District of Columbia and could see emergency hearings in the case as soon as this week, according to CNN.
All three news outlets had hinted at legal action, saying they would vigorously defend their First Amendment rights.
“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting,” the outlets said in a joint statement posted on X. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”
Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to a request from Reuters for comment outside normal business hours.

‘I lost my children, and I’m afraid of losing my baby again’: a day in the life of a pregnant woman in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:00:23 UTC
20:00:23 KST

As the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, this week, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each will tell the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the ongoing conflict.
Alaa Hessi takes each step deliberately: raises her foot to land heavily on the stair above, takes a breath, slides her hand up the railing. Resting atop an uneven mess of rubble, the wooden staircase judders with each motion. Her movements are slowed by the heavy melon of her pregnant belly.
At the top of the stairs, she pauses for breath, then walks on to the platform that once formed the upper storey of her family’s home. A tent is pitched where the house stood. Beneath her feet are the ruins of the house where she raised her three children, Waseem, 10, Mohannad, 7, and Khawla, 5. And where they died, all three killed by an Israeli airstrike that levelled the home.
In about one month*, Alaa will give birth again.
Daybreak
 The sound that wakes me in the morning is the buzzing of flies inside the tent, and the noise of our neighbours.
Privacy in the tents is nonexistent, as is safety. Everyone here hears each other’s secrets. We hear people when they go to the bathroom. We can even hear them breathing. The window of my tent faces the yellow line directly. You can see the Israeli army positions from here, and sometimes they fire at us.
My husband and I love drinking tea in the morning, but making tea has become a challenge, because Israel has prevented cooking gas from entering Gaza and gas is extremely scarce. We still rely on firewood and open flames for cooking and preparing hot drinks. Gathering wood and making a fire is enough to exhaust me.
After I drink my tea, I tidy the tent and try to cook as early as possible before the sun becomes too intense. I also hand-wash my husband’s clothes and my own, which is physically exhausting now that I am eight months pregnant*.
Morning
Alaa opens the window – a tarpaulin flap at the side of the tent. A hole out into open air. As her eyes adjust to the brightness, it is clear that everything, as far as can be seen, is destroyed. The landscape is a mass of shattered concrete and twisted steel.
 Today, I have a prenatal appointment, to check on the baby’s progress.
The place is far away, and I walk there – usually there is no vehicle that can give me a ride. It’s 34C, and walking through bombed streets filled with rubble and insects in the heat of the day is extremely hard. The place where I get prenatal care is a tent, not a proper healthcare facility.
The doctors have prescribed me nutritional supplements for my pregnancy. I have been pregnant before, and I can tell this pregnancy is different: no matter how much I try to make up for the nutritional deficiencies and food deprivation I lived through in the war, my body remains exhausted. Food is scarce. My husband buys me fruits and vegetables and refuses to eat them himself, because he can only afford small amounts.
When I learned that I was pregnant, I felt two completely opposite emotions. I was happy that I would have a child, but I also cried constantly because I missed my children – Waseem, Mohannad and Khawla. Everything reminds me of them. When I crave certain foods, I remember Waseem, because I loved those foods when I was pregnant with him.
I do not tell nurses at the clinic about my circumstances and my children who died, because even the healthcare workers are emotionally exhausted. They are unable to offer comfort or psychological support. My story is not unusual in Gaza. Many women here have lost their children.
After the appointment with the nutritionist, I also have an appointment with the maternity psychologist. They tell me to focus on my breathing: take a deep breath, hold it and let it out slowly.
Then I walk home.
Afternoon
Tackling the stairs again, Alaa heaves a blue backpack up to the tent. It contains some of her dead children’s clothes, which she hopes the new baby might someday wear. Many of them were damaged by the bomb blast – ripped, their edges burned, but still wearable. She carefully unfolds a Snoopy T-shirt and a hat with two fluffy pompoms, pulls out a scarf for Castleview AFC – a small football club in Cork – that her son Waseem treasured. “He wore it all the time, even in summer. I would say, ‘Waseem it’s too hot, take it off!’ And he would say, “No, I love it.’”
 I spend the afternoon with my brother, trying to decide how to store the clothes for the new baby.
He suggests a sturdy cardboard or wooden box. The thing that we are worried about is the rats: the rats are everywhere. We hear them every night, and they always find their way into the tent. I sewed up the place where they entered, and they chewed a new way in – today we found another hole in the side of the tent.
I wonder if we could use rat poison, but my brother fears that then the rats will die here in the tent and spread disease.
For the baby who’s coming, all I want is a safe place where the rats can’t reach. The baby will be so small, and I am terrified for him. I would like to have a proper crib for him, but cribs are hard to find in Gaza now, and the tent is already overcrowded.
What I wish the world outside Gaza understood is how humiliating life in a tent really is. It is difficult, degrading and profoundly inhumane. Death still surrounds us in every direction.
Evening
As late afternoon approaches, Alaa scrolls through her photos of her children. The smartphone that holds them, like so many in Gaza, is old, and its screen is cracked – after a long blockade, new smartphones are now being shipped in, but they are expensive, and many families cannot afford them. The children’s voices chime thinly from the speaker. Khawla and her older brother teasing each other. “Mama, I’m the sweet one!” Khawla shouts. Mohannad laughs, calls back: “No – I’m the sweet one!”
 I only really speak about my children with my husband. He is the only person who carries the same pain and truly understands what is in my heart.
When I become weak, he gives me strength. When he struggles, I try to comfort him and support him emotionally. We spend hours talking about our children – their personalities, the things they loved and the way they behaved. We even visit their graves together.
This place still holds the memories of my children. It reminds me of our beautiful life together before. When I look at this rubble, I remember my children – the life I shared with them, raising them, preparing food for them and teaching them. Everything beautiful disappeared after they were gone.
Sometimes, fear controls me because I lost my children, and I’m afraid of losing my baby again. I hope my new baby will live a better life than the one his siblings experienced, and that he will be safe.
* Shortly after this story was reported, Alaa gave birth to a healthy baby boy. She named him Waseem, after his older brother.

Millions of dollars in funding but still no plan: can Quebec save its caribou from extinction?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:00:23 UTC
20:00:23 KST

The caribou of Quebec are at breaking point. The province, home to 15% of Canada’s population of woodland caribou, has seen numbers crash to about half of what they were a decade ago. For years, local First Nations people, researchers and environmental groups have criticised the provincial government’s lack of action on protecting caribou, an animal considered a keystone species by Indigenous peoples.
A recently announced agreement between the federal and Quebec governments has raised hopes that the province will finally be compelled to release a protection strategy. The federal government has committed C$25m (£13m) to the province for caribou over five years, with an additional C$15m for the First Nations communities on whose land the herds live.
But one detail of the announcement has caused concern: the continued reliance on maternity pens. Pregnant caribou have been rounded up and enclosed in pens in the hopes that the secure environment will give them and their calves a better chance of survival. But experts say this cannot be a longterm solution.
Quebec has herds throughout the province, the majority of which are woodland caribou. There are 13 woodland herds, with 6,800 to 8,900 animals in total. A caribou’s average lifespan is 10 to 15 years; females have a single calf a year, with fewer than half usually surviving their first year.
The woodland herds were listed in Canada’s 2003 Species at Risk Act, but 12 of the herds are at risk of extinction in the next 20 years, says Prof Martin-Hugues St-Laurent, an animal ecologist at the University of Quebec at Rimouski.
The new funding agreement focuses on only the three most critically endangered herds: in Val d’Or, Charlevoix and Gaspésie. The six remaining animals of the Val d’Or herd were placed in a protective pen in 2020, and hopes were high that the animals would breed and thrive in safety, ready for rerelease. But by summer 2026, the herd had grown by just one animal.
The Charlevoix herd was penned in 2022 and numbers 48 animals; the Gaspésie herd was penned in 2023 and has 20 animals. Currently, the Val d’Or and Charlevoix herds are penned throughout the year, while it is intended that some of the Gaspésie caribou will be released every few years. Seven were released this year to join the small number of wild caribou, the first reintroduction since the animals were penned.
“When you do not have any confidence that those animals will be able to survive in the wild because you have not solved the problem in the wild then sometimes you convert this maternity penning experiment into a complete permanent penning experiment,” says St-Laurent.
Alain Branchaud, director of the Quebec branch of the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society (SNAP Québec) says the penning experiment has delivered mixed results so far.
“The Charlevoix population is doing OK, but nothing happened for the Val d’Or population and two females died from the Gaspésie initiative, so it’s not working well,” he says.
Justina Ray, president and senior scientist of the Wildlife Conservation Society Canada (WCS), says that while there is some evidence that maternity pens do help sustain the population, they do not address the underlying problem of habitat loss.
“The introduction back into the wild is less of a success story if you haven’t repaired the things that are driving population decline to begin with,” says Ray, pointing to a lack of specifics and accountability in the recent funding agreement.
Quebec’s caribou herds are well studied, but that information has not translated into conservation measures such as habitat restoration, despite a decade of federal and provincial money put towards caribou monitoring and recovery, says St-Laurent. “Some, maybe more cynical people, could say that we are the best at monitoring the decline.”
Two of Quebec’s major industries, logging and mining, operate within the caribou’s home ranges. To thrive, woodland caribou need about 65% undisturbed forest, but most of Quebec’s caribou populations live in areas that have less than 40% undisturbed, says Daniel Fortin, a biologist at Quebec City’s Laval University.
If caribou are released from pens into an environment that has substantially changed, that habitat is no longer familiar to them and they cannot rely on the historical knowledge that aids survival, says Fortin. Although they will slightly shift their habitat in response, they are still more likely to die.
But not moving out of degraded habitat also means they are more likely to die, he says. “Putting individuals in pens is a last resort – something that you can do just before extinction,” says Fortin. “Anything else than habitat restoration is a Band-Aid.”
There are more than 300,000 miles (500,000km) of dirt roads crisscrossing Quebec’s forests, mostly to access logging areas, on public land. That distance is the length of a trip to the moon and halfway back to Earth, points out St-Laurent. These roads make it easier for wolves to access caribou herds and also change the forest cover. That in turn attracts more moose, which attract more wolves who hunt them.
When these roads appear, cabins, shacks and fishing and hunting camps soon follow, says St-Laurent, making closing these roads an unpopular choice. The Quebec government is investing into “interim” measures such as wolf culls and penning, he says. “But because of the public opposition to those road closures and habitat restoration efforts, they’re not investing as much money as needed there.”
The Quebec government still does not have a caribou strategy, says Branchaud, even though the creation of one was announced a decade ago. He says the province’s ministry of the environment, climate change, wildlife and parks did have a proposal for one in 2024 but it was rejected by Quebec’s natural resources and forests ministry. The release of a partial strategy was announced in 2024 but has yet to materialise, he says.
The ministry of the environment, climate change, wildlife and parks declined to be interviewed for this article.
Pascale Déry, Quebec’s environment minister, has been criticised for previous remarks suggesting she did not believe caribou were endangered. A previous minister intended to send the Val d’Or herd to a zoo. That plan was cancelled after an outcry.
The Wendat Indigenous First Nation, on whose territory the Charlevoix herd lives, said in a statement: “The Wendat nation has been committed for many years to the conservation and recovery of the Charlevoix yenchehk [caribou] … The nation’s position remains consistent: the protection of the Charlevoix yenchehk is a critical issue, as is the preservation of other species.”
The other Indigenous communities where the herds are found – the MicMac, or Mi’gmaq, of Gespeg ; the Anishnabe of Lake Simon; and the Pekuakamiulnuatsh of Mashteuiatsh – declined or did not respond to requests for comment.
WCS’s Ray says Quebec’s approach is partially modelled on a successful initiative in British Columbia province, which also included pens. But that plan, she adds, was more holistic and also involved local First Nations, controlling predators and conserving habitats from the outset.
One thing that does help forest preservation in Quebec is the economy, says Fortin. As the US is a major buyer of the province’s forest products, when the economy there slows, so does the logging. “It’s a bit sad,” he says. “In other words, it’s not the laws, it’s really the economy that’s been driving it.”
But Quebec is running out of forests to log, says St-Laurent, and the increasing number and severity of wildfires in the province caused by climate breakdown is expediting the decrease of loggable trees.
“The [loggers] have to access the last remnant of forest that was in protected areas for caribou. So this is a debate that is far bigger than just caribou,” he says.
