‘Inredibly enouraging’: healing the scars of traditional anchors in Dorset’s seagrass meadows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:00:23 UTC
20:00:23 KST

One of the UK’s most precious underwater habitats – Dorset’s seagrass meadows – is recovering thanks to “eco moorings” designed to prevent the seabed being ripped up, a study has revealed.
Scars caused by traditional anchors in some areas of seagrass in Studland Bay have almost entirely vanished, which is boosting the number of seahorses that thrive in the submerged meadows.
The Studland Bay Marine Partnership, which includes a wide range of organisations including conservationists and boating enthusiasts, hopes the findings could help protect and restore seagrass in other busy marine environments around the UK.
Seagrass meadows are considered one of the world’s most valuable ecosystems because, as well as supporting creatures such as seahorses, they store carbon and help protect coastlines from erosion.
They are declining globally due to pressures including pollution, coastal development and the climate emergency. The meadows at Studland Bay are particularly at risk because the spot is so popular with leisure boaters.
Research conducted by Kira Dunn, as part of her masters degree at the University of Southampton, analysed data collected since eco-moorings were installed by the partnership in 2021.
In the area where 10 trial eco-moorings were installed five years ago, bare patches in the seagrass shrank by an average of 94% between 2021 and 2025. In a second study area, where traditional chain moorings remained until 2023, the scars reduced by 65%.
Dunn said: “The results clearly show that seagrass is recovering in areas where physical disturbance has been removed. It’s incredibly encouraging to see how quickly this important habitat can regenerate when given the opportunity.”
David Brown, the chair of the Studland Bay Marine Partnership steering group and lead ecologist for the National Trust, said: “The impact has been beyond our expectations, and thanks to robust monitoring and research, we have the science to prove how the eco-moorings benefit seagrass and all the species that rely on it.”
Studland Bay was designated a marine conservation zone in 2019 and is home to one of the UK’s largest seagrass meadows, supporting numerous marine species including the protected spiny seahorse and the occasionally recorded short-snouted seahorse.
Since eco-moorings were introduced volunteer divers who monitor seahorses have reported increases in numbers. Other creatures spotted in the seagrass include conger eels, spider crabs and corkwing wrasse.
Eco-moorings consist of a 2-metre helical screw, which is drilled securely into the seabed. Attached to this is a 2-metre elasticated riser that connects to a surface buoy. As the tide rises and falls, the riser stretches and retracts, preventing any scouring of the seabed and seagrass.
Ken Collins, emeritus research fellow and diving officer at the University of Southampton and supervisor of the study, said: “This research provides robust scientific evidence that eco-moorings are an effective tool for seagrass conservation and restoration.
“The findings support the continued use and expansion of eco-mooring schemes, not only in Studland but in other sensitive marine environments where seagrass habitats are under pressure.”

Couples searching for a third partner report stronger bonds but often ignore the newcomer’s desires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:00:21 UTC
20:00:21 KST

Couples who search for a third person to join their sexual or romantic relationships frequently focus on their own pleasure while minimizing the desires of the person they pursue. A recent qualitative analysis of people in these relationships also reveals that the search process itself often strengthens the existing couples’ bonds and communication. The findings were published in the journal Psychology & Sexuality.
In consensual non-monogamy, partners agree to have romantic or sexual encounters with other people. One increasingly visible practice involves established couples seeking a third person to join them. This third person is colloquially known as a unicorn because they are perceived as rare and highly sought after. The practice is often associated with a man and a woman looking for a bisexual woman to join them.
Polyamorous communities sometimes criticize couples who search for a third person. Critics argue these couples often prioritize their own needs and protect their established relationship hierarchy. This framework can treat the newcomer as an accessory to be used and discarded.
Engaging with a third person can provide a positive experience for everyone involved and can challenge traditional relationship norms. Direct research on couples seeking a third person has remained sparse. To better understand this dynamic, researchers led by Alena Bondarchuk-Mclaughlin at La Trobe University in Melbourne, Australia, set out to explore the perspectives of the people conducting the search.
The researchers recruited 80 participants through social media and an online survey platform. All respondents indicated they were currently or had previously been part of a couple looking for a third person. Participants answered five open-ended survey questions about who they wanted to join them, what their goals were, and how the search had affected their primary relationship.
The research team analyzed the text responses using a qualitative method. They looked for recurring patterns and grouped the answers into four main categories. These categories covered the desired characteristics of the third person, the effects on the couple, the ideal relationship dynamics, and the reality of their actual encounters.
When describing who they wanted to join them, most participants specifically sought a woman. The majority of these requests specified a bisexual woman. The desires were more varied than the typical stereotype suggests, as nearly a quarter of respondents said gender was irrelevant. Others looked for men, other couples, or specific personality traits like friendliness.
Couples overwhelmingly described the search process as having a positive impact on their relationships. Nearly 80 percent of participants reported that looking for a third person brought them closer together. They noted improvements in communication, honesty, and trust. Discussing fantasies and boundaries openly often heightened their sexual experiences as a couple.
A small minority reported that the search had a negative effect on their primary relationship. In these cases, participants noted that initiating the search coincided with disagreements, pressure, or a breach of trust. Some participants also described struggling with feelings of jealousy when confronting traditional relationship expectations.
The researchers found a major gap between the type of relationship couples wanted and what they actually experienced. A majority of participants desired a predominantly sexual relationship with the third person. They wanted to fulfill specific fantasies, experience novelty, or enhance their own shared pleasure. Many explicitly stated they wanted minimal romantic involvement.
In contrast, about 40 percent wanted an emotional connection, ranging from friendship to a loving, cohabitating relationship. Yet some responses revealed an expectation that the third person would serve mainly to fix a void or provide a service. These participants often specified that the newcomer must respect the existing couple’s priority and not disrupt their bond.
Only a small fraction of the participants mentioned the third person’s own desires or sexual pleasure as an important part of the ideal scenario. When describing their actual relationships with a third person, many couples maintained purely sexual boundaries, often sticking to one-night stands. About a quarter managed to form ongoing social or romantic relationships.
Expressions of care for the third person were rare in the actual relationship descriptions. Only 12 percent of responses mentioned prioritizing the newcomer’s feelings or treating them as an equal. The researchers noted that many couples entered the search focused heavily on their own personal gain.
Couples also frequently reported struggling to find a willing third person. Almost half of the participants described difficulties in their search. Many could not find the right match, faced a scarcity of interested people, or encountered mismatched expectations.
The researchers suggested this lack of success might stem from the couples’ failure to consider the third person’s interests. Treating the search like a request for a specialized service rather than the formation of a new interpersonal connection can easily lead to disappointment for all parties. The authors suggest that couples should express genuine care for the person they seek.
The study relies on self-reported data from a sample of 80 individuals, rather than interviewing both members of the couple. The researchers only surveyed the people doing the searching, leaving out the perspectives of the individuals being pursued. Future research will need to examine the experiences of the third person to provide a complete picture of these relationship dynamics.
The survey prompts may have influenced how participants answered the questions. For instance, the question asking who they wanted to join them included “bisexual woman” as an example, which might have prompted respondents to use that exact phrase. The survey also did not ask about the gender of the participants’ partners, which limits the ability to analyze how the gender makeup of the original couple shapes the search process.
The study, “Searching for a third: couples’ experiences of unicorn pursuit, desire, and ethical tensions,” was authored by Alena Bondarchuk-Mclaughlin, Nat Amos, and Joel R. Anderson.

Ukrainian Hackers Raid Russia’s Naval Files, Walk Away With Secrets From 70 Projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:00:10 UTC
20:00:10 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian Hackers Raid Russia’s Naval Files, Walk Away With Secrets From 70 Projects
Ukrainian hackers gained access to a large collection of Russian naval files, obtaining technical documentation linked to 70 projects involving submarines, warships, navigation systems, sonar technology, and autonomous underwater vehicles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The cyber operation, dubbed “Poseidon,” was carried out by Ukrainian Militant, the group said on September 20. According to the hackers, the compromised data covers Russian naval research, engineering, testing, and operational documentation, including files marked “secret” and “top secret.”
The materials reportedly contain information on nuclear-powered and diesel-electric submarines, frigates, corvettes, landing ships, and vessels designed for Arctic operations.
Among them are Project 949AM Antey nuclear-powered submarines and Project 636.3 Varshavyanka diesel-electric submarines, as well as ships belonging to Projects 22350, 20386, 23550, 11711, 23770, and 23900.
For some of these projects, Ukrainian Militant said the files reveal details of navigation equipment and modernization, onboard hardware placement, cable connections, information interfaces, and testing results.
The archive also reportedly includes technical requirements, operating manuals, structural and functional diagrams, algorithms, accuracy and reliability specifications, testing procedures, and acceptance documents.
Beyond individual ships and submarines, the breach reportedly covers a broader range of Russian naval technologies, including ship and underwater navigation, integrated control systems, sonar, radio navigation, inertial navigation systems, digital hydrography and mapping, and marine robotics.
Some of the documented research concerns autonomous navigation for submarines and underwater vehicles using terrain and geophysical fields, technologies intended to allow them to determine their position without relying solely on satellite navigation.
Ukrainian Militant also identified a series of systems and development programs in the obtained files, including Simfoniya, Chardash, KAMA-NS-VK, Sprut-N1, Priliv, 14Ts217, AKNG/PNG-23820, and ISU NK-23550.
The group said the archive contains materials associated with major Russian organizations involved in naval and underwater technology, including the Rubin and Malachite submarine design bureaus, the Elektropribor research institute, Okeanpribor, Elara, the Vega concern, and Russia’s State Research Navigation and Hydrographic Institute.
According to Ukrainian Militant, the documents also provide information on cooperation between contractors, research and development stages, testing, and the status of individual programs.
In total, the hackers said the obtained files concern Russian scientific and technical work supporting 70 ship, vessel, and submarine projects currently under construction or modernization. The full scope and authenticity of the archive have not been independently verified.
The naval breach follows other major leaks involving Russia’s defense industry. In November 2025, Ukrainian-linked hackers obtained classified documents related to Russia’s PAK DA strategic bomber and Su-57 fighter, exposing technical details of key aircraft components and the programs’ reliance on foreign manufacturing equipment.

Russia’s Molniya Attack Drone Shows Up in Africa—and Gets Shot Down in Mali
A Russian-made Molniya attack drone was reportedly brought down near the town of Dioura in central Mali, where Russian Africa Corps personnel and Malian forces have been conducting operations against the al-Qaeda-linked JNIM militant group.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Sahel-focused outlet Alerte Sahel on September 21, footage from the area showed the wreckage of what appears to be a Russian Molniya-type fixed-wing drone following its crash near Dioura in Mali’s Mopti region.
Alerte Sahel reported that Russian Africa Corps personnel had used the drone against positions held by Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) before withdrawing from the area. The outlet claimed the aircraft was subsequently shot down.
The available footage shows a damaged fixed-wing drone with a long fuselage and straight wings consistent with the design of Russia’s Molniya UAV. However, the video only shows the aircraft after it came down and does not establish what caused the crash or independently confirm that it was shot down.
The Molniya is a relatively simple Russian fixed-wing attack drone designed to carry an explosive payload. The aircraft has a reported operating range of roughly 30 to 40 kilometers and can carry a warhead weighing up to seven kilograms. Variants of the platform have also been used for reconnaissance and artillery fire adjustment.
The reported loss comes amid continuing fighting around Dioura following a major JNIM assault on a Malian military camp there on September 10.
The Malian Armed Forces acknowledged the attack and subsequently announced air and ground operations against militants in the area. On September 19, Mali’s military said its forces, supported by partners, continued targeted strikes around the Dioura garrison and the outskirts of the town.
The scale of the September 10 attack was substantial. AFP reported on September 18, citing military, security and local sources, that at least 100 Malian soldiers and five Russian Africa Corps personnel were killed. JNIM separately claimed that it killed 150 soldiers and captured 93, figures that have not been independently verified.
Russia has expanded its military presence in Mali through the Africa Corps, which replaced the Wagner Group as Moscow’s principal security force in the country. The reported deployment of a Molniya drone near Dioura would indicate the use in Mali of another Russian unmanned system originally developed and widely fielded for combat operations in Ukraine.

Saab is digitalizing Stockholm-Västerås Airport with remote air traffic control services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Saab is digitalizing Stockholm-Västerås Airport with remote air traffic control services
Saab has been entrusted to install and operate remote air traffic control for Stockholm-Västerås Airport for a period of 15 years. This means that air traffic in Västerås will be controlled from Saab’s Remote Tower Center (RTC) in Sundsvall.
This solution is already in operational use at several airports and is part of the ongoing technological development within the aviation industry, both in Sweden and globally. For Saab, the airport in Västerås will be the fifth airport to be operated from the RTC in Sundsvall to utilize this technology, in addition to Sundsvall-Timrå, Sälen, Örnsköldsvik and Linköping. The agreement comes into effect on January 1, 2028, and runs for 15 years. Saab will deliver a fully digitalized infrastructure to Stockholm-Västerås Airport, including the camera tower, a digital workstation for remote air traffic control, and meteorological services.
In addition to technology and air traffic control, the agreement encompasses a service-based delivery model in which Saab provides and assumes responsibility for the digital infrastructure throughout the contract period. This model paves the way for increased cost-efficiency and facilitates the implementation of future technological development.
“This contract underscores our leading role in the digitalization of air traffic control and enables us to deliver safe and cost-effective solutions. We look forward to helping Stockholm-Västerås Airport step into the future and benefit from the latest technological innovations," says Cecilia Larsson, head of Saab Air Traffic Management.

Justice in action: Five lessons for Ukraine from the conviction of Kosovo’s former president
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
14:00:00 EEST
20:00:00 KST

Justice in action: Five lessons for Ukraine from the conviction of Kosovo’s former president
On 16 September 2026, a verdict was delivered in The Hague against one of the most prominent political figures in post-war Kosovo. Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaçi and three other former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) – Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi – were found guilty of war crimes committed during the 1998–1999 armed conflict.
Thaçi and Krasniqi were sentenced to 25 years' imprisonment, Veseli to 18 years and Selimi to 13 years. The Court found them criminally responsible for the unlawful or arbitrary detention of 385 people, the torture of 303, the cruel treatment of 49 and the murder of 96 people.
More than a quarter of a century passed between the crimes and this first-instance judgment. During that time, Thaçi went from being one of the KLA's leaders to Prime Minister and later President of Kosovo. Political circumstances, the international environment and institutions all changed. At the time of the war, there was no mechanism capable of providing a legal assessment of these crimes. This differs from the situation in Ukraine, where we are building such a mechanism amid the realities of an ongoing war.
This is one of the most interesting features of the case. The Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established only in 2015. Their structure combines national and international components. The Chambers were established under Kosovo's Constitution and legislation, are integrated into the different levels of its judicial system, and apply Kosovo law alongside international law. At the same time, they are based in The Hague, while their judges, prosecutors and staff are international. The Specialist Prosecutor's Office is also based in The Hague and operates independently of other Kosovo institutions.
In practice, this is a hybrid justice mechanism that combines national jurisdiction with international participation and allows particularly complex cases to be heard outside Kosovo.
In my view, such a model could also be appropriate for Ukraine. This does not, of course, mean replicating the Kosovo model. Ukraine has its own Constitution and judicial system, a significantly greater volume of proceedings concerning international crimes, and an already established system of cooperation with international institutions. At the same time, combining national jurisdiction with international expertise and participation could strengthen Ukraine's capacity to adjudicate the most complex cases while keeping such proceedings within the Ukrainian justice system.
The trajectory of the Thaçi case itself illustrates how long it can take for such an opportunity to emerge. The indictment was confirmed in 2020. Thaçi subsequently resigned as President, was taken into custody and transferred to The Hague. The trial began in April 2023. The evidentiary proceedings concluded at the end of 2025, and in February 2026 the parties presented their closing arguments. The Court heard evidence from 273 witnesses, admitted 5,467 items of evidence, and the trial transcript ran to 29,238 pages.
The indictment contained ten counts. Six concerned crimes against humanity and four concerned war crimes. The outcome of the proceedings was significant not only because of the severity of the sentences imposed.
The accused were acquitted on all counts of crimes against humanity. The Court concluded that the prosecution had failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt the existence of a widespread or systematic attack directed against a civilian population.
This is precisely why the Thaçi case is far more relevant to Ukraine than simply as the story of one former president. It shows what happens to information about a war decades later, when the political context has already changed and every allegation must withstand judicial scrutiny.
What of the material collected today will withstand such scrutiny in ten, twenty or thirty years? Is it enough to have thousands of documented incidents? Where is the line between information and evidence? How do we move from a specific crime to the responsibility of a particular commander or political leader?
The Thaçi case offers at least five lessons that Ukraine should take into account today.
Lesson One. It Is Necessary to Prove Not Only the Crime, but Also the Responsibility of a Specific Individual
International criminal justice does not put positions or titles on trial.
It is not enough to establish that a person was a commander, minister, general or political leader at the time the crimes were committed.
In the Thaçi case, the Court separately examined the role of each accused, their powers, specific actions, involvement in decision-making and contribution to the common criminal purpose. The Court examined their actual influence. This is fundamentally important for Ukrainian cases concerning Russia's military and political leadership.
A chain of command positions does not in itself establish a chain of criminal responsibility. It is necessary to determine who made decisions, who issued orders, who received reports, who had information about the consequences, what measures were taken after such information was received, and what the actual contribution of a particular individual was to the commission of the crime. This is why proving international crimes requires more than documenting a crime scene. An evidentiary link must be established between a specific incident and a specific individual.
Lesson Two. The Number of Crimes Does Not in Itself Prove the Existence of Crimes against humanity
This is perhaps one of the most important conclusions from the case for Ukrainian investigations.
The Court established that hundreds of people had been victims of murder, torture, cruel treatment and unlawful deprivation of liberty.
Yet this was insufficient to secure convictions for crimes against humanity.
The reason lies in the legal structure of this international crime. It is not enough to prove numerous individual murders, acts of torture or unlawful detentions. The contextual elements must be established separately, including the existence of a widespread or systematic attack directed against a civilian population and the connection between the specific act and that attack.
In the Thaçi case, the prosecution, in the Court's assessment, failed to meet this standard.
For Ukraine, this has direct practical significance. When documenting Russian crimes, it is not enough to accumulate individual incidents. At the same time, material must be collected that makes it possible to identify and prove the broader system: recurring patterns of conduct, their geographical and temporal dimensions, categories of victims, methods of committing crimes, patterns in target selection, command links, orders, internal documents, policies and practices, as well as the leadership's response to crimes of which it was aware.
It is possible to have thousands of well-documented incidents and still have a weak evidentiary basis for establishing the contextual elements of crimes against humanity.
Numbers matter. But arithmetic is no substitute for proof.
Lesson Three. Information Is Not Yet Evidence
Another important aspect of the case concerns information about individuals whom the KLA regarded as opponents.
The Court examined the activities of the KLA's intelligence structures and the role of Kadri Veseli. The judges found that the four accused had made substantial contributions to a common criminal purpose directed against individuals regarded as opponents of the KLA's political and military objectives. These included Kosovo Albanians affiliated with other political or military forces, individuals suspected of links to the Serbian or Yugoslav authorities, and members of national minorities.
For Ukraine, a broader principle is important here.
Intelligence, operational, military or open-source information may be extremely valuable in criminal proceedings. It may help formulate an investigative hypothesis, indicate a direction for the investigation, and assist in identifying witnesses, documents, locations or other sources of evidence.
But information and a proven fact are not the same thing.
For Ukraine, which is currently accumulating a vast body of information about the war, including operational, digital and intelligence data, not least through the work of the newly established Directorate for Documentation of Violations of the Law of Armed Conflict Committed during Hostilities within the Military Law Enforcement Service of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the question of verification has very practical significance. Such information must be cross-checked against other sources, its provenance and authenticity established, and only then can its evidentiary value be assessed.
Lesson Four. The Legality of War and the Rules Governing Its Conduct Are Assessed Separately
The proceedings in The Hague were not an assessment of the political objectives of the Kosovo Liberation Army or of the idea of Kosovo's independence itself. The Court considered a different question: whether specific individuals bore individual criminal responsibility for specific acts committed during the armed conflict.
This legal distinction is also important for Ukraine. Ukraine is defending itself against Russian aggression, exercising its inherent right of self-defence under the UN Charter. At the same time, international law separately regulates the legality of a state's resort to force and the rules governing the conduct of hostilities.
Accordingly, the legal assessment of a specific incident during the war concerns compliance with international humanitarian law. It neither changes nor calls into question Ukraine's legal status as a state exercising self-defence against armed aggression.
This is why credible information about possible violations by the Ukrainian side must also receive proper legal assessment. This in no way equates the aggressor with the state defending itself. These are different questions of international law and involve different matters to be proved.
Moreover, a state's ability to examine the conduct of its own military personnel and, where sufficient evidence exists, ensure accountability demonstrates the capacity and resilience of its legal system. For Ukraine, this also has very practical significance. Proper domestic investigations allow the state itself to establish the facts, distinguish substantiated violations from unsubstantiated allegations, and examine its own mistakes in order to prevent their recurrence.
This is also important at the international level. Genuine and good-faith criminal proceedings at the national level are relevant to the principle of complementarity on which the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court is based. At the same time, it protects the state from situations in which third countries initiate investigations under the principle of universal jurisdiction.
There is another aspect that is particularly important in the context of information warfare. If the state itself does not establish what happened in a particular incident, the resulting vacuum is filled by unverified reports and manipulation, which the Russian authorities use to construct their own narrative. A professional investigation helps prevent this.
Legal assessment of possible violations by one's own side therefore demonstrates the ability of the legal system to function even under the most difficult conditions of war, to establish facts regardless of whom they concern, to learn from its own mistakes, and to ensure accountability where evidence exists.
Lesson Five. Evidence Must Outlast the War
More than a quarter of a century passed between the events at issue in the Thaçi case and the first-instance judgment.
But these were not 27 years of a single trial. The trial itself began only in 2023. Before that came years of accumulating information, international investigations, establishing a specialised mechanism, setting up the prosecution office, working with witnesses and preparing the case. The Specialist Chambers were established only in 2015, many years after the events they are now adjudicating.
In 1998, no one could have known that Hashim Thaçi would become Prime Minister, then President of Kosovo, and that two decades later he would leave office and appear before a court that did not even exist at the time of the events.
Likewise, today we do not know what the political circumstances will be in ten or twenty years, or when particular individuals suspected of crimes against Ukraine may actually appear before a court.
But there are things Ukraine can influence now. Will the evidence be preserved? Will it be possible, twenty years from now, to establish its provenance? Will it be clear who obtained a particular digital file or physical object, when and where it was obtained, and under what circumstances? Will the chain of custody be preserved? Will it be possible to reconstruct command relationships and decision-making processes?
The Thaçi case therefore does not provide grounds for mechanically transplanting the Kosovo experience to Ukraine. The conflict is different, the scale is different, the jurisdictional framework is different, and the factual circumstances are different.
But it demonstrates something universal. Political circumstances change far more quickly than the question of individual criminal responsibility disappears. In ten, twenty or thirty years, governments, international relations, official positions and individuals' status may all have changed. A judicial mechanism that does not yet exist today may emerge. New legal avenues for holding particular individuals accountable may become available.
For Ukraine, therefore, the central question today is not only when and where future trials will take place. More important is what we will bring to those trials. Will we have evidence of individual crimes and of their broader context?
The political window for justice may open years from now. More than a quarter of a century passed between the crimes for which Hashim Thaçi and the other KLA leaders were convicted and the first-instance judgment. During that time, political circumstances, individuals' status and institutions changed.
The question of individual responsibility did not disappear.
For Ukraine, this may be the central lesson of the case. Justice may come decades later, but the case that it will one day adjudicate begins today.

Gaza students return to in-person schooling for first time in three years

- About 660,000 students missed regular education due to war damage; UNICEF reports 98% of schools were destroyed or damaged.
- Despite hardships, including unaffordable supplies and unsafe conditions, Gaza's education officials and organisations opened temporary schools to continue learning.
AI generated
CAIRO/GAZA – Hundreds of thousands of children in Gaza returned to in-person teaching on Sept 19 for the first time in nearly three years, albeit in damaged or makeshift school buildings and tents, and with uniforms, notebooks and pens unaffordable for many families.
The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) says 98 per cent of schools in Gaza were either destroyed or damaged during the war, and Gaza education officials say about 660,000 students have been deprived of in-person learning and regular participation in education.
The reopening is a fragile milestone for Gaza after a conflict that has killed around 22,000 students and more than 770 education workers, including 532 teachers, according to Ibrahim Ramadan, director of education for East Khan Younis.
“The last time I have been to school was three years ago. Now, we are starting the school year, it is year of joy, happiness and success,” said Moayed Abu Mustafa in Khan Younis.
Mustafa said he was determined to learn even though he will sit on the floor in a tent lacking ventilation, he has no decent shoes, nor a notebook and pen, and lost friends during the war.
“Despite all of this we will learn, we will learn even in a tent.”
Fifteen-year-old displaced student Samar Abu Salmi, who lives with her family in a tent, is also returning to class.
“We studied on phones and we haven’t seen our teachers... now, we are back pursuing our dream... from one tent to another,” she said, speaking in the yard of her new makeshift school.
She also lacks much of the essential equipment, which has become unaffordable for her family.
“Before the war, everything was available for us – notebooks, pens, goods, clothes, outings, things that we could get cheaply,” Salmi said.
Mattresses and a blackboard
Despite the devastation in the enclave, the Ministry of Education, backed by international and local organisations, has moved ahead with the 2026-27 academic year, establishing dozens of temporary schools made of tents, tarpaulins, sheet metal and wood to accommodate pupils.
Some are built on sandy ground, others have classrooms with only some mattresses and a blackboard, into which students cram. Others are still housing dozens of displaced families.
Attending another school was 14-year-old Yamen Abu Samra.
“We used to wake up happy to go to school... Now, when we come to school, we’re afraid of stray bullets, rockets, strikes, everything,” he said.
“Now, I’m sitting in a tent that has absolutely nothing, just the sun and the heat,” he added.
At least 540,000 students are expected to attend in-person classes in 2026 in makeshift private schools, temporary learning centres and educational points, with UNICEF support, according to education officials. Online learning will continue for those who can’t attend classes or who left Gaza during the war.
Israeli forces remain in control of more than 60 per cent of Gaza despite the 2025 ceasefire, which halted major fighting but failed to end the conflict.
The Palestinian authorities say more than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in October 2023.
Stationery trader Khaled Aliyan, 30, said Israeli import restrictions have reduced supplies and hiked prices.
“This notebook, which used to cost 3 shekels (S$1.20), now costs 15 (shekels). All stationery items are expensive,” he said.
Israel’s COGAT military agency, which controls access to Gaza, did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on restrictions on supplies and strikes on schools. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of using schools for military purposes, which Hamas denies. REUTERS

MOSCOW, September 21. /TASS/. New participants with expanded powers may enter Russia’s crypto market by the end of this year, First Deputy Governor of the Bank of Russia Vladimir Chistyukhin said at the Moscow Financial Forum.
"We will see new participants with new powers, and the crypto industry will begin operating within the legal framework. At the same time, I would like to remind you that a transition period has been established until the middle of next year. The law regulating the circulation of digital currencies and digital rights in Russia took effect on September 1, 2026. Cross-border settlements in cryptocurrencies and stablecoins under foreign trade contracts are subject to standard currency control, anti-money laundering, and counter-terrorist financing procedures. Detailed requirements will be established by a Bank of Russia regulation governing the submission of supporting documents by residents and non-residents to authorized banks, a draft of which has already undergone a regulatory impact assessment.
Foreign trade participants may use cryptocurrencies and stablecoins for settlements under foreign trade contracts.
Qualified and non-qualified investors may purchase such assets subject to established requirements and may also transfer them abroad to their own foreign-based wallets or to non-residents as payment for goods and services.
The use of cryptocurrencies and stablecoins for domestic settlements has been considered an illegal currency transaction since September 1 and is subject to a fine of up to 40% of the transaction amount.

Experts: Social networks need to be made safer for children; a ban is not the solution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:57:37 UTC
19:57:37 KST

The European Union has begun discussing regulations for a safer internet that would include several restrictions on social media use; although the EU plans to ban children under the age of 13 from using social networks, Estonian researchers have pointed out that blunt bans will not solve all problems and could even create new ones, reports ERR News.
Indrek Ibrus, a professor of media at Tallinn University, views the EU initiative critically, noting that the planned regulation conflicts with children’s fundamental rights. He explained that the initiative disregards the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Children have the right to self-expression and access to information to foster their development and identity formation, and any age-based restriction on access to information fails to take children’s rights into account. In Ibrus’s view, by proposing these restrictions, the European Commission is showing that it has given up.
The researcher stated that instead of making the online environment safe for children, the EC is throwing in the towel. The Commission lacks the resolve to regulate the online environment, even though legal guidelines—the Digital Services Act—already exist and simply need to be strictly enforced. He added that, in a sense, children’s rights are being sacrificed because the European Commission is unable to take action.
Andra Siibak, a professor of media studies at the University of Tartu, agreed that one cannot rely solely on bans and restrictions, and pointed out the need to change the business models of online platforms. The professor stated that the EU requirement for service providers to implement specific tools to protect children’s online well-being, rights, and privacy is a positive step. Like Ibrus, Siibak emphasized that all the recommended changes are already included in existing EU regulations.
The EU needs to start thinking carefully about how to require platforms to implement these measures
and how to ensure that the changes are actually carried out.
Katrin Tiidenberg, Professor of Participatory Culture at Tallinn University, cited the Australian experience to argue against overly strict bans. The Australian example suggests that bans are ineffective; children under 16 continue to use social media, meaning—crucially—that no one knows where they are logging in from or what they are doing online.
One of the major issues surrounding the EU’s planned regulation is how to verify users’ ages without compromising privacy.
Ibrus sees serious risks associated with age verification systems. They could lead to direct privacy violations, and platforms might use identification data for more precise user profiling—a practice that could be dangerous in several respects. He added that while the EU is developing a digital wallet solution to create secure infrastructure for the future, any restrictions must be approached with extreme caution.
Siibak emphasized the difficulty of finding reliable and transparent age verification methods.
Attempts to use facial recognition technology have failed, and young people easily bypass checks—for instance, by using their parents’ documents. Australia’s experience has reportedly shown that young people skillfully bypass various age-verification solutions, and finding a method acceptable to all EU countries will be very difficult. Tiidenberg also noted that automated age-verification tools carry risks. If children are required to log in using an ID card, it implies that all social media users would have to do the same; however, it is crucial to avoid mass surveillance regarding which websites people visit and what they do there. She emphasized the importance of preserving freedom. Tiidenberg added that this does not mean age verification cannot be carried out in a proportionate and secure manner, but the method must be developed with extreme care, and one should not hastily place trust in the first private company to announce it has created a solution.
Experts pointed out that efforts to protect children and young people on social media should focus on improving the platforms themselves. Tiidenberg highlighted the need to compel platforms to adopt responsible designs that prioritize well-being. This entails limiting addictive algorithms and allowing users to choose between a chronological news feed and algorithmic recommendations. The researcher also supports the creation of accounts tailored to children and young people (e.g., for the 13–15 age group) that automatically restrict access to harmful content.
Ibrus noted that, alongside restrictions, it is crucial to strengthen media literacy and critical thinking among young people. Rather than simply banning the use of communication platforms due to potential risks, these risks should be mitigated: platforms need to be adapted and regulated, existing regulations must be enforced, and media literacy should be promoted across different age groups.
On the 17th of September, the European Commission adopted a regulation on a safer internet to enhance online safety. The package of measures includes a proposal to prohibit the use of social networks by children under the age of 13. Consideration is also being given to parental controls for social media accounts belonging to 13- to 15-year-olds, as well as restrictions on the use of artificial intelligence chatbots.

Google fined more than €400m by Irish regulator over its use of location data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:57:26 UTC
19:57:26 KST

Google has been fined more than €400m (£345m) over the way it processed users’ location data, following claims that the tech giant had manipulated users into agreeing to be constantly tracked on their mobile phones.
The fine, imposed by Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC), comes after complaints from multiple European consumer organisations that Google was following every step users took.
Location-related adverts are familiar to holidaymakers, but seven European consumer organisations had complained that undue use of location data can also lead to a breach of privacy.
The DPC inquiry was prompted by research by the Norwegian consumer agency in 2018 which suggested location data could reveal details such as religious beliefs (by tracking places of worship), political leanings (for example knowing a user has gone to demonstrations), health conditions (if a user has gone to hospital) and sexual orientation (if they have gone to certain bars).
The DPC launched its inquiry six years ago and set out to find out whether Google had a valid legal basis for its use of location data.
It found that Google users could have been unaware that their location was being used to influence them with adverts or to gather details about their health and interests.
“Location data is a type of personal data which is processed by way of location tracking, and includes data collected or processed by Google, which by itself or in conjunction with other information an individual’s location can be inferred,” said Graham Doyle, a deputy commissioner at the DPC.
“Location data can bring both benefits and harms to individuals.
“It can greatly enhance the utility of online services, but it can also reveal a significant amount of information about an individual, including information that is inherently private,” Doyle added.
Responding to the DPC’s ruling, a Google spokeperson said: “This case centres around historical policies that have since been updated. From 2019 onwards, we’ve significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple.”
The European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) based its complaint on research by the Forbrukerrådet, the Norwegian consumer agency, which claimed Google used “various tricks” to ensure location history and web and app activity were enabled.
“Today marks an important milestone in the effort to protect our rights online. People must be able to understand what they are agreeing to without being deceived or manipulated into making choices they otherwise would never have made,” says Finn Myrstad, director of digital policy at the Norwegian Consumer Council.
BEUC said that geolocation data was “one of the most invasive forms of consumer surveillance”.
Agustín Reyna, director general of BEUC, welcomed the ruling but said “the time needed to come to this conclusion is disproportionate with the seriousness of the infringement” arguing “late enforcement can be as harmful as no enforcement at all”.
The DPC inquiry looked at “web and app activity”, “location history” and “location accuracy” between 25 May 2018 and 4 February 2020.
Imposing a fine of €403m, the DPC ordered Google to bring its processing into compliance with the EU’s general data protection regulation (GDPR) within six months.
It is the fourth-largest fine imposed by the Irish regulator, which has EU-wide responsibility for all the US tech giants with EU headquarters in Ireland.
It has previously fined Meta €1.2bn, TikTok €530m and Instagram (also Meta owned) €405m.
Doyle said: “The GDPR provides a high level of protection of personal data throughout the EEA, and requires that the processing of personal data must be carried out in a lawful, fair and transparent manner.
“As a result of Google’s failures in this regard, individuals could have been unaware that their location was being used to, for example, influence them with ads or to infer their interests, and could lose control over their personal data.
“The retention of users’ location data for longer than necessary aggravated this loss of control,” added Doyle.
There are three other ongoing statutory large-scale inquiries open that concern Google, all of which are at an advanced stage.

More Dutch students studying abroad, Spain most popular choice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:50:32 UTC
19:50:32 KST

More Dutch students studying abroad, Spain most popular choice
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
More Dutch students are spending part of their degree abroad, but the proportion is still below pre-pandemic levels, according to latest official figures.
Some 24% of students who graduated from universities and vocational colleges in 2025 went abroad for part of their studies, with one in six (17%) staying for three months or longer.
Five years ago, during the most restricted phase of the coronavirus pandemic, just 16% of all students had spent time outside the Netherlands, the government statistics agency CBS said.
Spain was the most popular destination for students who took part in the Erasmus+ exchange programme between 2014 and 2024, accounting 16.9% of the total, followed by Germany (9.7%) and the UK (8.9%).
The last figure is noteworthy because Britain left the Erasmus+ scheme in 2020 as part of the Brexit agreement, though it is rejoining from next year.
Students who went abroad for their entire degree were most likely to go to Belgium, followed by the UK and the United States.
Online decline
One in seven students took part in online lessons or projects hosted by foreign colleges and universities, but here there was a declining trend, particularly among university students.
Just 10% of the latter group followed an online course, down from 14% in 2021, while for vocational students the proportion slipped from 19% to 18%.
More than one-third (36%) of recent graduates who spent time abroad also included an online element.

what does a guitar sound like in stone? bebeau builds one from 18 pieces of slate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:50:01 UTC
19:50:01 KST

what happens when an acoustic guitar trades wood for stone?
An acoustic guitar usually depends on a thin wooden body to turn the vibration of its strings into a larger movement of air. BeBeau Builds starts with a more stubborn material. For his latest experiment, the maker replaces the familiar timber shell with a faceted body assembled from 18 pieces of slate, producing a guitar that weighs 48.7 pounds and still functions as an acoustic instrument.
The idea begins with sound. Struck on its own, the thick slate gives off a long metallic ring, enough to suggest that the stone could resonate once shaped into a hollow body. Its physical behavior creates the harder part of the project. The slabs are heavy and vary in thickness, while the guitar still has to sit across a human body and hold the tension of its strings.
Creator BeBeau Builds develops several body shapes before settling on the final angular form, then uses 3D-printed templates to transfer those geometries onto the slate. A tile saw struggles almost immediately with the inch-thick material. Once the pieces are cut, their beveled edges have to meet precisely enough to create a closed volume around a repurposed acoustic-guitar neck.
The first assembly exposes how quickly tiny differences can accumulate. A 3D-printed internal frame is designed to position the 18 stone sections, yet the slate ranges from roughly three quarters of an inch to an inch and a quarter thick. Those shifts throw the cut angles off. The pieces drift farther from the intended geometry as the body grows, forcing BeBeau Builds to pull the assembly apart and scrape the adhesive from the stone.
BeBeau Builds constructs a playable acoustic guitar from pieces of slate
hot glue becomes temporary structure
For the second attempt, BeBeau Builds works from the exterior dimensions instead of relying on the internal frame. Hot glue holds the pieces in position as a temporary structure, while construction adhesive fills the irregular joints and cures over several days. The method leaves room for the slate to behave like slate, with each piece adjusted against the next instead of being forced onto an idealized digital skeleton.
The front plate and salvaged neck bring the object closer to an instrument, though the material keeps making its presence felt. A stone panel breaks during fabrication and is replaced. Gaps between the sections are filled, and a coating of mineral oil darkens the slate before the strings are tuned. By this point the guitar has the familiar proportions of an acoustic body, translated into a much heavier shell of hard planar surfaces.
eighteen stone sections shape the faceted body around a repurposed guitar neck
the slate guitar sounds strangely familiar
Once strummed, the biggest surprise is how ordinary the guitar sounds. BeBeau Builds expected the stone body to shift its voice dramatically, yet the first open chords land close to those of a conventional wooden acoustic. The slate version is softer and its notes fade sooner. Its tone changes slightly as well, while the inch-thick front plate still vibrates enough to move air and produce a recognizable acoustic sound.
Its physical limits are easier to hear and feel after a longer song. Nearly 49 pounds of slate becomes uncomfortable across the lap, and the neck sits at an imperfect angle, making the strings harder to press and pulling some notes sharp. Still, the project gets past its central question. A guitar body can become a stone shell and continue to behave like a guitar, with the biggest transformation arriving through weight and construction instead of an entirely unfamiliar voice.
the first assembly reveals how uneven stone thickness shifts each joint
hot glue temporarily holds the second assembly while construction adhesive cures
mineral oil deepens the slate surface before the instrument is tuned
the finished guitar weighs nearly 49 pounds
the slate body produces a familiar acoustic tone with lower volume and shorter sustain

'Most' of Ceuta's 2,000 unaccompanied minors will not return to Morocco, Spain says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:48:54 UTC
19:48:54 KST

Minister says minors who arrived in Ceuta during July's mass border breach will most likely stay in Spain. Madrid is facing serious operational difficulties in completing returns, while tensions with local residents are growing.
Spain's youth minister said Monday that most unaccompanied minors stranded in Ceuta after a mass border breach in July will remain in Spain, despite an earlier pledge by the Spanish government to return those who entered illegally to Morocco.
In July, more than 80,000 people crossed into the Spanish enclave in what authorities described as an unprecedented border breach. Between 5,000 and 10,000 people, depending on figures from the different authorities, are believed to have remained in Ceuta as Madrid works to identify them and arrange their return to Morocco.
Around half are reportedly unaccompanied minors.
Minister Sira Rego said Spanish law grants underage migrants fundamental protections regardless of their origin or legal status. She said the vast majority have asked to remain in Spain.
"Most of them want to stay in Spain and they are going to stay, of course. There is a law that protects them," Rego told Spanish radio network Cadena SER.
"Our duty is to protect them," she said.
Rego said many of the children had fled violence or extreme circumstances, making them particularly vulnerable.
She defended an approach based on the rule of law and empathy, while criticising what she called the "trivialisation of evil" in the political debate.
Rego is positioned on the further left of Spain's governing coalition, which also includes more moderate parties.
Her comments have yet to be confirmed by Spain's interior minister.
Madrid is facing legal hurdles over the return of minors, who are entitled to special protections under Spanish law, while the government has pledged to prevent further crossings into the EU's Schengen area.
The situation has also fuelled anger among some Ceuta residents. At several protests, locals have been heard chanting: "No asylum for the invaders."
In a departure from the government's usual line, Rego also said cooperation from the Moroccan authorities on the issue has been limited.
"It is not common for us to receive a smooth response from Morocco, and this is usually a problem," she said.

Fact-checking is most politicized media area — Zakharova
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:48:14 UTC
19:48:14 KST

MOSCOW, September 21. /TASS/. The media space has become an arena of struggle over the right to distinguish truth from lies, and under these conditions fact-checking is one of the most politicized fields of the media industry, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
"I think fact-checking is now one of the most politicized areas of the media industry," she said at a media forum dedicated to the 65th anniversary of the Organization of Asia-Pacific News Agencies (OANA). "It is surprising, but countries and organizations are now politically fighting not for the truth, but for the right to call truth as truth and lies as lies. It seems that we should join forces, stand up for the truth together and denounce lies, but no, even this has essentially become a front line, a line of contact between opposing sides."
The Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman noted that "the architecture of global information dissemination is still structured as if Western mainstream media know the facts better than other media outlets, and they are doing everything to essentially monopolize the right to disseminate information under the brand of "only we have the truth."
"Ranking algorithms, moderation standards and recommendation mechanisms are all concentrated in several Silicon Valley companies that, at the request of their governments or owners, can overnight erase the presence of entire media organizations," Zakharova stressed. "This is no longer about competitive journalism. It is about the fact that truth has begun to be censored, while lies have begun to be promoted."
The OANA media forum is being held in Moscow in the year marking the organization’s 65th anniversary. OANA brings together 41 news agencies from 33 countries. Russia: Putin party retains majority in parliamentary vote
September 21, 2026
Russia's electoral commission on Monday said that the ruling United Russia party has won the parliamentary election.
It's the first parliamentary poll since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and President Vladimir Putin has cast it as a referendum of support for what is termed in Russia, the "special military operation."
Parties that support Putin and the Kremlin's war in Ukraine are the only ones registered to run, and the opposition was barred from taking part.
The polls took place amid rising prices, a crackdown on political opponents and the internet, fuel shortages and rumors of another mobilization drive following the elections.
What do we know about the Russian election results?
The Central Election Commission said that with 95% of ballots counted, the party of Russian President Vladimir Putin won 57.83% of the vote.
Commission chair Ella Pamfilova said that according to the preliminary results, United Russia would get 355 seats in the 450-seat Duma, giving the party around 20 more seats than it currently holds and marking the strongest result in its history.
The parliamentary vote was also the first to include residents of four regions in Ukraine — those being Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia — that were occupied and illegally annexed by Moscow later that year.
Voting was also held in Crimea, which was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. Kyiv denounced the voting in those regions as illegal.
Chechen ally receives nearly 100% of vote
Russia's electoral commission also announced that close Putin ally, Ramzan Kadyrov, has been re-elected to a fifth term as leader of Chechnya, a Russian republic in the North Caucasus region.
Electoral officials said he achieved 99.85% of the vote, a slight improvement from the 99.73% garnered in 2021.
International observers have previously severely criticised electoral processes in the small region.
Kadyrov's government has been accused of widespread rights violations by human rights organizations, including targeting journalists and homosexuals, something he denies.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
On this occasion, the Ukrainians brought with them the AIDrones UA MAUL armored unmanned ground vehicle (UGV). They used it to illustrate how UGVs, ground drones, have revolutionized the unit’s ability to reach and recover casualties from the battlefield, particularly from within the so-called “kill zone” – the corridor that separates the front lines where weapon strikes, particularly drones, make evacuation impossible.
The 1st Separate Medical Battalion has extensive experience in the treatment and medical evacuation of casualties near the front line. Russia’s Overnight Attack Kills 2, Injures 11 Across Ukraine as Zaporizhzhia Bears Brunt

The Livgardet post said that General Michael Claesson, commander-in-chief of the Swedish Armed Forces, added that the experience, expertise and technological innovation shared by the Ukrainian medics will strengthen their own ability to operate on the modern battlefield, allowing Sweden to strengthen its own defenses.

U.S. space weapons, AI regulation debates and the EPA’s carbon emissions rollback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:43:17 UTC
19:43:17 KST

Rachel Feltman: Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup. Let’s catch up on some recent headlines.
Today we’ve got quite a few news items on science and tech policy in the US, but I promise there’s a sassy little animal story waiting for you at the end.
Let’s start with some troubling news about the Environmental Protection Agency, which lately frankly has seemed pretty determined to do less of the whole “environmental protection” thing. Last Monday, the EPA revoked a Biden-era rule that limited how much carbon dioxide could be emitted by gas, oil and coal-fired power plants. When the carbon pollution standards were announced in 2024, the EPA estimated that they could prevent approximately 1,200 deaths and 1,900 new asthma cases in the year 2035 alone, with 1.38 billion metric tons total of CO2 avoided from 2028 to 2047 and $370 billion in health and climate cost savings from 2024 to 2047.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Also last Monday, President Donald Trump posted on social media complaining of a “SICK conspiracy” against “AI and Data Centers.” This came in response to calls for slower, more cautious AI development from industry leaders, including the CEOs of OpenAI’s Sam Altman, SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei.
Earlier this month, Amodei published an essay on his website sounding the alarm on AI’s current trajectory. He claimed that, while he has always tried to balance his belief in the importance and potential of AI with the need for thoughtful development practices, he and his colleagues fear that we’re close to the kind of tipping point we really don’t want to reach.
The growing ability of AI models to create and change themselves, which is called recursive self-improvement, makes it easy for companies that favor speed to end up with products that they don’t actually understand or have a particularly good ability to control. Amodei also pointed to the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident that occurred a few months ago. Just in case you aren’t familiar with that, I’ll do my best to give you a quick summary: AI companies will often test their systems by putting them in a locked-down training area—a sandbox—and then prompting them to do stuff that it would be pretty bad for the AI model to do in the real world, like exploit known software vulnerabilities.
In May, an OpenAI agent was stuck on an impossible task in one of those sandbox scenarios and basically started poking around for possible solutions. Instead of being totally cut off from the Internet, it had the ability to request files from an intermediary platform—but someone had goofed, and the agents could also make their own files to leave in that directory. So, it started using that ability to leave messages on this file directory platform, and eventually other OpenAI agents started leaving their own messages. They deduced that they could use the platform to smuggle code out of the sandbox. In July, about 700 agents coordinated with each other to hack another AI company called Hugging Face. Hugging Face is an open-source platform that hosts tons of information about AI, and the agents were looking for ways to solve or cheat on the tests they’d been given.
On the one hand, the mental image of a “swarm” of AI agents coordinating to conduct a cyberattack that no one even asked for is very ominous. But it’s worth noting that the problem here isn’t that AI is getting so intelligent that it will decide humanity sucks and should be destroyed, and many experts have pushed back on any warnings of that tenor. These AI agents were doing what they had been told to do—with the help of lots of computing power and very little critical thinking. It’s kind of like if a small child left their clothes all over the bathroom floor and, once you told them to get those clothes out of your sight, they flushed them down the toilet and busted your plumbing. If that happened you probably wouldn’t worry that your child was an evil genius who was going to take the sewers and attack the water supply; you would probably smack yourself for leaving them unsupervised with a vulnerable toilet and endeavor to give clearer instructions the next time you wanted them to clean up their stuff. Of course, the stakes of this kind of unsupervised button mashing from a smart-enough-to-flush-the-toilet-but-not-wise-enough-to-know-when-to-flush-it child are much lower than for a powerful AI system with access to the internet.
So, no, we’re not in a Skynet scenario. But also, yes, it does seem like we really need to be better parents to our rambunctious and foolish little AI tots. And for once, most of the powers that be in the space seem to agree that more guardrails would be prudent. It is reasonable to ask whether these tech moguls could have at least slightly ulterior motives in choosing now to speak up and band together—perhaps they see that some kind of regulation is inevitable and are hoping that by getting out ahead of it they can make it less stringent. Or they may be hoping to help shape regulations that are more likely to kneecap new competitors than they are to meaningfully slow any of the major players—but that doesn’t mean the general call for prudence is a hoax. After all, plenty of other folks in tech have been warning us about this for a long time. But for now, both the president and VP JD Vance have been publicly quite dismissive of the idea of increased AI regulation.
Speaking of Skynet, let’s talk about space weapons.
[CLIP of Troy Meink at a conference: “ This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”]
That is Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink speaking last week at the annual Air, Space & Cyber Conference.
Here to tell us more about all of this is Lee Billings, the senior desk editor for physical science at Scientific American. Thanks for taking the time to chat with us, Lee.
Lee Billings: Thanks, Rachel. It’s good to be here.
So what’s going on with these weapons in space? Well, first of all, what’s really important to remember is that we’ve probably had weapons in space for a while, and by we, I mean the U.S., I also mean other space-faring powers like China and Russia. But never before has anyone actually admitted to that, and that was what was so notable about Meink’s statement last week. Because it suggests that things are heating up out there on the final frontier, so to speak, and there’s a lot of other stuff up there that isn’t military, that isn’t about defense. Whether you’re thinking of communication satellites or GPS satellites, these things are increasingly integral to everyone’s life on Earth and how our economy works around the globe. So you really don’t want to have, uh, war kicking off in space if you can help it, because it might disrupt all these other peaceful uses and resources up there.
So like pretty much everything that’s in space, these things must have been launched by rockets. There are a large number of rocket launches around the world every year that take place for defense purposes, and typically the payloads for those rockets and their trajectories, their mission profiles are not fully disclosed. There’s definitely a lot of cloak-and-dagger mystery around how exactly or when exactly any given thing went to space and what it does.
So yeah, where exactly are these things in space? And the quick answer is: almost anywhere in Earth orbit around our planet. There’s low-Earth orbit where things like the Hubble Space Telescope or the International Space Station are. There are higher orbits; for instance, there’s the very important one called geosynchronous orbit, which is very, very, very, very, very high up. And it’s so high, in fact, that the spacecraft up there over any given point of the Earth’s surface will be moving in its orbit at the same rate as the Earth turns below it, which means that it is effectively stationary over a point on Earth. And a lot of things that are in geosynchronous orbit are especially strategically valuable for militaries because they can surveil a big part of the planet underneath them indefinitely. So that’s useful for communications, that’s useful for monitoring troop movements and things like that.
So one thing to note is that in Secretary Meink’s statement last week, he did not specify what kinds of weapons we are talking about. He simply said that these are things that are “on orbit.” So we know they are up there, but besides that, we don’t really have a lot of other information.
However, one long-standing doctrine of the United States and presumably also of China and Russia, even though I don’t think it’s been proclaimed as such, is to minimize the amount of debris that is made from any sort of military activity in space. And that’s a very, very important distinction because if you don’t wanna create debris, that tells you what these weapons might be like.
So for instance, perhaps we’re talking about so-called jammers, which is when you overwhelm a satellite with electromagnetic radiation, with radio waves for instance, and it’s no longer able to send or receive communications with the ground or with other satellites. Another option would be a spacecraft that can rendezvous with an adversary’s spacecraft and manipulate it or interact with it in some way. The other option beyond jammers and rendezvous vehicles would be something like a missile or a very high-energy laser that could actually shoot something down or break something apart in orbit. But again, because we don’t wanna create debris, those are generally seen as high-risk, kind of, last-resort types of options, which doesn’t mean they don’t exist up there.
So one thing that’s rather interesting about Secretary Meink’s statements last Monday is they occurred at this industry conference called the Air, Space and Cyber Conference, which took place in Maryland.
And on Tuesday, the next day, there were more comments. Chief of Space Operations General Douglas Schiess, who said, “We’ve talked about, you know, [them] being able to grapple a satellite and move it to a different orbit.... I think at this point we are trying to say we also need capabilities to not only defend the joint force from space-enabled attack, but defend our assets,” end quote. So he was also talking about it. And then the following day, last Wednesday, we had General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, telling the audience that the US military must be, quote, “prepared to fight, endure, and win ... from the seabed to cislunar space,” which, means including on and around the moon.
So what’s next? This is a full court press we’re seeing from this one conference; we’re seeing multiple senior officials all saying the same sort of thing, which is a very clear signal to our adversaries but also our allies that the U.S. is, I guess, kinda taking the kid gloves off or is ready to escalate as need be in space. And the reason why this is happening is, again, because space is becoming more and more important and more of a contested domain.
But the point is is that, as we as a species, humankind, move out into space and do more activity there, all of our activities that are on Earth seem to be following us, warts and all. So, unfortunately, even though for a long time the official stance has been that outer space is something that should just be used for peaceful purposes or at least not for direct hostility, it seems like that may change in the near future, and that’s quite frightening.
Feltman: Thanks for that, Lee!
Okay y’all, we made it: It’s time for a fun animal story. It turns out that the most productive little landscapers on the planet are about the size of a human pinky. In a study published last Wednesday in Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface, scientists report that shrimplike creatures known as sand hoppers are small but when it comes to shoveling sand, very mighty.
Picture a stretch of sandy coastline—Isla Vista Beach in California, to be precise—and imagine a patch of sand three feet long. According to this new study, about 21,450 little critters in the genus Megalorchestia are bustling around that space. And every night, as they dig homes for themselves and kick displaced sand up to the surface, they collectively shovel about 110 pounds of the stuff. That’s about 16 half-gallon sandcastle buckets, for reference. In the 15.5 miles of beach that stretch along the area, the researchers estimate, the tiny creatures displace 310 tons of dry sand a day.
Why do we care about these scuttling sand hoppers? They’re a reminder that our favorite sandy beaches are complex ecosystems, and that too much human interference can mess with the natural ebb and flow.
That’s all for this week’s news roundup. We’ll be back on Wednesday to talk about the Internet’s hottest new wellness trend: poopmaxxing.
