Nearly six in 10 Danish companies with more than 10 employees now use artificial intelligence, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark. That’s almost four times the share recorded three years ago.
In 2026, 59 percent of these companies use AI, up from 15 percent in 2023. The share was 42 percent in 2025.
The uses of AI include analyzing text, converting spoken language into machine-readable code, generating images and videos, and automating work processes.
Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, said it has seen AI move from being mainly a topic of discussion to a tool used in daily business.
“Companies’ use of artificial intelligence is here to stay, and we can see that the large companies are the furthest ahead,” Frederikke Saabye, industry director at Dansk Erhverv, said.
According to the business organisation, companies see greater efficiency as the main benefit of using AI. A lack of employee skills, knowledge and time are the biggest barriers to making greater use of the technology.
IT-Branchen, an industry association representing technology companies in Denmark, said the wider use of AI also increases the need to consider issues such as quality, transparency and data security.
“The more the technology spreads, the more important issues of quality, transparency, data security, and not least human judgment become,” IT-Branchen’s CEO Natasha Friis Saxberg said, adding that the development makes broader AI knowledge and training more important, including upskilling and continuing education for employees.
The Danish government plans to charge tourists 20 DKK per overnight stay in Copenhagen and Aarhus and introduce a levy on cruise ships, according to government sources and a memo obtained by Børsen.
The previously undisclosed measures would help fund tax cuts that the minority government will seek support for this autumn. The plans require backing from other parties, expected to come from the center-right opposition.
The government wants to abolish the 7.5% intermediate tax on annual income between 641,200 DKK and 777,900 DKK. It also plans to remove the top-top tax on income exceeding 2,592,700 DKK.
Corporate tax would fall from 22% to 19% over three years. The ceiling for share savings accounts would rise to 500,000 DKK over the same period, and taxes on shares would be reduced.
Planned funding measures include keeping the duty on chocolate and sweets, reducing the research and development deduction for companies and raising taxes on dividends received by major shareholders.
The government also wants to limit interest deductions to 150,000 DKK for individuals and 300,000 DKK for couples. Estates worth more than 10 million DKK would face a tax rate 15 percentage points higher than today.
The tax cuts are not fully covered by higher taxes and duties. The government plans to use about 1.5 billion DKK from available public funds in 2027, rising to about 2 billion DKK in 2029.
Denmark’s government consists of the Social Democrats, Socialist People’s Party, Moderates and Social Liberals. It does not have a parliamentary majority.
Danish stocks fell for an eighth consecutive trading day Tuesday as rising oil prices and interest rates weighed on the market.
At midday, the C25 index of major Danish companies was down 0.75 percent from Monday’s closing level. The index stood at about 1,845, down 70 points, or 3.7 percent, from its latest peak on September 3.
Jacob Pedersen, an investment strategist at Danish bank Middelfart Sparekasse, said higher oil prices were pushing up interest rates.
Denmark’s largest companies generally carry less debt than businesses in other countries, making rising rates less of a direct problem for them, Pedersen said.
“But we cannot get around the fact that there is a risk in these rising interest rates in terms of the fact that it can drag some growth out of the economy, and that will also hit Danish companies,” he said.
Slower economic growth could reduce company revenue. Higher interest rates can also make stocks less attractive compared with bonds, which offer higher fixed returns when rates increase.
Pedersen said he did not expect an immediate major downturn in Danish shares. He described the market as strong because it has a large number of pharmaceutical and transport companies, which are less affected when consumers have less money to spend.
However, widespread selling by nervous investors would also affect Denmark because much of its stock market is owned by foreign investors.
“If everyone runs for the exit, it will also be felt in the Danish stock market,” Pedersen said. He added that such a decline would be driven more by market behavior than falling company earnings.
Denmark has rejected Russia’s claim that a Danish military helicopter acted “provocatively” before a Russian frigate fired two flares toward it Monday.
Russian Ambassador Vladimir Barbin said Danish helicopters had repeatedly performed “dangerous maneuvers” near Russian warships.
“The latest incident shows that the communication problems are not on the Russian navy’s side, but on the Danish side,” Barbin wrote to the Danish news agency Ritzau.
Denmark’s Armed Forces said the frigate fired two signal or distress flares toward an Air Force Fennec helicopter in international waters off Gedser. The helicopter was conducting routine photographic monitoring of the ship.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates called Barbin’s account “a Russian excuse” and denied that Denmark had provoked the frigate.
“What we do to monitor our own immediate area is completely legal, and it does not give the Russians any alibi whatsoever to start firing at us, even if it is only with flares,” Rasmussen told Danish newspaper Ekstra Bladet.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats also said the helicopter had a legitimate reason to be there and was following normal practice.
Barbin said Russia would investigate the incident. He also cited an alleged encounter on August 27, 2025, when a Danish helicopter flew low over the Russian warship Viceadmiral Kulakov near the German island of Fehmarn.
The ambassador said that helicopter created a collision risk and failed to answer radio calls or warnings. Ritzau has asked the Danish Defense Ministry for comment on that allegation.
Denmark has summoned Barbin to the Foreign Ministry for talks about Monday’s incident.
The Danish government will require police to register all potential crimes as criminal cases and end the practice of shelving reports without a proper investigation.
The Justice Ministry announced Tuesday that it would implement all recommendations from the National Audit Office, Denmark’s independent public spending watchdog. The disputed police practice is known as “washing cases.”
“Citizens must naturally be able to have confidence that the police handle their case properly and correctly, regardless of where in the country you live,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said.
“In the future, all potential criminal cases must be registered as actual criminal cases,” he added.
The Public Accounts Committee, a parliamentary oversight body, strongly criticized police in May after receiving a National Audit Office report on the practice. Cases were reportedly shelved partly to save resources.
The new government reshuffled senior police leadership in June. Top positions in the National Police and PET, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, changed hands.
Several justice spokespersons in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, said they had no confidence in National Police Commissioner Thorkild Fogde after he said he did not know about the practice. Fogde was later removed from the position.
The ministry did not say whether police would receive additional funding. Wammen previously said he was open to providing more money and noted that a multiyear agreement had already increased funding and training.
The National Police and Director of Public Prosecutions must regularly report on future developments to the political parties behind that agreement.
Two earlier State Prosecutor reports were not used because the National Audit Office identified issues they had missed, Wammen said.

Did Zara Larsson pull out of Abu Dhabi Grand Prix over Sudan?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:36:13 UTC

Breadcrumb
Did Zara Larsson pull out of Abu Dhabi Grand Prix performance over Sudan war?
Swedish pop star Zara Larsson has said she will not perform at the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix after facing calls to withdraw over allegations surrounding the UAE's role in Sudan's civil war, although her name was still appearing on the event's line-up.
Larsson was scheduled to perform alongside Scottish singer Lewis Capaldi on 3 December as part of the Yasalam After-Race Concerts on Yas Island.
Questions over whether she had officially pulled out emerged after a fan urged her on social media to "read about what UAE is doing to Sudan" and cancel the performance.
"I will not be going to Abu Dhabi," Larsson replied, according to screenshots of the subsequently deleted exchange.
She later expanded on her decision, saying she had considered the issue and decided against performing, while stressing that her reasons went beyond politics.
"I wanna perform and spread joy and music for people in every country, because no single person is their government," she wrote. "I've met so many wonderful people from every corner of the world and I know this to be true in my heart."
Larsson said her initial comment may have appeared impulsive, but that she had spent time considering the decision.
"Maybe it came off as a impulsive response to a comment, but I have spent some time thinking about everything and decided that to not do the show aligns with me the most right now, for many different personal reasons beyond politics."
However, despite Larsson saying she would not perform, her name was still appearing on the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix concert line-up at the time of reporting.
Ticketmaster continued to list Larsson alongside Capaldi for the 3 December concert, while the Yasalam website also advertised her among the artists due to perform during Grand Prix weekend.
The wider line-up includes Imagine Dragons, The Chainsmokers and The Script.
Larsson also appeared to indicate that a more formal statement about her decision could follow.
The controversy comes amid scrutiny of the UAE over allegations that it has supported Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) during the country's civil war.
The UAE has repeatedly denied providing military support to the RSF.
The RSF has been accused of widespread atrocities and crimes against humanity during the conflict. Human Rights Watch reported earlier this year that Colombian fighters linked to atrocities in Sudan had been trained by a security company based in Abu Dhabi.
The United Nations has described Sudan as the world's largest humanitarian and displacement crisis, saying in August that around 13 million people had been displaced amid mass killings, sexual violence, child recruitment and attacks on civilian infrastructure.

US and China Discuss Alerting Each Other to AI National Security Threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:34:43 UTC
19:34:43 KST

Talks have begun between US and Chinese officials to propose a mechanism for the two countries to notify each other of artificial intelligence incidents which could threaten national security.
The framework, called the US China AI Dialogue, would also see representatives from both countries meet again to discuss the technology and try to align on common goals and threats, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
“We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important,” Bessent told reporters on Sunday.
Bessent said the discussions picked up from where they had been left off after US President Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing in May. Since then, public safety concerns about the technology have grown. Security incidents over the summer, including OpenAI’s agents hacking Hugging Face, highlighted the capabilities of frontier models and how the industry’s safeguards have failed to keep pace.
Fears reached a fever pitch earlier this month after Anthropic employees warned AI could be on course to wipe out humanity. In recent weeks, leaders of the biggest frontier laboratories, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk, have called for a slowdown in development of the technology while they set safety standards. In an essay suggesting steps for laboratories and governments to pace the technology’s development, Amodei had asked for government assistance in establishing international coordination, including with the Chinese Communist Party.
Trump has so far mostly brushed off their calls, despite growing bipartisan support for regulating the industry. The US government already has sufficient criminal and regulatory power over developers, his administration has argued.
He’s not alone. Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia, which builds AI infrastructure, pointed out that AI firms are already subject to cybersecurity and damage liability laws. “Apply that first,” he said in an interview with CBS News over the weekend. “Don’t let this doomsday narrative allow someone to relieve them of the laws that currently exist.”
Trump has said any slowdown could cede the US lead in the technology to China—a danger because, in his own words: “WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!” His chief science advisor David Sacks previously warned that “China is very unlikely to join a global agreement” on pacing the technology. Thomas Wolf, cofounder of open-source AI platform Hugging Face, which Nvidia recently agreed to buy, has questioned whether the US can build global cooperation while “explicitly stating you want to design it to keep widening your own lead.” “That seems like a pretty counterproductive way to start the conversation to me,” he wrote on X in response to Amodei’s essay.
The US is currently trying to temper China’s advance in AI by restricting exports of advanced chips and chipmaking technology to China. Officials did not discuss these US export controls in this weekend’s meetings, said Bessent, which also featured trade discussions and were “very successful” ahead of this week’s visit to Washington by Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Seven Ethiopian armed groups announce anti-government alliance
ADDIS ABABA, Sept 21 - Seven Ethiopian armed groups, including longstanding enemies who fought on opposite sides of a 2020-2022 civil war, said they have formed an alliance aimed at overthrowing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.
The announcement of the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival brought together a geographically and ethnically diverse body of groups ranging from Tigray in the north to Somali Region in the south. Some remain at loggerheads with other members over territory and other issues.
Spokespeople for Abiy and the federal government did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Last month, after reports of a possible coalition of armed groups, an adviser to Abiy said any such formation would seek to wreak havoc but would not be able to overthrow the federal government.
The new alliance, announced late on Sunday, includes the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Amhara Fano National Movement. Fano, a coalition of armed groups from the Amhara region, fought in support of the federal government against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, which resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths and was marked by ethnically driven atrocities.
Fano subsequently rose up against the federal government in a conflict that has killed thousands in Amhara since 2023.
Many of the groups have accused the government of centralising power and marginalising the regions. The government says it has launched a national dialogue meant to address longstanding political divisions and internal conflicts.
"We, the peoples' forces concerned with the survival of Ethiopia's peoples, bear the historic responsibility of overthrowing this regime," said the statement read out by Fano leader Zemene Kassie and broadcast on Tigrayan television.
The announcement of the alliance, which also includes groups from the Oromia, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz regions, follows reported skirmishes between federal and Tigrayan forces.
In May, the TPLF reasserted control over the region's political administration in violation of the 2022 peace deal that ended the Tigray war after accusing the federal government of failing to uphold the agreement.
The Ethiopian military has carried out several drone strikes against Tigrayan forces in recent months, according to data from the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data project.
The federal government has not commented on the reported strikes, but the military said last week that nearly 300 Tigrayan fighters had surrendered to it.
Ethiopia has also accused its neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea of supporting insurgent groups, including the TPLF and Fano. Eritrea has denied this. REUTERS

The war's relentless daily attacks underscore the absence of any significant progress in diplomatic efforts to stop the fighting, more than four years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbour.

The Russian Defence Ministry said on Monday that its air defences overnight downed 244 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions and the waters of the Black Sea.

Moldova reports another drone incursion

Moldova’s Ministry of Defence said on Monday that part of the country's airspace in the north was temporarily closed overnight after surveillance systems detected an “aerial object” entering its national airspace shortly after midnight.
In recent weeks, Moldova’s airspace has been violated multiple times and drone debris has been found on its territory.
With electronic jamming knocking drones off course, it was not clear whether the drones were Russian or Ukrainian, though officials have often singled out Moscow for blame.
Moldova’s pro-Western President Maia Sandu has repeatedly condemned Russia for its war on Ukraine and earlier this month said Moscow’s “brutal war is reaching our border” following Russian strikes along Moldova’s frontier with Ukraine.

Suspected poisoning kills 10 lions at wildlife reserve in Tanzania
Ten lions have been found dead in a suspected poisoning incident at Tanzania's UNESCO-listed Ngorongoro Conservation Area, according to the authorities.
"The Ngorongoro Conservation Area Authority (NCAA) regrets to inform the public that ten (10) lions were found dead on September 18, 2026 in the Ndutu area," the wildlife reserve said in a statement.
Authorities said preliminary findings suggest that the lions died after "ingesting poison," adding that an expert investigation was ongoing "to determine the cause of the incident and identify those responsible."
Ngorongoro has been the scene of long-standing tensions between the authorities and the local nomadic community. Clashes have sometimes turned deadly since the government launched an eviction program in 2022.
The Tanzanian government argues that population growth is encroaching on wildlife habitat, with the number of people living in Ngorongoro rising from about 8,000 in 1959 to more than 100,000.
According to UNESCO, Ngorongoro Conservation Area is home to a population of about 25,000 large animals, including the densest known population of lions.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature classifies lions as vulnerable and says their numbers are declining. Threats facing the species include habitat loss, declining prey populations and human-wildlife conflict.
Since June, at least 20 elephants have died in Kenya's Amboseli ecosystem, near the Tanzanian border, from suspected pesticide poisoning, although authorities could not establish whether the deaths were accidental or deliberate.
Kenya has previously recorded incidents of elephants being poisoned as a result of poaching and human-wildlife conflict. But officials say it's the first time in decades the region has recorded elephant deaths on this scale, according to CBS News' partner network BBC News.

"These changes are long overdue and will make a significant difference, but focusing on prosecution alone will not be enough," said the British premier.

South Korea beats foreign student target, but struggles to keep them
New university rankings show while South Korea has enjoyed an international student boom, gaps in support and post-graduation outcomes remain
First launched last year and described as the country’s most internationalisation-focused assessment to date, The Korea Times University Rankings assess institutions on seven indicators, including the ratio of exchange and international students to total enrolment, diversity of the cohorts’ nationalities, proportion of international students meeting language proficiency requirements, and foreign student retention rate.
This year’s evaluation aims to look beyond the number of international students to assess how well South Korean universities are building the broader ecosystem needed for globalisation.
Results show that while the universities have been good at attracting and managing international students, many still lag in areas such as international faculty, financial support and post-graduation outcomes.

RX Architects expands Sussex home with extension "immersed in the garden"

RX Architects expands Sussex home with extension "immersed in the garden"
UK studio RX Architects has returned to a house it previously completed in Sussex to add an extension, designed to blend in with the existing timber-clad form.
The original home, named Druim, was completed in 2020 on the Rye Nature Reserve in East Sussex. The project involved altering a half-built structure that had been sold with the site.
While the original project focused on views of the nature reserve and sea, RX Architects looked to improve the home's connection to the more private rear garden with the Druim Extension.
"The main opportunity was to enhance the private rear gardens and connections to the northern aspect to the outside space," studio director Rob Pollard told Dezeen.
"The original design didn't allow this, due to budget limitations at that time, making it more complex to adapt the originally built structure," he explained.
"We wanted the new adaptations to tie in seamlessly with the original house, as we had only completed the original property seven years ago or so. Therefore, we used the same contractor and materials on the scheme."
Druim Extension houses an expanded dining area, which is wrapped by full-height glazing and sliding doors that open onto a patio and the home's garden.
This space, which connects to the existing kitchen to the east, has been organised around a solid wood table, large skylight and log burner at its centre.
Tucked into the glazed, garden-facing corner of this dining space is a large window seat, shaded by deep soffits clad in narrow timber planks that continue inside to define the extension's ceilings.
"The rear extension provides a break and depth to the rear elevation which sits neatly into the landscape – but internally it creates a genuine sense of being outdoors and immersed in the garden, which the original property didn't have," Pollard explained.
"The clad ceiling, overhanging soffits, glazed elevations and corner window seat have a real sense of calm, as they are completely sheltered from the southern aspect, which is more exposed to the harsh winds from the coast," he added.
As well as expanding the interior, Druim Extension also prompted a reorientation of the existing spaces around a new boot room and entrance hall, providing direct access to the staircase, which was previously accessed from the living room.
To the west of the entrance, a glazed linking corridor replaces a paved path leading to the home's annexe, helping to shelter the home's garden from coastal winds while still allowing views through.
"Turning the stair allowed the living room orientation to shift, providing a better aspect for views out to the sea and nature reserve," Pollard said.
"The glazed link gives the whole building more of a horizontal emphasis, but also provides a fantastic rear courtyard to the garden, which gives views through it to the sea and nature reserve."
Elsewhere in Sussex, DeDraft recently updated a modernist home set within a garden, using a palette of warm wood and ceramic tiles to echo the original design.
Other projects by RX Architects include Seabreeze, a coastal home in East Sussex that was finished in pale pink-toned concrete to evoke Mediterranean beach houses.

Why K-Pop Took Off When C-Pop Didn’t
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:30:03 UTC
19:30:03 KST

It’s not often that an 18th century folk song can be said to be the inspiration for a pop concert. But those who attended the finale of BTS’ “ARIRANG” North American concert tour at Los Angeles’ giant SoFi Stadium earlier this month will long remember the tens of thousands of fans who waved South Korean flags and sang along to the traditional Korean melody.
The four-night run in LA was the finale to a tour of 31 sold-out shows, with combined attendance of approximately 1.92 million, according to figures released by the band’s agency. For comparison, Beyoncé’s 2023 Renaissance tour sold about 1.73 million tickets across 35 North American shows.
The flag-waving scenes from the SoFi capped a banner year for Korean pop, following BTS’s World Cup final halftime performance. Earlier in the year, Golden, from KPop Demon Hunters, collected a Grammy, followed by an Academy Awards performance and the Oscar for best original song.
Those performances and prizes will have brought smiles to the faces in Seoul’s foreign-policy circles, where there is a keen appreciation for the soft power that K-Pop brings South Korea. In Beijing, it will have led to much gnashing of teeth.
For more than a decade, China has looked on with undisguised envy as its Korean neighbor has accumulated soft power through cultural exports. As far back as the 2014 National People’s Congress, the Communist Party heavyweight Wang Qishan marveled at the reach of Korean culture, citing popular TV dramas like My Love for the Star and the breakout dance hit Gangnam Style by Psy, arguably the first K-Pop star to break big worldwide.
The interest went beyond public musing: Beijing resolved to learn from Seoul’s example. China’s culture ministry signed an agreement with its South Korean counterpart, providing for annual cultural-industry forums and cooperation in marketing cultural products abroad.
But it is one thing for Beijing to study Seoul’s cultural outreach, and quite another to match it. China, despite possessing a vastly larger population, an extensive diaspora, and the world’s fourth-largest recorded-music market, has failed to produce a music machine comparable to the international following of the marquee K-Pop acts. And while Taiwan’s Mandarin-language stars and Hong Kong’s Cantopop veterans have their own histories, they haven’t as yet spawned an act as ubiquitous as Blackpink or Stray Kids.
The audience Wang wondered about now extends well beyond America and Europe. Blackpink’s leading Spotify markets in 2024 included Indonesia, Mexico, the Philippines, and Brazil, spanning across the Global South, where Beijing has invested billions in the pursuit of soft power. These audiences' affection for K-pop reaches across linguistic and political boundaries, giving Seoul a welcome that its diplomats would struggle to arrange.
One obvious reason for China’s failure to produce pop stars of global reach is the sheer size of the domestic market. “A concert tour of 10 Chinese cities is probably as big as if they go around the world,” Anthony Fung, professor of journalism and communications at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, told the Financial Times. Why spend years trying to understand Brazilian teenagers when there is so much money to be made in familiar surroundings? Chinese musicians have perfectly sound commercial reasons to focus on the home market, regardless of their government’s geopolitical ambitions. Korean companies, with fewer customers at home, had more reason to take on the risks and costs of finding fans abroad.
That incentive would have achieved little without companies willing to adapt to foreign tastes. Korean agencies combined intensive training with production and promotion, recruited performers internationally, and hired foreign songwriters and choreographers. They built acts whose appeal survived the loss of the lyrics. For instance, fans didn’t need to understand Korean to dig Psy’s dance moves. The resulting music would not satisfy a purist’s definition of national, but its borrowings helped it travel: Korea’s entertainment industry learned to please people elsewhere.
Those listeners could also help find the next audience. YouTube let fans share performances without waiting for local broadcasters to discover them; viewers could join in by making videos of their own. When Gangnam Style passed a billion views in December 2012, YouTube reported that it had already drawn at least a million views in nearly 75 countries. Fourteen years later, KPop Demon Hunters shows how much further this can go. The Sony Pictures Animation film distributed by Netflix made Korean pop culture its selling point. In other words, American businesses now have their own reasons to keep the world interested in Korea.
Chinese performers, on the other hand, face greater difficulty getting that circulation started. YouTube and Instagram are blocked at home, separating their domestic following from the platforms where potential foreign fans congregate. They can release music overseas, of course. But their most enthusiastic supporters cannot pass it along as easily, so a hit on a Chinese platform has further to travel before it reaches a Mexican listener. Beijing’s determination to police what enters the country complicates its ambition to export what comes out.
The policing also reaches into the relationship between performers and fans. In 2021, China’s internet authorities abolished online rankings of entertainers and tightened supervision of fan accounts. Broadcasting regulators banned idol-development shows and demanded political correctness from entertainers, expressing special disdain for supposedly effeminate men. Some restrictions addressed legitimate concerns about children being induced to overspend. But a state that prescribes acceptable masculinity is doing much more than protecting young consumers: It is claiming jurisdiction over the tastes that pop music exists to indulge.
This is an expensive preference for a government seeking friends. Joseph Nye, the political scientist who developed the concept of soft power, wrote that “popular entertainment often contains subtle images and messages about individualism, consumer choice, and other values that have important political effects.” The messages themselves—lyrics about youthful love and angst—needn’t concern foreign policy to help a foreign minister. A country that others around the world have encountered as a source of pleasure has a better chance of receiving a sympathetic hearing when it asks for support. Seoul still needs persuasive policies, but K-pop gives it an advantage over governments whose principal introduction to foreign publics is a dispute or a threat.
China itself has supplied a demonstration of how stubborn that affection can be. Beijing’s unofficial restrictions on Korean entertainment, imposed after Seoul agreed to host an American missile-defense system, have not prevented Chinese fans of K-Pop from traveling abroad to see the performers they love.
Seoul has good reason to encourage an industry capable of sustaining such loyalties. Chinese officials might point to the Korean government’s support for entertainment companies to argue that the state has a useful role in cultural exports, but public assistance doesn’t entitle officials to supervise the relationship with the audience. Foreign listeners bring tastes no ministry can predict, and successful performers need room to accommodate them. China can afford the studios, the training, and the promotion. Its leaders must decide whether they can tolerate a pop star whose first obligation is to please the fans.
Meanwhile, back in the US, there is every expectation that K-Pop will continue to break new ground in 2027: BTS and Blackpink feature prominently in speculation about who will perform in next year’s Super Bowl halftime show. The best Chinese officials can hope for is to score tickets to the game.

Bambu P2S Combo 3D Printer Review: My Own Little Plastics Factory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Easy for anyone to use. Consistently perfect prints. Enclosed chamber for temperature control. New tool-free nozzle-swap feature. AMS add-on makes multicolor printing a breeze.
TIRED
Speed causes a lot of shaking—needs a very stable surface to sit on. Filament waste disposal makes a mess. Fumes from high-temperature filaments are still very intense.
Does the average consumer actually need a 3D printer? Isn’t it just for people who want to sell fidgets at the flea market, design obscure brackets in CAD, or print groups of Warhammer figurines?
Yes, they do, and no, it isn’t.
Photograph: Kat Merck
In my four weeks of testing the Bambu Lab P2S Combo, I have printed a sponge holder for my kitchen sink; caps and parts for my hydroponic gardens; various clips and hangers; a Mason jar lid organizer; a shovel; a couple of funny signs; plant pot coasters; a shoehorn; truck bed tie-downs; a pair of earrings; and, of course, a Benchy—every piece perfectly smooth and looking like it was purchased from a store. Owning a 3D printer is like having an Amazon fulfillment center right in your house.
While I'm no stranger to 3D printing—I owned the open-frame Bambu Lab A1 before I started testing 3D printers—I have never used a machine as easy to operate as the P2S. In fact, when we reviewed Bambu Lab’s P2S predecessor, the popular and bestselling P1S, earlier this year, tester Brad Bourque declared it the easiest-to-use 3D printer he’d ever tried, claiming its lack of complicated steps and futzing has changed the way he thinks about 3D printing.
The P2S builds on the already excellent P1S design with a new 5-inch color touchscreen, tool-free nozzle swapping, a beefed-up 1080p 30-frames-per-second camera with improved AI failure detection, and a redesigned airflow system. I wasn’t exactly in love with the latter, but one complaint for a system with thousands of failure points is more than enough to earn the P2S a solid A-grade.
Detail of identical pigeon figurine printed on white Bambu Lab PLA: A1 on left, P2S on right.
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
It Really Is That Easy
If you own another brand of mid- or lower-tier 3D printer, any Bambu Lab machine will already feel like an upgrade. Much like an iPhone, any Bambu Lab printer will work seamlessly right out of the box, with easy-to-use software and intuitive design elements. With a little assembly, you’re ready to go.
The large touchscreen allows you to perform many functions and troubleshooting right on the machine. These printers are easy for even the most clueless newbie to use and understand—so much so that some call the company “the Apple of 3D printing.” (Even better, the company’s free, flagship Bambu Studio software is open source.)
What makes both the P1S and P2S worth the upgrade from the A1 is the enclosed chamber that provides environmental control for acrylonitrile filaments like ASA and ABS, which require high temperatures to melt and are notoriously prone to warping. In the P2S, Bambu Lab incorporates a new airflow system that switches modes depending on the filament—it pulls in cooler air for more easily melted PLA, or retains air (and therefore heat) for ASA and ABS.
However, I did notice that when printing in ASA (note that the P2S comes with only a rough-textured build plate; I had to buy the smooth $30 engineering plate separately), the resulting fumes were overwhelming—I had to close the door, open the windows, and turn on an air purifier. There is a carbon filter in the back of the device, but during high-heat prints, the airflow is supposed to circulate inside the unit; instead, it seemed to leak out around the door and other cracks.
Video: Kat Merck
Fumes are emitted from all 3D printers, so this is not really a flaw on the company’s part, just an indication that the redesigned airflow system has room for improvement. Make sure you keep the printer in a room with a door that can close if you’re printing with any kind of impact-modified plastics. Bambu Lab’s helpful Wiki also offers a 3D-printable exhaust kit that can redirect fumes outside.
And speaking of locations, you will also want to ensure the 15 x 16 x 19-inch P2S is on a very firm surface—perhaps even on the ground. At 600 mm per second, the nozzle moves vigorously, which will shake whatever it’s on. I was using a low wooden table, but since I found myself using the printer near-daily, the shaking eventually loosened the table’s leg joints, resulting in multiple X-Y axis error messages on the machine. Research showed this to be a somewhat common issue, almost always resolved by finding a firmer surface.
I was not able to test the AI failure detection, as none of my 30-plus prints failed (aside from a couple of mismeasurements on my end), but I did have occasion to view through the 1080p camera—if you download the free Bambu Handy app, it will store a little time-lapse video of your object being printed, which is fascinating to watch.
In Living Color
The “Combo” in the name refers to the Automatic Material System (AMS) that sits on top of the printer. (You can also buy it separately at $299.) It holds four spools of filament that auto-feed to your project—a game changer if you’re printing something with multiple colors. Without it, a multicolor print would necessitate stopping the print, removing the spool of filament, and installing a new one on the side. For the P2S, the AMS also has the ability to dry the filament—this removes any absorbed ambient moisture that would create steam when heated and mess up your print.
The AMS add-on allows for seamless multicolor prints.
Photograph: Kat Merck
I tested the P2S on the West Coast in late summer, when the humidity was very low, so my filament stayed below 40 percent relative humidity, according to the built-in hygrometer—it didn’t need drying. However, if you live in a humid region, springing for the AMS will be a massive time-saver.
With the P1S, if you needed to swap out a different nozzle, it was something of an ordeal—you basically have to unplug everything and take apart the assembly with screws. On the P2S, the front of the nozzle head is magnetic and pops right off—simply unclip the old nozzle and clip in the new one. Another massive improvement if you find yourself swapping nozzles often.
The P1S’s automatic nozzle cleaning function that “poops” filament blobs out the back of the machine is still in effect on the P2S. I’d been warned, but I was still surprised to see the amount of detritus it left on the floor, especially during multi-color prints. I highly recommend that a “poop chute” or collection basket be one of your first prints. (And there are plenty of fun designs for using the waste filament blobs once they’ve accumulated, from creative games to a “poop Atlas” filament waste world map.)
Do You Really Need One?
Yes, unless you need a dual-nozzle printer or a commercial-grade unit that can also laser cut and engrave—features this printer doesn’t offer. The ability to print and customize useful household and garage objects, art projects, and toys easily and quickly—with minimal fuss—makes the P2S worth every penny. This is doubly so if you have some basic engineering skills, as importing files into Bambu Studio is a cinch.
Bambu Lab-brand filaments start at about $15 a roll with spool. Note that we flagged some app inconsistencies when using non-Bambu filaments with the P1S, but I did not have any non-Bambu filaments on hand to test in the P2S, so I can’t vouch for whether this issue has been fixed.
While the P2S may well be overkill if you only want to print the occasional fidget or figurine, if you regularly find yourself in need of some annoyingly specific organizer, replacement cap, or bracket, this machine could well pay for itself over time in both convenience and material costs.
Kat Merck is a commerce editor for WIRED, where she covers smart bird feeders, indoor gardening systems, kitchen composters, and all things sustainable home tech. As a forestry major at California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, Kat practiced axe throwing on her college logging team and trained as a wildland firefighter ... Read More

EU nears deal to break impasse over French request to remove Usmanov from sanctions

2026-09-21
10:27:49 UTC
19:27:49 KST

EU sanctions on Russia are at risk of expiring as France pushes to remove Uzbek-Russian Usmanov from the blacklist in a deal that could secure the release and pardon of two French nationals in Azerbaijan.
EU ambassadors are nearing a deal to break the deadlock over France’s request to delist Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov from the sanctions list as part of a package that could see two French nationals released from prison in Azerbaijan.
The Irish presidency, which runs the EU Council for six months under the bloc’s rotating presidency system, proposed a compromise to delist Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, another Russian businessman, in exchange for an unprecedented 36-month renewal of the sanctions regime to avoid a similar impasse in future, diplomats told Euronews.
Ambassadors met on Monday morning but failed to strike a deal. They are set to reconvene at 14.00 CET as pressure to reach an agreement mounts.
"The contours of a deal are emerging," a diplomat said.
The French position has taken negotiations to the brink as a deadline to roll over sanctions on more than 2,600 people and entities accused of supporting Russia's war in Ukraine is set to expire at midnight on Tuesday if no agreement is reached.
Unanimity is required to renew the sanctions every six months.
After days of consultations, diplomats are preparing for an outcome in which Usmanov is removed, even if that prospect remains politically hard for many to stomach.
"Multiple ideas are floating around," a second diplomat said.
Uzbekistan, alongside other Turkic states, has lobbied for two years to have Usmanov, who holds Russian and Uzbek citizenship, removed from the sanctions list, appealing to the EU institutions and multiple member states.
His lawyers have also pushed for his delisting.
Euronews understands that Uzbek authorities and France have reached an agreement behind the scenes that would see Usmanov removed from the list in exchange for Azerbaijan releasing two French nationals from prison. The deal has angered several member states, which fear the precedent it could set.
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev will issue a pardon as part of the deal.
The EU sanctioned Usmanov in the early days of the full-scale invasion over his "close ties" to Russian President Vladimir Putin and interests in "key sectors" of the Russian economy that provide "substantial" revenue to the state.
The 73-year-old businessman denies the allegations.
France has not confirmed the swap, and French officials have refused to comment beyond referring to a national security issue without providing details.
Since September 2024, Paris has warned against travelling to Azerbaijan over the "risk of arrest, arbitrary detention and unfair trial".
"In the event of arrest or detention, respect for fundamental rights is not guaranteed," the French foreign ministry says in a notice that remains active.
As negotiations drag on in Brussels, Ukraine has asked allies to keep both Usmanov and Fridman on the blacklist.
"How can anyone seriously discuss sanctions delisting while Russia's war continues?" Vladyslav Vlasiuk, sanctions advisor to the Ukrainian president, said on Monday.
"Delisting without a fundamental change in conduct sends exactly the wrong signal: pressure is temporary, accountability is negotiable, and sanctions can simply be waited out."

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung has added high-resolution drone imagery to its online spatial information platform, allowing the public to view building models and land information remotely, per a press release issued Monday.
The city’s Land Administration Bureau said it uses high-performance drones to produce orthophotos, which are aerial images corrected to provide an accurate, map-like view. The images support cadastral surveying and are available through the city’s 158PLUS Spatial Information Platform.
The bureau said the platform contains about 107,500 3D building models created using initial property registration data collected from 2021 through the second quarter of 2026.
Users can also access property boundaries, transaction-price records, and drone imagery online. Bureau Director-General Tseng Kuo-chun (曾國鈞) said the service reduces the need for in-person visits, printed documents, and transportation.
The city said the 3D spatial data and drone imagery can be used to assess access to sunlight, simulate wind patterns, and analyze building energy consumption. The information can support green-building development, disaster-risk analysis, land development assessments, and cadastral surveying.
The bureau said it plans to expand the platform’s 3D data and drone imagery while increasing data integration among city departments.

Israeli warplanes carried out strikes overnight and into Monday morning on the outskirts of Kfar Tebnit and the Ali al-Taher woodland on the outskirts of Nabatieh al-Fawqa in the Nabatieh district, Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA) said.
Israeli artillery also intermittently shelled Nabatieh al-Fawqa, Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh, and Khallet Mayfadoun, located between Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh and Mayfadoun, during the night, the agency said.

In the Marjayoun district, Israeli artillery struck Wadi al-Salouqi and the outskirts of Touline, while Israeli forces fired illumination flares over Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh, Markaba, Houla, and Hadatha.
Israeli forces conducted heavy machine-gun fire toward Sarbin, Hadatha, the outskirts of Mays al-Jabal, Wadi al-Salouqi and Wadi Zibqin, NNA reported.
Israeli military vehicles were simultaneously reported moving in Hadatha, Beit Yahoun, Rachaf, and Mays al-Jabal.
In the morning, Israeli warplanes struck the valley of Zibqin, while heavy artillery shelling targeted the towns of Mansouri and Majdal Zoun and nearby valleys in southern Lebanon, according to the agency.
Before dawn, Israeli forces also fired illumination flares over several villages in the western and central sectors and blew up homes in Mansouri.
Since March 2, Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed at least 4,386 people, injured 12,407 others and displaced more than 1 million, according to Lebanese authorities.
The attacks have continued despite a US-brokered “framework formula” agreement signed by Lebanon and Israel on June 26, which provides for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of Hezbollah.
Israel continues to occupy areas in southern Lebanon, some for decades and others since the 2023-2024 war, while its forces have advanced more than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) into Lebanese territory during the current offensive.

France and Slovakia's threat to scupper 3,000 EU sanctions to protect two Russian oligarchs gathers steam

2026-09-21

France and Slovakia's threat to scupper 3,000 EU sanctions to protect two Russian oligarchs gathers steam
Editor's note: This is a developing story.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Resistance to a French-Slovak proposal to drop EU sanctions against two Russian oligarchs began to crumble in a meeting of EU ambassadors on the morning of Sept. 21, with an afternoon meeting set to finalize the agreement.
If EU countries fail to vote unanimously to renew the bloc's 3,000 sanctions in relation to Russia's war on Ukraine for another 12 months, all of them will lapse.
The technical vote has been held hostage by France and Slovakia, who want to delist the oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman.
read also
Slovakia has held the position for some time, repeatedly demanding that the oligarchs be delisted, but France's decision to support the move came as a surprise to some.
Paris has joined the demand because it is allegedly being requested by Azerbaijan, which France told EU countries is holding two of its nationals as political prisoners.
"Two countries are insisting on delistings due to national security concerns, and are ready to block the rollovers," one national diplomat told the Kyiv Independent.
The deadlock has led to multiple tense discussions among EU ambassadors, who were cut off from their phones, and a week-long delay in the decision before the Sept. 22 deadline.
To avoid letting all 3,000 sanctions listings lapse, several EU diplomats confirmed, on condition of anonymity, that some countries are beginning to cave in to the French-Slovak demand.
One proposal on the table, first reported by Euronews and later confirmed by the Kyiv Independent, is to roll over the sanctions for 36 months rather than 12, in exchange for the delisting of the two men.
But while a European Council Presidency spokesperson told journalists that ambassadors will reconvene in the afternoon "with the aim of finalizing agreement," that does not mean a new consensus has been achieved.
"We're not there yet... it is, of course, very difficult," the national diplomat said.
A second national diplomat said, "We will be asking for things in return if it goes that way."
Ukraine's sanctions envoy Vladyslav Vlasiuk voiced frustration on social media over the latest EU ambassadors' meeting, asking, "How can anyone seriously discuss sanctions delisting while Russia's war continues?"
"Delisting without a fundamental change in conduct sends exactly the wrong signal: pressure is temporary, accountability is negotiable, and sanctions can simply be waited out," Vlasiuk said.
The two sanctioned individuals, Fridman and Usmanov, are both considered members of Russian leader Vladimir Putin's inner circle.
Fridman is a co-founder of the Russian conglomerate Alfa-Group, whose subsidiary provided insurance for vehicles used by Russian forces in Ukraine, and reportedly serviced the Main Office of Special Programs, which is responsible for guarding Putin.
Usmanov made his fortune in metal and mining operations following the collapse of the Soviet Union. He was referred to as "one of Putin's favorite oligarchs" in the EU's original 2022 sanctions decision.
An EU diplomat told the Kyiv Independent that "in theory," the deadline could be postponed again, but that they were "not sure an extra week would lead to a change in positions."
Doing so would be entering uncharted waters. The diplomat said it is not even clear whether there are technical or legal reasons that would prevent repeatedly prolonging a sanctions rollover for short periods.
EU ambassadors in Brussels are expected to meet again at 2 p.m. local time, "with the aim of finalizing agreement," an EU Council Presidency spokesperson told journalists.

Kremlin reacts to Ukraine’s attack on Russian elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:24:55 UTC

Kremlin reacts to Ukraine’s attack on Russian elections
Ukraine has failed in its attempts to derail Russia’s parliamentary elections through mass attacks during the vote, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
The comments came after Moscow and its suburbs were hit by a huge Ukrainian drone raid overnight Saturday into Sunday. The attack killed two civilians in the capital suburbs and damaged an oil refinery, residential buildings, and civilian infrastructure. Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said the “unprecedented” raid involved more than 1,600 UAVs on all directions.
The three-day vote wrapped up late on Sunday, with preliminary results showing the ruling United Russia party far ahead of its rivals and retaining its commanding majority in the State Duma.
With more than 95% of precinct protocols processed as of Monday, United Russia had 57.82% of the party-list vote, followed by the Communist Party with 13.8%, the LDPR with 8.99%, and New People with 7.96%, while A Just Russia scored slightly above the 5% threshold for party-list seats, according to Central Election Commission data.
Around 113 million people were eligible to vote, including more than 1.8 million registered abroad, with final turnout exceeding 59%.
Speaking to reporters on Monday, Peskov weighed in on Ukrainian attacks both on Moscow and frontline regions during the elections. “It is sabotage. It is also an attempt to disrupt these elections,” he said, stressing that the effort “had no effect.”
Russia’s frontline areas – including new regions which voted for the first time in the parliamentary elections – also came under Ukrainian strikes.
Rodion Miroshnik, the head of the Foreign Ministry’s mission tasked with documenting alleged Ukrainian war crimes, said 74 buildings housing election commissions had been damaged or destroyed in ten Russian regions during the vote.
“This is material confirmation of planned actions by Kiev and its partners aimed at disrupting elections in Russia,” he said. “Kiev, which is not seeking to hold elections at home, is investing in attempts to disrupt elections in Russia, but without result.”
Denis Pushilin, the head of Russia’s Donetsk People’s Republic, said mobile election commissions had played a major role in allowing people in frontline areas to vote despite the risks. He also portrayed the vote as completing the region’s political integration into Russia.
Valentina Matviyenko, the speaker of the upper chamber of the parliament, argued that the election results had demonstrated Russia’s resilience in the face of Western pressure. “The West has once again failed: The voting results confirmed that the idea of inflicting a strategic defeat on us by dividing us from within and splitting our society is hopelessly doomed,” she said.
Matviyenko added the “main and indisputable result” of the election was the “highest degree of self-respect” shown by Russian society.
United Russia chairman Dmitry Medvedev called the vote a “real result” but said it also marked “the start of a great deal of work.” “Having received such a mandate from the electorate, we must now set about implementing our national program,” he said. “I have no doubt whatsoever that our party… will rise to the challenge... We will prevail.”
China, meanwhile, has congratulated Russia on the election, saying that Beijing “firmly supports the Russian people’s independent choice” and that it is ready to continue working with Moscow to implement agreements between Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and take bilateral relations “to new heights.”

Far-right AfD and left-wing Die Linke win German state elections
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:24:09 EEST
19:24:09 KST

Germany’s Alternative for Germany won the state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday, while far-left Die Linke finished first in Berlin, dealing another electoral setback to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union.
The AfD secured about 38.2 per cent in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, ahead of the centre-left Social Democrats on 35.5 per cent, according to preliminary results reported on Monday.
The CDU received 4.9 per cent, leaving the party just below the 5 per cent threshold for representation in the state parliament.
The result gave the AfD its second first-place finish in a state election this month, following its result in Saxony-Anhalt.
Merz described the result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania as a “disaster” for his party. He rejected speculation about his position and said he intended to continue the federal government’s programme of economic, tax and welfare reforms.
“What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness, and patience,” Merz said after the vote.
Berlin produced a different result but another defeat for the CDU. Die Linke received 25.7 per cent of the vote. The CDU followed on 18.8 per cent, with the AfD on 16.3 per cent, the Greens on 14.3 per cent and the SPD on 12.1 per cent.
Berlin’s election authority announced the preliminary second-vote result early on Monday after voting for the city’s House of Representatives took place on Sunday. Almost 2.49 million people were eligible to vote.
Die Linke’s first-place finish does not by itself give the party control of Berlin’s government. It will need support from other parties to form a governing majority.
The two elections add pressure on Merz 16 months after he became chancellor. His CDU-led federal government has pursued changes to pensions, taxation, healthcare and other areas while Germany continues to face weak economic growth and concerns over living costs.
The AfD has gained support on issues including migration, energy policy and opposition to Germany’s military and financial support for Ukraine. Other main parties continue to rule out coalition agreements with the AfD, limiting its route to government even where it finishes first.
Germany has 16 federal states with powers in areas including education and policing. State elections do not determine the federal government, though their results affect the political position of national parties and their representation in the Bundesrat.

New air traffic control failure delays flights at British airports

- The issue on Sept 21 is separate from a software defect two weeks earlier that caused 2,000 flight cancellations and costly disruptions.
- Airlines like easyJet and British Airways warned customers of delays, with easyJet criticising NATS’ system resilience and calling for stronger preventive measures.
AI generated
LONDON – Flights at several British airports were delayed on Sept 21 owing to an air traffic control failure, Britain’s National Air Traffic Services (NATS) said, less than two weeks after a separate issue halted flights across the country.
Manchester, Glasgow and Belfast airports were experiencing delays, which the air traffic control provider said was related to an issue at its Prestwick centre in Scotland.
London’s Gatwick and City Airports said there would be some disruption.
Airline easyJet said it had cancelled some flights, while British Airways warned its customers that they were likely to experience disruption on Sept 21.
In response to queries from The Straits Times, a Singapore Airlines spokesperson said on Sept 21 that none of its flights are affected.
New issue behind delays
NATS said the delays on Sept 21 were “unrelated to the issue two weeks ago”, when around 2,000 flights were cancelled owing to a software defect.
“Airports south of Manchester are broadly unaffected. However, flights heading north and flights departing Scottish airports are currently subject to some delay,” the air traffic control provider said in a statement.
A previous outage in August 2023 cost airlines £100 million (S$170.7 million) and caused travel chaos. Ryanair, Europe’s biggest airline, has been calling for NATS chief executive officer Martin Rolfe to step down.
According to easyjet, the disruption on Sept 21, which did not appear to be as severe as the failure two weeks earlier that delayed hundreds of thousands of people, underlined the weakness in the air traffic operator’s systems.
“This, once again, calls into question the resilience of NATS’ systems and demonstrates the need for firm actions to prevent these repeated failures,” easyJet said. REUTERS

Russia Announces Election Results Cementing Putin's Power; EU Slams 'Veneer Of Democracy'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:19:13 UTC
19:19:13 KST

Officials in Moscow have announced a new record victory for President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party in what the European Union dismissed as “sham elections” on September 21.
The Central Election Commission said United Russia gained nearly 58 percent of the vote, winning 355 seats in the 450-seat State Duma in the first election to the body since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In a highly managed process on September 18-20, voters could choose from several parties that are all approved by the Kremlin and fully support Putin. Results showed dozens of Ukraine-war military veterans will now be lawmakers.
The only party opposing the war on Ukraine, Yabloko, was excluded from the poll. Its leader, Nikolai Rybakov, scrawled “for peace” on his ballot with a bright marker pen and posed with it for photographers at a polling station in St. Petersburg.
'Setback For Russian Democracy'
Most of Russia’s political opposition is now in prison or in exile. Dmitry Gudkov, in the latter group, told Current Time “they didn’t let anyone [from the opposition] run, they kicked out election observers, there was clearly widespread ballot stuffing.”
Gudkov is a member of the Russian Democratic Forces, an exile opposition group at the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE). He said he believed it would soon declare the Duma elections illegitimate.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has already done so, noting among other things that voting also took place in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.
“The so-called Duma elections marked another major setback for Russian democracy,” she wrote in a social media post on September 21. “The veneer of democracy is all that remains in Russia. I have proposed measures against those facilitating these sham elections in occupied Ukrainian territories.”
Turnout was given at 59.32 percent, an uptick on previous years that was trumpeted by election commission chief Ella Pamfilova.
Last time round, in 2021, it was 51.7 percent, while in 2011 -- when allegations of electoral fraud led to huge opposition protests in Moscow being brutally suppressed by security forces -- the figure was 60.2 percent.
The reliability of official figures has been widely questioned, however, with examples such as Chechnya --where longstanding regional boss Ramzan Kadyrov was recorded as receiving 99.85 percent of the vote -- seen as particularly glaring.
“In Chechnya, it’s not even mass falsification. Nobody even counts any votes,” Maksim Glikin, chief editor of exile publication Mozhem Obyasnit, told Current Time. “They just write down the required numbers and put them out.”
What Now?
In any case, the elections have once again delivered a pliant Duma that will rubber stamp legislation submitted to it by the Kremlin -- as was generally expected. Attention now returns to the brutal war of attrition in Ukraine.
In the weeks preceding the poll, there was widespread speculation that it would be followed by a new wave of mobilization to boost army ranks that are reported to suffer some 30,000 casualties every month.
“Ukrainian intelligence have warned that the Kremlin plans to use the parliamentary elections as a stage-managed show of public support to launch a new wave of mobilization,” Dominika Hajdu, director for policy and programming at GLOBSEC, a think tank, told RFE/RL.
“The mobilization would help Russia sustain its offensive pressure, given its willingness to absorb high casualties, but its battlefield impact will likely be limited, as recent fighting has been shaped mainly by drones and air-strike capabilities rather than manpower alone,” she added.
Fighting continued with Russian strikes on a university, a shopping center, and other facilities injuring six people in Zaporizhzhya, according to Ukrainian emergency services on September 21.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Russia was open to reopening trilateral peace talks but that “we are continuing the special military operation” -- a preferred term used by officials to describe the invasion.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said late on September 20 that he’d spoken with US President Donald Trump and that the two would meet at the UN General Assembly this week.
In a social media post, Zelenskyy said the meeting "could change a lot" and that he and Trump "got through a lot" during their discussion.

Merve Berker
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that his administration's planned 250-foot (76-meter) triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery will also serve as a military complex housing drones, snipers and ammunition.
Trump said on his Truth Social platform that he had agreed to convert the planned arch "at the strong request" of the US military and "for National Security purposes."
The planned "Military Complex/Triumphal Arch" will "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas," he said.
He added that the facility would store "large quantities of sniper ammunition."
"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," he stated.
The administration had previously presented the arch as a tourist attraction commemorating the US' 250th anniversary, with plans including an observation deck, according to Washington Post.
Construction could begin as early as November, while a federal judge is considering a legal challenge seeking to halt the project.
Veterans, advocacy groups and historic preservationists have opposed the project, arguing that the structure would overshadow the nearby Arlington National Cemetery and is too large for the site.
Republican Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat whose district includes the cemetery and Reagan National Airport, criticized the proposal to use the site for drones.
"Putting a drone launching site directly in the landing path for DCA is a stupid, dangerous, and unworkable idea," the Post quoted Beyer as saying.
The White House did not respond to the newspaper's questions about Trump's announcement, while the Interior Department also did not comment.
A Pentagon spokesperson said there was nothing to add beyond Trump's statement.
The administration has said it does not need congressional authorization for the arch, citing authorization granted by lawmakers about a century ago for a similar project near the site.
Trump administration officials have said they will obtain "all necessary approvals" before construction begins.

UK's Burnham heads to US with pragmatism in mind for Trump meeting
LONDON, Sept 21 - Prime Minister Andy Burnham heads to New York on Monday for the United Nations General Assembly, his first foray into global diplomacy and a test of his vow to press British interests even if they are at odds with US President Donald Trump.
Burnham, a former mayor of Greater Manchester in northwestern England with limited experience of foreign affairs, is expected to meet Trump for the first time on Tuesday, and has set out a different approach to his predecessor, Keir Starmer, who went out of his way to win over the US leader.
Instead, Burnham has said he will disagree with Trump if it is in his nation's interest, while describing himself in his first interview after becoming Britain's seventh prime minister in a decade in July as someone "who tries to work with people".
At a meeting of world leaders due to focus on Ukraine, the Middle East, climate action and AI, Burnham will hope to double down on his call in Kyiv last month for more air defence support to protect the nation from Russia's bombardment in its more than four-year war, including the delivery of US Patriot systems.
TWO LEADERS SHOULD GET ON, SAYS FORMER AMBASSADOR
Kim Darroch, a former UK ambassador to Washington, said he believed Trump would want the meeting with Burnham to go well after falling out with other leaders, such as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
"I think he'll (Trump) want this meeting to go well, but even so, there will be unpredictability attached to it," Darroch told Sky News on Sunday.
"But Burnham, I think, is personable. He has charisma. He's sort of instantly likeable. I suspect they'll sort of hit it off because Trump cares much more about personal chemistry than about ideological divides."
Burnham has had at least two calls with Trump since becoming prime minister on July 20, describing the exchanges as warm and cordial, with his team pointing out that the US leader did not push back against Britain's move to block imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
In a shift from Starmer's more cautious approach, Burnham said at the time the move was a way to assert British values: "It is more important than ever that Britain stands for something."
Twelve nations signed the statement saying they would introduce, or were considering introducing, a ban on goods from settlements, the strongest collective action taken by Western countries against Israel's moves into the West Bank. Israel rejects the assertion that the settlements are illegal.
The coordinated action could signal a meeting of minds between Burnham and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who last week attended a match of their favourite English football team, Everton. Sitting side by side, the two celebrated and hugged when Everton scored the winner against Wolves.
Carney has argued for closer cooperation among so-called "middle powers", arguing that countries such as Canada should work together to protect their interests in a world increasingly shaped by great-power rivalry and US protectionism.
SPECIAL RELATIONSHIP
But Burnham will not want to antagonise Trump, his team says, and will be happy to find areas to maintain the so-called "special relationship" with the United States by making "pragmatic decisions in the best interests of the country".
With Washington pushing NATO countries to do more to support the alliance, Burnham has said he wants to increase defence spending and investment to create home-grown jobs, but has so far said little about when and how he will do so.
His finance minister, John Healey, will present a budget on October 28, when he will want to set out how to fill a funding hole in Britain's Defence Investment Plan rather than setting out longer-term goals for defence spending.
But several leaders in the defence industry have voiced concerns about the government's commitment after Burnham said earlier this month his ministers would "do everything to support national security, but it can't come at the expense of social security". REUTERS

Shares of U.S.-listed companies exposed to Greenland surged on Monday after the U.S. and Denmark reached a deal on security arrangements on the Arctic territory.
Shares of Greenland Energy soared more than 154% during premarket trading, with Greenland Mines seen up over 70% and Critical Metals Corp nearly 27% higher.
The agreement, which is expected to be signed during the United Nations General Assembly this week, will see the U.S., Denmark and Greenland enter into a pact to develop a significant military presence on the territory, while blocking Washington's adversaries from building their own bases there.
It follows several months of U.S. President Donald Trump's threats to annex the self-governing Danish territory, with the president insisting Greenland is critical to U.S. national security.
Announcing the deal, Trump said via Truth Social on Friday that the U.S. would "FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America."
Trump said the agreement would come at no cost to the U.S., adding that Washington would "immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many."
Key details of the agreement have not yet been made public.
Greenlandic and Danish officials sought to reassure citizens over the weekend that the deal would respect the island's right to self-determination and the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom.
"It is joyous that we are about to make an agreement that will ensure and strengthen the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western Alliance," Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a statement.
"The agreement recognizes Greenland's interests and our place in the international cooperation. It is to the benefit of us all," he added.
Greenland Energy is an oil and gas exploration firm focused on trying to unlock the hydrocarbon potential of the Jameson Land Basin on the island's east coast.
The Texas-based company, which has links to Trump, recently delayed plans to drill for oil in Greenland after the island's government issued a "strong warning" to its joint venture partner for bringing equipment ashore without permission.
Greenland Mines, meanwhile, is a natural resources company working on the Skaergaard Project, which ranks among the world's largest undeveloped palladium, gold and platinum deposits.
Critical Metals Corp, for its part, is a mining company focused on critical metals and minerals and is developing the Tanbreez rare earths mine in southern Greenland.

An artisanal miner on torture and ill treatment by Rwanda Backed M23 fighters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:16:13 UTC
19:16:13 KST

In eastern DRC, Rwanda-backed March 23 Movement (M23) fighters have committed horrific human rights abuses against artisanal miners while facilitating the trafficking of gold and coltan to neighbouring Rwanda with the help of Rwandan authorities. The miners recount horrific encounters with the fighters which include summary killings; torture and ill-treatment; arbitrary detention; forced labour and forced recruitment. In this interview one of the miners tells Amnesty International of his ordeal in a mine shaft in the hands of the M23 fighters. From daily beatings to being left inside the shafts for hours and being denied his rightful wages. This is his story which is replicated across the mines.
Since the last time I spoke with you, the situation has gotten worse. I have a lack of funds that is linked to many things [including] because I was beaten in the mine shaft. Because of the bad conditions [at the mine] I can’t work every day. I now work four times a week. I usually work around five hours a day and I am only paid 5,000 Congolese francs (US$2.17). There are around 120 diggers in each mine shaft. The boss gives the manager money, and he brings food (to diggers). We get one beignet [a piece of fried dough] and water for the day.
We’ve seen a lot of things that we can’t forget. The fact we must stay in the mine shaft against our will, the fact our bosses beat us, they beat people and they end up in the hospital.
Miner, DRC
There are Rwandans in the area who sometimes use force against us. When they come, they wear civilian clothes, but when there is an atmosphere of war, they wear military-style uniforms. I’ve seen them change [from civilian clothes to military uniforms] several times. They are my bosses. I work for them.
We’ve seen a lot of things that we can’t forget. The fact we must stay in the mine shaft against our will, the fact our bosses beat us, they beat people and they end up in the hospital.
I was beaten this year. I was in the mine shaft and had been at work for three hours. The only thing I heard were the blows of the stick hitting me. Then I lost consciousness. It was the manager who beat me. He was Congolese, a colleague, but comes from Rwanda. There was no dispute that led to the beating. You just meet someone and he starts beating you. The managers are our intermediaries between us and our bosses. We shouldn’t be beaten by our colleagues. That’s why we believe there was an order that was behind it.
When I woke up in the hospital, I noticed all the bandages all over my body. On my head, arms, feet, joints and one on my stomach. I spent three days in the hospital.
There are Rwandans in the area who sometimes use force against us. When they come, they wear civilian clothes, but when there is an atmosphere of war, they wear military-style uniforms. I’ve seen them change [from civilian clothes to military uniforms] several times. They are my bosses. I work for them.
Miner, DRC
Others suffered the same thing I did. It’s not every day, but it happens maybe four times a week. They are taken to the hospital. There are sometimes other people who stand up for them, and they are saved. Others are left to die. I’ve seen people who died and were buried in the mine shaft.
I want everyone to know that the expensive telephones they are buying are made from expensive minerals, and the telephones they use come to them after a lot of blood has been spilled. I want advocacy done so that the minerals are extracted in a legal way and so the diggers are also treated legally. That’s why we need someone to carry our voices far so that when we are digging, there is no blood spilled in the mine shaft.
Thank you [Amnesty] for thinking of us. Continue your work so that you know what we are facing. Continue your work so we can live a peaceful life like everyone else. Let the world know that we need advocacy so we can put in place the laws of the country here.
To have people monitoring the situation, that would be a good thing. When the observers are doing their work, [M23] wouldn’t be able to commit abuses. They commit a lot of abuses. When they do bad acts, the observers could write reports about them.
If you carry our voices to those far away, that will be good for us. That would be a big help.
