UAL turns Atterbury Flat guest apartment into riotous student design archive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:15:44 UTC
19:15:44 KST

UAL turns Atterbury Flat guest apartment into riotous student design archive
The University of the Arts London has transformed a drab guest quarters at one of its colleges into a colourful showcase that lets visitors eat, sleep and bathe in student and graduate design.
The two-bedroom Atterbury Flat – located on the Chelsea College of Arts campus, a Grade II listed former Royal Army Medical College building – has been used to host visiting professors and dignitaries since the university moved into the premises in 2005.
But University of the Arts (UAL) lecturer Zoë Tynan-Campbell saw an opportunity to turn it into something more – a living and "live-in" archive of student work that had so far gone largely uncollected by the university.
UAL is the second top-ranked university for art and design in the world, with six colleges including Central Saint Martins under its banner, allowing her to draw from a deep well of talent.
Working with alumni Abigail Rigby and Bhairavi Yogasivam as co-curators, Tynan-Campbell engaged more than 400 students and graduates from 58 courses across all colleges in the endeavour, ultimately purchasing 117 works for the first round of acquisitions.
These range from fantastical pieces that attracted attention at graduate shows – like a colour-changing chair and a conceptual coffee table made of 160 kilograms of stacked paper – to widely available products from companies established by UAL veterans.
The latter category includes refillable soap by Blackmarket, foldable clothes hangers by Easy Hang and cookware hand-moulded from Indian river clay by Tiipoi.
Many of the pieces were made specifically for the flat, including bathroom tiles and a matching sink in a gradient of greens by ceramicist and County Hall Pottery director Emma Louise Payne, as well as a giant pencil by multidisciplinary designer Neha Ratanchand for signing the guestbook.
No object is too small to be unworthy of creative attention – a pair of scissors, a pack of tarot cards, several tea towels and a recycling bag made of recycled bags are among the alumni contributions – but some ordinary furniture from the old flat remains, awaiting replacement as the archive expands.
"Part of the intention is asking questions around what we collect and what we value," said Tynan-Campbell. "Because we have a fine art collection as an institution... but most of it is paintings and photographs and 2D work, basically."
"So this is us saying, okay, well, we have six universities, we have so many different disciplines, why is only fine art worth collecting?" she continued. "Why are we not collecting the narratives, the stories, the objects that all these other courses are producing?"
"And of course, there's loads of practical reasons why not. One is space, which is why this is perfect, because we didn't have to build a space. This was here, and it was a blank canvas."
The Atterbury Flat was unveiled last week at the London Design Festival and will continue serving as a temporary home for visiting professors and other guests now that the event is over.
Dezeen had the pleasure of a night's stay during the festival and can report that the mismatched wooden door handles by product design student Nora Hinsch function, the precisely honed mugs by architect-turned-ceramicist John Robertson are perfect to cradle, and the softly psychedelic 3D-printed botanical bedside lamps by Yichun Lu are soothing to watch alone in the dark.
Tynan-Campbell sees the takeover of the Atterbury Flat as a new model for commissioning and archiving student work. As far as she is aware, it is the first archive of this type, doubling as a residence at a university.
The project saw £61,686 paid directly to students and grads for their work – 91.98 per cent of the total budget.
In addition to selecting the pieces and shepherding new commissions to completion, Tynan-Campbell and her co-curators took charge of the interior and spatial design, using a colour palette adapted from a work by Molly Cook as a jumping-off point.
Tynan-Campbell had discovered Cook in the first room at the first degree show she scouted, where the multidisciplinary designer presented a project that involved the careful study of a location through photography, drawing and listening to arrive at its idiosyncratic colour palette.
The graphic print she made using the same methodology for the Atterbury Flat hangs in the kitchen and was provided as a reference to the other participants.
"We set out [on this project] saying, this is an act of radical trust in what your students can do," said Tynan-Campbell. "Give them the opportunity, not an external agency or firm. I feel like literally every one of them really rose to the occasion."
The Atterbury Flat was on show from 12 to 20 September as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party secured a majority in the State Duma, Russia’s lower house, following the country’s first parliamentary elections since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022.
In a widely expected result, the ruling party won around 58% of the vote for the 225 deputies elected via party lists, according to preliminary data from Russia’s Central Election Committee. Another 225 will be elected in single-mandate seats, where United Russia candidates are also dominating. Voting took place over the course of three days, with polls closing Sunday evening.

“I have proposed measures against those facilitating these sham elections in occupied Ukrainian territories,” she added. Trump to be sued by MS NOW, CNN, Politico to reverse White House ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:14:06 UTC
19:14:06 KST

MS NOW, CNN and Politico are set to sue President Donald Trump on Monday morning and to ask a federal judge to reverse his total ban on those three media outlets from the White House.
Journalists from the outlets were prevented from entering the White House on Saturday, a day after Trump announced he would bar them from working there.
"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the lawsuit says, arguing that the ban has already "severely impeded the ability of" the three outlets to cover Trump and his administration.
"Presidents from the earliest days of the Republic have disagreed with and complained about the tenor and content of press coverage of their administrations," the civil complaint, set to be filed in U.S. District Court in Washington, notes.
But "the Constitution protects the liberty and property interests that news organizations and White House reporters have in their press credentials and the access those credentials afford them to cover the White House for the benefit of the public," the suit says. "No official can deprive Plaintiffs of those interests on a whim — with no notice, no process, and no warning — as the President did here."
Trump, in announcing the ban in a Truth Social post Friday, accused the outlets of writing fiction and lies about him, and warned, "Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow." The president cited what he called "cumulative stories" by the three news organizations, adding, "You get sick of it."
The suit alleges the ban violates the Due Process Clause of the U.S. Constitution by failing to give the outlets advance notice and an opportunity to challenge it, without establishing clear standards for Trump's decision.
The complaint also says the ban violates the Constitution's First Amendment by retaliating "against protected newsgathering and speech."
And it says the ban violates the First Amendment for a separate reason: it bars the three media outlets "from a nonpublic forum for unlawful reasons." Those reasons include so-called viewpoint discrimination, or targeting the outlets for their perceived "motivating ideology or the opinion or perspective."
In a joint statement on Monday, the three outlets said, "This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes."
Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting," the statement said. "Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."
The White House and the Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC about the lawsuit.
The three outlets will file a joint motion asking a judge to issue a temporary restraining order barring Trump and other defendants from taking further action to enforce the ban and requiring them to immediately restore so-called hard pass press credentials to the plaintiffs, which give their reporters access to the White House.
In addition to Trump, the defendants are his assistant for communications, Steven Cheung, White House Chief of Staff Susan Wiles, and Sean Curran, director of the U.S. Secret Service.
The named plaintiffs are the three outlets and three White House reporters: Akayla Gardner of MS NOW; Betsy Klein of CNN; and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett. All three journalists were denied entry to the White House on Saturday and had their hard passes taken away by a Secret Service officer there, the suit says.
On Sunday night, the White House removed CNN from its scheduled rotation as the pool network for the White House travel pool. The pool is set to travel Monday with Trump for his visit to New York for the United Nations General Assembly.
The lawsuit cites the White House's removal of CNN from Monday's pool schedule as an example of the ban "causing irreparable harm to" the outlets.
The suit is being filed in the same court where The Associated Press has a pending lawsuit against the White House for a ban on that wire service's journalists working in certain restricted spaces in the White House, including the Oval Office and on Air Force One. The White House's partial ban on the AP came in February 2025 after the wire service refused to reflect Trump's renaming of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America in how it routinely refers to that international body of water.
Trump told reporters on Friday that the latest ban is worth implementing, even if it is overturned by a judge.
"I think it's good to point it out, whether it survives or doesn't," he said.
The Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, in a statement after Trump's announcement, suggested he would lose a legal challenge to the ban because of the U.S. Constitution's First Amendment protections for the media.
"The First Amendment prohibits the president from punishing journalists because he doesn't like their coverage, just as it prohibits him from punishing universities because he doesn't like the courses they offer, or from punishing law firms because he doesn't like the clients they represent," said Jameel Jaffer, executive director of the institute.
"With so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you'd think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now," Jaffer said.
MS NOW, in a statement Saturday, had said, "The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars."
"MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy," the network said. MS NOW also vowed to "continue to report on the President, the administration, and the issues that impact the American people."
CNN and Politico issued similar statements, which referred to their constitutional right to report news without government interference.
White House Correspondents' Association President Jacqui Heinrich, in a statement Saturday, said, "The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably."
"That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting," Heinrich, a Fox News correspondent, said.
In the AP's lawsuit, Judge Trevor McFadden ruled in April 2025 that Trump's partial ban of the agency's journalists violated the First Amendment and ordered that the AP be given the same access as other members of the presidential press pool to the Oval Office, other restricted areas of the White House and Air Force One.
"The Court simply holds that under the First Amendment, if the Government opens its doors to some journalists — be it to the Oval Office, the East Room, or elsewhere — it cannot then shut those doors to other journalists because of their viewpoints," wrote McFadden, who was appointed to the federal bench by Trump.
"The Constitution requires no less," the judge said.
Rather than allowing The Associated Press access to places the White House press pool goes to cover the president, the White House said it would abolish the so-called wire pool, which included the AP, Bloomberg and Reuters. The wire pool for decades had traveled with presidents to bring news coverage to news consumers around the world. It has not been reinstated.
A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, in a 2-1 vote in June 2025, blocked McFadden's ruling from taking effect while Trump appealed it.
The panel heard oral arguments in the appeal in November, but has not issued a decision.
Disclosure: CNBC and MS NOW are divisions of Versant Media.

MOSCOW - The pro-Putin ruling United Russia party retained its decisive majority in the national Parliament, near-complete election results showed on Sept 21, while the anti-war Yabloko party appeared to have won a tiny foothold in one regional Parliament.
President Vladimir Putin had cast the three-day election to the State Duma - the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022 - as a test of support for the war.
Elections for some regional parliaments and governors were held at the same time.
In a tightly controlled political system, which critics say does not tolerate genuine dissent, under which many of Yabloko’s candidates were barred, few surprises were expected.
But political analysts said it was important to the authorities that the process itself was seen to be relatively smooth.
Officials from Putin down had cast the vote as a way of showing enemies that Russia was united.
With over 95 per cent of the vote counted, Ella Pamfilova, chair of the Central Electoral Commission, said United Russia had won a resounding victory with 57.83 per cent, up from the 49.8 per cent that it won in the last parliamentary election, in 2021.
United Russia was set to control 355 seats or nearly 80 per cent of the 450-seat Duma, a total that includes results in individual constituencies.
That would maintain its constitutional majority - enabling it to pass laws and initiate amendments to the Constitution without the support of other parties.
Pamfilova said three other parties had made it into Parliament - the Communists with 13.81 per cent, the ultra-nationalist LDPR with 8.98 per cent, and the New People party with 7.96 per cent.
Just Russia was just under the 5 per cent threshold needed to enter Parliament, but had “a big chance” of making it, she said.
All of those parties have voted in the same way as United Russia on major issues in recent years.
In Chechnya, Ramzan Kadyrov, a close Putin ally, was re-elected to a fifth term as leader with an official tally of near 100 per cent.
Pamfilova said turnout among Russia’s 111 million voters - which she put at 59.3 per cent - was a record for such an election, which continued despite a heavy Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow on Sept 20, the last day of voting.
She also called the vote “clean” in the face of allegations from opposition activists in exile of widespread rigging.
Yabloko, the only registered anti-war party in Russia, failed to win any seats at a national level.
But in Novgorod, about 480km north-west of Moscow, with nearly 97 per cent of votes counted, it appeared to have cleared the 5 per cent barrier by one percentage point to enter the regional Parliament.
“More than 12,000 Novogorod residents supported Yabloko,” the party, which supports a ceasefire in Ukraine, said in a statement.
“Peace, freedom and a life free from fear are values that have struck a chord in people’s hearts and souls.” REUTERS

Russia’s Rassvet Already Gets at Least Two Daily Hour-Plus Windows Over Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:12:35 UTC
19:12:35 KST

- Category
- World
Russia’s Rassvet Already Gets at Least Two Daily Hour-Plus Windows Over Ukraine
Russia connected residents of a settlement in the Nenets Autonomous Okrug to a remote electronic voting system through its Rassvet satellite network on September 20, its first trial with real users rather than company engineers, Militarnyi reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Ukrainian defense outlet cited Ella Pamfilova, head of Russia's Central Election Commission, who announced the test's success.
Militarnyi described how low-orbit satellites operated by the developer, Bureau 1440, relayed data to a ground terminal in the settlement. The signal then passed to a user's tablet over Wi-Fi, opening a connection to the voting platform, the outlet noted.
Earlier company trials had verified the link with engineers alone, Militarnyi explained. Pamfilova declared the experiment a success, the outlet added.
Russia's Central Election Commission now plans to assess extending the technology to other regions with limited access to telecommunications, according to Militarnyi. The country has 37 regions containing hard-to-reach territories where the system could apply, the report stated.
Militarnyi wrote that Bureau 1440 is deploying Rassvet as a low-orbit satellite communications network. The company placed its first 16 satellites of the target group in orbit in March 2026 and added a further 16 in July, according to the outlet.
According to the company's own account, the system relies on 5G NTN technology to connect its satellites to ground terminals. Bureau 1440 is separately developing inter-satellite laser communication and has claimed data transfers between spacecraft over distances of up to 1,000 kilometers at speeds of up to 10 Gbit/s.
Militarnyi emphasized that those figures come from the company itself.
The outlet noted that Russia accelerated the rollout after successfully blocking Starlink along the front line. Russian units had earlier relied on terminals from the American Starlink service.
In January 2026, Ukraine reported that Shahed drones were operating via Starlink, prompting Kyiv's defense ministry to appeal to SpaceX, the outlet added. A domestic network would end Moscow's reliance on an external provider that could be pressured to cut service, according to Militarnyi.
Militarnyi indicated that Rassvet could eventually support more than communications, potentially assisting drone control, operational coordination, and real-time data transfer. In principle, the outlet added, terminals could be fitted to drones, aircraft, and even missiles.
Even so, the satellites were already providing at least two daily "communication windows" over Ukraine as of July 2026, each lasting more than an hour, Militarnyi reported.
The voting trial comes against a rollout that has repeatedly fallen short of its targets. The first Rassvet-3 group launched on March 23, and a second followed on July 19, yet six months on, none had reached the planned operational altitude of 800 kilometers.
Most of the initial batch settled near 507 kilometers, one satellite reentered the atmosphere on June 6, and two from the second group have drifted low enough to risk the same fate.

Ukrainian Drones Reportedly Strike Bashneft Oil Refinery 1,600 km Inside Russia
Ukrainian strike drones reportedly targeted the Bashneft oil refinery complex in Ufa, Russia, on September 21, reaching a major Russian oil refining hub located roughly 1,600 kilometers from Ukraine’s state border.
On September 21, Ukrainian strike drones reportedly targeted the Bashneft oil refinery in Ufa, Russia, in response to Moscow’s attacks on Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Exilenova+ reported that Ukrainian Defense Forces strike drones had reached Ufa, while Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of Occupation, said the Bashneft refinery had been hit.
“Breaking news. Ufa. The Bashneft oil refinery has been hit,” Andriushchenko said.
The extent of the damage and other details surrounding the reported strike remain unclear.
Ufa is one of Russia’s major oil refining hubs, hosting three large facilities: Bashneft-UNPZ, Bashneft-Novoil, and Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim. All three belong to the Bashneft group and together make up a major refining complex.
According to RBC-Ukraine, the facilities have a combined annual processing capacity of more than 23 million metric tons of crude oil and produce gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel, lubricants, and other petroleum products.
The refineries are located roughly 1,600 kilometers from Ukraine’s state border.
The reported attack follows other recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian military and industrial facilities. The strike caused extensive damage to a warehouse reportedly used for military purposes. According to the assessment, the building suffered a roof collapse across an area measuring approximately 60 by 40 meters.

France Moves to Shield Critical Defense Sites From Russian Drone and Cyberattacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:12:02 UTC
19:12:02 KST

- Category
- World
France Moves to Shield Critical Defense Sites From Russian Drone and Cyberattacks
France is preparing nationwide defenses against an intensifying campaign of Russian hybrid attacks, with its intelligence services bracing for the possibility of a large-scale assault.
France Télévisions reported on September 19 that internal planning now points to autumn 2027 as an accelerated scenario, brought forward from an earlier horizon of 2030.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The threat has sharpened in recent months, according to France Télévisions, taking the form of cyberattacks against the French military and government ministries. Fabricated videos generated by artificial intelligence have also targeted candidates ahead of the presidential race, part of a wider pattern of operations striking several European countries.
In an unprecedented step, the government convened all of France's prefects in an emergency session, France Télévisions reported. Beginning next week, each department is to stand up a security and defense staff drawing together local police and military commanders, education officials, business leaders, and emergency responders.
President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged on September 18 that the security climate had shifted and that France, like its European partners, was readying itself. "I asked the government to prepare a plan to protect our critical infrastructure," Macron stated. The plan extends to the most sensitive sites of France's defense industrial and technological base, guarding against both drone and cyberattacks.
According to a confidential note reviewed by France Télévisions, the infrastructure judged at risk includes power plants and electrical grids, rail networks, telecommunications, and drinking-water distribution. Macron summoned the country's presidential candidates to the Élysée Palace's new high-security crisis room on September 18 to alert them to the danger.
France's principal airfields are already prepared against drone incursions, but the exposure runs wider, according to retired Air Force General Patrick Dutartre. "One can imagine that all sensitive sites associated with defense could be targeted," Dutartre noted.
The Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, rejected the idea that Moscow menaces Europe. "Some European leaders openly declare that they are preparing for war against Russia," Putin claimed, arguing they were merely trying to rescue "plummeting popularity ratings."
France Télévisions reported that the country's intelligence services are readying for a possible wave of massive Russian attacks, with the projected timeline steadily contracting. While planners once looked toward 2030, the reporting indicated that autumn 2027 is now the reference point.
The interference shadowing the presidential race is not new. Paris prosecutors opened an investigation in August 2026 into a campaign that circulated fabricated videos aimed at former Prime Ministers Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal. 
The falsified clips carried the branding of established French news outlets and were tied to the Russia-linked networks Storm-1516 and Matriochka. The physical threat has been just as concrete: in early August, an explosive-laden drone was discovered beside a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Germany's Leipzig airport, a plot US intelligence has linked to Russian services.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,660 Troops, 75 Artillery Systems, and 1,728 UAVs in One Day
Russian forces lost an estimated 1,660 personnel over the past day, along with 75 artillery systems and 1,728 operational-tactical UAVs, according to figures released by Ukraine’s General Staff on September 21.
The latest figures bring Russia’s total estimated personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, to approximately 1,519,650.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In addition to personnel and drone losses, the General Staff recorded the loss of five Russian tanks and four armored combat vehicles over the previous 24 hours. Russian forces also lost three multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), three air defense systems, 516 vehicles and fuel tankers, 17 unmanned ground vehicles, and 13 pieces of special equipment.
According to the General Staff, Russia’s cumulative equipment losses have reached 12,361 tanks, 25,365 armored combat vehicles, 50,142 artillery systems, 2,149 MLRS, 1,662 air defense systems, and 527,693 operational-tactical UAVs.
Recorded losses also include 442 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 5,111 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines. The General Staff estimates that Russia has also lost 151,861 vehicles and fuel tankers, 2,712 unmanned ground vehicles, and 4,729 pieces of special equipment since February 2022.
The strike came amid continued intense fighting across Ukraine, with 238 combat engagements recorded over the past day.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has continued targeting Russian military and energy infrastructure. Overnight on September 20, Ukrainian strike drones and cruise missiles targeted the Moscow Oil Refinery in Kapotnya, triggering a large fire at the facility.

&quot;United Russia&quot; wins a record number of seats in Russia&apos;s State Duma - Russian media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
13:11:45 EEST
19:11:45 KST

"United Russia" wins a record number of seats in Russia's State Duma - Russian media
Kyiv • UNN
After 95% of the protocols have been counted, the party has received 57.83% of the votes and is leading in 209 constituencies. Russia's Central Election Commission is expected to announce the final results after September 25.
The "United Russia" party is securing a "constitutional majority" in the Russian parliament and the largest faction in the State Duma of the Russian Federation in its history — about 355 of 450 seats. Russian media are reporting these preliminary election results announced by Russia’s Central Election Commission, UNN writes.
Details
After 95% of the protocols had been counted, "United Russia" had won 57.83% of the vote on party lists. In single-member constituencies, the party’s candidates are leading in 209 of 225 constituencies.
As the Russian service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty notes, the party’s final result may amount to between 348 and 356 seats. This would be the largest faction of "United Russia" in the party’s history.
Russian media also report that "United Russia" announced that it had elected 86 participants in the war against Ukraine to the State Duma of the Russian Federation, but later "clarified" that there were 49. They could have formed the second-largest faction in the new legislature, the Russian service of the BBC notes.
The Central Election Commission of the Russian Federation plans to announce the final results no earlier than September 25 — additional time has been provided to consider possible complaints.
The "elections" took place amid criticism over the absence of genuine political competition. The federal list of "Yabloko" — the only registered party that openly opposed the war — was removed from the elections by Russia’s Supreme Court.
Russia also did not invite OSCE observers. OSCE PA President Pere Joan Pons called the absence of independent international observation a violation of Russia’s commitments and part of an "alarming trend" of rejecting transparency and democratic accountability.
During the voting, "Yabloko" and the Communist Party of the Russian Federation reported that observers had been denied access to polling stations and removed from them. There were also reports of sealed ballot boxes being opened, problems with issuing paper ballots, and the inability to verify certain turnout data.
By the evening of September 20, the "Elections 2026 — Let’s Observe Together!" platform had counted more than 900 complaints submitted to election commissions, about one-third of which concerned observers’ rights. At the same time, the Prosecutor General’s Office and the Interior Ministry of Russia stated that they had recorded no serious violations capable of affecting the conduct of the elections.
Ukraine’s reaction
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine issued a statement, noting that Russia’s holding, from September 18–20, of so-called elections to the State Duma of the Russian Federation in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine is a farce staged by the occupying state, has nothing to do with democratic elections, and creates no legal grounds for extending Russia’s jurisdiction to any part of Ukraine’s territory.
"No ‘vote’ organized by Russia at gunpoint changes the internationally recognized status of these territories. Temporary occupation does not confer sovereign rights on the occupying state. Ukraine recognizes neither the holding of these illegal ‘elections’ nor their null and void results. We call on foreign states, international organizations, and other subjects of international law likewise not to recognize these actions by Russia or regard them as an expression of the legitimate political will of people in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. We warn against any participation in this illegal undertaking, which will have legal consequences in national and international jurisdictions," the statement says.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs emphasized: "Any ‘elections’ in modern Russia are merely a farce. After more than a quarter-century of Putin’s rule, democracy, freedom of speech, political-party pluralism, and any respect for basic civil liberties are absent in this country."
"We call on the international community to call things by their proper names: the so-called ‘elections’ to the State Duma of the Russian Federation are merely a performance designed to create the illusion that the population supports the aggressive policy of the regime in Moscow," the statement says.

Over 3,000 migrants remain on streets of Spain's Ceuta, says government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:10:00 UTC
19:10:00 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
More than 3,000 migrants, including several hundred minors, are still living on the streets of Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta, the government said Monday.
Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres gave the estimate in an interview with Spanish public broadcaster TVE on Monday.
Torres said transfers to accommodation facilities designated under a government decree would continue in the coming days, with another site to be opened if necessary.
"We hope that in just a few weeks everyone will be relocated and the return files will begin to be processed," he said.
Between 150 and 200 migrants are voluntarily returning to Morocco each day, according to Torres, with 160 doing so over the past 24 hours.
He said only people entitled to international protection and minors who cannot be reunited with their families would remain in Spain, adding that most of the recent arrivals from Morocco were not expected to qualify for protection.
The government intends to transfer unaccompanied minors to mainland Spain to prevent overcrowding in Ceuta.
Torres also condemned an attack on Sunday on a Ceuta Assembly lawmaker whose car was pelted with stones, calling the incident "unacceptable."

German car exports drop 4% in first 7 months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:09:14 UTC
19:09:14 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
Germany exported around two million new passenger cars between January and July 2026, marking a 4% volume decline compared with the same period last year, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) reported on Monday.
The total value of new car exports dropped by 8.9% to €73.5 billion ($84.4 billion).
Shipments of combustion engine cars decreased by 2.9% to a million units during the seven-month period.
Electric car exports also fell by 2.9% to 560,000 units, while hybrid vehicle shipments dropped by 8.2% to 380,000.
The UK, the US and Italy remained the main destinations for German cars, receiving 32.7% of all new car exports.
Exports to the US declined by 2.6% in volume to 245,000 vehicles and 17.1% in value to €9.6 billion.
While combustion engine vehicle exports to the US surged by 31.7%, electric and hybrid car shipments plummeted by 56.1% and 50.3%, respectively.
On the import side, Germany brought in approximately 1.3 million new cars from January to July, reflecting a 16% volume increase compared with 2025.
China became the top supplier of new cars to Germany, with imports surging 120.9% to 175,000 vehicles.

Trump's favorite 2026 campaign target is Biden: nearly 900 mentions and counting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:09:03 UTC
19:09:03 KST

Trump’s favourite 2026 campaign target is Biden, nearly 900 mentions and counting
- Donald Trump has mentioned Joe Biden nearly 900 times in 2026, using him as a key political target to shift focus from his own presidency ahead of the November midterm elections.
- Trump blames Biden for issues like inflation, immigration, and foreign policy failures, despite public opinion often holding Trump responsible for economic problems.
- Trump’s frequent attacks extend to personal jabs and international crises, aiming to keep Biden at the centre of political debate and rally Republican support.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump has invoked Joe Biden’s name almost 900 times in 2026, a Reuters review shows, keeping his predecessor at the centre of debate as Republicans fight to hold their fragile grip on Congress in November’s midterm elections.
Trump has made Biden, a Democrat, his political target on average three times a day across speeches, comments and Truth Social postings, blaming him for problems ranging from inflation and immigration to munitions shortages, even as the former president, 83 and battling Stage 4 cancer, has largely withdrawn from public life.
The tactic reflects Trump’s effort to keep Americans focused on the perceived failures of the previous administration rather than on voters’ concerns about his own presidency with just six weeks left until the Nov 3 midterm elections.
Democrats “delivered you four years of disaster, bedlam and death under sleepy Joe Biden,” Trump, 80, told the party faithful at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Sept 9.
“Donald Trump always needs a foil and it’s better to have a single person than a party,” said Republican strategist Ryan Williams. “He’s done this throughout his time in office. He can use it to try to deflect any problems he’s currently facing.”
The Reuters review examined Trump’s references to Biden from January, when the 2026 election cycle began taking shape.
The findings underscore Trump’s effort to keep the focus on Biden as his own approval ratings have sagged, the war with Iran has dragged on, and the cost of living remains stubbornly high.
Since Jan 1, Trump has called out Biden by name at least 890 times, spanning almost 200 events and interviews and around 190 Truth Social posts in 2026, the Reuters review found.
He invoked Biden at least 210 times on the economy, 168 times on immigration and 138 times on foreign policy and national security matters, while also blaming him for a range of other domestic issues.
He has criticised Biden at events as varied as first lady Melania Trump’s movie premiere, the National Prayer Breakfast and the traditional Easter Egg Roll on the White House South Lawn.
During July’s NATO meeting in Turkey, Trump set a record for the number of mentions in a single day – 16.
He blamed Biden for a shortage of military munitions, the cost of housing and denigrating the steel industry.
While presidents often blame their predecessors – as Biden did Trump – Trump’s focus on Biden 20 months into his second term stands out for both its persistence and volume.
“Joe Biden is the worst president in American history, and President Trump has spent every day cleaning up his mess and making the United States of America stronger than ever before,” said Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman defending Trump’s repeated references to his predecessor.
T.J. Ducklo, a spokesman for Biden, declined to comment for this story.
Meghan Hays, a former senior Biden White House official, however, attacked what she called Trump’s “obsession.”
“Nine hundred mentions in less than a year isn’t governing, it’s an obsession. Joe Biden beat him once and Trump still hasn’t gotten over it. He’s more focused on re-litigating 2020 than lowering the cost of gas and groceries for the American people,” she said, referring to Biden’s victory in the 2020 election that Trump falsely claims was stolen from him.
Rowing back on economy
In February, Trump told an interviewer he owned the economy.
Now, with public opinion polls showing Americans souring on Trump’s economic stewardship, Trump is blaming affordability issues on Biden.
“I hope everyone realises that price increases throughout America were caused by Sleepy Joe Biden and the Biden Administration, not by ‘TRUMP,’” the president posted on Truth Social last week.
Some Trump supporters at the midterm convention in Dallas told Reuters they believed that Biden was to blame for inflation 20 months after he left office.
Opinion polls, however, suggest it is Trump who draws most Americans’ ire over inflation.
Inflation soared to more than 9 per cent during Biden’s presidency, fuelled in part by Covid-19 pandemic disruption to supply chains, the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the Biden administration’s spending to stimulate the Covid-19-racked economy.
Trump won election mainly on his promise to bring down prices, but they have remained stubbornly high, in part because of his war on Iran.
Averaging 4.95 per cent a month during Biden’s four years, year-on-year inflation has averaged 2.94 per cent a month since Trump took office and stood at 3.4 per cent in August.
“Politics is always about the future and never about the past, so blaming your predecessor does not work. Especially for an incumbent. He must defend his own record to help his party,” said veteran Republican strategist Charlie Black, who has sometimes criticised Trump.
Immigration
After the economy, immigration is the issue on which Trump most frequently invokes Biden.
As Trump’s expanded deportation campaign drew nationwide criticism and protests in 2026, he repeatedly sought to shift responsibility to his predecessor, arguing that Biden’s policies had enabled record levels of illegal immigration along the US-Mexico border.
After federal immigration agents killed two American citizens protesting in Minnesota in January, for example, Trump blamed the “open border policies of Biden” for “all of the time that we spend talking about Minnesota.”
The president talks about the high level of border crossings under Biden and the tougher Trump administration immigration policies so much that he recently acknowledged that his White House advisers were trying to get him off the topic.
“Even my speechwriters, they say, ‘Sir, nobody wants to hear about the border anymore. You’ve done it,’” Trump recounted in the Oval Office in August. “Biden couldn’t do it,” he added.
Iran, Ukraine conflicts
Under pressure to end the war on Iran he started nearly seven months ago, Trump has invoked Biden at least 37 times.
He accuses his predecessor of not having been aggressive enough against Tehran during his 2021-2025 presidency and of “creating a monster with Iran” in 2015 with the Iran nuclear deal negotiated by then-President Barack Obama while Biden was vice- president.
Biden’s policy toward Iran was to increase economic pressure on Tehran, a position Trump has now adopted amid sporadic clashes with Iran.
Trump initially denied media reports that US stockpiles of missiles and interceptors were dwindling rapidly in the war, but in May, he started blaming Biden for the shortages.
“I’d like to have more (munitions) to be honest, but so much was given to Ukraine by Biden,” Trump told reporters on Air Force One on July 27.
Trump has blamed Biden for international crises around the world at least 138 times.
This ranges from Ukraine and Iran to the US withdrawal from Afghanistan and being too soft on China.
Personal jabs
Trump has also taken a number of personal jabs at Biden over his mental acuity and his use of the autopen to sign some documents, a practice used by many presidents.
Sitting at a picnic table and signing eggs at April’s White House Easter Egg Roll, Trump told the group of children surrounding him that Biden “gave everything to the autopen because he was incapable of signing, let alone running a country.”
A favourite stop on the tour Trump gives guests at his “presidential walk of fame” near the White House Rose Garden is a display dedicated to Biden.
While other presidents are represented by photos of themselves, Biden is represented by an image of an autopen.
Trump has invoked Biden even when addressing local issues such as the renovation of the Reflecting Pool on Washington’s National Mall, arguing, without providing any evidence, that the project’s problems stem from neglect during Biden’s presidency or from reconstruction efforts that predated his return to office.
The pool now sits empty, two months after the initial renovation.
Trump has blamed vandals for the project’s problems, but the Justice Department acknowledged in August that recent “flawed” renovation work led to the pool’s peeling, a problem tied to work undertaken during Trump’s administration. REUTERS

“Joe Biden is the worst president in American history, and President Trump has spent every day cleaning up his mess and making the United States of America stronger than ever before,” said Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman defending Trump’s repeated references to his predecessor.
T.J. Ducklo, a spokesman for Biden, declined to comment for this story.
Meghan Hays, a former senior Biden White House official, however, attacked what she called Trump’s “obsession.”
“Nine hundred mentions in less than a year isn’t governing, it’s an obsession. Joe Biden beat him once and Trump still hasn’t gotten over it. He’s more focused on re-litigating 2020 than lowering the cost of gas and groceries for the American people,” she said, referring to Biden’s victory in the 2020 election that Trump falsely claims was stolen from him.
Rowing back on economy
In February, Trump told an interviewer he owned the economy.
Now, with public opinion polls showing Americans souring on Trump’s economic stewardship, Trump is blaming affordability issues on Biden.
“I hope everyone realises that price increases throughout America were caused by Sleepy Joe Biden and the Biden Administration, not by ‘TRUMP,’” the president posted on Truth Social last week.
Some Trump supporters at the midterm convention in Dallas told Reuters they believed that Biden was to blame for inflation 20 months after he left office.
Opinion polls, however, suggest it is Trump who draws most Americans’ ire over inflation.
Inflation soared to more than 9 per cent during Biden’s presidency, fuelled in part by Covid-19 pandemic disruption to supply chains, the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the Biden administration’s spending to stimulate the Covid-19-racked economy.
Trump won election mainly on his promise to bring down prices, but they have remained stubbornly high, in part because of his war on Iran.
Averaging 4.95 per cent a month during Biden’s four years, year-on-year inflation has averaged 2.94 per cent a month since Trump took office and stood at 3.4 per cent in August.
“Politics is always about the future and never about the past, so blaming your predecessor does not work. Especially for an incumbent. He must defend his own record to help his party,” said veteran Republican strategist Charlie Black, who has sometimes criticised Trump.
Immigration
After the economy, immigration is the issue on which Trump most frequently invokes Biden.
As Trump’s expanded deportation campaign drew nationwide criticism and protests in 2026, he repeatedly sought to shift responsibility to his predecessor, arguing that Biden’s policies had enabled record levels of illegal immigration along the US-Mexico border.
After federal immigration agents killed two American citizens protesting in Minnesota in January, for example, Trump blamed the “open border policies of Biden” for “all of the time that we spend talking about Minnesota.”
The president talks about the high level of border crossings under Biden and the tougher Trump administration immigration policies so much that he recently acknowledged that his White House advisers were trying to get him off the topic.
“Even my speechwriters, they say, ‘Sir, nobody wants to hear about the border anymore. You’ve done it,’” Trump recounted in the Oval Office in August. “Biden couldn’t do it,” he added.
Iran, Ukraine conflicts
Under pressure to end the war on Iran he started nearly seven months ago, Trump has invoked Biden at least 37 times.
He accuses his predecessor of not having been aggressive enough against Tehran during his 2021-2025 presidency and of “creating a monster with Iran” in 2015 with the Iran nuclear deal negotiated by then-President Barack Obama while Biden was vice- president.
Biden’s policy toward Iran was to increase economic pressure on Tehran, a position Trump has now adopted amid sporadic clashes with Iran.
Trump initially denied media reports that US stockpiles of missiles and interceptors were dwindling rapidly in the war, but in May, he started blaming Biden for the shortages.
“I’d like to have more (munitions) to be honest, but so much was given to Ukraine by Biden,” Trump told reporters on Air Force One on July 27.
Trump has blamed Biden for international crises around the world at least 138 times.
This ranges from Ukraine and Iran to the US withdrawal from Afghanistan and being too soft on China.
Personal jabs
Trump has also taken a number of personal jabs at Biden over his mental acuity and his use of the autopen to sign some documents, a practice used by many presidents.
Sitting at a picnic table and signing eggs at April’s White House Easter Egg Roll, Trump told the group of children surrounding him that Biden “gave everything to the autopen because he was incapable of signing, let alone running a country.”
A favourite stop on the tour Trump gives guests at his “presidential walk of fame” near the White House Rose Garden is a display dedicated to Biden.
While other presidents are represented by photos of themselves, Biden is represented by an image of an autopen.
Trump has invoked Biden even when addressing local issues such as the renovation of the Reflecting Pool on Washington’s National Mall, arguing, without providing any evidence, that the project’s problems stem from neglect during Biden’s presidency or from reconstruction efforts that predated his return to office.
The pool now sits empty, two months after the initial renovation.
Trump has blamed vandals for the project’s problems, but the Justice Department acknowledged in August that recent “flawed” renovation work led to the pool’s peeling, a problem tied to work undertaken during Trump’s administration. REUTERS

Guidance: Land Open Systems Architecture (LOSA)
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:05:00 BST
19:05:00 KST

Land Open Systems Architecture (LOSA)
Land Open Systems Architecture (LOSA) is the Ministry of Defence’s approachs to support land capability integration.
Documents
Details
Land Open Systems Architecture (LOSA) is the Ministry of Defence’s approach to using open standards, common data models and defined interfaces to support land capability integration. It helps systems exchange information more consistently, reduces bespoke integration effort, and makes it easier to upgrade or replace digital capabilities throughout their service life.
LOSA is supported by a set of core products: the Land Data Model (LDM), Generic Vehicle Architecture (GVA), Generic Soldier Architecture (GSA) and Generic Base Architecture (GBA). The LDM acts as the parent data model from which the GVA and GSA data models are derived. The Generic Architectures provide more specific approaches for vehicles, soldier systems and base infrastructure.
What LOSA does
Although LOSA is rooted in the land environment, its principles may support wider defence integration where common data models, open standards and defined interfaces are needed. It gives programmes, suppliers and integrators a consistent way to design digital and data elements so that systems can exchange information with shared meaning, rather than relying on bespoke project-by-project integration.
By promoting common architecture and reusable integration patterns, LOSA helps defence platforms work together more effectively and makes future upgrades easier. It supports interoperability across platforms, soldier systems and base infrastructure, while also helping UK land capabilities align more easily with NATO, allies and industry partners.
Who should use LOSA
You should use LOSA if you are working on systems, services or equipment that need to exchange data or integrate with other MOD, allied or industry systems.
LOSA is intended for MOD delivery teams, suppliers and systems integrators involved in the design, procurement, development or integration of defence capability. Although LOSA has strong roots in the land environment, its principles can also support wider defence integration where systems need to share information, use common data models or apply open standards.
This may include vehicles, soldier systems, sensors, communications equipment, command-and-control applications, software services and deployable or fixed infrastructure. LOSA is most relevant where systems need to work together, share information with common meaning, or remain adaptable as technology changes.
Why LOSA is relevant
Modern land capabilities are increasingly data-centric: sensors, communications, platforms, soldier systems, software services and command-and-control applications all need to share information quickly and consistently. Without a common approach, each programme can end up creating bespoke interfaces and data mappings, making systems harder to integrate, upgrade and reuse across the land environment.
LOSA is relevant because it provides the open architecture principles, common data models and defined interfaces needed to manage this complexity. By separating data and integration approaches from individual proprietary solutions, LOSA helps reduce vendor lock-in, gives MOD greater freedom to upgrade or replace components over time, and enables a wider range of suppliers to deliver compatible capability. In doing so, it supports the Land Industrial Strategy’s focus on innovation, competition and interoperability, while helping enable the Defence Investment Plan’s ambition for a more integrated, digitally enabled and adaptable force.
International collaboration
The LOSA approach and the LDM are actively used to enable interoperability between NATO members by providing a common way to describe, structure and exchange data. This helps different nations’ platforms, sensors, soldier systems and command applications share information with consistent meaning, reducing the need for bespoke integration work between individual systems.
This is particularly important for coalition operations, joint experimentation and multinational capability development, where UK systems must be able to work alongside allied systems. By promoting open standards, shared data models and reusable integration approaches, LOSA helps the UK collaborate more effectively with NATO partners and supports a more coherent approach to future capability integration.
Benefits
The LOSA products
LOSA is supported by four key products. These provide the foundations for common architecture, interfaces and data exchange in the land environment.
LOSA booklet
The LOSA booklet provides a short, accessible introduction for users who need to understand LOSA before accessing more detailed material. The booklet can be found at the top of this page.
Contact
Contact the LOSA team if you need access to LOSA guidance, standards or supporting material.

Italy moves to cap foreign students with limited Italian skills in classrooms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:03:20 UTC
19:03:20 KST

Giada Zampano
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
Italy’s conservative government led by Premier Giorgia Meloni plans to introduce a decree limiting the number of foreign students with poor Italian-language skills in classrooms, sparking criticism from educators and migrant advocates who say the measure risks creating new barriers to integration.
The proposal would give legal force to a guideline introduced in 2010 that recommended foreign students account for no more than 30% of a class but was rarely enforced, particularly in neighborhoods with large immigrant populations.
Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara has said the cap would apply only to non-EU students with little or no knowledge of Italian, rather than to all foreign pupils. Schools would assess language proficiency and educational preparedness, with the limits aimed at students requiring significant language support.
The decree is also expected to require some foreign parents to attend Italian-language courses and to ban the wearing of burqas and niqabs in schools.
Supporters say the measures are needed to improve educational outcomes and integration, but critics argue they focus on restrictions rather than investment in schools serving large immigrant populations.
Italy has about 930,000 foreign students, equal to 11.6% of the national school population, according the latest data available. Nearly two-thirds, about 607,000, were born in Italy, while roughly 323,000 were born abroad.
Although the national figure is well below the proposed threshold, immigrant populations are concentrated in some urban neighborhoods and northern regions, raising questions about how the policy can be implemented in practice.
School leaders have warned that some schools, particularly in migrant-heavy districts, have few alternatives for placing students. Antonello Giannelli, head of Italy's National Association of School Principals, has said schools cannot simply refuse admission to children.
Education unions have called instead for increased funding for language instruction, specialized teachers and cultural mediators. According to official data, students without Italian citizenship are significantly more likely to leave school early than their Italian peers.
Legal experts have also warned that strict enforcement could raise constitutional concerns if children are required to attend schools far from their communities in order to comply with classroom limits.
Speaking on Sunday at a youth festival organized by her nationalist conservative Brothers of Italy party in Rome, Meloni defended the package as a way to strengthen integration.
"For us, anyone who comes to Italy and wants to build their future here must learn our language, understand our culture, and respect our rules," she said. "It is the only serious way to welcome them."
Meloni said the decree would also prohibit the burqa, the full-body veil worn by some Muslim women, and the niqab, which covers the face except for the eyes. She did not refer to the hijab, the headscarf worn by many Muslim women.
The measures are the latest in a series of initiatives by Meloni's right-wing coalition aimed at tying immigration more closely to integration requirements, an issue that remains at the center of political debate in Italy.

A simple guide to the Yemen conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:01:30 UTC
19:01:30 KST

A simple guide to the Yemen conflict
Here’s a brief history of Yemen’s war – from the Houthi takeover in 2014 to the latest escalation.
Yemen is back in the global spotlight after the Iran-aligned Houthi group earlier this month made military gains against the forces loyal to the internationally recognised government, tightening its grip over the Red Sea coast.
The latest escalation in the Arab region’s most impoverished nation follows a period of relative calm that had largely held since the United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022 between the Iran-aligned group and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
The Houthi takeover of northwestern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, in 2014 had drawn Saudi military intervention. The fighting left tens of thousands dead and millions displaced, creating a humanitarian crisis.
In 2023, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis agreed to a UN roadmap towards a permanent ceasefire after direct talks, but the roadmap was never formalised.
Here’s a simple guide to Yemen’s war, from the Houthi takeover in 2014 to the latest escalation.
From the 2014 Houthi takeover to the expansion of the Saudi-backed government
- The Houthis took over vast swaths of northwestern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014, and months later assumed control of the government, forcing President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi to flee to Aden and then to Saudi Arabia.
- Alarmed by the rise of the Iran-aligned Houthis on its border, Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the internationally recognised government of Hadi in March 2015, carrying out thousands of attacks. Saudi Arabia sees Iran as a regional threat due to the latter’s financial and military power, as well as support for armed groups like Hezbollah.
- In this period, Houthi rebels targeted strategic infrastructure across Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), including airports, gas fields and oil tankers in the Red Sea. According to data analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, Saudi Arabia’s military intercepted more than 4,000 Houthi missiles, drones and other standoff weapons between 2017 and 2022.
- In 2019, the UN reported that about 24 million people (80 percent of the population) needed some form of assistance, making Yemen “the world’s worst humanitarian crisis” after nearly five years of war. The country also experienced the world’s worst cholera outbreak, amid the war‑damaged health and water systems. Millions of people were exposed, and hundreds of thousands of suspected cases were recorded.
- After seven years of conflict, the UN-mediated truce took effect in April 2022, bringing a marked de-escalation in fighting, even while a low-intensity conflict had remained since.
- In January of this year, Yemen’s internationally recognised government expanded its control of the southern and eastern parts of the country after the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council (STC) announced its dissolution.
- The UAE’s backing of the STC, which called for the secession and independence of southern Yemen, strained Saudi-UAE ties, with Riyadh asking the Emirati forces to leave the country.
Who are the main players?
The Houthis
The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (supporters of God), are an armed group in control of mainly northwestern Yemen and several areas close to Saudi Arabia. Since September 10, they have tightened control over the country’s Red Sea coast, a vital shipping lane.
The Houthis from Yemen’s Zaidi Shia minority emerged in the northern mountainous region of Saada in the 1990s, demanding a greater share of power.
They capitalised on the widespread public anger against the weak transitional government that came to power after longtime President Ali Abdullah Saleh was forced to step down following the 2011 Arab Spring protests.
The Houthis initially allied with military units loyal to former President Saleh as they captured the Red Sea port of Hodeidah in October 2014. In January 2015, they seized the presidential palace in Sanaa, forcing President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi to flee to the southern port city of Aden. Hadi later moved to Saudi Arabia, from where he ran his government-in-exile until his resignation in 2022.
The Houthi group then spent years, with Iran’s backing, fighting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia.
Seen as part of a regional alliance known as the “axis of resistance” and backed by Iran, the Houthi group nevertheless has its own base, its own interests, and its own ambitions.
The group has gained international prominence for its attacks on Israel and shipping in the Red Sea since the start of Israel’s genocide in Gaza in October 2023.
Saudi Arabia
Riyadh entered the Yemen war when it led a military coalition against the Houthis in March 2015, seeking to restore the government of then-President Hadi.
Houthis have accused Riyadh of carrying out hundreds of attacks in support of the internationally recognised government battling the Houthis in the latest fighting.
Presidential Leadership Council
The PLC was established in 2022 when former President Hadi formally transferred his powers to the new eight-member body.
It represents the internationally recognised government of Yemen, with a mandate to manage the country’s political, security and military affairs, and to steer negotiations towards a permanent ceasefire. It is chaired by Rashad al-Alimi, an adviser to Hadi and former interior minister with the government of the late President Saleh.
Its membership is drawn from a mix of northern and southern politicians and military-linked leaders in a bid to unite major anti-Houthi forces under one roof.
The PLC is backed by Saudi Arabia and the alliance that Riyadh leads. Since taking over complete control of southern Yemen after the dissolution of the STC, the PLC aims to unite Yemen, including the areas controlled by the Houthis.
Islah party
The Yemeni Congregation for Reform, better known as Islah, is a Sunni Islamist movement with historical ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. It is a faction within the recognised PLC-led government but has long had an independent identity. Its major stronghold has long been Marib, the country’s sole gas-producing region with one of its largest oilfields.
National Resistance Forces
The National Resistance Forces is a government-aligned military faction led by Tareq Saleh, nephew of the late former President Saleh.
The force has maintained ties to Saudi Arabia and, like the Islah party, is part of the PLC. It aims for a unified Yemen, positioning itself as a counterweight to both the Houthis and southern secessionists.
Who controls what in Yemen?
The Houthi movement controls Sanaa, the capital, and most of northwestern and northern Yemen, including the entire Red Sea coastline and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the busiest global maritime routes. The control over Bab al-Mandeb by the Iran-aligned Houthis has raised concerns about navigation amid the closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran in response to the US-Israel war on Tehran.
The internationally recognised government, meanwhile, controls much of the rest of the country.
What is the humanitarian situation?
More than 112,000 people have been displaced in Yemen and close to 3,000 have fled the conflict to Djibouti, according to the UN.
The International Organization for Migration estimated that 22 million Yemenis, nearly half the population, are in urgent need of humanitarian aid.
The UN Security Council, meanwhile, has condemned the Houthis’ continuing attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying they have caused civilian casualties, including women and children, and damaged energy infrastructure.
What do we know about the latest fighting?
Tensions escalated in July after Yemen’s government forces claimed an attack on an airport in Sanaa, preventing an aircraft from Iran from landing. More attacks followed, and it further escalated in late August when the Houthis launched a major offensive, saying the 2022 truce had been violated by government forces.
The Saudi Arabia-led coalition on Saturday evening said on X that it “successfully intercepted and destroyed” a missile attack attempting to target Riyadh – the first attack on the capital since the Yemen conflict erupted in July.
The coalition added that the Houthis had tried to target “civilians and civilian infrastructure” in several cities in the west of the kingdom, including the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, an important export hub for Saudi oil, which were additionally thwarted.
The Houthis confirmed they had targeted “sensitive sites” in Riyadh, as well as Aramco facilities in Yanbu.
“The message from the Yemeni group is that despite the Saudi bombardment campaign across Yemen, it will continue to step up its attacks and meet escalation with escalation,” said Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa.
The incident comes days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca on Wednesday, denouncing it as a “cowardly terrorist attack” on Islam’s holy city. The Houthis strongly denied the accusation, calling it a “worn-out lie”.
Meanwhile, on the ground in Yemen, the armed forces of the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government and the Houthis are engaged in fierce fighting in southern Marib as well as Taiz, Lahj, al-Jawf and al-Bayda.
The Yemeni army also said 13 soldiers were killed in two days of clashes with Houthi forces in the southwestern provinces of Taiz and Lahj.
On September 10, the Houthis made their most crucial gain in this bout of fighting by seizing the crucial Red Sea city of Mocha, expanding control over the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Despite appeals from Riyadh for United States President Donald Trump to strike the Houthis directly, Washington has so far held back, wary of opening a new front while still fighting a costly war with Iran.
Meanwhile, US officials have met Houthi representatives in Oman over the weekend. The Houthis reportedly assured Washington that vessels not linked to Saudi Arabia would not be targeted.
The Houthis have banned the passage of Saudi ships, adding pressure on Riyadh, which has used the Red Sea as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. Last week, the Houthis also attacked the East-West pipeline, disrupting the export of Saudi oil and causing global oil prices to cross $100 per barrel.

Sound guardians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:01:00 UTC
19:01:00 KST

For Abidin, a Balik elder who lives in East Kalimantan in Borneo, Indonesia, the sounds of nature aren’t merely a backdrop but a vital part of how he navigates the world. But as the rainforest around him has become more developed, the calls of creatures once heard everywhere have grown scarce. And that process is speeding up. To relieve Indonesia’s capital city of Jakarta, which is sinking due to overdevelopment and vulnerable to climate change, the government is building a new one, Nusantara, close to Abidin’s home. The noise of construction and city life is beginning to overpower the soundscape he relies on, and researchers suspect they may already be pushing wildlife away.
In this short documentary, the US director Leah Varjacques traces an effort to record the sounds of the rainforest before they’re altered forever. The film follows Abidin working with a research team that includes Wendy Erb, a bioacoustic scientist from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology in New York, to collect audio from caves, treetops and everywhere in between. In doing so, they hope to create a record for posterity so that the rainforest’s soundscapes – and the culture and ancestral knowledge embedded within them – are never fully erased.
