Neuroscientists uncover a previously unknown brain benefit of very slow running
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:00:16 UTC
19:00:16 KST

A recent study published in Imaging Neuroscience indicates that engaging in a very slow jog for just ten minutes can improve a person’s mood and enhance their ability to focus. The research suggests that the gentle, rhythmic bouncing of running at a low intensity provides a measurable boost to brain regions involved in mental control and emotional regulation.
Human beings have a long evolutionary history of running, a form of movement that provides widespread physical and mental health benefits. The prefrontal cortex, a brain area located behind the forehead that is responsible for complex thinking and emotional control, appears particularly responsive to aerobic exercise.
Earlier work has shown that different forms of activity can stimulate this brain region. For example, a 2014 study revealed that even very mild, low-effort pedaling on a stationary bike is enough to activate the prefrontal cortex and improve mental focus. Building on that concept, researchers later found that a 2021 study of a ten-minute session of moderate-intensity running boosts mood and strongly activates the same brain areas.
But moderate running can be physically taxing, elevating the heart rate to a level that might feel uncomfortable or stressful for older adults or people who are not regularly active. This research progression led scientists to wonder if the gentlest possible jog could still deliver these same brain and mood benefits without the physical strain.
The research was led by Hideaki Soya, a professor emeritus at the Institute of Health and Sport Sciences at the University of Tsukuba, and Ryuta Kuwamizu, an assistant professor at the university, alongside Chorphaka Damrongthai and colleagues at the Soya Laboratory. “Running is widely believed to benefit the brain, but studies combining rigorous brain imaging with tightly controlled running protocols have been relatively limited, partly because exercise intensity is much easier to control on a bike,” Soya and Kuwamizu told PsyPost.
The researchers wanted to test running under controlled laboratory conditions at the very bottom of the intensity range, using speeds that could also be used for walking. “If the benefits were still present at such a low intensity, running could become accessible to people who cannot, or simply do not want to, run hard,” they explained.
To measure mental performance, the researchers focused on executive function, a term for the mental skills that help people pay attention, manage time, and switch focus. They were especially interested in whether the physical characteristics unique to running, such as the vertical bouncing of the head with each step, might play a role in how the exercise affects the brain.
To explore this question, the researchers recruited 24 healthy young adults. Each participant completed two separate sessions on different days. One session involved sitting quietly on a treadmill for ten minutes to serve as a resting control condition, while the other session involved running on the treadmill at a very slow pace for ten minutes.
The researchers tailored the running speed to each person’s fitness level, ensuring it remained at a very light intensity. For the men in the study, this averaged about 3.4 miles per hour, and for the women, it averaged about 2.4 miles per hour. These are speeds that most people could comfortably walk, but the participants were instructed to maintain a running form with small steps.
Before and after each session, participants completed a brief survey assessing their mood on two dimensions: arousal and pleasure. They also completed a computer-based task called the Stroop test to measure their executive function. The Stroop test asks participants to look at color words, such as the word “RED,” printed in an unmatched color like blue ink, and then quickly identify the ink color rather than the written word. This creates a mental conflict, and the extra time it takes to answer correctly is a measure of cognitive interference.
To observe brain activity, the researchers used functional near-infrared spectroscopy. This non-invasive imaging technique uses light sensors placed on the scalp to measure changes in blood oxygen levels in the brain. Because exercise can cause changes in skin blood flow and heart rate that might interfere with these readings, the researchers waited five minutes after the running session before measuring brain activity.
During a separate two-minute run, the team also attached a small sensor to the participants’ heads to measure vertical head acceleration. This allowed them to capture the rhythmic bouncing motion of the participants’ steps.
The researchers found that the ten-minute slow run provided noticeable benefits compared to the resting session. Participants reported feeling more energetic and experiencing a more pleasant mood after the very light run.
“Notably, the increase in pleasant mood was particularly strong, suggesting that slow running may be especially effective at improving how people feel,” the researchers noted. They were surprised to see that the increase in pleasant mood appeared particularly pronounced compared with what they had observed with very-light-intensity pedaling in their previous studies.
Performance on the Stroop test also improved. Following the slow run, participants reacted faster to the conflicting color words, which suggests a temporary sharpening of their executive function and focus.
The brain imaging data supported these behavioral changes. After the slow run, the researchers saw increased blood oxygen levels in specific left-sided areas of the prefrontal cortex while participants completed the Stroop test. These specific regions, known as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the frontopolar area, are heavily involved in overriding impulses and managing complex tasks.
When the researchers analyzed the head acceleration data, they noticed an interesting pattern. The amount of vertical bouncing a participant experienced during their run positively correlated with how much their pleasant mood increased. This provides evidence that the physical sensation of rhythmic up-and-down motion might be one of the mechanical factors that make running feel enjoyable.
“Intriguingly, this increase in pleasant mood was correlated with the magnitude of each runner’s head acceleration, raising the possibility that the gentle bouncing rhythm characteristic of running may itself contribute to why running feels good,” the researchers said. “Importantly, this head acceleration reflects the rhythmic vertical motion of the whole body, rather than simply movement of the head.”
The practical significance of the study lies in its cost-benefit balance, demonstrating that a very easy, walking-compatible pace with very low physiological strain is sufficient to produce measurable improvements. “If you have avoided running because it seems too demanding, slow running may offer a very accessible way to begin,” Soya and Kuwamizu added.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that a ten-minute bout of very light-intensity exercise dilated the pupils and was associated with increased left prefrontal cortex activation and better executive function. The current results also align with a study covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that short bursts of light-intensity physical activity increased blood flow to the prefrontal cortex, though that earlier study tested brief desk movements in children without directly measuring cognitive performance.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding this study. The experiment involved a small group of healthy young adults, meaning the results might look different in older populations or those with specific health conditions.
“Please do not read this as ‘slow running is better than harder running’ or as a claim that everyone should switch to slow running,” the researchers cautioned. “For those who enjoy brisk or vigorous running, it remains an excellent form of exercise for body and brain.”
They emphasized that their point is about the floor, not the ceiling, showing that measurable brain benefits of running can already appear at its very lowest intensity.
The study also relied on brain imaging equipment that lacked short-separation channels, which are specialized sensors used to filter out superficial blood flow in the scalp. While the researchers used specific timing and analytical techniques to reduce this noise, future studies using more advanced sensors could help confirm that the observed signals originate entirely from within the brain.
Additionally, the researchers compared running only to a resting state. Because they did not include a walking condition at the same speed, it is difficult to completely separate the effects of the running motion from the general effects of being upright and moving.
The team noted that the relationship between head acceleration and pleasant mood is currently exploratory and correlational, meaning causality is not yet established. “By directly comparing running with walking, we aim to determine whether the rhythmic vertical acceleration characteristic of running contributes to changes in mood and brain function,” they said.
Looking ahead, the researchers plan to test slow running in populations who may benefit from it most, including older adults, people with low fitness, and those with depressive symptoms. They also hope to better understand the neural mechanisms through which slow running influences the brain, such as how it might engage arousal-related catecholaminergic systems—neural pathways involving dopamine and noradrenaline.
“Our long-term goal is to establish slow running as an evidence-based, easily accessible daily habit for maintaining mental and cognitive health across the lifespan,” they explained.
“Running is one of the most fundamental human movements, yet many people feel that it is not for them,” Soya and Kuwamizu concluded. “We are beginning to think that slow running may be more than simply running slowly. It may be a form of locomotion in which we move slowly while preserving the gentle, rhythmic vertical oscillation characteristic of running—and enjoy the pleasant ‘vertical groove’ created by that rhythm.”
The study, “Slow running benefits: Boosts in mood and facilitation of prefrontal cortex function even at very light intensity,” was authored by Chorphaka Damrongthai, Ryuta Kuwamizu, Yudai Yamazaki, Naoki Aoike, Dongmin Lee, Kyeongho Byun, Ferenc Torma, Kazuki Hyodo, Worachat Churdchomjan, Michael A. Yassa, Kazutaka Adachi, and Hideaki Soya.

Expect ‘high tide’ of Chinese biotech deals as threat of US curbs fades: analysts
Stocks jump on reports Washington will allow most licensing deals under ‘substantially softer stance’ than had been feared, analysts say
US-China biotech deals are expected to thrive because Washington is reportedly leaning away from sweeping restrictions, according to analysts, giving Chinese healthcare firms a major boost following Beijing’s ambitious five-year plan for the sector.
Out-licensing deals between China and the US would “ride on a high tide” in the favourable environment, said Nomura’s head of China healthcare research Jialin Zhang, in a research note on Sunday.
The US Treasury Department was drafting investment rules for American pharmaceutical firms that would preserve their ability to license most Chinese drugs, barring links to pathogens or weaponisable biotechnology, Reuters reported on Friday, citing unnamed sources.
That stance would represent a “substantially softer stance” than had been feared based on restrictions outlined in two US bills earlier this year, said Tony Ren, head of Asia Healthcare Research at Macquarie, in a note on Monday.

We Have a Climate Imagination Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Earlier this year I stood in a draughty sports hall, facing rows of 10-year-olds sitting cross-legged on the scuffed floor. I asked them a question: “What does climate change mean?”
Small hands shot up: “The sea rises and floods everything,” one child said. “Fires are gonna burn all the forests,” another added. “We all die.”
The litany of apocalypse continued until I interrupted with a second question. “And what can we do about it?”
Silence.
After some shuffling, one girl tentatively offered: “Solar panels?” Then a louder boy called out, “Recycle!” His classmates nodded.
And that was pretty much it.
I've worked in climate communication for nearly 30 years, interspersing sessions with CEOs, activists, and politicians with talks to school kids. Over those decades, I’ve watched the average 10-year-old acquire an increasingly sophisticated picture of the climate crisis they will inherit. They can imagine burning forests, flooded cities, dying species, and an uninhabitable planet. Many of them seem to understand climate science better than some CEOs.
But ask these children to picture what we do about it, and suddenly their extraordinary imaginations contract to a recycling bin.
To be clear, I am enthusiastically in favour of recycling—just not as our answer to a planetary emergency. But I understand why I’m still hearing that inadequate response. Since the greenhouse effect and global warming first entered mainstream public consciousness in the 1980s, we’ve offered people ever more detailed maps of the apocalypse with barely a sketch of the way out.
The climate movement, of which I’m a proud member, has been complicit in this communications crisis. Most messages shared by progressive forces are merely an ad nauseam echo of: climate change is real, humans are to blame, and the consequences are catastrophic. I call this framing the earned dystopia, and it’s so ubiquitous most pre-teens can parrot it.
After so many years, can we not imagine a different story?
One reason for this imagination deficit is that storytelling has been treated as merely the spoonful of sugar to help the scientific medicine go down. Storytellers are asked to act as the marketing department for climate science.
But if that subservient role for storytellers was ever needed, it’s increasingly futile now that climate change has started communicating itself. Our growing count of horrifying floods, fires, storms, and droughts capture headlines without my help.
We have clear science and brutal direct experience of climate change, so why haven’t politicians and populations sprung into action?
The logic of the climate crisis is clear. What we’re missing is the magic.
Long before humans measured atmospheric carbon, we whispered tales of flood and fire. Stories have always helped us understand who we are and what we might become. Increasingly, researchers are proving this singular power of stories to spark ideas, possibilities, and acts of imagination.
I believe part of this magic comes from stories’ purpose in curating emotions rather than evidence.
Today, we don’t particularly lack information about heat pumps, electric vehicles, or regenerative agriculture. More details than you could ever want are just a click away. What we’re missing is an emotional architecture for change; how it feels to want a different future and to believe we can reach it.
That’s where great storytelling could change everything. Our ability to enter a story and temporarily experience the character's world as our own is called narrative transportation. Studies prove that this experience of emoting along with fictional people can directly influence real people’s attitudes, intentions, and even our behaviors. Few other mechanisms can achieve the same effect.
Climate politics has sensed this power, but translated it into the narrower language of “public narrative.” Politicians now plot narratives for electrification and renewables. Campaigners construct counter-narratives to fossil fuels. Brand teams test sustainability narratives against each other. In climate circles, everyone is searching for the breakthrough narrative that will finally unlock action. But too often the term is simply a cypher for messaging. And messaging is not the same thing as mythology.
A political narrative tells us how to understand an issue while mythology helps us understand ourselves. And climate change is mythological in scale. It contains terrifying monsters, underdog heroes, unexpected allies, destruction and rebirth. Or at least it should. My problem is with the enormous cultural library of apocalyptic narratives compared to a surprisingly small shelf of fables that foreshadow a better ending.
We need a plot twist in climate storytelling, moving beyond the threat and into the thrilling adventure of solving it. Tales of the messy decades in which billions of people change how they power homes, grow food, travel, build cities, and protect one another from a climate that has already changed
That’s a job for storytellers.
Culture makers are beginning to catch on. I’ve been invited by television and film writers, social-media creators, and brands to help climate solutions appear in comedy, drama, adventure, and everyday life. Ever more box-office hits, like The Wild Robot, Avatar, and the upcoming Digger, reflect our fight against climate and nature crises. Sesame Street is helping kids cope with extreme weather. New climate fiction novels weave answers into stirring worldbuilding. These all work because they are compelling and moving stories above all, not climate science lectures dressed in a thin veil of narrative. Many other scriptwriters, novelists, social media creators, musicians and artists must add to this list.
I passionately believe that climate solutions are the most important story of this century.
When I return to that classroom over the coming years and ask the same two questions, the first answers will remain frightening. But when I ask what we can do about it, I hope every hand will shoot up, because we’ll have filled kids' imaginations with enough possibilities that they can start inventing answers we haven’t thought of yet. That will be a good day.

We Need to Stop Talking Like Climate Change Is Partisan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

This summer of disasters has shown us that climate impacts are not political, and it is past time we stopped talking about them as if they were. A flood doesn’t knock on your door and ask who you voted for in the last election before it sweeps your house away, nor does wildfire smoke distinguish between Republicans and Democrats before it chokes the air.
People who raise awareness about climate change know that how you communicate your message matters, and there’s much to learn from them. We surveyed the top organizations and individuals who regularly communicate about climate change across the U.S. and Canada. Almost none said that advocating for candidates or policies was the goal of their work. Their top priority was helping people understand what’s happening and why it matters: we’ve always had heatwaves and droughts, storms, and floods—but the faster the planet warms, the worse these events get.
Climate change is loading the weather dice against us, and its effects are growing. A recent study estimated that deaths caused by extreme heat are vastly under-reported. Air pollution, whether from burning fossil fuels or wildfire smoke, is responsible for a growing list of health impacts, from increased risk of asthma and dementia to premature death. The financial toll of climate change is also on the rise as climate-related expenses, including rising utility bills and insurance premiums, are already adding at least $400 to $900 to yearly household budgets. And as we have seen over the past few years, there are no climate havens: we are all at risk.
Here’s the thing, though: when people connect what’s happening to why it’s happening, their support for all sorts of climate action grows. This fact is true in the U.S., in Canada, and in dozens of other countries too. Why? Because we need solutions at scale that make the easiest, most affordable choice the best choice for the planet and our future. This requires action at every level: individual, community, and corporate action, but also government policy that enables and accelerates the rest.
Even as the impacts from climate change grow, data show that we still aren’t hearing or talking about it enough. Just under half of Canadians and 41% of Americans read or hear about climate change once a week. Only 20% of Americans discuss global warming with family and friends a few times a month or more. And nearly half, 44%, say they never discuss it at all.
Why aren’t we hearing about it more? Why do so many articles about the devastation of the Nepal floods, the soaring costs of home insurance, or the escalating health risks of wildfire smoke fail to make the connection between these issues and climate change?
There are many reasons, but one is the fact that polarized public discourse has made climate conversations more difficult, and even well-meaning efforts to “move climate change up” people’s priority list often fundamentally misrepresent the risks. The reality is that climate change doesn’t need to move up any list; it is already impacting any homeowner’s, farmer’s, teacher’s, or parent’s top concerns. But that connection isn’t always obvious: it needs to be made, again and again.
Given this contraction in public climate conversations, we wanted to learn from those who are still doing climate communication. What’s working, and how can we amplify it? Here’s what we found.
The first and most important lesson is that talking about climate change means talking about everyday life. When we asked climate newsletter writers, podcast hosts, people who regularly post on social media, and those building climate content for non-profits, their response was clear. Their first priority is to connect the climate crisis to other concerns people face: our jobs, our health, the places we love. They don’t set up climate change as a rival to those worries. Instead, they understand that climate change is already shaping the things people worry about. When we connect the dots between what we love and how climate change threatens it, it becomes obvious that nearly all of us have our own reasons to care and act.
The second priority climate communicators identified was shifting public perceptions and norms. And this issue is equally vital. Three years ago, 71% of Canadians and 63% of Americans reported they were worried about climate change. But most people keep their worries to themselves and underestimate how many others share their concerns. When people don't hear their neighbors, coworkers, and friends talking about climate change, they’re less willing to bring it up themselves. Conversely, of everything people can learn about climate change, knowing that others care best predicts whether people speak up. And here's why it matters: if we don't talk about climate change, how will we know who else cares about it—and if we think we're alone in our concern, why would we act?
Climate communicators are not pushing to make this a partisan issue—in fact, only 4% prioritized advocating for elected officials or candidates. Instead, they’re working to inform and educate their audiences about climate action, climate science, risks, and impacts, in hopes of equipping others to talk about climate change themselves.
Climate communication that isn’t polarizing and connects directly to what we already care about is exactly what we need; we just need more of it. Yet only 41% of the communicators surveyed report having received any financial support for their climate communication in the past five years. A third work entirely alone, and two-thirds work either alone or with a small team of ten or fewer colleagues. Even with these limitations, they are producing content and getting the word out: nearly eight-in-ten say they’re publishing content about climate change at least once a week.
We know that climate shocks, like the ones we’ve experienced this summer, open windows of opportunity: people who live through climate change-exacerbated extreme events are more supportive of climate science and climate action and are more civically and politically engaged. On this warming planet, we all need to learn from what the few who are talking about climate change are already doing. Research has shown that friends and family are trusted messengers who can initiate a pro-climate conversation loop. We all need to become climate communicators and stop letting those who want to delay climate action as long as possible polarize it and silence us.
To care about climate change today, one doesn’t need to be anything other than a human being living on planet Earth. And when we stop talking about climate change like it’s a political issue and start talking about it as a shared challenge that we all need to work together to solve, that’s when we’ll finally be able to start talking about saving ourselves.

Press review: State Duma set to keep five parties while Europe faces record fuel prices

MOSCOW, September 21. /TASS/. The single voting day to elect lawmakers to the 9th Russian State Duma has ended, with the lower chamber of the Russian parliament set to include the same five parties and United Russia retaining the majority of seats; Europe is grappling with record-high diesel and gasoline prices, seeking a way out; and the US and Denmark seem to have found a way out of the crisis over Greenland. These stories topped Monday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Media: Russian State Duma to include same five parties following election, with United Russia retaining its leadership
The Single Voting Day 2026 has ended in Russia. The results of the elections held September 18-20 will determine the 450 members of parliament, as well as new governors and regional lawmakers. Preliminary results indicate that United Russia maintains a solid lead in the party-list vote. It is followed by the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), the Liberal Democratic Party of the Russian Federation (LDPR), New People, and the A Just Russia - For Truth, according to the Russian Central Election Commission’s report as of the end of September 20. Meanwhile, unprecedented cyberattacks from abroad and drone raids sought to actively disrupt the voting.
At the time all polling stations in Russia closed, voter turnout for the federal parliamentary elections stood at 56.66%, the CEC reported. This figure has already surpassed the turnout rates from the 2021, 2016, 2003, and 1993 elections. Meanwhile, the final turnout on the electronic voting platform exceeded 90%. The final election results will not be announced until September 25 at the earliest. In addition to the parliamentary elections, Russians elected regional lawmakers and municipal authority representatives in 39 regions, as well as regional heads in eight regions through direct voting.
The political system successfully passed a stress test by ensuring that the elections were held under wartime conditions, including drone attacks, new sanctions, and problems in the fuel market, Konstantin Kostin, head of the Civil Society Development Foundation and former head of the presidential administration’s Domestic Policy Department, told Vedomosti. "This fact, along with United Russia’s lead, is an important argument in support of Russia’s position in international relations and at the negotiating table," he emphasized.
Most Russians support the current course, while a minority believes their vote can make a difference. "Two factors - the desire for stability and the demand for change - overlap, resulting in a very high voter turnout," Kalachev noted. Boycotting the election as a form of protest does not seem to have been very popular, he said.
The Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics, as well as the Kherson and Zaporozhye Regions, participated in parliamentary elections for the first time in history as Russia’s full-fledged subjects. According to Central Election Commission (CEC) Deputy Chairman Nikolay Bulayev, these regions are already fully integrated into the country’s overall electoral system. The same technologies are used there as throughout the country.
However, as AI and the digital ecosystem of elections become more complex, cybersecurity issues are also the rise, Dmitry Orlov, CEO of the Agency for Political and Economic Communications, told Izvestia.
Nevertheless, the political system’s ability to respond to these challenges remains paramount, a task that the 2026 campaign successfully met, the expert pointed out.
Vedomosti: How record-high diesel and gasoline prices affecting Europe
French President Emmanuel Macron called French fuel prices "unbearable" on this X page. On September 18, he met with representatives of major political parties to discuss the situation in the fuel market. As of September 17, gasoline averaged 2.6 euros per liter in the EU and 2.12 euros per liter in the eurozone.
EU governments have three main tools at their disposal: a temporary reduction in the tax component of prices, targeted assistance to vulnerable households and transportation companies, and measures to ensure greater supplies to the European market, Vladislav Belov, deputy director of the Institute of Europe, told Vedomosti. Abnormally high prices for diesel and gasoline are becoming an additional factor holding back economic growth in the EU, the expert noted. According to him, high diesel fuel prices increase costs in freight transportation, agriculture, construction, and parts of the manufacturing sector, and are then passed on to consumer prices through supply chains. Therefore, if current price levels persist in the medium term, one can expect additional inflationary pressure, a decline in real incomes and consumer demand, as well as a deterioration in the competitiveness of European manufacturers, Belov emphasized.
European countries lead the world in motor fuel prices primarily due to taxes, Alexander Frolov, deputy director of the MGIMO International Energy Policy and Security Institute, pointed out. The situation in the Middle East has worsened the disruption of Russian fuel supplies to the global market caused by attacks on Ukraine, which has driven up prices and exacerbated the chronic energy crisis that Europe has been facing since the late 2010s, the expert stressed. With the severing of business ties with Russia and the strategy to phase out its hydrocarbons by the end of 2027, the safety net has vanished, and the search for replacements in alternative markets only drives up prices, Frolov said. "Europe is affected by any upheaval on the periphery, which could previously be offset by Russian supplies combined with conservation measures," he stressed.
The causes of the fuel price crisis are the same across all regions of the world, but for the US, a key factor is the exceptionally high profitability of oil and petroleum product exports, which diverts fuel from the domestic market, Alexey Belogoriyev, research director at the Institute for Energy and Finance Foundation, emphasized. Europe, on the other hand, is a net importer: these are fundamentally different starting points, he said. The expert also stressed that EU countries are indeed experiencing the consequences of decades of "dieselization" of passenger vehicles and the severing of energy ties with Russia. Public perception of the crisis is similar in the US and Europe, but the economic consequences for European consumers are more severe, Belogoriyev noted.
Kommersant: What US should expect from new Greenland deal
The US and Denmark appear to have reached an agreement to resolve the crisis around Greenland. President Donald Trump announced that the parties will soon conclude a deal under which the Americans will, on the one hand, be able to significantly and indefinitely expand their military presence on the island and, on the other hand, prevent any attempts by their opponents to gain a foothold in this strategically important region. And although the US already had extensive rights and capabilities in Greenland, Trump considers this a diplomatic breakthrough.
The conflict between Washington and Copenhagen over the status of Greenland, which is officially part of Denmark with autonomous status, has lasted more than a year and a half and is approaching a resolution. Washington will apparently no longer attempt to buy the island, threaten to seize it by force, or persuade its residents to revolt against the central government. The US president did not disclose the text of the draft agreement but revealed its three key components. First, he said, it will be open-ended. Second, it will allow the US to significantly expand its military presence on the island, something the Americans, according to him, intend to do "immediately." And third, no US opponents will be able to establish military bases or make significant investments on the island without written approval from the Americans.
Meanwhile, it remains unclear whether this truly constitutes a diplomatic breakthrough, as Trump is eager to portray it, until the text of the new agreement is made public. Both American and European media outlets have pointed out that the US already held extensive rights and capabilities on the island under the 1951 US-Danish agreement on the defense of Greenland. They argue that the White House has achieved nothing new and that the deal merely allows the US administration to "save face."
According to international security expert Konstantin Bogdanov, American interest in Greenland is longstanding and predominantly military in nature. "Greenland’s primary significance lies in its convenient location as a forward early-warning outpost. There is a radar station there that is part of the US missile and nuclear strike warning system, oriented toward the north and northwest - that is, toward the potential trajectories of ballistic missiles launched from Russian territory, as well as cruise missiles launched over the Arctic," he told Kommersant.
Over the past 10 to 15 years, he noted, the US has reacted nervously to China’s attempts to initiate investment and infrastructure projects in Greenland. "In its current form, the agreement preserves and strengthens US priority in Greenland, eases concerns about the emergence of Chinese influence there (including the possibility of deploying technical intelligence assets), and, most importantly, resolves the diplomatic crisis in relations with Copenhagen that arose due to President Trump’s clumsy remarks," the expert concluded.
