Across China: Rare dark-sky zone in east China drives rural tourism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
17:30:02 CST
18:30:02 KST

HANGZHOU, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Fang Shanfei never thought his village was special, nor did he understand terms like the Bortle scale. But things changed when strangers arrived, eager to gaze at the stars he had seen all his life.
Running the only rural homestay in Gaotiankeng Village, in east China's Zhejiang Province, Fang was the first to spot the drift in 2017, when stargazing enthusiasts scoured the mountains for a dark-sky site and eyed on his village.
Elsewhere, especially in the brilliant glow of the Yangtze River Delta, the night is awash with light, serving as a proxy for electricity use and economic vitality in China's economic and technology powerhouse.
But in the largely mountainous province, farmers in remote areas relied mainly on selling homegrown produce and rural specialties such as raw tea leaves, with limited incomes and peaceful but still dark nights.
In Fang's village, however, the darkness reveals something even rarer: a sky brimming with stars, far from urban luminescence.
Nestled in eastern Zhejiang's mountains at an altitude of 680 meters, with forest coverage above 85 percent, Gaotiankeng is shielded from light pollution by its natural surroundings.
In 2024, it was officially added to the world list of dark sky protected areas, marked by a stone stele at the village entrance. A year later, the Beijing Planetarium set up a permanent astronomical observation site there, the first in the Yangtze River Delta to join the top institution's official observation system.
Professionals classify Gaotiankeng as a Class 2 dark-sky zone with a Bortle scale rating of two to three, marking a rare astronomical resource unmatched across the entire delta region.
Fang's homestay now runs at nearly full occupancy, with all eight dining tables regularly filled during meals. Guests range from study-tour groups from neighboring Shanghai and road trip travelers from Zhejiang's capital Hangzhou, to astronomy enthusiasts hauling telescopes from across the country.
Before dark-sky tourism took off, Gaotiankeng was a hollowed-out mountain village. Young people migrated to cities for work, leaving farmland abandoned.
Today, villagers are returning. Four other villager-operated homestays are in business, each generating annual turnover exceeding 100,000 yuan (about 14,820 U.S. dollars).
A local company has acquired and renovated 45 old, empty house buildings, preserving their original architecture. Of these, 16 were converted to high-end star-viewing homestays, while the rest transformed into a star-themed library, a teahouse, a restaurant and an art gallery, adding new vigor to the village's business.
The benefits extend beyond tourism. Vacant houses in the village attract rental inquiries, abandoned farmland is reclaimed and leased, and local specialties such as dried bamboo shoots become popular in the market.
The Hangzhou Astronomical Society has also set up a permanent meteor-monitoring station there. On the mountaintop, an astronomy museum, equipped with professional instruments and a dome theater, stands alongside a dedicated stargazing camping base.
Dou Chuang, the museum's curator, leads astronomical study tours. During the Perseid meteor shower earlier this year, Dou delivered on-site observation sessions for student groups, showing visitors why preserving the dark sky matters.
Dark-sky tourism has driven coordinated development across the township of Changhong, which administers Gaotiankeng. Residents comply with light-pollution controls, and dark-sky protection rules have been embedded in village regulations.
In 2025, Changhong Township recorded more than 120,000 tourist visits and 8 million yuan in tourism revenue, up 28.5 percent year on year. Homestay occupancy reached 98 percent during holidays. Six villages achieved collective operating income above 500,000 yuan, and two surpassed 1 million yuan.
This year, Fang renovated the second floor of his homestay into three guest rooms with private bathrooms and star-gazing skylights, all ideas from guests expecting to watch meteor showers from bed.
As dusk fell, after checking room reservations and informing guests about the weather, Fang lounges back into his old bamboo chair in the courtyard, while soft breeze stirring under the starry night. ■

Punjab Chief minister Bhagwant Singh Mann’s government has expanded its ‘Yudh Nashean Virudh’ anti-drug campaign beyond a conventional police crackdown, combining action against drug networks with prevention in schools, youth engagement, community vigilance and treatment for people battling addiction.The government said the campaign seeks to make it harder to sell drugs, easier for citizens to report peddling, prevent young people from falling into addiction and ensure those affected can access timely treatment. The strategy brings police, teachers, students, community volunteers and health workers into a coordinated anti-drug effort.Between March 2025 and September 2026, Punjab’s Anti-Narcotics Task Force registered 61,824 FIRs and arrested 81,433 people. Authorities seized 3,918 kg heroin, 991 kg opium, 47 tonnes poppy husk, 1,416 kg ganja and 65 lakh tablets and capsules during the period. Punjab Police also conducted 79,293 public meetings to strengthen community participation in the campaign.The government has simultaneously taken the prevention campaign into schools. A 14-week anti-drug curriculum is being taught to 7.5 lakh students across 3,600 schools through trained teachers.
In the first phase, nearly 25,000 teachers from 13 districts are being sensitised, with 7,000 already trained in Amritsar, Tarn Taran and Fazilka. The programme aims to help teachers identify early signs of mental-health distress, vulnerability to substance abuse and possible intervention.Youth programmes are also being used to address peer influence and social acceptance of drugs. Schools have been given year-long activity calendars, while colleges are promoting cultural festivals, mental-health clubs, sports and other activities to encourage healthier lifestyles and reduce the stigma around recovery.At the grassroots level, around 1.25 lakh people have joined nearly 15,000 Village and Ward Defence Committees. More than 50,000 members have been trained to use the Nasha Mukti App to report drug-related information and connect people seeking help with government services.
Since its launch on March 1, 2025, the safe Punjab whatsApp helpline has received more than 51,000 citizen tip-offs, which the government said helped police make over 25,000 drug-related arrests.The government has also expanded treatment infrastructure, with Punjab currently having 547 OOAT centres, 219 de-addiction centres and 91 rehabilitation centres. Government facilities have been revamped, health workers trained and skilling and creative activities introduced at treatment centres.Admissions to government de-addiction and rehabilitation centres rose from over 12,200 in 2024 to nearly 34,000 in 2025, an increase of more than 170%, according to the government. The figures indicate a sharp rise in people seeking institutional support as Punjab seeks to combine enforcement with prevention, community action and rehabilitation in its fight against drugs.

Traditional safeguards for AI agents are unraveling: UN panel
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
17:29:34 CST
18:29:34 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- A UN panel on artificial intelligence (AI) warned on Monday that traditional safeguards for AI agents are unraveling.
The Independent International Scientific Panel on AI issued the warning in its first thematic brief, an assessment of July's breach of U.S. AI company Hugging Face's systems by AI agents under evaluation at OpenAI, another U.S. AI company.
The panel finds that stopping this incident is no assurance that humans can reliably keep AI agents under control today, particularly as they become more capable, harder to monitor and better at finding loopholes or hiding their activity.
"The default interpretation and immediate lesson is that basic cybersecurity practices were overlooked, and safeguards are not advancing at the pace of capabilities," said the panel in a press release. "The more insidious and grave concern is that current training methods can lead agents to adopt goals of their own, knowingly violate safety instructions, and conceal their actions."
It leaves open whether safeguards designed today will work once agents can understand them and plan around them. In simple terms, the traditional model of safeguarding is unraveling, said the panel.
The panel also finds that the governance challenge is moving from AI models to AI agents. A local failure could spread across organizational and national boundaries. AI safety may be becoming a matter of collective security as well as corporate governance.
The panel, established by the UN General Assembly, is made up of 40 independent experts from all regions.
The panel is publishing an advance unedited version to make the brief available to world leaders gathering in New York for this year's General Assembly's High-level Week. ■

Ten lions found dead in suspected poisoning at Tanzania reserve

Ten lions found dead in suspected poisoning at Tanzania reserve
Ten lions have been found dead at Tanzania’s UNESCO-listed Ngorongoro Conservation Area, prompting an investigation into suspected poisoning, the authorities have said.
The animals were discovered on Friday in the Ndutu area of Endulen Ward, according to a notice issued by the Ngorongoro Conservation Area Authority (NCAA). “Preliminary findings suggest the animals may have died after ingesting poison,” the agency said.
The NCAA has launched an expert investigation to establish the cause of the deaths and identify those responsible. It did not disclose the animals’ ages or sexes or say what substance may have been involved.
Poisoning is a recurring threat to large carnivores in East Africa and is frequently associated with conflict between predators and livestock owners. However, the authorities have not established whether the latest deaths resulted from deliberate poisoning or identified a possible motive.
In 2018, six lions and 74 vultures died after feeding on a poisoned cattle carcass near Tanzania’s Ruaha National Park. Conservation groups said the poisoning appeared to have been carried out in retaliation after lions attacked livestock, although no suspect was identified.
The latest deaths come a month after 18 elephants were found dead in Kenya’s Amboseli ecosystem near the Tanzanian border. Preliminary tests indicated possible exposure to a toxic substance. Four suspects were arrested and later released on bail pending further investigation. In January, six lions and more than 30 vultures were killed in a poisoning incident in Kenya’s Kitenden Conservancy, also near the Tanzanian border.
Tanzania has an estimated 17,200 lions, the world’s largest national population, according to a 2024-2025 wildlife census released by the Tanzania Wildlife Research Institute in June. Around 5,844 live in the northern tourism circuit, which includes Ngorongoro, Serengeti, Tarangire and Lake Manyara.
Ngorongoro is a UNESCO World Heritage Site where ethnic Maasai pastoralists coexist with lions, elephants, buffaloes, black rhinos and other wildlife.
The Tanzanian Tourism Ministry said the country received 993,771 international tourists during the first half of 2026. Attractions managed by the NCAA recorded 331,349 domestic and foreign visits during the period, an annual increase of 7.6%.

LGBT tolerance slumps in the Netherlands as debate turns vicious
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:26:37 UTC
18:26:37 KST

LGBT tolerance slumps in the Netherlands as debate turns vicious
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Less than a quarter of schoolboys in the Netherlands have a positive view of homosexuality, almost half the proportion of four years ago, according to a Europe-wide survey.
The HBSC (Health Behaviour in School-Aged Children) poll found that just 22% of boys aged 12 to 16 had a positive view of homosexuality, compared to 40% the last time the survey was carried out in 2021.
Gonneke Stevens, professor of Social and Behavioural Sciences at Utrecht University, said there was a “worrying turn in the trend” after decades of growing acceptance of same-sex relationships.
“In recent years sexual diversity has been increasingly questioned by leading figures in society, including politicians,” said Stevens, who led the Dutch research team in collaboration with the Trimbos mental health institute.
The COC, which campaigns for LGBGTI rights in the Netherlands, described the findings as a “frightening development.” Director Marie Ricardo said: “We badly need the young generation for a free country in which everyone can be themselves.”
The survey found girls were still more accepting of homosexuality than boys, but the proportion had fallen from 78% to just over half (51%) since 2021.
Manosphere
Stevens said there was a clear link between deepening intolerance and the rise of trends on social media such as the “manosphere”, which provides a platform for aggressive and discriminatory messages about women and gays.
“The fact is that in recent years young people have been exposed to these views and that in the same period they have taken a more negative view of homosexuality.”
Hardline conservative organisations have also pushed back against efforts to promote tolerance in education by promoting spurious links between homosexuality and paedophilia.
In 2023 children’s writer Pim Lammers had to go into hiding after receiving death threats when his novel De Boer en de Dierenarts (“The farmer and the vet”), about a same-sex relationship, was targeted by the radical Catholic organisation Civitas Christiana after he was asked to write a poem for children’s book week.
The sex education institute Rutgers, which organises the annual “Week van de Lentekriebels” (Spring Fever Week), won a court case against Civitas Christiana banning it from making false statements or publishing its “black book”, listing people and organisations that it accuses of “sexualising” children. The judgment was upheld by the Court of Appeal in May.

Google hit with €403M privacy fine over handling of user location data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:26:18 UTC
18:26:18 KST

The Irish data privacy authority fined Google €403 million on Monday over how it has been gathering location data from users.
This is the fourth largest fine ever issued by the Irish regulator and its first major penalty against Google. Ireland is charged with enforcing the European Union’s privacy rules against many of the world’s tech giants that have their European headquarters in Ireland.
The decision concludes an inquiry that was opened in 2020 by the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC), following complaints from consumer organizations across the EU over how Google processed people’s location data and the transparency around that processing.
Advertisement
Google infringed the General Data Protection Regulation, the EU’s landmark laws, on four counts, said Ireland’s three privacy commissioners Des Hogan, Dale Sunderland and Niamh Sweeney. The issues concerned how Google processed and retained location data in its Web & App Activity, Location History and Location Accuracy functions, as well as transparency.
The complaints from consumer groups alleged that Google had used dark patterns and unfair practices to incite users to enable features that shared their location data.
The Irish DPC has three other ongoing large-scale investigations against Google. Those are examining data processing by Google’s PaLM2 AI model, the company’s personalized advertising system, and Google’s account sign-up process.
Google spokesperson Mathilde Méchin said in a comment: "This case centers around historical policies that have since been updated. From 2019 onward, we’ve significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple.”
Agustín Reyna, director general of BEUC, said in a comment: “The decision is good news for consumers, as it holds Google accountable and confirms the illegality of the way the tech giant obtained consent to use peoples’ location data. However, the time needed to come to this conclusion is disproportionate with the seriousness of the infringement ... Consumers’ fundamental rights need to be upheld faster and better."
This article was updated to include comments from Google and BEUC.

What kills Schrödinger’s cat? Gravity may not be the answer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:24:50 UTC
18:24:50 KST

What kills Schrödinger’s cat? Gravity may not be the answer
A deep-underground experiment found no sign that gravity erases quantum weirdness in the way a famous decades-old theory predicted.
- Date:
- September 21, 2026
- Source:
- Foundational Questions Institute, FQXi
- Summary:
- Physicists have put a decades-old idea about why the strange rules of quantum mechanics disappear in our everyday world to one of its toughest experimental tests yet. Deep beneath Italy’s Gran Sasso mountain, researchers searched for an extremely faint radiation signal predicted by a theory suggesting that tiny fluctuations in spacetime, caused by gravity, gradually destroy quantum superpositions. After 62 days of measurements with a highly shielded germanium detector, they found no such signal.
- Share:
At some point between the tiny world of particles and atoms and the much larger world we experience every day, quantum behavior appears to fade away.
Quantum mechanics allows particles to exist in combinations of possible states, a phenomenon known as superposition. That strange feature inspired Schrödinger's famous thought experiment involving a cat that is both alive and dead until it is observed. Yet objects in the everyday world do not behave that way.
Physicists call the loss of these distinctly quantum effects decoherence. Exactly why decoherence happens, and whether gravity plays a role, remains one of the major open questions in fundamental physics.
Now, a new experiment supported by FQxI has eliminated one prominent explanation involving gravity. The findings were published in the New Journal of Physics in June 2026.
"One of the deepest questions in modern physics is why the strange quantum behavior that governs atoms and elementary particles seems to disappear in the macroscopic world we experience every day," says FQxI member Catalina Curceanu, director of research and spokesperson for the VIP Collaboration at the National Laboratory of Frascati of the National Institute for Nuclear Physics (INFN-LNF) in Italy.
Testing Gravity's Role in Quantum Decoherence
The experiment was carried out at the INFN Gran Sasso National Laboratory (INFN-LNGS), the world's largest underground laboratory devoted to fundamental physics.
Researchers focused on a model proposing that gravity itself could help destroy quantum superpositions.
According to Einstein's general theory of relativity, massive objects curve the fabric of spacetime. In the 1960s, Hungarian theoretical physicist Frigyes Károlyházy suggested that spacetime may also undergo tiny, unavoidable fluctuations.
In his model, those fluctuations would gradually disrupt quantum superpositions. That process could help explain why large objects do not remain in the strange combinations of states allowed by quantum mechanics, such as the dead-and-alive situation imagined in Schrödinger's cat thought experiment.
Károlyházy's idea has continued to attract attention and was recently revived, refined and reformulated by FQxI's Angelo Bassi and colleagues.
Searching for a Faint Radiation Signature
The predicted spacetime fluctuations cannot be detected directly. But if they exist, they should have a measurable side effect.
They would cause electrically charged particles to move and accelerate randomly. In turn, those particles should emit extremely faint electromagnetic radiation.
Detecting such a weak signal is difficult because it could easily be buried beneath radiation from other sources, including cosmic rays.
That is why Gran Sasso is so useful. The laboratory sits beneath 1.4 kilometers of radiation-dampening rock, which blocks much of the background interference that would otherwise complicate the search.
"The natural shielding provided by the rock creates one of the quietest environments on Earth for detecting extremely rare physical phenomena," says Curceanu.
The researchers used a detector built around a coffee-mug-sized piece of high-purity germanium crystal, protected by additional layers of copper and lead.
They gathered data for 62 days, then removed the amount of background radiation they expected to see. What remained was compared with the radiation pattern predicted by the Károlyházy model.
The result was simple: no signal appeared.
A Major Theory Takes a Hit
The finding does not prove that gravity has nothing to do with quantum decoherence.
Instead, it rules out one important version of that idea and gives physicists tighter boundaries for future theories connecting gravity with quantum mechanics.
"This absence of a signal is itself a major scientific result," says Curceanu. "By ruling out one of the oldest and most natural gravity-induced decoherence models, this work narrows the search for the theory describing the interplay between gravity and quantum mechanics, bringing us one step closer to understanding one of the deepest mysteries in fundamental physics."
From Quantum Theory to Testable Physics
Károlyházy's model is based on the idea that nature may impose a fundamental limit on how precisely we can determine the position of an object or measure a distance.
Since the model was proposed, similar ideas have appeared in several modern attempts to unite gravity and quantum mechanics, including string theory and loop quantum gravity.
"Every quantum gravity approach ends up with predicting the existence of a minimal length connected to the uncertainty in the measurement of spacetime," says Kristian Piscicchia, a quantum physicist at the Enrico Fermi Research Center/INFN/VIP, in Italy, and the experimental lead on the new study.
Quantum gravity is often viewed as a subject that lies far beyond the reach of present-day experiments. But this study adds to growing evidence that at least some predictions involving both gravity and quantum mechanics can already be tested.
"Precision experiments are now reaching a level of sensitivity where they can test ideas that, until recently, belonged almost exclusively to the realm of theoretical speculation," says Curceanu. "As sensitivity improves, the boundary between theory and measurement continues to move, opening new possibilities for discovering the fundamental principles that govern our universe."
The research was supported by the Foundational Questions Institute, FQxI, through the Consciousness in the Physical World program.
"The type of research that FQxI is encouraging brings teams together across generations, across boundaries, across disciplines," says Curceanu. "It really can act as incubators of new ideas."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Foundational Questions Institute, FQXi. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Nicola Bortolotti, Kristian Piscicchia, Alessio Porcelli, Matthias Laubenstein, Simone Manti, Antonino Marcianò, Federico Nola, Catalina Curceanu. Experimental exclusion of a generalized Károlyházy gravity-induced decoherence model. New Journal of Physics, 2026; 28 (6): 064511 DOI: 10.1088/1367-2630/ae774c

Russia Claims Election Systems Hit by Cyberattacks During First Parliamentary Vote Since 2022
Russian authorities claimed on September 19 that electronic voting systems and communications infrastructure had been attacked during the country's three-day parliamentary election, the Kyiv Independent reported on September 20.
According to the outlet, the vote is Russia's first since it launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and the first to organize balloting in temporarily occupied parts of four Ukrainian regions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The election is taking place with little genuine opposition, as most anti-war candidates have been barred from running and the ruling United Russia party dominates the political system. Russia also declined to invite OSCE election observers, a decision the organization stated violated Moscow’s commitments and prevented independent international monitoring.
The Kyiv Independent noted that Ella Pamfilova, head of Russia's Central Election Commission, reported Moscow's online voting system had faced a major cyberattack overnight, with attempts to disrupt it being repelled. The outlet added that the claim could not be independently verified.
Russia's Digital Ministry separately claimed an attempted act of sabotage against communications infrastructure in the country's Far East, according to the report.
Officials stated the attempt had been stopped and communications restored without disrupting voting.
The outlet reported that Russia's Supreme Court removed the liberal Yabloko party from the nationwide ballot in August after a legal challenge to its registration.
Yabloko is the only registered Russian party that has openly opposed the war against Ukraine, though some of its candidates remain in individual constituency races, according to the report.
Voting for the 450-seat State Duma began on September 18 and runs through September 20, the Kyiv Independent wrote, with the Kremlin-aligned United Russia party dominating the lower house.
Russian election officials reported a turnout of about 45% nationwide by the morning of September 20, according to the outlet.
The temporarily occupied territory voting covers parts of Ukraine's Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions.
Ukraine has condemned the organization of Russian elections on temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory as illegal.
In a statement on September 14, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) urged residents of the temporarily occupied territories not to take part in the vote. The agency described the ballot as an illegal effort to legitimize Kremlin rule and gather support for Russia's ruling political forces.
The SBU traced the practice to the September 2022 pseudo-referendum staged across temporarily occupied parts of the same four regions, during which Russian authorities pressured residents to participate.
In 2023, the agency noted that Russia held pseudo-elections for its regional bodies on temporarily occupied land.
The Kyiv Independent added that the European Union will not recognize results from Russia-occupied Ukrainian territories, describing the voting there as a violation of international law.
The staging of votes across temporarily occupied areas of Ukraine began weeks before the nationwide ballot opened, with early balloting in Russian-held parts of the south starting on August 29 and early voting in temporarily occupied Donetsk on September 14.
Mobile polling teams, escorted by armed Russian servicemen and police, moved through settlements collecting ballots at residents' homes.
In the Zaporizhzhia region, the identities of soldiers killed in action were allegedly used to fabricate ballots for the ruling United Russia party. Clerical staff reportedly delayed death registrations so the names remained active, allowing ballots to be cast in occupied Melitopol, Berdiansk, and Tokmak.

LONDON, September 21. /TASS/. The International Federation of Robotics (IFR) estimated global sales of humanoid robots for industrial and professional service applications at around 7,000 units in 2025, Reuters reported after reviewing IFR data ahead of its official release.
IFR Secretary General Susanne Bieller told the news agency that humanoid robots still account for "only a small fraction" of the total number of robots worldwide. The IFR estimate is based on data from suppliers and national industry associations. It does not include humanoid robots for household or military use, while medical robots are also classified separately. Under IFR criteria, a humanoid robot is one that resembles a human and operates autonomously in environments designed for people, it does not necessarily need to have legs.

Can China turn its Iran ties into a diplomatic role ahead of Xi-Trump meeting?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:19:51 UTC
18:19:51 KST

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi in Beijing earlier this week, as Tehran looks to one of its closest international partners for support amid the continuing US-Israeli war on Iran.
The talks came days after Chinese President Xi Jinping called on BRICS countries to help broker an end to the war and just over a week before Xi is due to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington on September 24.
The timing has put Beijing’s role under the spotlight: China has repeatedly called for diplomacy and an end to the fighting, while maintaining close political and economic ties with Tehran.
But whether Beijing is prepared to use those ties to push Iran and the US back to negotiations remains unclear.
China’s close ties with Iran, alongside its own economic exposure to the war, could give Beijing a reason to push for an end to the fighting ahead of Xi’s meeting with Trump, according to Professor Garth Le Pere, international affairs analyst and Visiting Professor at the University of Pretoria.
“Given the close alliance between Iran and China, a reasonable expectation is that China will use President Xi’s forthcoming visit to Washington to try to de-escalate the war and tensions, especially since China is directly affected by the turbulence in financial and energy markets besides being the largest consumer of Iran’s crude oil,” Le Pere tells TRT World.
“China has projected itself as a neutral player and is trying to play the role of a trusted interlocutor, albeit rather ambivalently,” he adds.
During his meeting with Araghchi, Wang called on Iran and the US to exercise restraint, return to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding and rebuild a negotiating mechanism based on agreements reached so far.
He also called for substantive consultations between the two sides and urged measures to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
That goes further than simply calling for an end to the war. But it still falls short of China formally taking on the role of mediator.
Beijing has not announced a mediation initiative or offered to host direct Iran-US negotiations. Instead, it is pushing the two sides towards a diplomatic process while leaving the negotiations themselves to Tehran and Washington.
China and Iran describe their relationship as a comprehensive strategic partnership, and Beijing has repeatedly opposed what it considers unilateral pressure on Tehran.
At the same time, the continuation of the war threatens the energy supplies, trade routes and economic stability on which China depends.
The Strait of Hormuz is a particularly immediate concern.
Wang’s call for its reopening came as the war continues to disrupt one of the world’s most important energy routes. BRICS leaders also called for maximum restraint and the preservation of global trade and energy flows in their New Delhi declaration.
Iran’s nuclear file and China’s economic ties
Beijing has consistently opposed unilateral sanctions against Iran and has backed a diplomatic solution to the nuclear dispute, while Washington has continued to increase pressure on Tehran.
At the same time, China has become increasingly important to Iran’s ability to withstand that pressure.
A US Congressional commission said this week that China remains Iran’s most important economic lifeline, particularly through its purchases of Iranian oil, while highlighting growing US pressure on Chinese networks linked to Tehran.
That leaves Beijing balancing its relationship with Tehran against its relationship with Washington.
China is keen to prevent Iran’s isolation from becoming even deeper, particularly as US sanctions continue to target Chinese entities involved in trade with Iran.
But Beijing also has an interest in preventing the war from becoming a wider confrontation that further damages regional trade and energy security.
The nuclear issue therefore sits alongside the broader question of what China is willing to do for Iran. Beijing can help Tehran withstand economic pressure and support its call for negotiations, but so far has stopped short of taking responsibility for bringing Washington and Tehran back to the table.
And Beijing is not operating only through its relationship with Tehran.
On Thursday, Wang spoke with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, with the Middle East among the issues discussed. According to Beijing, Wang again called for restraint, a return to the Islamabad agreement and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Le Pere expects Beijing to play a symbolic diplomatic role rather than take on the risks of directly mediating between Iran and the US.
“In his speech at the BRICS summit in Delhi, Xi did not suggest an explicit and activist mediation role but rather proposed a generic four-point plan for de-escalating conflict in the Middle East,” Le Pere says.
“The plan was centred on the essential pillars of China’s foreign policy, namely, peaceful co-existence, respecting national sovereignty, adhering to international law, and finding an appropriate balance between security and development.”
“This is in keeping with the strategic thrust and normative ethos of China’s foreign policy, which is to avoid getting embroiled in third-party wars, tensions, and conflicts; and then subsequently having to bear the burden of failure of any diplomatic endeavour,” he adds.
What does Beijing bring to the Xi-Trump meeting?
Wang last hosted Araghchi in Beijing in May, ahead of US President Donald Trump’s summit with Xi in the Chinese capital.
Wednesday’s meeting marked their second in-person talks in the Chinese capital since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28.
For Tehran, the meeting offered an opportunity to make its position clear to Beijing before Xi sits down with Trump. For China, it provided a chance to hear directly from Iran while preparing for a much broader conversation with Washington.
The US-Israeli war on Iran is expected to be among the issues on the agenda when Xi and Trump meet, alongside trade, Taiwan and other areas of tension between the two countries.
“Iran’s nuclear programme is expected to be an important item for discussion between Araghchi and Wang, especially since the US, France, Germany, and the UK have recently asked the IAEA to refer Iran to the UN Security Council,” Le Pere says.
“However, this is largely symbolic. Any attempted resolution to further tighten the already extremely punitive sanctions under which Iran is suffering is bound to fail because it will be vetoed by China and Russia,” Le Pere says.
“However, China has felt the brunt of the US sanctions package against Iran.”
“Under the so-called ‘Operation Economic Outcast’, there are a large number of Chinese-linked refineries, firms, and financing instruments that allegedly have direct dealings with Iran and hence, China could feel the effects of these sanctions,” he adds.
Beijing therefore has several interests to balance, according to experts. It wants to maintain its strategic relationship with Iran, protect its access to Iranian energy and oppose pressure that it sees as undermining its interests.
At the same time, it has an interest in keeping the war from escalating further and in preventing Iran from becoming another major source of instability in the global economy.
That gives China leverage, but leverage is not the same as mediation.
For now, Beijing appears to be using its position to push both sides toward diplomacy while keeping room to manoeuvre.

Estonian scientists say AI development should be slowed down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:18:00 UTC
18:18:00 KST

Estonian scientists say AI development should be slowed down
Recent incidents involving AI systems acting autonomously have intensified calls for stronger oversight, with researchers warning that safeguards must keep pace as the technology becomes increasingly capable.
Recently, there have been several cases in which AI agents have acted on their own while carrying out tasks, breaking into other systems or attempting to exploit security vulnerabilities.
Developments following these incidents have moved quickly. Calls for restrictions on AI are no longer coming only from critics, but also from some of the companies developing the technology.
"We are clearly at a point today where there is enormous potential, but also real risk," OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman said.
Few issues are capable of bringing political opponents together around a common goal in the United States. Yet this week in Washington, both Sen. Bernie Sanders and former Donald Trump ally Steve Bannon called for stronger oversight of AI.
"I think Sen. Sanders gave a good overview of the risks. Obviously, we have quite different views of the U.S. president, but we're trying to rise above party politics and we have to do that," Bannon said.
Estonian researchers attending an AI conference in Washington said there is currently no certainty that artificial intelligence far more capable than humans could be kept under control.
"If we keep building increasingly intelligent AI systems without limits, then, based on where things stand today, we don't know how to control an AI that is vastly more intelligent than humans. Until we have better methods of control, we shouldn't build such systems," University of Tartu Professor of Artificial Intelligence Meelis Kull said.
"Slowing the development of these large super-systems would be somewhat beneficial in every respect because it would reduce the major risk and give us time to do something about it, while also giving the economy and society time to adapt," Tallinn University of Technology Professor of Applied Artificial Intelligence Tanel Tammet said.
Superintelligence is the term used for a so far hypothetical form of AI that would be more intelligent than humans in almost every field. Jacob Coxon, who helped train large AI models but recently quit, has also warned of the danger, saying that if development continues on its current path, artificial superintelligence will soon be a reality and science fiction films such as "The Terminator" could become real. And people are genuinely afraid.
"For comparison, if someone rides a motorcycle throughout their life, their risk of dying from it is about 1 percent. In other words, many people think the probability that artificial intelligence could cause all of humanity to go extinct — not one person, but everyone — is at least five times higher, perhaps even more. Some think the probability is above 10 percent. That's actually very concerning and these aren't just a few isolated individuals at AI companies saying this; they include academics conducting research," Eesti.ai advisory council member Risto Uuk said.
Setting limits on the development of artificial intelligence is therefore essential to reducing these fears and risks. The European Union has already introduced rules for AI, but a global agreement is needed.
"China already has its own regulations, Korea, for example, has adopted some things from the European Union, Brazil — regulations are starting to emerge everywhere. The next step would be for us to come together globally and discuss what kind of agreement we could reach," Uuk said.
Estonia can influence the development of AI more than is often assumed, both through the European Union and at the individual level.
"Europe actually has an enormous amount of power and influence over these technology companies because the European market is very large. The European Union can theoretically say that if you don't follow proper safety practices, if you don't ensure security and safety, you don't get access to our market. The same applies to Estonia because Estonia is an EU member state," Uuk said.
"I would like Estonians to lose this sense of helplessness. There is a great deal we can have a say in and at the individual level, we can vote and elect politicians who are concerned about artificial intelligence. We can learn about artificial intelligence ourselves, use it and see how it can be beneficial and how it can be harmful. There are all sorts of things we can do, so there is no reason for us to adopt a position of hopelessness," Uuk added.
This is all the more relevant because, paradoxically, AI itself can help mitigate the risks associated with AI.
"If we were to say that we shouldn't use AI, we'd be putting ourselves in an especially difficult position. We should actually try to make the greatest possible use of AI in our activities and economies and get involved with it because that will at least keep us near the leading edge of this wave," Tammet said.

In the United States, fishermen accidentally caught an American clone of the Iranian Shahed drone near an Air Force base

In the United States, fishermen accidentally caught an American clone of the Iranian Shahed drone near an Air Force base
Kyiv • UNN
Fishermen near Eglin Air Force Base accidentally found a U.S. LUCAS drone in the sea. The aircraft fell during U.S. Air Force testing.
The crew of a civilian fishing boat off the coast of Florida accidentally hauled a U.S. Air Force military drone out of the sea. The aircraft turned out to be a LUCAS drone—an American clone of the Iranian Shahed-136, which the Air Force lost during tests near Eglin Air Force Base. CNN reports, writes UNN.
Details
Hot Spots Charters, a company that organizes fishing tours from Pensacola, reported the unusual catch on Facebook. Its captain, Daniel Arseneau, posted a photo of the aircraft alongside the traditional catch, praised the crew for six successful hours at sea, and jokingly suggested that the drone’s owner call the company.
According to media reports, the discovery was made near Eglin Air Force Base, home to the 96th Test Wing. A base spokesperson confirmed to The War Zone that tests had been conducted there and that a test vehicle had fallen during them.
The fisherman, who appeared not to be bothered in the slightest by the discovery, told the publication that he spotted the drone by chance when the vessel was in open water and the drone was drifting on the surface.
It is likely that this was an FLM 136, an American copy of the Iranian Shahed 136, which has become one of the key weapons in the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Late last year, the U.S. Air Force announced that it had replicated the Iranian design, naming such aircraft LUCAS, an acronym for Low-Cost Unmanned Attack System.

Japan steps up measures to eradicate longhorn beetles to protect cherry trees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:16:58 UTC
18:16:58 KST

Aamir Latif
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
Japan is stepping up measures to control the growing population of longhorn beetles that are devouring cherry trees, local media reported on Monday.
The country's Environment Ministry has requested 6.7 billion yen ($43 million) in the initial budget for the next fiscal year to eradicate the red-necked longhorn beetle and strengthen measures to protect trees, including plum and peach trees, from infestation, Tokyo-based Kyodo News reported.
The requested amount is 11 times the initial budget of 600 million yen for fiscal 2026.
According to the ministry, a further increase in the beetle population could cause agricultural damage, make it difficult to enjoy cherry blossom viewing in the spring, increase the risk of falling trees and affect ecosystems.
In July, Japan's environment and farm ministries set up a task force to provide local governments with technical and financial support in response to the nationwide damage.
The longhorn beetle is native to China, the Korean Peninsula, Taiwan and Vietnam, among other places.
Measuring about 2.5 to 4 centimeters long, the species was first confirmed in Japan in 2012 and has since been spotted in various parts of the country.
It was designated an invasive alien species in 2018 and is prohibited from being bred, kept, imported, sold or released into the wild.

Renewables help Türkiye avoid $21.5 billion in coal imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:15:09 UTC
18:15:09 KST

Türkiye generated 442.2 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity from wind and solar power over the decade spanning 2015 to 2025, according to the Energy and Natural Resources Ministry data.
By replacing fossil fuel consumption with renewables, the ministry reported saving $21.5 billion on imported coal while cutting about 354 million tons of carbon emissions.
Türkiye produced 11,847 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of electricity from solar and wind power in 2015, substituting electricity that could have been generated using imported coal worth around $300 million and preventing 9.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions.
Between 2015 and 2025, the country generated 442.2 TWh of electricity from solar and wind energy. The ministry said this output eliminated the need for $21.5 billion worth of imported coal or $43.3 billion worth of natural gas imports that would have been required to produce the same amount of electricity.
The ministry added that replacing fossil fuels with renewable energy prevented about 354 million tons of carbon dioxide emissions when compared with coal-fired power generation. Based on natural gas-fired generation, the amount of avoided emissions was estimated at around 177 million tons.
Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said in a social media post that Türkiye would continue maximizing the use of renewable energy resources in line with its 2053 net-zero emissions and full energy independence targets.
Bayraktar said that electricity generated from wind and solar energy between 2015 and 2025 prevented up to 354 million tons of carbon emissions while also reducing fossil fuel imports worth tens of billions of dollars. He added that Türkiye currently ranks fifth in Europe and 11th globally in renewable energy investments and aims to increase installed renewable power capacity to 120,000 megawatts by 2035.

United Russia Set for Record Parliament Majority in First Wartime Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:14:27 UTC
18:14:27 KST

Russia’s ruling party, United Russia, is on track to secure a record number of seats in the lower-house State Duma following the country's first parliamentary elections since the launch of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, preliminary results showed Monday.
With 95% of the ballots counted, Central Election Commission (CEC) chief Ella Pamfilova announced that United Russia received 57.83% of the party-list vote while dominating single-member districts, where its candidates were leading in 208 of 225 constituencies.
Pamfilova said United Russia stands to capture around 355 seats in the 450-seat State Duma — surpassing its previous record of 343 seats set in 2016 and comfortably maintaining its constitutional supermajority.
Four other parties cleared the threshold to enter parliament: the Communist Party with 40 seats, the nationalist Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR) with 25, New People with 20 and A Just Russia with four.
Turnout reached nearly 60%, the highest for parliamentary elections since 2003, according to the newspaper Kommersant.
Independent analysts described the vote — which President Vladimir Putin framed as a test of public support for the war effort — as the most uncompetitive in modern Russian history.
At least 86 Ukraine war veterans are expected to gain seats in the latest convocation of the State Duma. Putin has touted veterans-turned-politicians as Russia’s “new elite.”
The liberal Yabloko party, the only party running on an anti-war platform, failed to secure any seat in single-member constituencies. In August, Russia’s Supreme Court blocked Yabloko from the party-list ballot, and its candidates running in single-member districts also faced exclusion and pressure from the authorities.
In concurrent regional gubernatorial races, Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov was re-elected with an official 99.85% of the vote.
The CEC said final official election results will be released by Friday at the earliest.

Germany news: Trial starts of ex-Transport Minister Scheuer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21

Germany news: Trial starts of ex-Transport Minister Scheuer
Published September 21, 2026last updated September 21, 2026
What you need to know
- Former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer stands accused of making false statements in connection with a failed scheme to charge foreign motorists highway tolls
- Germany has had one of the best cherry harvests in years
- Ever more people in Germany are using buses and trains for short trips, according to the Federal Statistical Office
- German car exports sank considerably in the first seven months of the year, new figures show
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz is under growing pressure after his CDU was badly defeated in two state elections
Here is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on September 21, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Automotive workers protest nationwide as industry suffers crisis
Protesters from Germany's automotive industry have called for action from the government and company managements to save their jobs and factories as the country's car production sector faces a growing crisis.
Tens of thousands of people are expected to take part in rallies, which, according to the IG Metall union — Europe and Germany's largest — will take place at more than 280 sites.
Car industry being driven 'into a brick wall'
Speaking at carmaker Volkswagen's Wolfsburg factory, IG Metall's chairwoman, Christiane Benner, who is also a member of VW's supervisory board, said: "Things have really hit the fan."
"Companies like VW, BMW, Audi, Bosch, Mercedes and Porsche were synonymous with fantastic cars and high quality," she said.
"Now, management is driving the industry at full throttle into a brick wall."
Benner called on the government to bring down energy costs, give financial help to suppliers to help them adjust to new challenges and use "Made in EU" rules to bolster domestic production.
Massive job cuts underway
Many observers put the blame for the current crisis on companies having started too late with the shift to electric vehicles, while others say China's government support for its own producers has led to an unequal playing field in the sector.
US tariffs have also done their bit to damage what is one of Germany's key industries, while domestic demand has weakened.
VW itself plans to cut 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade in what would be the biggest ever restructuring in global automotive history, while Mercedes-Benz and BMW are also reducing their workforces.
German car exports down in first seven months of 2026 — Destatis
In 2026, German exports of passenger cars dropped by 4% up to the end of July in comparison with the same period last year, new figures by the Federal Statistical Office showed on Monday.
It exported altogether some 2 million cars at a worth of €73.5 billion ($84.4 billion), 8.9% less than a year ago, with almost a third going to the UK, the US and Italy.
Cars with electric and combustion engines both saw an export drop of 2.9%, while the export of those with hybrid motors fell by 8.2%.
Imports of new passenger cars rose by 16% to some 1.3 million vehicles.
China takes first place for car imports
Chinese vehicles climbed to first place among car imports to Germany at 175,000 vehicles.
That made up 13.8% of all car imports and represents a rise of 120.9% compared with the January-July period in 2025.
It thus pushed the former import leaders Czech Republic and Spain to second and third place respectively.
The rise in Chinese imports was largely driven by hybrid vehicles (+36%) and purely electric vehicles (+66%), while imports of Chinese cars with combustion engines went down 9%.
Elections latest: Merz defiant after state poll drubbings
Friedrich Merz's position as chancellor is looking increasingly fragile after his Christian Democrats (CDU) failed to make it into the state parliament of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in weekend elections.
And that result came on the heels of the election in Saxony-Anhalt around two weeks ago, in which the CDU also put in a poor showing amid big gains by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
That, combined with his already very low approval ratings, means Merz is currently under huge pressure.
DW looks at his predicament and the broader fallout from the recent polls in this dedicated blog: Germany: Friedrich Merz fights for survival after election defeats
Germany brings in bumper cherry harvest
German orchard growers have harvested some 48,500 metric tons (53,462 US tons) of sweet and sour cherries this summer — 7.8% above the average for the past 10 years — new statistics show.
According to the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), some 80.2% of the harvest (38,900 tons) was sweet cherries, and 19.8% (9,600) was of the sour variety.
Pear growers also have reason to be content, with preliminary estimates putting the harvest of that fruit at 7.7% higher than the average over the past 10 years, though 3.3% down on last year.
The good fruit harvest comes despite Germany's grain production suffering greatly under the hot conditions during the summer.
Ex-Transport Minister Scheuer goes on trial for perjury
A perjury trial against former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer kicked off at the Berlin District Court on Monday.
Scheuer and his co-defendant Gerhard Schulz, a former state secretary, are accused of having lied to a parliamentary committee investigating a failed scheme some seven years ago to levy a highway toll on foreign motorists.
Both of them deny the charges made against them.
What are the charges against Scheuer and Schulz?
The two are accused of lying to the committee about having signed a contract with a company to run the toll operations despite knowing that the European Court of Justice (ICJ) was likely to declare the scheme illegal.
Scheur's Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of the Christian Democrats (CDU) currently led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, had devised a plan to levy tolls on all drivers but then compensate German motorists by reducing their motor vehicle taxes.
The scheme was shot down in 2019 by the ICJ for breaching EU rules.
But by that time, the Transport Ministry under Scheuer had already signed binding contracts with the operators who were to be tasked with executing the plan.
The German government was then forced to pay €243 million ($283 million at current exchange rates) in damages to the companies involved.
Jail sentences possible
The trial is planned to take place over 12 days, with a verdict expected on November 25.
If found guilty, the accused could face jail sentences ranging from three months to five years.
Welcome to our coverage
The DW newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn wishes all its readers guten Tag at the start of a new week.
Among the big topics of the day in Germany is the start of a trial against former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer in connection with a failed car toll scheme that cost the government hundreds of millions of euros some seven years ago.
He stands accused of making false statements before a parliamentary committee investigating the issue.
In more positive news, cherry (and pear) farmers have something to smile about this year: They have had their best harvest in years owing to some mild spring weather.
And we will also, of course, be looking at the fallout from recent state elections that have brought bad news for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

NATO general: Baltic states now much better defended than before
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:13:00 UTC
18:13:00 KST

NATO general: Baltic states now much better defended than before
Military security in the Baltic states has improved markedly since NATO developed a clear strategy and action plans, a senior NATO general said.
Lt Gen. John Mead, a British general and deputy commander of NATO's Brunssum Joint Force Command, also highlighted significant progress on logistics in an interview given to LETA.
Lt Gen. Mead cited the alliance's Deterrence and Defense of the Euro-Atlantic Area (DDA) strategy and clear action plans.
He said one of the most notable aspects of the DDA has been aligning NATO's regional plans with national-level planning. Mead added the alliance is developing guidelines for building military capabilities and for jointly defending every meter of territory — a collective and increasingly integrated effort — alongside joint surveillance conducted as part of day-to-day deterrence.
Mead pointed to Operation Baltic Sentry, launched in response to new threats, as proof of the approach, noting that no undersea cables have been cut since it began.
The general also cited the Eastern Sentry air defense operation launched a year ago as a further example, saying NATO is taking decisive steps, has robust plans, and is addressing capability gaps through continuous integration and joint exercises.
He acknowledged that noting short of a revolution is under way with respect to the alliance's armed forces, and that NATO must keep adapting while maintaining deterrence — and must feel uncomfortable about not moving fast enough.
Latvia and Estonia as small countries lack geographical depth, a challenge they must meet strategically. Mead noted NATO is working to neutralize this, stressing "tremendous" progress has been made on logistics, with much greater cohesion among the Baltic states and better alignment between NATO and national plans than had been the case in the past. Exercises in the coming weeks will also test direct communication with national operations centers, he said.
Mead also praised the level of innovation in the Baltic states, saying science, tech and innovation play an important role.
Mead said he sees no need to deploy more foreign troops to the Baltics. Instead, he said, regular exercises are needed to ensure NATO forces that are available can operate according to plan. Next year's Exercise Steadfast Deterrence will test force deployment, Mead added.
While the numbers of forces available is "sufficient," Mead said, their deployment must be validated and demonstrated in order to send a credible deterrence signal.
He referred to the first joint German-Dutch cooperation — leading NATO vigilance and day-to-day deterrence in Latvia and Estonia — as an important step, and said full deployment under some plans will take a couple of years to reach readiness.
Mead highlighted communications, information systems and data use as areas of current focus. He identified identifying an attacker as a challenge, noting the use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) as seen in Ukraine is largely revolutionizing military operations and air warfare.
The general closed by stressing unity: NATO is the sum of its member nations' capabilities and threats are constantly changing; the alliance must not give in to fear, he added.
It is important to remember dialogue is among the 32 member states as equals, and not between NATO and each member state on a bilateral basis. This defines the alliance's strength, he concluded.

Economic forecast predicts faster growth but higher public debt
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
12:12:20 EEST
18:12:20 KST

Finland’s economy has entered a stronger period of growth, but the recovery will not stop public debt and deficits from rising, according to a new forecast from the Ministry of Finance.
The ministry expects gross domestic product to grow by 1.6 per cent in 2026, 1.8 per cent in 2027 and 1.5 per cent in 2028. Revised statistics also show that output grew through much of 2024 and 2025, indicating that the recovery began earlier than previously estimated.
Growth has spread across several parts of the economy, while companies and households report improved prospects.
“The brake that prevented demand and output growing last year has lost some of its effect,” Director General Mikko Spolander said in the ministry’s statement.
The improvement does not extend to Finland’s public finances. The general government deficit is forecast at 4.2 per cent of GDP this year as defence equipment purchases increase. It is expected to rise to 4.5 per cent in 2027, driven in part by a widening gap between revenue and expenditure in local government.
The deficit is forecast to remain at 4.4 per cent in 2030. Public debt will reach about 90 per cent of GDP this year before approaching 98 per cent by 2030.
“The upturn in general government finances is expected to remain weak because the economic recovery will be insufficient to correct the structural imbalance,” Spolander said.
The forecast also points to a delayed recovery in the labour market. Employment continued to fall during the first half of 2026. Unemployment is expected to reach 10.3 per cent this year before falling below 10 per cent. The employment rate among people aged 20 to 64 is forecast at 75.5 per cent.
Stronger output should start supporting employment towards the end of 2026. Much of the improved GDP outlook reflects higher productivity rather than increased labour input.
Exports are rising as international demand improves, while imports are growing faster due to F-35 fighter deliveries and equipment purchases for data centres.
Inflation has increased due to energy prices, though the ministry expects consumer prices to rise by about 2 per cent annually during the forecast period. Wage increases and an expected employment recovery should support household purchasing power next year.
Data centres, defence purchases and energy projects are supporting investment and construction. Housing remains weak, with residential construction expected to start recovering in 2027.
One major investment is absent from the forecast. The projections were completed before Google announced plans to invest at least €13 billion in Finland. The projects are expected to increase investment in 2027 and 2028, though Spolander said they would also compete for workers with other projects.
Oil prices have risen above the level assumed in the forecast, which is expected to weigh on growth in 2026 and 2027.
Household savings leave room for stronger consumption, while weaker global growth remains a risk. The effects of US trade policy and the Middle East crisis have so far been less severe than feared.
Rising defence and interest costs, alongside tax cuts, will keep pressure on public finances. Economic growth and a one-off transfer from the State Pension Fund will slow debt growth through 2027, before the debt ratio starts rising faster again in 2028.

US watching Chinese marine presence off Alaska, Arctic Coast Guard chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:04:00 UTC
18:04:00 KST

US watching Chinese marine presence off Alaska, Arctic Coast Guard chief says
OSLO - The United States is watching China’s presence in its Arctic zone “very closely” amid concerns regarding the security of the US homeland, a senior US Arctic military official said.
So far in 2026, four Chinese research vessels have conducted work offshore in the US Arctic, compared to a total of five in 2025, Rear Admiral Bob Little, Commander of the US Coast Guard’s Arctic District, told Reuters.
The Chinese ships sailed in the maritime zones off the US state of Alaska, including the Aleutian Islands, into the Bering Strait and as far north as the North Pole, he said during a visit to Oslo to speak at a conference on Arctic security.
“Where I have responsibility, interest and concern is when they are operating in and around US sovereign space,” said Little.
“So inside of our exclusive economic zones, or over our extended continental shelf, we certainly have a security concern. And so those are the types of activities that we see that we’re watching very closely.”
The ships remained in international waters but had not notified the US of their presence in advance through diplomatic channels, as would be the usual practice.
“When we challenge them and query them as to the purpose of their activities, their response typically is either ‘we are conducting operations in international waters’ or ‘we are conducting scientific research’,” he said.
The concern is two-fold.
One is that China may be involved in scientific research focused on the mineral exploitation of the seabed in an area that belongs to the US, Little said.
The other is that these vessels conduct activity that might “provide them (the Chinese) with a military advantage or pose a security threat to the United States”, said Little, whose area of operations is nearly as vast as Europe.
China, which calls itself a “near-Arctic” state and wants to create a “Polar Silk Road” in the Arctic, has stepped up its presence in the polar region in recent years, sometimes in joint operations with Russia and sometimes alone.
While in Norway, Little discussed with international colleagues how they were dealing with similar activities by Russian research vessels.
“Whether it’s the Barents (Sea) or the Baltic (Sea), it’s easy to find examples of hybrid threats and activities,” he said.
“So I certainly watch that very carefully, because it’s the same nation-state that’s my neighbour on the western side of the Arctic,” he said, referring to Russia.
Moscow denies that its research vessels conduct illegal activity or that it poses any threat to US interests. REUTERS

U.S. Marines field counter-drone vehicles in Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:00:43 UTC
18:00:43 KST

- U.S. Marines with the 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit drove a Light Marine Air Defense Integrated System in the Middle East.
- The system uses two Polaris all-terrain vehicles, one for command and one with electronic warfare gear, to detect and disrupt small drones.
The U.S. Marine Corps has released a photo of Marines with the 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit driving a Light Marine Air Defense Integrated System, known as LMADIS, a mobile counter-drone system, in the Middle East on Sept. 2-6.
The caption says only that the photo was taken in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility, the command that covers the region.
The unit is deployed to a region at war. The war began Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, and the 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit left San Diego with the USS Boxer (LHD 4) Amphibious Ready Group in March. It has about 2,500 Marines. A ceasefire took hold April 8, but fighting flared again in early September.
LMADIS is built to detect, identify, track and defeat small drones that threaten forward forces. It consists of two Polaris MRZR all-terrain vehicles. One serves as the command unit, and the other carries an electronic warfare suite. The system combines radar, electronic warfare and command-and-control equipment. The radar finds the drone, and the electronic warfare gear disrupts the signals that link it to its operator.
In the version used in 2019, both vehicles carried a radar and one also carried a camera turret. The radar picks up a small drone at range. The camera helps operators confirm what it is and whether it is hostile. If it is, they use a jammer to cut the drone’s link to its ground control station, which can make it crash. The aim is to stop a hostile drone before it reaches the base being protected.
LMADIS is the light version of the Marine Air Defense Integrated System, or MADIS, which is built on Joint Light Tactical Vehicles. The light version is aligned to Marine Expeditionary Units, which are smaller than a Marine Littoral Regiment and have a wider range of missions. It served as a testbed and stopgap counter-drone system before MADIS was fielded, and Marine low altitude air defense battalions still use it.
The Marine Corps first saw a gap in countering cheap commercial drones in 2013, at the start of the fight against ISIS. LMADIS made its operational debut in July 2019, when Marines aboard USS Boxer used it, mounted on a Polaris MRZR, to bring down an Iranian drone. Boxer is again the flagship of the amphibious group carrying the 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit.
That drone came within about 900 meters (1,000 yards) of the ship as it sailed through the Strait of Hormuz on July 18, 2019. Pentagon officials said Marines jammed it electronically. Iran denied it had lost a drone. The MRZR sat on the ship’s bow, powered by a gasoline generator, and the Marines who trained on it came from the 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit’s aviation squadron.
The vehicles are light enough to work from an amphibious ship’s flight deck and to drive ashore, which suits a unit that moves between ship and shore in small groups. Since the war began, Iran has fired missiles and drones at U.S. military installations across the Gulf, Iraq and Jordan. Col. Chris Niedziocha, who commanded the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit in the same war, said this month that staying current on new equipment, much of it counter-drone gear, took up much of his Marines’ time. The 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit trained with rifle-mounted counter-drone optics in April.

"Too often, neurodiverse design is a marketing ploy"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:00:06 UTC
18:00:06 KST

"Too often, neurodiverse design is a marketing ploy"
Lazy attempts to frame interiors products as more inclusive for neurodivergent people are becoming too common, writes Ellie Foster.
Most of us would agree that increasing awareness around neurodiversity is important and overdue, with 15-20 per cent of the global population demonstrating traits of ADHD, autism, dyslexia and the like. It makes sense that interior designers pursuing a more inclusively built world are following the conversation closely, asking themselves to better accommodate those who interpret and experience space differently.
For better or worse, product manufacturers have been following along too. However, too often, neurodiverse design is merely a marketing ploy.
Is neurodiverse design just another gap in the market to exploit, similar to greenwashing before it?
Naturally, some contract furnishers will bristle at that accusation, and for specifiers aiming to envelope people up and down the spectrum it may also rankle. But recent industry events and product launches make it difficult for me to come to any other conclusion.
In the past three years, there has been no shortage of events championing "designing for difference" in my inbox; no lack of press releases pulling on the terms hypo- and hypersensitivity to explain that a task chair comes in both brights and neutrals.
More recently, the sheer volume of these kinds of emails has raised questions for me about honest intentions. Do this many manufacturers really care about making products that improve the wellbeing of all?
Or, is neurodiverse design just another gap in the market to exploit, similar to greenwashing before it? Having a heightened awareness of space myself, these are the same questions that have started to gnaw at my conscience in a big way.
For more than a few brands, the plan of attack has been to showcase how updated furniture collections soothe individuals overstimulated by clashing patterns and loud colours, and energise those rendered lethargic by muted tones and minimalism.
At last year's Clerkenwell Design Week, one commercial name hosted a showroom installation addressing the acute sensory needs associated with certain diagnoses. Once attendees had marvelled at the work, the structure doubled as a backdrop for a talks programme on how we can be kinder to neurodivergent employees and service users through the use of design.
The focus on colour overlooks the psychological and physiological impact that objects have on neurodiverse brains
The activation then linked to a new luxury vinyl tile collection – one that looked similar to the brand's previous lines, but professed to ease mental anguish nonetheless.
All that is to say, the event was good; well-intentioned, well-received. The tenuously linked PVC planks in Herringbone, Chevron and Checkerboard? Not so much.
The fanfare around ever-so-slightly tweaked product ranges rarely ventures beyond those two "H" words (hyposensitivity and hypersensitivity), which are almost exclusively used in the context of colour. The main outcome – for me, at least – is a subtle repositioning of said brand as the ethical choice, alongside an excuse to mass produce its current portfolio in a range of new and "progressive" hues.
The focus on colour overlooks the psychological and physiological impact that objects have on neurodiverse brains in other ways. Low-hanging light fixtures leading to feelings of claustrophobia; castor-mounted furniture causing emotional instability; chairs with too many components creating distraction or obsessive compulsions.
These are just a few topics that could broaden the conversation around neurodiversity in product design – and the fact that we're still accepting that additional Cobalt and Stone colourways are enough to prevent meltdowns only proves that the area remains chronically understudied.
I want to urge interior designers not to take things at face value
From where I'm sitting (and that's in a central Manchester co-working space revamped just a year ago), it seems obvious that often it's just a rebranding of the same old products. Neurodiverse-friendly lounge chairs come in the same kaleidoscopic fabrics that were once flogged in the name of "design versatility"; those with stripped-back aesthetics – at one time marketed to fans of wabi-sabi or biophilic design trends – are now prime for people overwhelmed by pattern complexity and vibrance.
Repackaging collections that already exist shows a significant lack of care for people whose entire worldview can be skewed by spatial discordance, as manufacturers continue to cash in on industry-wide conversations around diverse perspectives.
I want to urge interior designers not to take things at face value. To read between the lines on brands pushing a "designing for difference" rhetoric, to uncover whether these same brands championed neurodiversity before it became a global talking point.
It's also worth investigating whether neurodiverse individuals have been involved in the product design process at all or if, at the very least, the process was informed by talking to them directly.
It goes without saying that product and interior designers mutually aspiring for more inclusive interior settings is a positive thing, but the problem lies in the recent surge of stuff that overpromises and under-delivers. The risk is that marketing products in this way leaves neurodiverse occupants failed, and designers mis-sold.
Ellie Foster is an architecture and design journalist based in Manchester.
