ICE Shooting of Immigrant in Texas Under Investigation: What to Know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:00:04 UTC
18:00:04 KST

The Department of Homeland Security’s investigative arm is leading a probe into a federal agent’s shooting of an immigrant from Venezuela in Austin, Texas, on Sunday afternoon.
Protesters immediately gathered at the scene to denounce the latest instance of violence involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, with videos on social media showing them paralyzing traffic. Texas law enforcement was deployed to the scene to respond and attempt to disperse the gathering, CBS Austin reported, detaining multiple protesters and firing pepper balls into the crowds.
“I’m very angry about this,” Austin Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said in a press conference about the shooting, adding that local police were not involved in the incident, which happened during a traffic stop.
Watson said he was not surprised by ICE’s involvement, given “the nature of ICE and the way ICE is doing its business these days.”
Watson and other Texas Democrats have also called for independent investigations into the incident. James Talarico, who’s campaigning for a U.S. Senate seat, said he was “closely following” the reports and urged a probe that released available footage of the shooting. “Previous incidents have shown that this agency cannot be trusted to report all the facts,” Talarico said in a statement released to the media.
The District Attorney’s Office in Travis County, which includes Austin, requested to partner with city police in the investigation and for the federal government to cooperate in providing access to evidence. It added: “As has occurred in other jurisdictions, it is possible that this incident included violations of state law.”
Rep. Greg Casar (D, Texas) wrote a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and acting ICE director David Venturella seeking a congressional briefing on Sept. 28, and asked the agencies to publicly release all body and dash camera footage from federal officers present at the scene and recorded communications between agents before and after the shooting.
Casar and Watson claimed that ICE activity in Austin has increased in recent weeks amid President Donald Trump’s implementation of his strict anti-immigrant agenda. “It’s a disturbing pattern,” Casar said, “and it has got to stop.”
Here’s what we know so far.
What happened?
The shooting occurred near the intersection of Anderson Square and Research Boulevard in Austin. The Texas Tribune reported that Texas state troopers received a call at around 12:50 p.m. from ICE officials, citing Sheridan Nolen, a spokesperson for the state’s Department of Public Safety. The officials reportedly asked for help to pursue a blue Toyota Corolla.
But Nolen said that before the state troopers arrived, an ICE agent had shot a man, and upon the troopers’ arrival, they treated the driver of the Toyota Corolla.
Austin-Travis County EMS received notification from city police of a shooting around 12:56 p.m. CT, according to its chief Rob Luckritz. They identified a man who sustained a gunshot wound to the torso, with Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis adding that preliminary information pointed to a “small foot pursuit” happening before the shooting.
Authorities then added that the man was transferred to the Dell Seton Medical Center in stable condition.
What do we know about the people involved?
Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, an Austin immigration lawyer who said she had been hired to represent the man who was shot and his wife, identified the man who was shot as a 28-year-old Venezuelan named Wilber Rafael Garces Perez.
The Tribune reported, citing Lincoln-Goldfinch, that Perez had a work permit and had entered the U.S. legally. According to Lincoln-Goldfinch, Perez was delivering for DoorDash when the shooting occurred.
A DHS spokesperson said, without naming Perez, that the Venezuelan immigrant who was shot “illegally entered our country under the Biden Administration and had a final order of removal.” The man is stable and “in federal custody pending removal,” the spokesperson added.
In videos posted to her social media, Lincoln-Goldfinch said Perez’s wife had not been informed of her husband’s condition since and that she was turned away at the hospital’s premises before being informed several hours later that her husband was already in ICE custody.
“If ICE deports him, the key witness to their shooting disappears,” Rep. Casar posted on social media. “He must not be removed from this country, and he must receive proper medical care.”
As for the ICE agent, who has not been publicly identified, when authorities were asked about his whereabouts, Mayor Watson said: “We do not know that. But my hope would be that an agent that’s involved in an officer-involved shooting would not leave the city; certainly not leave the state.”
Is this part of a pattern?
Sunday’s shooting involving federal immigration agents follows another widely reported shooting in July. In Houston, an ICE agent shot and killed 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican national, while conducting a traffic stop. ICE said Salgado Araujo was not the intended target of the operation, though the DHS has claimed, without proof, that Salgado Araujo was in the country illegally and attempted to ram ICE vehicles.
Since Trump’s return to the White House, his Administration has deployed federal agents to Democrat-run cities around the country to carry out the President’s strict immigration agenda, and these agents have been involved in multiple high-profile violent incidents.
Among the first people killed in such operations was 23-year-old U.S. citizen Ruben Ray Martinez. A federal agent fatally shot Martinez in South Padre Island, Texas, on March 15, 2025.
Shootings involving federal agents, such as those of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, have sparked debate over how immigration policy is enforced nationwide. Demands for accountability over the shootings, mainly from Democrats, have triggered funding battles and partial shutdowns of the DHS.

In Europe, Today's Children Will Live Through Nearly Twice as Many Fire Weather Days Than Their Grandparents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:00:04 UTC
18:00:04 KST

Children born in Europe now will live through almost twice as much extreme fire weather as their grandparents (an 84% increase), according to a new study published today in the journal Environmental Research Letters.
A child born in Europe in 2025 will live through more than three additional years of extreme fire weather compared with someone born in 1950, the researchers found.
The largest increases are projected in the Mediterranean—a region already hard hit by wildfires. There, people born in 2025 are projected to face up to 2.5 times the exposure to extreme fire weather than those born in 1950—the equivalent of over five additional years of extreme fire weather over their lifetime. That’s for a scenario where global warming increases by 2.6°C above pre-industrial temperatures by 2100, as is currently predicted under current global climate and energy policies.
To map out potential outcomes, researchers used climate model projections for fire weather known as the Fire Weather Index. Fire weather refers to the hot, dry, and windy conditions that make fires more likely to ignite, spread faster, and become harder to suppress—conditions that are becoming more common due to climate change. They define extreme fire weather as days when the fire weather index exceeds the top 5% of days for that country over 1985-2014.
“It doesn't mean that there [will be] a wildfire on all of those days, but it does mean that the risk is much higher,” says Rosa Pietroiusti, lead author of the study and PhD researcher at Vrije Universiteit Brussel.
Portugal, the European country that has seen the highest proportion of its area burned in recent decades, can expect to see extreme fire weather days more than double under current climate policies, from 14 days per year from 1950 to 1970, to 32 days per year by 2100.
Each additional degree of global warming by the end of the century adds around 272 days of extreme fire weather to the life of a Portuguese child born in 2025. A child born in Greece can expect to see 473 additional days of exposure to extreme fire weather during their lifetime, while children in Spain and Italy will see 448 days.
Exposure to wildfire smoke comes with a number of immediate health impacts, including stinging eyes, wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath. Over time, long-term exposure can cause and exacerbate diseases in the lungs, and heart, and has been shown to lead to cognitive impairment and memory loss. Long-term exposure to wildfire smoke is also associated with higher risk of death.
The study notes that rapid measures to reduce emissions could reduce exposure in all regions. If we limit warming to 1.5°C by the end of the century, “a lot of exposure could be avoided,” says Pietroiusti. “While younger people will be more exposed than older generations under all pathways, every fraction of a degree of warming counts, and every fraction of a degree of avoided warming can reduce the hazard that we're exposing young people to during their lives.”
The world, however, has strayed far from that goal. A U.N. report published at the beginning of September found that the planet is set to pass the 1.5°C threshold for global warming set out in the Paris Agreement within the next few years. Optimistic scenarios estimate temperature rise peaking at 1.8°C, while other estimates predict even higher peaks.
Europe is the world’s fastest warming continent. Temperatures have risen by approximately 0.56°C per decade since the mid-1990s—more than double the global average.
This summer alone brought several severe heat waves to the continent, with the European Forest Fire Information System reporting that wildfires burned over 668,000 hectares (over 1.6 million acres) across the E.U., including Belgium’s worst wildfire in a century and the largest recorded wildfires in France and Spain since data collection began. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen recently proposed a new European Heatwave Plan as well as a future European firefighting fleet of airplanes to address the realities of climate change, calling this summer “the summer of truth.”
“We're really seeing that these conditions are not just climate model projections and simulations and results,” says Pietroiusti, “but they're really real world conditions and risks.”

After 8 Years in Space, ‘BepiColombo’ Is Finally Approaching Mercury
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

BepiColombo has been on a bit of an Odyssey. The space probe—named after an acclaimed Italian scientist who developed the “gravity assist” trick that enables interplanetary journeys today—was originally scheduled to arrive at Mercury last year. However, after a malfunction with the propulsion, the probe was forced to change course so it could reach Mercury at reduced power. As a result, the arrival date was pushed back by nearly a year, and now after eight years in space, BepiColombo is beginning its descent to low orbit around Mercury.
On September 3, ground control confirmed that the propulsion module had successfully separated from the rest of the craft, marking the final phase of the joint mission between the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). After a bumpy journey—reaching more than 200 million kilometers from Earth—transmissions from the probe indicated all went smoothly.
Mercury has only been explored twice before, both times by NASA probes. Because even without propulsion mishaps, Mercury is especially challenging to reach due to it’s position as the closest planet to our sun. When traveling towards the center of our solar system, a spacecraft is essentially “falling” from Earth towards the much greater gravity of the sun. That’s the easy part. The hard part is to not keep falling. Getting to Mercury therefore requires a lot of fuel not to travel there but to engage rockets to put on the breaks.
Spacecraft can also use the gravity of other planets as a means of slowing down, but that involves taking a more convoluted path, looping between celestial objects. To-date, BepiColombo has traveled approximately 6 billion miles (9.9 billion kilometers), swinging around Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times for a total of nine gravity assist maneuvers to control its velocity.
Furthermore, being so close to the Sun, Mercury’s surface can be intensely hot—over 800 degrees Fahrenheit or about 430 degrees Celsius. And because the small planet has essentially no atmosphere, temperatures drop to -290 degrees Fahrenheit (-180 Celsius) at night. BepiColombo therefore needs to survive not just these extremes, but the daily swings between them.
Once in position, BepiColombo will break into two separate spacecraft: the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), which will study Mercury’s surface and internal structure, and the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (dubbed “Mio”), which will investigate the planet’s magnetic field and tenuous atmosphere. This is the first time multiple probes will orbit Mercury simultaneously, with the goal of gaining a more comprehensive picture than any single probe could capture on its own.
Mio will enter a higher elliptical orbit oriented to circle across the poles. MPO will then lower its altitude further and is scheduled to reach its final orbit in March of 2027. Even after the probes take their positions, full-scale observations will not begin immediately. The probes must go through a series of procedures—such as the deployment of Mio’s essential sunshield—before conducting scientific observations, which are scheduled to begin in April 2027.
The two probes will attempt to uncover answers to much that remains unknown about the swift planet. Some key questions include why Mercury has an extremely large iron core relative to its size; why ice exists in permanently shadowed craters at the poles despite the scorching heat; why it’s the only rocky planet other than Earth to possess its own magnetic field; and the true nature of the mysterious depressions known as “hollows” that dot its surface.
Answers to into these questions are expected to provide crucial clues for how terrestrial planets—including Earth—formed and evolved within the solar system. Astrophysicists also plan to use precise orbital data from the mission to test Einstein’s general theory of relativity, because—due to its proximity to the sun—Mercury is an ideal testing ground for verifying the gravitational distortion of spacetime.

Bronze in Nagoya, but Iran’s basketball still has questions to answer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:59:00 UTC
17:59:00 KST

Bronze in Nagoya, but Iran’s basketball still has questions to answer
TEHRAN - Iran’s men’s basketball team left Nagoya with a bronze medal and, perhaps more importantly, a reminder of what this group can produce when its confidence, shooting and defensive intensity come together.
The 79-70 victory over China secured Iran’s first Asian Games medal since 2018 and the delegation’s first medal in Aichi-Nagoya.
 
 The result was particularly significant because of the manner in which it was achieved. After a disastrous 77-51 semifinal defeat to South Korea, Iran could easily have allowed disappointment to define the final game of its campaign. Instead, the team recovered from a 17-12 first-quarter deficit, improved its perimeter shooting and dominated the third quarter 26-15. Matin Aghajanpour led Iran with 21 points, while Arsalan Kazemi once again provided physical presence and rebounding. China, meanwhile, struggled to contain Iran from three-point range and committed 16 turnovers.
 
 That contrast perhaps tells the larger story of this Iranian team. Its ceiling is clearly higher than its recent inconsistency suggests. In Nagoya, Iran lost its opener to Qatar 59-53, then beat Chinese Taipei, Jordan and Bahrain before the heavy semifinal defeat to Korea. The bronze-medal game showed that the problem is not necessarily a lack of talent, but the team’s ability to reproduce its best level from one game to the next.
 
 That issue will become even more important in the coming months. Iran’s next major challenge is the FIBA Basketball World Cup 2027 Asian Qualifiers, with the fifth qualifying window scheduled for November 23-December 1.
 Iran is in Group E alongside Australia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Jordan and Syria, with the results from the previous round carried forward. The top three teams in each second-round group, plus the best fourth-placed team alongside host Qatar, will qualify for the World Cup.
 
 For coach Sotiris Manolopoulos, therefore, the Nagoya bronze is both an achievement and a warning. The medal can strengthen belief in a developing generation, but it should not hide the weaknesses exposed against Korea and during parts of the Asian Games. Iran needs greater offensive consistency, more reliable three-point shooting and better execution under pressure.
 
 The encouraging point is that the core of this team has already shown it can compete. The next step is turning occasional performances like the victory over China into a standard rather than an exception. The bronze medal has restored Iran’s place on the podium. The World Cup qualifiers will show whether this team is ready to build something bigger.

The elections, held on Sept. 20, were the first state polls in both regions in which 16- and 17-year-olds were eligible to vote.

The EU still cannot agree on sanctions against russia — France and Luxembourg are making matters more complicated with their demands
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

The EU still cannot agree on sanctions against russia — France and Luxembourg are making matters more complicated with their demands
Kyiv • UNN
France and Luxembourg are making demands regarding the EU sanctions list. The current restrictions on nearly 3,000 individuals expire on September 22.
EU ambassadors are once again considering the issue of sanctions against Russia today, September 21, targeting nearly 3,000 individuals and organizations. Time is running out – the current restrictive measures expire tomorrow, September 22, at midnight, and no further temporary extension is expected. UNN reports this, citing RMF24.
France is blocking the deal
France, the publication writes, "remains the biggest problem." Paris is demanding that Russian oligarch Alisher Usmanov be removed from the EU sanctions list. Officially, France cites national security considerations. However, Brussels is aware that Azerbaijan is pressuring Paris, promising to release two French citizens in exchange for a concession in the Usmanov case, the publication notes.
For some EU countries, however, the problem lies in the principle itself – they do not want the EU's sanctions policy to be subject to pressure from a non-EU country. If France succeeds in having Usmanov excluded, a precedent may be created, and other non-EU countries may try to use such situations as bargaining chips in the future, the publication explains.
However, in recent days, a middle-ground idea has also emerged. The Financial Times reported on the possibility of keeping Usmanov on the list but limiting some of the sanctions against him rather than removing him entirely.
This option may be more acceptable to some EU countries that do not want to revoke the entire sanctions list. An EU diplomat told RMF FM that this option was not officially discussed during the ambassadors' meeting on Friday, September 18.
Not only France
The French demand, the publication writes, complicates the situation, as other countries are beginning to put forward their own expectations.
From the very beginning, it was clear that Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico wanted Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman to be removed. Slovakia was the first to voice its objections. However, according to RMF FM, Bratislava will certainly withdraw its objections if France does so. In other words, if Paris gives in, Slovakia will not want to remain alone in blocking the entire deal.
However, another demand emerged on Friday – this time from Luxembourg. Luxembourg, the publication writes, does not want to lag behind France. If Paris succeeds in removing Usmanov from the EU sanctions list, Luxembourg wants Mikhail Fridman (who is involved in a dispute with Luxembourg over frozen assets worth $16 billion) to also be removed from the list. This demonstrates how quickly the French demand inspired other countries, which began putting forward their own demands, the publication notes.
What happens next if there is no deal
There is very little time for negotiations. The current sanctions list is valid only until midnight on Tuesday, September 22. EU countries have already agreed to a short one-week extension. This time, no further extension is planned, the publication writes.
"This means that if there is no unanimity, sanctions against approximately three thousand individuals and organizations will expire by Tuesday evening," the publication says.
For the EU, the publication notes, this will be not only a legal and political problem but also a very serious image problem. Therefore, it is difficult to imagine that the EU will be unable to reach an agreement, the publication writes.
Radio Free Europe journalist Rikard Jozwiak noted that EU ambassadors are once again planning to meet on this issue on Monday, September 21, at 14:00 Brussels time, following a morning meeting that produced no result.
"The deadline is tomorrow. It is likely that, in the end, at least Usmanov (and perhaps even Fridman) will be removed from the list, and that the sanctions will be extended for 12 months instead of the usual 6," Jozwiak wrote on X.

Morocco turns back the clock with permanent return to GMT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:55:20 UTC
17:55:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Morocco turns back the clock with permanent return to GMT
Morocco has officially returned to Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), ending nearly eight years of operating on GMT+1 as the government responds to public concerns over the impact of the additional hour.
Clocks were turned back by 60 minutes at 2am on Sunday, under a decree issued on 25 June and published in the official gazette four days later.
The change is permanent rather than a seasonal adjustment, with the new decree repealing a 2018 measure that established GMT+1 as Morocco's standard time.
Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch announced the decision in June, saying the government had taken into account public expectations and discussions within the governing majority.
According to Morocco's official government portal, Akhannouch said the move was also intended to address problems associated with the GMT+1 system.
Morocco had operated on GMT+1 throughout most of the year since 2018, temporarily reverting to GMT during the Muslim holy month of Ramadan.
The system had long been a source of debate in the country, with some supporters arguing that the additional hour had offered economic and organisational benefits and allowed greater use of daylight hours.
Others, however, complained about its impact on everyday life, particularly during winter, when later sunrises meant schoolchildren and employees often began their days while it was still dark.
The new decree formally repealed the October 2018 decree that introduced the permanent additional hour starting from 20 September.
The measure was signed by Akhannouch and Amal El Fallah Seghrouchni, the minister delegate responsible for digital transition and administrative reform.
The return to GMT will affect working and school hours, transport schedules, public services and businesses across the country.
It could also alter Morocco's time difference with some of its major economic partners, particularly European countries that continue to switch between summer and winter time.

Australia’s deaths to outnumber births by 2060s, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:53:31 UTC
17:53:31 KST

Australia’s deaths to outnumber births by 2060s, report says
Number of Australians aged 85 or older projected to triple by 2065-66, according to government forecast.
Australia will see more deaths than births by the 2060s, hitting a milestone already surpassed by advanced economies including Japan, Germany and France, according to a government report.
In its latest Intergenerational Report released on Monday, Australia’s Treasury forecast that the country’s population will hit 39.3 million by 2065-66, 1.8 million lower than projected in its last outlook in 2023.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump administration readies sweeping sanctions against ICC, reports say
- list 2 of 4Powerful explosions at Syrian army site near Aleppo injure at least four
- list 3 of 4Imran Khan’s family says three sisters detained ahead of Islamabad march
- list 4 of 4Massive explosions at Syrian army weapons depot near Aleppo
The Treasury said it expects population growth to average 0.9 percent annually over the next four decades, compared with 1.4 percent over the prior 40 years.
The number of Australians aged 85 or older is projected to triple by 2065-66, with immigration accounting for all population growth as the fertility rate falls to 1.34, the Treasury said.
Despite plunging birthrates, the Treasury said it expects the economy to more than double in size by the mid-2060s, citing productivity gains due to artificial intelligence and greater workforce participation by women and older Australians.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers said that while Australia’s economy faces serious risks due to the demographic shift, it also holds “substantial” advantages compared with its peers.
“The report confirms Australia is better placed and better prepared to deal with rapid change than most countries, but despite our advantages we cannot be complacent,” Chalmers said in a statement accompanying the report.
The outlook comes as Australia, whose economic growth is largely dependent on migration-driven population growth, grapples with deteriorating living standards amid a long-term slowdown in labour productivity.
Australia’s 20-year average for annual productivity growth fell to 0.8 percent in 2023-24, compared with 1.8 percent in 2003-04, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
Greater labour productivity allows an economy to produce more goods and services with the same amount of man-hours, raising economic growth and boosting living standards.
The Business Council of Australia on Monday expressed scepticism about the assumptions in the government’s economic outlook, saying it “cannot be taken for granted” that long-term productivity growth will rise to 1.2 percent due to AI.
The council, which represents more than 120 of Australia’s largest companies, said real gross domestic product per person is almost $2,000 lower today than expected under the 2023 forecast, due to weak productivity growth.
“This is not a problem that starts 40 years from now – Australians are already paying the price for our failure to lift productivity through lower living standards,” Business Council Chief Executive Bran Black said.
“Every man, woman and child in Australia is almost $2,000 worse off because we haven’t achieved the path anticipated in the 2023 Intergenerational Report.”
Tim Robinson, a research fellow at the Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research, said that while AI may improve Australia’s lagging productivity, the “extent and timing” of the potential gains are uncertain.
“We’ve had a flat level of labour productivity for around a decade. Without it, the Australian economy can’t grow as fast without running into inflation issues, and people’s living standards don’t improve by as much as they did in the past,” Robinson told Al Jazeera.
“If the Australian economy achieves the productivity growth assumed in the Intergenerational Report, that would be a marked turnaround,” Robinson said.

Three postponements in a week: who is delaying the hearing of the medical negligence case involving Odrex doctors?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:51:42 EEST
17:51:42 KST

Three postponements in a week: who is delaying the hearing of the medical negligence case involving Odrex doctors?
Kyiv • UNN
Last week, the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa was supposed to continue hearing the case involving Odrex doctors; however, all three scheduled hearings were postponed. Two of them were postponed at the request of the defense.
Last week, three hearings were scheduled at the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa in the case of private Odrex clinic doctors Vitaliy Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska, who are accused of improper performance of their professional duties, which, according to the investigation, could have caused the death of businessman Adnan Kivan. All three hearings were postponed, two of them following procedural actions by the defense. Why the case, which has been heard for more than nine months, has stalled again was examined by UNN.
One of the hearings did not take place following a motion by Maryna Bielotserkovska’s lawyer to postpone the hearing because of her participation in another court proceeding. The court granted the motion and scheduled the next hearing for September 18.
However, even then it was impossible to proceed with further examination of the evidence. Vitaliy Rusakov’s defense once again moved for the recusal of the presiding judge, Viktor Chaplytskyi. The court considered the recusal motion and denied it, but was unable to continue examining the merits of the case because Rusakov himself failed to appear.
These are far from the first postponements. Since the beginning of the trial, dozens of hearings have been postponed or failed to take place following motions or failures to appear by the defense. Presiding Judge Viktor Chaplytskyi responded to the defense’s actions and appealed to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar.
Oleksandr Sytnykov, a retired judge of the Supreme Administrative Court of Ukraine, explained to UNN that ensuring a case is heard within a reasonable time is the court’s responsibility. Therefore, if lawyers’ repeated failures to appear or motions effectively block the progress of the case, the presiding judge must respond to the situation, since responsibility for compliance with procedural time limits also rests with them.
Undoubtedly, if a lawyer’s actions lead to the protraction of proceedings, the judge must respond. The judge is subject to procedural time limits and may also face disciplinary liability for failing to comply with them. Therefore, a situation may arise in which, due to constant postponements, the judge themselves comes under scrutiny regarding compliance with the time limits
Andriy Misiats, acting chair of the Higher Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar, also draws attention to the possible consequences of systematic failures to appear.
A combination of failures to appear may indicate not an accidental violation, but a certain pattern of a lawyer’s behavior and their unfair attitude toward their professional duties
He emphasizes that a lawyer’s participation in another proceeding may indeed be a valid reason for failing to appear if it is genuine and properly documented. At the same time, being occupied with another case alone does not automatically mean that a hearing must be postponed. Whether the actions of the lawyers for the Odrex doctors show signs of a disciplinary offense must be determined by the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar.
Why are the accused afraid of hearing the medical expert’s testimony?
All these postponements are taking place at the stage when the court is to hear the medical expert. The expert is to provide professional explanations regarding the medical documentation, expert conclusions, compliance with treatment protocols, and the medical aspect of the question of a possible causal relationship between the doctors’ actions and the patient’s death. The guilt of the accused, however, is determined exclusively by the court.
In May, the expert had already appeared in court, but at that time Rusakov’s lawyers initiated the issue of changing jurisdiction. Now that the case has once again approached the examination of the key medical component of the evidence, a series of so-called "procedural maneuvers" has continued.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz begins the week weakened by his center-right CDU party’s bruising losses to far-right and far-left rivals in two regional elections.
Just 16 months in office, Merz has seen his approval ratings plummet while his party has suffered a string of regional election losses against the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which also leads nationwide polls.
Fighting speculation that his CDU/CSU bloc may try to oust him, 70-year-old Merz took the unusual step of addressing the nation on TV Sunday, just minutes after the first exit polls were announced.
Merz admitted that his CDU had suffered a "disaster" in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state – and that was before the CDU dropped below five percent there in the ongoing count, meaning it got kicked out of parliament altogether.
While the AfD came first there, the center-left SPD party looks set to continue governing the state by forming a coalition with left-wing allies.
After the CDU was also soundly defeated by a far-left Die Linke in Berlin, Merz charged that "trust in our country's institutions is waning" and being "actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right."
"What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness and patience," Merz said. "I will demonstrate this as CDU party chairman and, above all, as chancellor of our country."
Analysts saw it as an attempt to gain the advantage before another hailstorm of criticism comes raining down.
"His extremely early move shows that Merz is staking a claim to define the narrative," political scientist Oliver Lembcke of Ruhr University Bochum told AFP.
Lembcke labeled this "leadership from a defensive position – and an attempt to prevent a personnel debate with an uncertain outcome from gathering steam."
ING bank economist Carsten Brzeski said about Merz's unusual TV address: "Read the appearance for what it was, an attempt to choke off the speculation about his possible resignation that has been building in recent weeks."
After Sunday's CDU crisis meeting, the chancellor has also cleared his calendar for the following days and skipped a trip to New York for the U.N. General Assembly, to deal with potential aftershocks from the votes.
Merz has been fighting off rumors for weeks he may be ousted by his center-right CDU/CSU bloc.
Names of hopefuls for the top job that have been floated include Hendrik Wuest, state premier of populous North Rhine-Westphalia, and Markus Soeder, the Bavarian state premier and head of the CSU, the regional sister party of the CDU.
However, no contender has made an open move for the job – perhaps fearing the act of disloyalty could backfire, or intimidated by the tough task of trying to revive the party's fortunes during one of its worst-ever crisis.
When Merz took office in May last year, he vowed to reboot a flagging economy, rebuild the military to deter Russia and reduce irregular immigration to soothe voters' fears and lure them away from the AfD.
But the AfD now leads nationwide polls and Merz's personal approval ratings hover just above 10%, not helped by his occasionally blunt and abrasive comments.
The latest elections came two weeks after the far-right, pro-Trump and Moscow-friendly AfD also dealt a stunning defeat to the CDU in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.
The string of election debacles comes as Merz has struggled to push through promised economic and social welfare reforms with his coalition partners the SPD.
Under-fire Merz received some badly needed support from CDU power brokers last week when eight state premiers declared jointly that Germany needs "stability now more than ever" rather than "discussions about personnel."
They refrained, however, from issuing a personal endorsement for Merz.

Egypt rejects European plans for refugee camps in 'return hubs'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:48:02 UTC
17:48:02 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt rejects European Union's plans for refugee camps on Egyptian shores
Egypt has categorically rejected a proposal by some European countries to create camps for the reception of refugees and asylum-seekers in non-European countries south of the Mediterranean.
During a meeting with European diplomats in Cairo on 10 September, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said his country refuses the mere discussion of such a proposal under all circumstances.
Egypt, he said, bears a huge refugee burden already.
The Egyptian rejection comes as some European nations actively discuss and advance plans for the creation of what has come to be known as "return hubs".
These are deportation or repatriation centres that could receive irregular migrants and rejected asylum-seekers who cannot be returned to their home countries.
The European nations advancing these plans, including Germany; Austria; the Netherlands, and Greece, suggest creating the aspired centres in African countries, including in North African countries southern Mediterranean.
Discussions about the creation of such hubs come almost four months after the European Parliament approved new legislation that allows member states to establish these centres in non-EU countries via agreements, provided that human rights and international law standards are met.
The new legislation and the aforementioned discussions highlight the intensity of the refugee and asylum problem in Europe, analysts in Cairo said.
Nevertheless, the same discussions also come at a tough time for North Africa where the refugee problem is equally intense, being exacerbated by escalating conflicts in the Middle East and Africa, they added.
"These conflicts have put North African countries at the receiving end of a large number of refugees," Mona Omar, a former assistant to the Egyptian foreign minister and a retired ambassador, told The New Arab.
This refugee burden, she added, comes with heavy economic pressures, given the fact that North African governments have to provide these refugees with all types of support, including food, healthcare and education.
"These pressures translate into higher inflation, public anger, and consequently domestic security threats," she said.
Heavy burden
Egypt hosts millions of refugees already, highlighting one of the reasons for its rejection of European discussions about the establishment of return hubs in it, observers said.
Sitting at the crossroads of a series of regional and continental conflicts, the Arab country is one of the world's largest refugee receiving states, they added.
Leading economic Khaled al-Shafie said Egypt's reception of such a large number of refugees puts a drain on its economy.
"The refugee burden saps the economy in general by depleting state resources and overstretches basic services," he told TNA.
He attributed part of Egypt's current economic hardships to the same burden.
Egypt hosts over 10 million refugees and asylum-seekers who have converged into it from neighbouring and regional states, escaping conflict and economic hardships back home, according to the Egyptian government.
Despite this, only 1 million of the foreigners the populous Arab country hosts are registered with the United Nations refugee agency, with the Sudanese constituting the largest number of these refugees and asylum-seekers.
Egypt prides itself, meanwhile, on building its distinct refugee and asylum-seekers hosting model by allowing those foreigners to live side by side with its own citizens, sharing services offered to these citizens by the Egyptian government.
Over the years, however, the same pride has shrivelled up to give way to a feeling of the real burden of hosting such a huge number of refugees, comparable to almost 9% of Egypt's overall population of 120 million.
Such a feeling of being weighed down by the refugee burden also came as the Egyptian economy felt the heat from regional unrest, including because of the war in Gaza, the current war in Iran and the unfolding unrest in the Red Sea.
This might explain the Egyptian leadership's repeated plea for the international community to share with Egypt its refugee burden, analysts said.
Treating symptoms
Whether the Egyptian government's refusal to host refugee deportation centres will affect relations with the EU remains to be seen.
Apart from its geostrategic importance, its influence in the Arab and Islamic worlds, the presence of the Suez Canal in it, and its role in brokering regional peace, Egypt acquires part of its appeal to Europe from its ability to function as a barrier for waves of illegal migrants to Europe, specialists said.
Perhaps the same appeal was the reason why the continent was keen to strengthen its relations with Cairo in different fields over the years, something that has grown quite noticeable in the past few years, they added.
The two sides upgraded their relationship to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2024.
The first Egypt-EU summit was held in Brussels in 2025 to seek ways to help the economically-struggling Arab country, in the light of a 2024 multibillion dollar aid package.
The second Egypt-EU summit is expected to be held in Egypt next year. The third edition of the Egypt-EU Investment Conference is also expected to be held on the sidelines of the summit.
During his 10 September meeting with European diplomats, the Egyptian foreign minister said his country is committed to managing the refugee issue in a comprehensive manner.
He called for addressing the root causes of migration by advancing development, creating jobs and enhancing border management.
In Cairo, analysts believe that EU states are only treating the symptoms, rather than the cause by planning to create repatriation centres in other countries.
Addressing the root causes of the refugee problem, they added, would come through a more active European involvement in conflict resolution in refugee-sending countries.
"You can't prevent migration waves to Europe without putting an end to conflicts in countries sending these migrants or refugees," Ambassador Omar, the former assistant to the Egyptian foreign minister, said.
"This is why I believe the creation of the planned return hubs in non-European states will solve the problem as long as these conflicts keep raging," she added.

Russia election results show Putin’s party winning: What we know

Russia election results show Putin’s party winning: What we know
With more than 90 percent votes counted, Putin’s United Russia appears poised for a landslide win. But analysts say warning signs for the Kremlin may lie in the results.
Early results emerging from Russia’s first parliamentary elections since the launch of the full-fledged war on Ukraine show President Vladimir Putin’s party dominating the vote — an outcome widely predicted.
The election, which began on Friday and ended on Sunday to elect members of the lower house of parliament, the State Duma, is projected to see Putin’s United Russia maintain its hold amid a tightly controlled election in which opposition to the president’s policies remains limited.
Despite the lack of alternatives to United Russia, the Kremlin had positioned the vote as a chance for residents to have their say since the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and amid economic hardship.
Most antiwar candidates have been barred from the ballot. Those who did run from the liberal Yabloko party said they feared for their freedom after two senior party figures were handed long jail terms before the election due to comments made about the Russia-Ukraine war.
Still, Yabloko’s leader, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstrably spoiled his ballot paper, writing his party’s name and the slogan “For peace”.
Here’s what we know:
What have early results shown?
The state news agency TASS reported on Monday that 90.43 percent of ballots had been counted, according to data from the Central Election Commission (CEC).
The CEC found that, as of Sunday night, voter turnout stood just below 57 percent.
United Russia led with 57.86 percent of the vote, with 225 deputies apportioned from party lists. In single-seat races, another 225 lawmakers will be chosen, and Putin’s party is also projected to win most of them.
So far, no surprises or upsets have been recorded.
TASS also reported, citing the Ministry of Digital Development, Communications and Mass Media, that more than 3.6 million people voted online.
Those voting included residents of four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed in 2022 – Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhia – as well as those in Crimea, which was taken in 2014. The United Nations and most of the world do not recognise Crimea and other occupied Ukrainian regions as part of Russia.
How have other parties fared?
Other parties, like the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), the ultranationalist Liberal Democratic Party of Russia (LDPR), New People and A Just Russia, all of which largely vote the same way as United Russia in parliament, trailed behind in the early election results but were still on course to win seats in the State Duma.
The vote breakdown showed the CPRF at 13.84 percent, the LDPR at 8.9 percent, New People at 7.94 percent, and A Just Russia at 4.95 percent, according to TASS.
But while the early results paint a predictable outcome, the Berlin-based think tank NEST, cofounded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, said the vote could produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain.
NEST said the votes received by the CPRF and New People might in many cases amount to a silent protest against Putin and United Russia — even if these parties do not actually challenge the president on most issues.
“The consequences of the war are increasingly being felt within the country, and accumulated anxiety and frustration may translate into votes for the systemic opposition parties that the Kremlin has allowed to remain on the ballot,” it said in a note.
What were previous outcomes and when are final results expected?
During the 2021 State Duma elections, United Russia kept an absolute majority in the 450-seat lower house, holding 326 seats.
The CPRF was the second-largest party, winning 57 seats. It has remained a major force in Russian politics since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
The CEC will announce preliminary results and turnout on Monday, but the final results are unlikely before Friday, by which time all ballots are likely to be counted and other procedures required by law are completed, TASS reported.
What has Ukraine said on the Russian election?
Ukraine had denounced the election, which involved voters from the annexed regions, with officials calling it illegal.
Moscow accused Ukraine of attempting to sabotage the election after a wave of Ukrainian drone attacks targeted Moscow and other regions on Sunday, which TASS called the biggest of its kind since the war began in February 2022.
The attacks killed three people in the Moscow region and two in the Russian-held part of Kherson, including an election official, according to the regional governor and the election commission.
Moreover, a facility at Moscow’s oil refinery, which has been targeted before, was also damaged.
On Monday morning, a man was killed and three others were wounded in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Bryansk region, according to acting Governor Yegor Kovalchuk.

September 21, 2026
Pakistan conducted airstrikes on northeastern Afghanistan on Monday on what Pakistani security officials described as militant hideouts, resulting in some deaths.
The two neighbors reported conflicting casualty tolls.
The Taliban government in Kabul claimed that three people were killed as it accused Pakistan of bombarding "civilian homes," while the Associated Press news agency cited two unnamed Pakistani security officials as saying that 28 suspected militants were killed.
Afghanistan's deputy government spokesperson Hamdullah Fitrat said that the strikes took place in the Kunar and Paktika provinces.
Fitrat wrote on X that one strike hit at around 3:00 am Monday (2230 UTC, Sunday) in Kunar's Nurgal district and "completely destroyed" a house, adding that three people were killed and four other members of the family were wounded.
He said that two locations were also hit in the Paktika province, claiming that a shop and an unoccupied house were destroyed.
There has yet to be an official statement from Pakistan on the strikes.
Strikes follow last week's militant attack in Pakistan
The reported strikes come after a suicide bombing and a 20-hour gun battle between militants and police on Friday, which took place at a district police headquarters compound in the Pakistani city of Kohat, situated near the Afghan border.
At least 31 people, including 16 police officers, were killed in the attack.
Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, a local militant group linked to the jihadist group Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for the attack.
The Afghanistan-Pakistan conflict
Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan have been tense since the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calm after former South Asian allies engaged in their worst clashes in years in February.
Pakistan declared that month that it was in an "open war” with Afghanistan, following a rise in militant attacks on civilians and security forces inside Pakistan.
Afghanistan launched retaliatory strikes after Pakistan carried out airstrikes inside Afghan territory and the cross-border fighting has since claimed the lives of hundreds of people.
Pakistan last mounted deadly airstrikes in Afghanistan in June.
Islamabad accuses Afghanistan of sheltering militant groups which launch attacks inside Pakistan's territory.
Main among these is the TTP, often referred to as the Pakistani Taliban and Baloch separatist groups from the border areas.
The Taliban has dismissed the allegations, saying that militancy in Pakistan is an internal problem.

17:43:54 KST

Signet Bank AS Group (hereinafter – the Group) maintained strong growth momentum in the first half of 2026, organically expanding across its key business areas – corporate lending, investment banking and investment management products. Growth was also supported by the continued development of the Signet Baltic Bond Fund (hereinafter – the Fund) and the provision of Banking-as-a-Service (BaaS) solutions to fintech companies through AS Magnetiq Bank.
According to the Group’s consolidated audited interim report for the first half of 2026, total operating income rose EUR 26.3 million, an increase of 11.5% compared with the same period in 2025, while the Group’s comprehensive income attributable to the Bank’s shareholders amounted to EUR 5.75 million, up 24% compared with the first half of 2025. The Group’s equity increased by 34.1% year over year to EUR 65.8 million, while total assets under management and administration (AUMA) grew to EUR 1.8 billion. The Group’s return on equity (ROE) was 21.42%, while return on assets (ROA) stood at 1.53%.
The Latvian economy recorded moderate growth in the first half of 2026, with gross domestic product (GDP) increasing by 2.8% compared with the same period in 2025. At the same time, inflation remained moderate, with annual inflation reaching 2.6% in July 2026. The outstanding volume of corporate loans in Latvia continued to increase, reflecting sustained demand for financing and active lending by banks. Positive economic dynamics and continued demand created favorable conditions for further growth of the Group’s loan portfolio and the acquisition of new corporate clients seeking financing.
During the first half of 2026, the Group issued EUR 176 million in new loans to support the development of local businesses. By the end of the first half of the year, the Group’s loan portfolio had increased by 68% compared with June 30, 2025, reaching EUR 428.3 million. As a result of the strong increase in lending volumes, the Bank met the criteria for a 100% exemption from the Solidarity Contribution applicable to credit institutions in Latvia since January 1, 2025.
One of the Group’s key areas of development and expertise is capital markets financing – organizing bond and equity issuances for Baltic companies. Signet Bank continues to be the leading arranger of corporate bond and equity issuances in Latvia and one of the leading stock exchange brokers in the Baltics. In the first half of 2026, the Bank arranged 19 bond issuances, helping companies raise EUR 160 million in financing. Transaction activity is expected to remain stable during the second half of 2026.
The Group continues to implement its long-term growth strategy by expanding and diversifying its corporate financing solutions, broadening its range of investment products, and increasing client assets invested in the Signet Baltic Bond Fund and portfolios managed by Signet Asset Management Latvia IPS.
In its first year of operation, the Signet Baltic Bond Fund has become an important product not only within the Group’s offering but also in the Baltic capital market more broadly. During its first 12 months, the Fund delivered a 7.6% return for investors, while its assets had reached EUR 12.6 million by the end of the first half of the year. It is a unique investment product and currently the only product of its kind in the Baltic region, allowing investors to gain exposure a diversified portfolio through a single investment of Baltic corporate bonds comprising bonds from more than 50 issuers. At the same time, investors retain the ability to increase or reduce their investment at any time due to the daily liquidity provided by the Fund.
“Until now, investing in Baltic corporate bonds has largely been more accessible to experienced investors with relatively large amounts of capital to invest. We saw a need to make this market more accessible to a broader range of investors, which is why we created the Signet Baltic Bond Fund. With a lower investment threshold, it provides a simpler way to invest in a diversified portfolio of Baltic corporate bonds. We expect the Fund to become an increasingly important part of the Baltic capital market in the coming years, while also helping channel private capital toward financing the growth of companies across the region. Following the admission of the Fund’s units to trading on the Nasdaq Baltic exchange, it has become an investment accessible to every resident of Latvia,” says R. Idelsons.
The Group’s other companies also continue their strategic development. Magnetiq Bank will continue investing in process automation, developing technology-driven lending solutions, and strengthening its integration into the Latvian and European Union fintech ecosystem by expanding cooperation with peer-to-peer payment platforms, crypto-asset service providers, digital lending platforms, and e-commerce businesses. Meanwhile, Primero Finance AS and SIA AgroCredit Latvia will continue developing their loan portfolios in their respective specialized market segments, complementing the Group’s overall range of financing services.
To support further growth in the Group’s business volumes, particularly its loan portfolio, the Group completed the largest new equity raise in its history during the first half of 2026, raising a total of EUR 10.5 million in additional equity capital through three separate issuances. Following these issuances, the Group’s total number of shareholders increased to 47 local and international private investors. The Group’s capital base was further strengthened through the issuance of EUR 2.5 million in Additional Tier 1 (AT1) bonds, as well as a EUR 5 million subordinated Tier 2 loan from the European Energy Efficiency Fund.
“Signet Bank Group has reached a stage of development where our priority is not only to continue growing, but also to deliberately increase the scale of that growth. A stronger capital base provides greater capacity to finance larger projects, expand our range of investment products, and continue improving access to capital markets financing for businesses. Our ambition is to strengthen the Group’s position as one of Latvia’s leading financial services groups, capable of providing companies and investors with a broad range of financing and investment solutions, while gradually increasing our role in the Baltic financial market as well,” R. Idelsons says, outlining the Group’s near-term objectives.

EU condemns elections to Russian State Duma in occupied Ukrainian territories
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
11:43:33 EEST
17:43:33 KST

The European Union has condemned the holding of elections to the Russian State Duma in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, assuring that it will never recognize them, and that sanctions will be applied to those involved in their organization.
A corresponding statement by High Representative Kaja Kallas on behalf of the EU regarding the elections to the State Duma of Russia held on September 18-20, 2026, and their non-applicability on the territory of Ukraine, was distributed in Brussels on Monday.
The European Union strongly condemned the illegal organization by the Russian Federation of so-called "elections" in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, namely in the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol, as well as in parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson regions, stating that these votes represented another blatant violation by Russia of international law, in particular the UN Charter, as well as the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of Ukraine.
In this regard, the EU called on Russia to respect Ukraine's internationally recognized borders and sovereignty, reiterating that it does not and will never recognize either the holding of these so-called "elections" in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine or their results. It assured that sanctions would be applied to persons involved in organizing these fictitious elections or running as candidates in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, as well as to those responsible for undermining the possibility of holding free and fair elections in Russia itself.
In addition, the European Union reaffirmed its unwavering support for the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders, urging that Russia must stop its illegal war of aggression against Ukraine, agree to a full, immediate, and unconditional ceasefire, and immediately, completely, and unconditionally withdraw its troops and equipment from the entire territory of Ukraine.
Regarding the elections in Russia itself, the High Representative stated that they once again highlighted the ongoing and deep erosion of democracy in Russia, which is taking place in an increasingly authoritarian political environment, noting that the lack of a level playing field for all participants was further complicated by Russia's illegal war of aggression against Ukraine and the ongoing illegal occupation of Ukrainian territories.
The statement emphasized that the Russian authorities continue to step up systematic and institutionalized domestic and transnational repression to prevent any democratic opposition forces from participating in the struggle against the status quo, and that the decision to bar candidates from the Yabloko party from participating in the elections on the federal list further limited the choice for Russian voters by removing one of the last opposition forces and the only party with an anti-war program from the electoral process.
The text also pointed to such facts as the large-scale abuse of administrative and judicial resources to eliminate all those who opposed Russia's illegal war of aggression, deprive Russian voters of a real choice regarding the future of their country, and significantly limit Russians' access to independent information, adding that the European Union and its member states will continue to support the important work of Russian civil society organizations, human rights defenders, and independent media.
Furthermore, the EU expressed regret over Russian's decision not to invite OSCE observers to these elections, stating that this once again demonstrated Russian’s disregard for the commitments undertaken by all OSCE participating states and deprived Russian voters and institutions of the opportunity to receive an impartial and independent assessment of the elections.

China Focus: Exhibition showcases AI-powered manufacturing, int'l cooperation opportunities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:42:22 CST
17:42:22 KST

HEFEI, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- At an exhibition booth, a dual-arm robot works with remarkable precision, gripping a delicate test tube with one arm while handling reagents with the other.
"It is more than a robot that simply executes pre-programmed commands," said Wang Wandong, assistant director of the Center for Scientific Intelligence and Innovation. An onboard foundation model for scientific research enables it to understand a research task, generate an experimental plan, and carry out tasks on its own.
The "thinking" robotic arm, according to Wang, offers a glimpse into how Chinese manufacturers are combining sophisticated hardware with increasingly capable homegrown artificial intelligence (AI).
At the Binhu International Convention and Exhibition Center in Hefei, capital of east China's Anhui Province, more than 1,200 companies are showcasing over 15,000 products across a 70,000-square-meter exhibition area as part of the 2026 World Manufacturing Convention that opened Sunday.
Humanoid robots play rock music, practice boxing and sing traditional Chinese operas, while sleek electric vehicles sit alongside displays of chips, electronic panels and other key components. Around them, exhibitors display technologies ranging from quantum applications to artificial intelligence.
China's manufacturing value-added accounts for nearly 30 percent of the global total, the largest share worldwide for over a decade. The country's manufacturing sector is placing greater emphasis on improving quality and efficiency, aiming for high-end technology and smarter, greener production.
Anhui, an inland province, has in recent years seen rapid growth in manufacturing sectors such as electric vehicles, semiconductors, quantum technology and robotics.
From January to July this year, the output value of Anhui's strategic emerging industries grew 17.3 percent year on year. During the period, the output of new energy vehicles, integrated circuits and robots increased 27.5 percent, 28.6 percent and 32.8 percent, respectively, year on year.
At the opening ceremony, Hefei-based Chinese memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) announced its latest fifth-generation technology platform, which improves product capacity, power consumption and stability.
The company, which went public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange's STAR Market in late July, became the most valuable listed company on the A-share market. Luo Xiaodong, vice president of CXMT, said that, in developing the new platform, the company introduced a tailored AI large model and digital simulation covering the entire production process, significantly improving R&D efficiency.
This year's convention also puts a greater emphasis on showcasing entire industrial chains, shifting from individual products to broader ecosystems, the event organizer said.
Anhui ranked first nationwide in automobile production, new energy vehicle production, automobile export volume and export value in the first half of this year.
In the intelligent connected new energy vehicle section of the exhibition, displays span the full chain, from complete vehicles and power batteries to chips and chassis. Industrial data showed that more than 3,000 core parts suppliers now support automobile manufacturing in the province.
The province's growing industrial clusters are bringing manufacturers, technology companies and suppliers closer together, strengthening links between innovation and production, analysts noted.
"Anhui is helping shape the future of manufacturing," said Peter Wilson, the British ambassador to China. He added that Anhui has developed a globally significant manufacturing base, built world-class industrial clusters and is a center for emerging technologies.
Xin Guobin, vice minister of industry and information technology, said at the opening ceremony that China welcomes industrial enterprises from around the world to share opportunities here.
China will continue to expand high-level opening-up and create a world-class business environment that is market-oriented, law-based and internationalized, he added.
China removed all market access restrictions for foreign investors in the manufacturing sector in 2024, and in its latest edition of the Catalog of Encouraged Industries for Foreign Investment, effective Feb. 1, it added and expanded relevant items in the advanced manufacturing sector.
"Partnership creates opportunity," said Wilson, adding that Chinese and British businesses have been contributing to each other's manufacturing sectors.
"Let's learn from each other, work together, empower each other, and succeed together," the ambassador said. ■

Cambodia's fuel prices continue to surge amid ongoing Middle East tensions
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:42:03 CST
17:42:03 KST

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Retail fuel prices in Cambodia continued their upward trajectory on Monday, driven by a surge in global oil prices fueled by ongoing tensions in the Middle East, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
In its latest announcement, the ministry said that the price of regular gasoline has risen to 5,250 riels (about 1.29 U.S. dollars) per liter. This marks a 9.3-percent increase from 4,800 riels just 10 days ago.
Diesel prices saw an even sharper jump, climbing 11.9 percent to 6,100 riels per liter, up from 5,450 riels in the previous period.
The ministry's data highlights a staggering long-term trend, showing that since the outbreak of the Middle East conflict, the retail prices of regular gasoline and diesel in Cambodia have skyrocketed by 36.3 percent and 58.4 percent, respectively.
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, warned that these hikes directly inflate transportation and production costs.
"This drives inflation and erodes consumer purchasing power, particularly for food and agricultural products," he told Xinhua. "Ultimately, this dampens overall economic activity and pushes food prices higher."
He added that the burden falls disproportionately on vulnerable segments of the population.
"The most affected are low- and middle-income households, informal workers, and small and medium enterprises, as they are forced to confront rising living and operational costs with very limited financial cushions," he said.
Cambodia remains highly vulnerable to global oil market volatility. The Southeast Asian nation relies entirely on imported petroleum and diesel, as its own offshore oil reserves have yet to be commercially exploited. ■

Dementia survey highlights diagnosis delays, carer burden in Australia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:41:47 CST
17:41:47 KST

CANBERRA, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- A national survey has found that many Australians living with dementia report positive wellbeing and support from family and friends, but face complex pathways to diagnosis and difficulties accessing support services.
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) survey, conducted between May 2025 and January 2026, collected responses from 266 people living with dementia and 1,648 carers, an AIHW statement said Monday.
Three in five people living with dementia reported receiving a diagnosis within three years of first noticing symptoms, while fewer than half said they were diagnosed within the first year, the survey found, adding that barriers included delays in seeking advice, delays in tests and specialist appointments, symptoms being attributed to other causes, and appointment costs.
The survey also highlighted the burden on carers. Nearly one-third spent 70 hours or more each week caring for someone living with dementia, while more than seven in 10 women and six in 10 men reported feeling overwhelmed by their responsibilities.
Around two-thirds of carers recorded low wellbeing, with those providing 70 hours or more of care a week reporting lower wellbeing than those providing fewer hours, it said.
Nearly 459,000 Australians are estimated to be living with dementia in 2026, with the number expected to exceed 1 million over the next 35 years, said AIHW spokesperson Bronte O'Donnell, noting that the findings would help Australia better understand how dementia affects people's everyday lives.
Monday marks World Alzheimer's Day, observed as part of World Alzheimer's Month. Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, accounting for an estimated 60-70 percent of cases worldwide, according to the World Health Organization. ■

Asian Games | Feature: Pan Zhanle swims past self-doubt
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:41:40 CST
17:41:40 KST

by sportswriters Zhang Can, Gao Meng, Liu Yichun
TOKYO, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Pan Zhanle had already accepted defeat before he touched the wall.
With just one meter to go in the men's 100-meter freestyle final at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Sunday, the Chinese world record holder thought he was going to lose.
But Pan found the finish first.
He edged South Korea's Kim Young-beom by just 0.04 seconds to win the title in 47.61, with another South Korean, Hwang Sun-woo, taking bronze in 47.79.
"I thought I was going to lose at 99 meters," Pan said.
Before the medal ceremony, Pan asked Kim about his wingspan. Kim told him it was 2.16 meters, while Pan's is just over 1.9 meters.
"So I really thought I was going to lose in that last meter," Pan said with a smile. "Maybe I was just lucky."
The relief was visible. Pan climbed onto the lane line to celebrate, a rare display of emotion for a swimmer who has often kept his post-race comments brief.
Minutes later, he was equally candid in the mixed zone, talking about the challenges he had faced over the past two years.
Three years ago at the Hangzhou Asian Games, Pan broke 47 seconds for the first time by winning the 100m freestyle in 46.97. In 2024, he set a new world record of 46.40 at the Paris Olympics.
But those performances became harder to reproduce. He won the 100m at the 2025 national championships in 47.77, missed the final at the Singapore world championships after clocking 47.81 in the semifinals, and won the National Games in 48.01. In March this year, he finished third at the Chinese Swimming Open in 48.05.
"Over the past two years, I have become less and less confident," Pan said.
He changed his training methods and competition habits and spent time training overseas. The experience, he said, did not necessarily produce immediate results, but changed the way he understood swimming and his own career.
"Training overseas gave me a better understanding of the sport and swimming," he said. "That kind of improvement is difficult to show directly, but it will affect my entire career."
The biggest change, however, was mental.
"Enjoy life, enjoy the competition, give my best in training and leave no regrets in the race," Pan said.
For him, enjoying competition does not mean losing the desire to win. It means accepting whatever the race may bring.
"I don't think I'm a naturally gifted or genius athlete," he said. "Winning is of course good, but losing can give you experience."
Pan still has three relay events to come in Tokyo, but for now his focus remains on the immediate task.
"I don't want to talk too far ahead," he said. "I just want to fully show my training level and form in competition, and leave no regrets." Enditem.

Loud audio, feet on seats to draw fines on Singapore buses
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:41:34 CST
17:41:34 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Singapore will introduce fines of up to 500 Singapore dollars (392 U.S. dollars) for disruptive behavior on public buses from Sept. 23, including putting feet on seats, playing audio loudly and littering, the Land Transport Authority (LTA) said on Monday.
The LTA said in a statement that the new regulations will apply to public buses, as well as bus interchanges and terminals, and are intended to foster a safer, more considerate and pleasant public transport environment.
More serious offenses, such as causing obstruction or danger to commuters at bus interchanges or terminals, or soiling any part of a public bus, interchange or terminal, carry a maximum penalty of 5,000 Singapore dollars.
Authorized staff, including ticket inspectors and bus interchange staff, may issue Administrative Notifications of Offenses to people suspected of committing an offense. The LTA will conduct follow-up investigations.
Bus captains will not be empowered to issue the notifications, so as not to affect their core duty of safely operating the bus. However, they may advise passengers to stop disruptive behavior or require them to alight if they fail to comply.
The LTA said it would continue to exercise discretion and fairness, particularly in cases involving commuters with physical or mental health conditions. ■

Torrential rain lashed the Izu Islands and the Kanto region in eastern Japan on Monday, prompting the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) to issue a Level 5 emergency warning for landslides for Oshima Town in the island chain, which is located about 100 km from Tokyo.
The weather agency said it is extremely likely that landslides had already occurred in the area and urged residents to remain on maximum vigilance and take immediate action to ensure their safety, including moving as far away as possible from cliffs and streams, or to higher floors of buildings if going to designated evacuation sites is considered too dangerous.
As of 2 p.m. local time, Typhoon Dujuan, located about 40 km northwest of Hachijo Island in the Izu Island chain, was moving northeast at a speed of 25 km per hour (kph). It had a central atmospheric pressure of 960 hectopascals, packing maximum gusts of 198 kph, according to the JMA.
The year's 25th typhoon is expected to pass near the Boso Peninsula in Chiba Prefecture, east of Tokyo, from the evening to late Monday.
In the 24 hours through noon Tuesday, the weather agency forecast up to 250 mm of rain in the Tokai region in central Japan, the Kanto region and the Izu Islands, and up to 150 mm in the Tohoku region in northeastern Japan.
The typhoon has disrupted transportation, forcing the closure of parts of highways, and may also cause delays and cancellations of bullet train services connecting Tokyo and western Japan on Monday afternoon. ■

China's grain industry to see annual output value exceed 4.5 trln yuan during 2026-2030
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:41:30 CST
17:41:30 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- The annual industrial output value of China's grain industry is expected to exceed 4.5 trillion yuan (666.8 billion U.S. dollars) during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), an official said on Monday.
The grain sector will better meet people's demand for higher-quality, more nutritious and healthier food, said Liu Huanxin, head of the National Food and Strategic Reserves Administration, at a press conference.
China's grain industry has maintained steady growth in recent years, with the total industrial output value of grain enterprises rising from 3 trillion yuan at the end of the 13th Five-Year Plan period (2016-2020) to over 4 trillion yuan at the end of the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025).
Liu said that despite current fluctuations in the international grain market, China's grain market has remained generally stable and the country's food security is well guaranteed.
Liu pointed to a recent forecast by the World Meteorological Organization, which showed that El Nino will continue to strengthen and could impact global food production. Meanwhile, geopolitical conflicts are disrupting transport routes, driving up fertilizer prices and production costs, and adding to uncertainties around global food security.
He said China's food security is underpinned by stable production, ample reserves and strong processing capacity.
On the production side, China's grain output has been supported by steadily improving production capacity and the country's vast territory, which allows different regions to offset each other's harvest fluctuations, Liu said.
China's annual grain output has stayed above 650 million tonnes since 2015, exceeding 700 million tonnes for the first time in 2024 and reaching 715 million tonnes in 2025. Per capita grain availability has surpassed 500 kg, higher than the global average, providing a solid foundation for the country's food security.
On the reserves side, China's grain stock-to-use ratio remains well above the international grain security threshold of 17 to 18 percent, Liu said. If abnormal market fluctuations occur, reserves can be used to regulate supply and demand and help stabilize the grain market.
China also has strong grain processing capacity. The country has about 24,000 grain processing enterprises engaged in grain and edible oil processing, food and condiment production, feed processing and deep processing, among other businesses. Processing capacity for flour, rice and edible oil is sufficient to meet domestic demand, Liu said. ■
