Three South Korean officers injured in blast near North Korea border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:40:18 UTC
17:40:18 KST

An explosion near South Korea's heavily fortified border with North Korea has injured three South Korean military officers, Seoul has said.
South Korea's Defence Ministry said on Monday that the explosion occurred during an unspecified operation in the Demilitarised Zone, a border buffer zone separating the two nations that is commonly referred to as the DMZ.
The cause was not immediately clear, the ministry said.
Officials did not say whether the explosion could have been caused by a landmine planted by North Korea, which has added mines, anti-tank barriers and other frontline fortifications in recent months as relations between the two countries have sharply deteriorated.
Two of the officers were airlifted from the site by helicopter, while the third was transported by land before being airlifted, according to the ministry. The officers are being treated at a military hospital near the capital Seoul.
The DMZ, which stretches 248 kilometres and is four kilometres wide, is one of the world’s most heavily armed borders. An estimated two million mines lie inside and near the border alongside barbed wire fences, tank traps and combat troops on both sides.
The zone is a legacy of the 1950–1953 Korean War, which ended with an armistice but no peace treaty.
Border tensions
Increased activity by North Korean soldiers near the military demarcation line has raised concerns in South Korea as Pyongyang strengthens its border defences amid prolonged tensions.
The South Korean military has not officially confirmed media reports that North Korean soldiers crossed the line more than 20 times during frontline operations in August alone.
In April 2025, South Korean troops fired warning shots after around 10 North Korean soldiers crossed the line in the eastern section of the DMZ. The North Korean soldiers retreated following audio warnings and the shots, with no clashes reported.
North Korean troops also crossed the border three times in June 2024, prompting South Korea to fire warning shots.
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has suspended virtually all cooperation and diplomacy with Seoul in recent years, declaring South Korea his country’s most hostile enemy amid a stalemate in nuclear negotiations with Washington.
Landmines have caused casualties on the southern side of the border before. North Korean mines have occasionally washed down swollen rivers into South Korea, killing or injuring civilians.
In August 2015, landmine blasts maimed two South Korean soldiers and triggered a sharp rise in tensions between the two countries.

Old balloons, new drones: U.S. Army tests both in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:40:16 UTC
17:40:16 KST

- U.S. Army soldiers launched micro-High-Altitude Balloons, one carrying an APOLLO-R drone, in Hokkaido, Japan, on Sept. 18 during Exercise Orient Shield 26.
- It is at least the third U.S. Army exercise this year with balloon-carried drones, after Morocco and Guam.
U.S. Army soldiers launched micro-High-Altitude Balloons at the Yausubetsu Training Area on Hokkaido, Japan, on Sept. 18, including one that carried an APOLLO-R drone. Observers from Japan, the United Kingdom and Australia watched the demonstration during Exercise Orient Shield 26, according to the title of the U.S. Army’s video.
Balloons are often seen as relics of earlier wars. The Hokkaido launch is at least the third U.S. Army exercise this year to feature balloon-carried drones. Earlier this year, during African Lion 26, the U.S. Army launched drone-carrying micro balloons from a vessel off Morocco, Naval News reported. On June 24, soldiers from the 3d Multi-Domain Task Force launched an Apollo R on an Urban Sky balloon at Orote Airfield, Naval Station Guam, during Valiant Shield 2026. That test looked at sensing from the stratosphere and at extending joint communications networks.
A micro-High-Altitude Balloon is a small balloon that lifts equipment high into the atmosphere. In the Hokkaido photos, one rises with the APOLLO-R attached. A second U.S. Army video shows soldiers recovering the balloons on Sept. 19.
Icarus, a Los Angeles aerospace company, builds the APOLLO-R. The Defence Blog reported in June that it is an autonomous, solar-powered aircraft designed to fly indefinitely at altitudes above 18,300 meters (60,000 feet). The balloon does the initial lifting. TWZ reported that the U.S. Army has supported the aircraft’s development through its xTech innovation challenge.
Russ Van Der Werff, vice president of stratospheric solutions at balloon maker Aerostar, has argued that balloons offer survivability advantages over aircraft such as the Global Hawk and the Reaper.
Orient Shield 26 is the 41st edition of the annual exercise and the largest so far, with about 3,700 personnel from U.S. Army Pacific, the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force and the Australian Army. The opening ceremony took place Sept. 17 at Camp Higashi-Chitose.
The U.S. Army has not said how high the balloon climbed, whether the APOLLO-R separated and flew on its own, or how many balloons were launched. The captions do not name the balloon’s maker or the unit that ran the launch, and they do not say what the drone collected or relayed.
Ukraine offers a wartime example with a different platform, the tethered aerostat, which stays anchored to the ground while it holds equipment aloft. The Defence Blog reported in March that Ukrainian company Aerobavovna had delivered specialized aerostats to Ukrainian forces for surveillance, communications relay and electronic monitoring linked to drone operations.
“To control a drone at long distances and at low altitude, the relay needs to be raised into the sky,” said Aerobavovna CEO Yuriy Vysoven.
Vysoven said another drone can do that job, but its time in the air is limited, while an aerostat can operate around the clock. He expects the market to move toward larger numbers of smaller, cheaper platforms instead of single systems costing hundreds of millions of dollars, because large radar aerostats placed near the front become targets.
The Defender reported in May that the company’s AB12TC aerostat can lift equipment to altitudes of 100 to 700 meters (330 to 2,300 feet) and operate for up to 72 hours in field conditions. According to company data cited in that report, more than 50 aerostat systems have been delivered to units of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, Special Operations Forces and National Guard. Vysoven said in March that Aerobavovna was preparing its first export sale, to a customer in the European Union.

Several manufacturers and suppliers have announced restructuring programs as they seek to cut expenses, raising concerns about widespread job losses and possible factory closures.

The Taipei City Government said the project is expected to reduce travel time between Nangang Station and the National Biotechnology Research Park from 20 to 30 minutes during rush hour to approximately five minutes. The new route is also intended to reduce congestion on existing roads serving the Jiuzhuang area.
The tunnel has separate space for pedestrians and cyclists. A four-meter-wide pedestrian and bicycle corridor, separated from vehicle traffic by a physical barrier, runs through the tunnel. The city government said the design will provide a safer and more comfortable route for people walking or cycling.
The project also incorporates disaster-response measures. The city government said the tunnel’s smoke-exhaust system was designed to standards comparable to those used for the Suhua Highway Improvement Project. The pedestrian corridor can also be converted into an emergency evacuation and rescue route when necessary, per a press release.
The city recently conducted a disaster-response drill inside the tunnel involving a simulated vehicle collision, fire, and smoke. Police, firefighters, environmental officials, and public works personnel participated in the exercise ahead of the planned opening.
Chiang thanked city government employees, engineers, and contractors involved in the project, saying the administration would continue addressing residents’ transportation problems and completing major construction projects.
Construction began in February 2022, and engineers broke through the tunnel in December 2023 after overcoming difficult geological conditions, including unstable slopes and shallow rock cover.

'Rules need to be upheld': Australia's push to change a contentious UN power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:33:32 UTC
17:33:32 KST

Australia would push to reform the United Nations if given a seat on its Security Council, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said on Monday, as she joined Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in New York for the United Nations General Assembly.
Speaking with SBS News, Wong said Russia's use of veto powers to exempt itself from repercussions during its invasion of Ukraine was an example of where Australia would seek reform.
"We've had a longstanding position as a country of reform of the veto, and we know it's been misused previously," Wong told SBS World News chief political correspondent Anna Henderson in New York.
"What happened in relation to Russia's invasion of Ukraine was that a permanent member of the Security Council used its veto to prevent any action being taken for its own breach of the charter. That was an example where we would like reform."
Fifteen countries sit on the Security Council, and its five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — have the right to veto any resolution or decision.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
In 2022, Russia vetoed a Security Council resolution that described its attempts to unlawfully annex four regions of Ukraine as “a threat to international peace and security”, demanding Russia “immediately, completely and unconditionally withdraw all of its military forces” from Ukrainian territory. Ten of fifteen members had voted in favour of the resolution, while four abstained.
Wong said that Australia was "for reform", but that Australians were "very practical people".
"We recognise rules need to be upheld; the UN needs to be reformed.
"We want to make sure, where it really matters, that we continue to be part of setting the direction about that reform."
Wong has backed Albanese's bid for a seat on the council, which Australia has not held since 2014. Asked whether the veto powers in their current state rendered the campaign redundant, Wong stood by the pursuit.
"We might be distant from New York, but we are not distant from the rest of the world, and the world does have an effect on what happens in our economy, in our lives.
"So what I would say is we want to be able to advocate for Australia's interests in every forum that matters, and the UN Security Council matters."
International law under 'pressure'
International law is under a "great deal of pressure", Wong said, but the best response would be for countries to "come together" and advocate for the observance of international law.
"You've got two options, don't you? You can throw your hands up and say, 'I give up'. Or you can say, 'This actually matters to many countries.'
"We're not a superpower, but we're a country with substance and power to work with others to try and ensure that we hold onto the rules that matter."
Asked whether Australia could hold the United States to account over accusations around the war in Iran, as well as its actions in Venezuela, Wong said it was a task for the international community to work out the rules that "we really want to hold on to, that matter to us".
"I think trading arrangements matter to us. They certainly matter to Australia, and we've been very clear about our difference with the Trump administration."
But Australia does not intend to join its like-minded international partners in broader sanctions on Israeli settlements on the West Bank, Wong said, referring to "targeted sanctions" announced earlier this month as the UK banned trade in the occupied territories, and nine European countries said they were considering the same.
"I've announced already that we would engage in targeted sanctions," Wong said, noting that no country that had announced it would engage in the sanctions on a blanket basis had yet implemented them.
"And we certainly will be working with them as they do that to understand how they intend to deal with that," she said, and added that she has a "very clear intention" of engaging in more action against settlements, "which are an obstacle to peace", and "engaging in behaviour which makes two states less likely" in the case of the E-1 settlement, a contentious development plan for a 12-square-kilometre corridor in the West Bank.
"We'll continue to work closely with our like-minded countries just as we did a year ago, when, with others, we recognised the state of Palestine, which was part of the precursor to the peace plan, which we want to see implemented."

Ukrainian climbers won "gold" and set two European records
Kyiv • UNN
Hryhorii Ilchуshyn and Yaroslav Tkach won the speed relay in Chongqing. The Ukrainians set a European record of 10.03 seconds.
Ukrainian climbers Hryhorii Ilchyshyn and Yaroslav Tkach won gold medals in the speed relay at the World Climbing Series stage in Chongqing, China. During the tournament, the Ukrainian duo broke the European record twice, defeating the United States team in the final. The National Olympic Committee of Ukraine reports this, UNN writes.
A World Climbing Series stage in speed climbing took place in Chongqing, China. One hundred athletes from five continents took part in the competition — 57 men and 43 women
On their way to victory, the Ukrainian duo broke the European record twice. First, in the quarterfinal against China's first team, the Ukrainians improved the continental record to 10.26 seconds. Then, in the final against Americans Samuel Watson and Zach Hammer, they set a new record of 10.03 seconds, winning "gold" after their opponents made a false start.
It is noted that the previous European record in the speed relay also belonged to the Ukrainian duo. Hryhorii Ilchyshyn and Yaroslav Tkach set it earlier this year at the World Climbing Series stage in Krakow — 10.31 seconds.
The speed relay is a new discipline that made its debut at the World Climbing Series level only this year and is currently being considered as one of the future main disciplines on the competition calendar

Ukraine Urges Global Shutdown of Russian House Centers, Citing Security Threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:31:15 UTC
17:31:15 KST

- Category
- World
Ukraine Urges Global Shutdown of Russian House Centers, Citing Security Threat
Germany closed the Russian House cultural center in Berlin on September 18, ending years of what Ukraine describes as malign Russian influence. Despite the shutdown, similar centers still operate in at least seven European countries, Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, warned on September 19.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Sybiha set out the assessment in a post on X on September 19, framing the network as a front for hostile operations. He identified Rossotrudnichestvo and the so-called Russkiy Dom, or "Russian House," centers as instruments of disinformation, destabilization, and espionage.
"Our shared European home is not the place for 'Russian houses' promoting war propaganda," Sybiha wrote. He commended the measures European authorities have taken to block the network across the continent.
The network's reach extends well beyond Europe, the minister noted. Its scale is even greater in Africa, Central and Eastern Asia, the Asia-Pacific, and South America, he added.
In several countries, the official infrastructure remains intact, Sybiha stated, and in some it is woven directly into Russia's diplomatic presence. He characterized the centers as part of a comprehensive Russian effort to wage a global battle for public opinion.
Ukraine has formally appealed to governments worldwide to recognize the network as a national security threat, the minister explained. Kyiv has presented arguments for restricting the centers' operations and closing them entirely.
The Berlin shutdown extends a steady contraction of Russia's overseas cultural network. At least 13 Russian Houses have closed worldwide since Moscow's full-scale invasion began in 2022, down from roughly 15 centers operating across the European Union before the war.
Slovenia became the first EU state to expel its branch in April 2022, followed by Romania's closure of the Bucharest center in February 2023 and the shuttering of houses in Slovakia, Croatia, North Macedonia, and Montenegro that same year.
Moldova's center ceased operations entirely on July 4, 2026, with officials citing subversive activity conducted under the guise of culture.

Moldova Reports Suspicious Drone-Like Objects and Explosion. Here's What We Know
Residents in central Moldova reported unidentified airborne objects and an apparent explosion early on September 20.
However, according to Moldovan emergency services reports cited by RBC the same day, police found no debris or evidence of impact to confirm that anything had fallen or detonated on the ground.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Moldovan police, the first alert came at around 01:50 a.m., when a resident of the village of Berezloji contacted officers in the city of Orhei. The man stated that he had seen a flying object resembling a drone.
A second call reached police in the city of Călărași at around 02:00 a.m. A resident of the village of Dereneu described a bright light in the sky, followed by an explosion.
Officers began checks across both areas, examining terrain inside and beyond the villages, police noted. The preliminary inspection uncovered no debris, no traces of an impact, and no fires that would confirm an explosion on the ground or the fall of any object.
Authorities have not confirmed the nature or origin of the reported objects. Police indicated that checks in the affected districts were continuing.
The reports add to a series of airspace incidents along Moldova's border with Ukraine in recent weeks. On September 17, an unidentified drone crossed into Moldovan airspace from the Odesa region during a mass Russian attack, leaving Ukrainian territory minutes later.
Earlier, on August 27, five drones entered the country's airspace during an overnight assault, tracking toward the Ștefan Vodă district before turning back.
On August 17, a Russian "Banderol" loitering munition crashed near the village of Tălmaza, following a drone explosion on August 9 near Krokmaz that damaged farm structures.

Türkiye begins serial production of first domestically developed high-speed train
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:30:45 UTC
17:30:45 KST

(AA Photo)
Türkiye has begun serial production of its first domestically developed high-speed train, Transport and Infrastructure Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu said, as the country moves to expand its indigenous rail manufacturing capabilities.
The train, developed by Turkish Rail System Vehicles Industry (TÜRASAŞ), is designed to operate at speeds of up to 225 kilometers per hour. The first train set is currently undergoing testing, reaching 250 kilometers per hour during dynamic running safety tests, Uraloğlu said.
Production of the second train set has now begun, marking the transition to serial production, according to the minister.
Türkiye aims to manufacture 14 electric high-speed train sets over the next two years, with seven planned for 2027 and another seven in 2028. Each eight-car train will have a capacity of 577 passengers and will be developed using domestic engineering capabilities.
Critical components, including the Train Control and Management System and traction system, are also being designed and manufactured domestically in cooperation with Turkish defense and technology company ASELSAN.
Uraloğlu said serial production will eventually be carried out at Türkiye’s first dedicated high-speed train factory, which is currently 90 percent complete. The 18,000-square-meter facility will bring production, assembly and testing operations under one roof once completed.
The factory is designed to have a production capacity of one high-speed train set per month, allowing Türkiye to scale up manufacturing as it seeks to strengthen domestic capabilities in railway technology and reduce reliance on imported systems.
The project is part of Türkiye’s broader efforts to expand its high-speed rail network.

====================================================================================================

More than 10,000 signatures collected to reduce number of Saeima MPs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:28:09 UTC
17:28:09 KST

More than 10,000 Latvian residents have signed an initiative on the ManaBalss.lv platform calling for the number of Saeima MPs to be reduced from 100 to 70. This means the initiative will now have to be considered by the Saeima.
“Article 5 of the Constitution of the Republic of Latvia stipulates that the Saeima consists of 100 representatives of the people. The figure of 70 MPs was chosen in order to maintain approximately the same ratio of residents per MP as Latvia had in 1993, taking into account the decline in population,” the initiative’s author, Ričards Bumbērs, explains.
“At that time, Latvia had a population of approximately 2.60 million and there were 100 MPs. At the beginning of 2026, the population stood at 1.845 million, while the number of MPs remained at 100. This means that one MP now represents approximately 18,450 residents, compared with around 26,000 residents per MP at the beginning of the period following the restoration of independence,” Bumbērs says.
One argument cited in support of reducing the number of MPs concerns the organisation of parliamentary work – fewer could mean better.
With 70 MPs, each member of parliament would be more visible and their work and voting record easier to track,
which, according to the initiative, could encourage MPs to work more effectively rather than simply “be present”.
Larger and more stable parliamentary groups could work more efficiently and reach agreements more quickly. In parliamentary committees, MPs’ expertise and activity are more important than their formal number. According to the initiative, a smaller parliament would make it easier to ensure that committees are staffed by MPs who genuinely understand the issues rather than simply “filling seats”.
A smaller number of MPs could also lead to shorter debates, fewer formal speeches and easier coordination.
The initiative also argues that the change could potentially strengthen MPs’ links with voters.
If each MP represented a larger number of people, there could be greater motivation and a stronger need to maintain genuine contact with their constituency.
“With 100 MPs, many can afford to be ‘Riga politicians’. With 70, that becomes more difficult – they would also have to work more with the regions,” the initiative argues.
According to Bumbērs, a smaller parliament could also encourage voters to concentrate their votes on parties that have a realistic opportunity to influence politics.
Another argument cited is potential savings for the state budget.
“The Saeima’s 2026 budget is planned at 40.28 million euros, of which approximately 31 million euros is allocated to remuneration for MPs and Saeima employees. Reducing the number of MPs from 100 to 70 would save approximately 1.5 million euros annually from the basic salaries of 30 MPs alone, based on 2026 remuneration levels,” the initiative states.
“Additional savings could come from MPs’ assistants, compensation and other costs
directly linked to the number of MPs, although the exact amount would have to be determined during the development of the reform. Reducing the number of MPs by 30 would also reduce expenditure on assistants’ salaries. Although assistants’ salaries are lower, this could provide an additional 0.6–1 million euros in annual savings.”
The initiative acknowledges that the financial savings alone would not be decisive for the state budget, but argues that they could form part of a more efficient system of public administration and set a precedent by showing that political institutions are also willing to review their own administrative costs.
“Taxpayers expect state institutions to regularly assess their costs and the efficiency of their work. Fewer MPs would not mean less democracy. Latvia needs an effective and accountable parliament, not the largest possible number of MPs,” the initiative states.
“However, this is not only about potential financial savings.
The issue particularly concerns those residents who feel alienated from political power and believe that public administration should be closer to the people, more accountable and more efficient.”
According to the initiative’s author, an equally important issue is the attitude of state authorities towards society and politicians’ willingness to take responsibility themselves at a time when many Latvian residents face economic difficulties, low wages, rising prices and limited public services.
“By reducing the number of Saeima MPs, the state authorities would demonstrate solidarity with the public and show that politicians are also prepared to seek more efficient solutions and reduce their own administrative costs. It would be a symbolic but highly significant step towards restoring public trust in state institutions.”
The proposed solution is to amend Article 5 of the Constitution of the Republic of Latvia,
stipulating that the Saeima would consist of 70 representatives of the people instead of the current 100 MPs, the initiative states.
The changes would be implemented through the constitutional procedure by adopting the necessary amendments to the Constitution. The reduced number of MPs would take effect after the next Saeima election, providing a clear transition period and avoiding disruption to the work of the current parliament.
The proposed reform would reduce the number of Saeima seats from 100 to 70; amend the Saeima Election Law accordingly, including the proportional distribution of seats among electoral districts; preserve a democratic and proportional electoral system; increase each MP’s responsibility for decisions; and make parliamentary work more efficient and transparent.
“This solution is not merely about saving state budget funds.
It would also send both a symbolic and practical signal that state authorities are prepared to apply the principles of efficiency and accountability to themselves. At a time when residents are being urged to save and use their money responsibly, state institutions must also be able to set an example.”
The solution could realistically be implemented within a reasonable timeframe – all that is required is a political decision and the procedure for adopting constitutional amendments prescribed by the Constitution.
“By reducing the number of Saeima MPs from 100 to 70, Latvia could potentially gain a more efficient, accountable parliament that is closer to society. A smaller number of MPs is not automatically a magic formula. These are only potential and conditional benefits that can materialise if the reform is implemented wisely and accompanied by other changes, such as improvements to parliamentary procedures, party-group discipline and transparency,” Bumbērs says.
In his view,
“a smaller number of MPs would mean that each representative would bear greater individual responsibility
for the decisions they make and for their work before society. It would be more difficult for MPs to hide behind a larger number of colleagues, while voters would find it easier to assess each MP’s contribution.”
“A smaller number means that each MP becomes more visible and accountable to voters. Decisions could potentially be made more quickly, debates could become more focused, and political fragmentation could decrease. These changes would also provide an important symbolic benefit – demonstrating that state authorities are prepared to start with themselves and apply the principles of efficiency to their own work.”
“This would strengthen public trust in state institutions and promote a sense that politicians and residents are on the same side – working together to build a responsible and fair country.”
“Reducing the number of parliamentary seats could also lower the costs associated with maintaining parliament in the long term. The state funds saved could be redirected to areas of greater importance to society – healthcare, education, social support and security,” the initiative states.

Iran shuts down French cultural center over security concerns
Iran has shut down a French-language center in Tehran, accusing the embassy-affiliated institution of operating illegally and engaging in activities which threaten the country’s national security.
Relations between Paris and Tehran have deteriorated despite France staying out of the war which the US and Israel launched against Iran in late February and denouncing the initial strikes as a breach of international law.
In July, two French diplomats were detained by Iranian security services, which accused them of interfering in the country’s internal affairs. They were subsequently expelled from the country. France retaliated in August by expelling two of Iran’s diplomats.
“Based on the Tehran prosecutor’s office’s order, the illegal center affiliated with the French Embassy in Tehran, which has operated for years under the guise of language instruction, has been closed,” the Iranian judiciary’s Mizan news agency said on Sunday.
Iranian authorities claimed that the institution had repeatedly ignored warnings to obtain the licenses required under the country’s laws and had conducted activities that “violated diplomatic conventions.” They also accused it of using language instruction as cover to promote projects opposed to Iranian-Islamic culture, identify and build networks, and facilitate the departure of skilled Iranians from the country.
France has condemned the closure as an attack on its cultural presence in Iran and said it would take “appropriate measures” in response. Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot has ordered the Iranian ambassador to be summoned.
The French Language Centre (CLF) offered French language courses in Tehran, with thousands of Iranians attending its classes each year, according to the French Foreign Ministry.
In January 2023, Tehran closed the French Institute for Research in Iran after the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo published dozens of cartoons mocking then-Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and Iran’s religious establishment. The images, some of which were graphic or sexually explicit, were selected through an international contest called “Mullahs Get Out” and were intended to support anti-government protests in Iran.

The head of Türkiye’s National Intelligence Organization (MIT), Ibrahim Kalin, met with Libya’s acting defence minister, Abdussalam Zubi, in Istanbul, as Ankara and Tripoli seek to deepen cooperation and support efforts to unify Libya’s divided institutions.
The Saturday meeting came as negotiations aimed at bringing Libya’s military and political institutions together have gained momentum, according to Turkish security sources.
Kalin and Zubi discussed developments in Libya and the wider region, steps to maintain Türkiye-Libya cooperation, and ongoing efforts to achieve political and military unity and preserve stability in the North African country.
Zubi thanked Türkiye for its efforts to advance unity in Libya, while Kalin reiterated Ankara’s determination to continue supporting Libya’s security and stability.
A relationship built around security, trade and the Mediterranean
Türkiye’s engagement with Libya has expanded considerably over the past several years, encompassing security, energy, trade and maritime cooperation.
A landmark step came in November 2019, when Türkiye and Libya’s then Government of National Accord signed a memorandum on the delimitation of maritime jurisdiction areas in the Mediterranean.
The agreement, registered with the United Nations, defines a maritime boundary between the two countries’ continental shelf and exclusive economic zone areas.
The accord has remained a central element of Türkiye-Libya relations and the wider geopolitical debate over maritime boundaries in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Ankara maintains that the agreement protects the maritime rights of both Türkiye and Libya and was concluded in accordance with international law.
The maritime understanding was followed in October 2022 by a separate memorandum on cooperation in hydrocarbons, covering scientific, technical, technological, legal, administrative and commercial cooperation on land and at sea.
The agreements have helped broaden the relationship beyond security cooperation, placing energy and the Mediterranean at the heart of Ankara-Tripoli ties.
Ankara backs efforts to consolidate Libya’s institutions
Türkiye has also increasingly framed its engagement around Libya’s territorial integrity, political unity and institutional consolidation.
In August, Kalin said Türkiye would continue supporting efforts to bring Libya’s eastern and western administrations together under a single Libyan framework, while Turkish and Libyan officials discussed measures to strengthen security and stability.
International and regional efforts have sought to establish unified institutions and pave the way for lasting political stability.
Against that backdrop, Ankara’s contacts with figures from different Libyan institutions have become an important component of its engagement with the country.
The latest Kalin-Zubi meeting underscores the breadth of that engagement, linking security cooperation with the broader effort to help Libya achieve political and military unity.

Acad. Traykov: Alzheimer’s disease can be diagnosed before symptoms appear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:22:08 UTC
17:22:08 KST

Author
Gergana Hrischeva
Interview
September 21 - World Alzheimer’s Day
Acad. Traykov: Alzheimer’s disease can be diagnosed before symptoms appear
The leading Bulgarian neurologist from Alexandrovska Hospital is a guest on the BNR specialized healthcare podcast "At the Centre of the System"
Monday 21 September 2026 11:25
Monday, 21 September 2026, 11:25
Academician Lazhezar Traykov
PHOTO Ani Petrova, BNR
Font size
Years can pass between the earliest changes in the brain and noticeable memory loss. Today, medicine has biomarkers, neuroimaging techniques and therapies targeting the underlying disease pathology. Why is early diagnosis becoming increasingly important, and what can we do to protect our brain health?
On September 21, World Alzheimer’s Day, the BNR health-related podcast "At the center of the system" explores why the focus is increasingly shifting from the question, “What should we do when a person starts to forget?” to a much earlier one: “How can we recognise and diagnose the disease process before it has caused significant neuronal loss?”
According to leading Bulgarian neurologist Acad. Lachezar Traykov, head of the Department for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Degenerative and Vascular Dementias at the Clinic of Neurology of Alexandrovska University Hospital, one of the major breakthroughs in modern neurology is precisely the possibility of moving diagnosis to an earlier stage.
Bulgaria has no fully comprehensive and official national statistics on the exact number of people living with Alzheimer’s disease, but according to estimates by the Alzheimer Bulgaria Civic Association and international studies, the number of people affected by dementia and Alzheimer’s disease in Bulgaria is estimated at between 70,000 and 100,000. According to the data of the World Health Organization, 18 million people are affected by the disease on a global scale.
Modern medicine increasingly views Alzheimer’s disease as a biological process that begins before the onset of clinical symptoms. According to updated Alzheimer’s Association criteria, pathological changes may begin while a person still has no noticeable cognitive impairment. Memory is among the functions most commonly associated with Alzheimer’s disease, but the clinical picture is more complex.
Cognitive abilities include attention, concentration, memory, language, orientation, planning and decision-making. Consequently, early changes do not necessarily manifest themselves as the classic “forgetfulness”.
“Memory is one of the first symptoms,” Acad. Traikov told BNR, but he also points to another domain that may be affected earlier, namely the "executive" functions.
These are the abilities that allow us to respond appropriately in unfamiliar situations, plan, weigh alternatives and make decisions. As an example, he describes the usual route to work. When the route is familiar, a person follows it almost automatically. But if a street is suddenly closed, they must quickly orient themselves, devise an alternative route and adjust their plans to the circumstances. Such situations can become more difficult in the early stages of cognitive impairment.
“This process of making a decision quickly, in an unfamiliar situation, and arriving at the right decision has proved to be the most vulnerable and one of the earliest indicators to emerge,” Acad. Traykov explains.
Of course, such difficulties alone do not establish the presence of Alzheimer’s disease. They may be associated with anxiety, depression, stress, other neurological conditions or individual characteristics. This is why specialists use a more detailed neuropsychological assessment.
From brief screening to a neuropsychological profile
Brief cognitive tests can be used for screening in clinical practice. They should not, however, be regarded as equivalent to a diagnosis.
“We do not settle for the one-minute screening test performed by GPs. It is only a screening tool. Our psychologists conduct a 40-minute assessment,” Acad. Traykov explains.
The aim is to establish a cognitive profile, identifying which abilities remain intact and which are impaired. This helps distinguish normal ageing from pathological cognitive decline and determine what additional investigations may be required.
Modern diagnostic guidelines also stress that biomarkers should be interpreted in the context of a comprehensive clinical assessment rather than treated as a standalone laboratory verdict.
What happens in the brain years before symptoms appear?
Alzheimer’s disease is associated with the accumulation of pathological proteins, including amyloid-beta and abnormally modified tau protein.
One of the key structures affected in the early stages is the hippocampus, a region that plays a crucial role in the formation and storage of new memories. As the pathological process progresses, neuronal loss and structural changes in the brain occur. These may be detected on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as atrophy.
“Patients with Alzheimer’s begin to develop atrophic changes. Some areas of the brain responsible for particular functions lose cells, and on scans this appears as a shrinkage of the tissue,” Acad. Traykov added.
MRI, however, is not in itself a specific test for Alzheimer’s disease. It is important for assessing brain structure, identifying atrophy and investigating other possible causes of cognitive impairment. Current diagnostic criteria include MRI among the tools used to assess neurodegeneration and cerebrovascular injury.
“The bad proteins” can now be tracked
One of the most significant developments in recent years has been the advancement of biomarker-based diagnosis. Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) obtained through a lumbar puncture can measure biomarkers associated with amyloid-beta and tau pathology.
Another important method is amyloid PET imaging. It uses a radiotracer that binds to amyloid deposits in the brain, making them visible on imaging.
Current criteria identify amyloid PET and certain combinations of CSF biomarkers as core diagnostic biomarkers. A positive result obtained with an appropriately validated test can establish the presence of the biological pathology of Alzheimer’s disease.
The blood test: a major breakthrough, but not a diagnosis “from the laboratory”
Blood-based biomarkers have generated even greater interest. Various forms of phosphorylated tau can be measured in plasma, particularly p-tau217, as well as combinations of other biomarkers. Research in recent years indicates that some of these tests can achieve diagnostic accuracy comparable to that of established CSF tests.
This does not mean, however, that every positive commercial blood test automatically indicates clinical Alzheimer’s disease. On the contrary, scientific criteria emphasise substantial differences between individual tests. Not all blood-based assays currently available have the required accuracy, and their results must be interpreted in light of the clinical picture and the likelihood that the patient actually has Alzheimer’s pathology.
Acad. Traъkov warns of the danger of people without cognitive symptoms ordering such tests themselves and then assuming, following a positive result, that they are already ill. This is particularly important because the presence of biological pathology is not synonymous with the presence of dementia.
Current scientific criteria make precisely this distinction: a person without cognitive impairment who has a positive biomarker is at increased risk of developing symptoms, but this does not mean that they already have a clinical syndrome of dementia.
Amyloid is not the whole story
One of the important conclusions is that the disease cannot be reduced simply to the presence of amyloid. At least two major protein systems are involved in the pathological process, amyloid-beta and tau. Current criteria regard them as reflecting different biological stages of the disease. 
Amyloid biomarkers and early phosphorylated tau biomarkers are part of the so-called Core 1 biomarkers, while certain tau biomarkers that emerge later and tau PET are used for further staging of the biological process.
This is also important for treatment: the presence and extent of pathological amyloid and tau changes may be relevant to determining the stage of the disease and whether a particular patient may be eligible for a given therapy.
Academician Lachezar Traykov and Gergana Hrischeva, author of the BNR podcast "In the Center of the System"
PHOTO Private archive
New treatment: from treating symptoms to targeting the underlying pathology
For decades, Alzheimer’s medications primarily addressed symptoms. They can temporarily improve or stabilise certain cognitive functions, but they do not eliminate the underlying cause of pathological protein accumulation.
In recent years, however, this situation has begun to change. Monoclonal antibodies target amyloid-beta and are intended for patients in the early stages of the disease.
In 2023, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted traditional approval to lecanemab after a confirmatory trial demonstrated clinical benefit. In July 2024, the FDA approved donanemab for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease. The therapy is intended for patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia, the population in which the drug was studied.
In the European Union, one of the two drugs received marketing authorisation in April 2025 for a specific group of patients with early Alzheimer’s disease, confirmed amyloid pathology and a particular APOE ε4 status.These therapies are not “anti-forgetfulness drugs” in the traditional sense. They are disease-modifying therapies targeting a pathological mechanism of the disease, and their effect is associated with slowing clinical decline rather than curing the disease.
Treatment also carries risks
The new therapies are not suitable for every patient. They therefore require an accurate diagnosis, confirmed amyloid pathology, careful patient selection and specialised monitoring.
The most important word remains “early”. Both drugs have been studied and are intended for the early clinical stages of the disease. This changes the logic of the entire system: the earlier the disease process is identified in an appropriate patient, the sooner the possibility of disease-modifying treatment can be considered.
“We have to emphasise that this medication works only in the very earliest stages,” Acad. Traikov stressed. This is where biomarkers become particularly important: they can confirm that Alzheimer’s pathology is indeed underlying the clinical picture.
Can we reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease, and what role does prevention play?
Not all cases of Alzheimer’s disease can be prevented. Age and genetic factors are among the principal risk factors that cannot be modified. There is, however, a substantial group of modifiable risk factors associated with the risk of dementia. These include controlling blood pressure, diabetes and lipid levels; maintaining a healthy body weight; engaging in physical activity; avoiding smoking; limiting excessive alcohol consumption; maintaining social engagement; and sustaining cognitive activity.
It is important, however, to distinguish between reducing risk at the population level and guaranteeing prevention of the disease in an individual. There is no way to promise that a particular lifestyle will definitely protect someone from Alzheimer’s disease. For this reason, the modern approach is better understood as a strategy for healthy ageing of both the brain and the cardiovascular system.
Exercise, nutrition and intellectual activity
Acad. Lachezar Traykov places particular emphasis on physical activity and the control of vascular risk factors. This is logical because the brain does not exist in isolation from the rest of the body. Hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, obesity and physical inactivity are associated with cerebrovascular damage and may interact with neurodegenerative processes. A Mediterranean-style diet, regular physical activity and maintaining normal blood pressure are among the broadly accepted strategies for reducing the risk of cognitive decline.
According to Acad. Traykov, however, prevention goes beyond diet and exercise. He highlights the particularly beneficial role of cognitive stimulation:
“Read, listen to music, interact with others more.”
And he warns:
“Online scrolling is an insult to the brain.”
Behind this striking formulation lies the idea that passive consumption of information is not equivalent to active cognitive engagement. Reading, music, learning, creative pursuits, social interaction and solving novel problems engage different neural networks.
And what do we know about “positive emotions”?
Acad. Traykov also emphasised quality of life, including social interaction, positive emotions, love, an interest in the arts and a sense of meaning. Here, however, the scientific discussion needs to be somewhat more cautious. There is no evidence that a person can prevent Alzheimer’s disease simply by “thinking positively”, or that a particular emotion in itself prevents the disease. There are, however, strong grounds for considering social activity, physical activity, cognitive engagement and psychological well-being as components of the broader model of healthy ageing.
“Let us enjoy the small things, the beautiful things, and learn to look for them.”
Alzheimer’s disease remains a progressive and currently incurable condition. But medicine is no longer in the same position it was several decades ago.
“We have more precise diagnostic criteria, increasingly effective biomarkers and the first therapies targeting a fundamental pathological feature of the disease. Early recognition matters. Diagnosis should be comprehensive, biomarkers should be used judiciously, new therapies are intended for carefully selected patients, and brain health should be maintained long before the first symptoms appear. I say this as a scientist. I have read extensively on the subject, and I am very pleased that scientific evidence is showing us the path by which the human brain will survive,” says leading Bulgarian neurologist Acad. Lachezar Traykov.
*Acad. Lachezar Traykov is a leading Bulgarian neurologist, recipient of national and international distinctions in medicine and science. He served as Rector of the Medical University of Sofia from 2020 to 2024 and has been a prominent advocate for the advancement of Bulgaria’s healthcare system. He was Executive Director of Alexandrovska University Hospital from 2009 to 2013 and currently heads the Department for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Degenerative and Vascular Dementias at the Clinic of Neurology of Alexandrovska University Hospital.

Developers finally believe in the City with a Future – new homes are emerging and the supply of commercial space is expanding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:21:30 UTC
17:21:30 KST

While new homes are being developed in Riga and elsewhere, the new-build housing market in Ventspils has stagnated for years. Despite strong demand for high-quality family homes, virtually no energy-efficient new development has entered the market in the past 15 years. High construction costs and the region’s limited market have so far discouraged developers from investing.
Businesses have also faced a long-standing shortage of suitable premises. According to Sanda Austere, Head of Real Estate Transactions at Latio, the situation is now beginning to change: a major renovation project offering new, energy-efficient apartments is under way in the residential segment, while promising building complexes are entering the commercial property market.
“New investment is flowing into the city, the number of economically active companies is increasing and new jobs are being created. This signals to developers that the slogan ‘City with a Future’ reflects reality and that there will be genuine demand here for both new housing and commercial space,” Austere explained.
The figures support this assessment. In 2024, the number of economically active companies in Ventspils increased by 3.5% to 2,249, while the stock of foreign direct investment in the city reached EUR 118 million at the beginning of 2026, equivalent to EUR 3,385 per resident.
Developers slow to respond to demand
The Ventspils apartment market is unusual because virtually no new apartment buildings intended for sale have been developed in the city over the past 15 years. Consequently, buyers’ choices are largely limited to standard Soviet-era apartment buildings.
Austere explained that developers in the regions face considerably greater difficulty in balancing construction costs with the prices local buyers are prepared to pay. Construction costs in Ventspils and Riga do not differ significantly, while sale prices in Ventspils are substantially lower. This creates a vicious circle typical of regional markets: buyers want new, energy-efficient homes, but developers remain cautious about whether such projects will be financially viable.
The gap between supply and demand is particularly noticeable among buyers seeking larger family homes. Almost half of all transactions in the Ventspils apartment market involve two-bedroom apartments, while homes with four or more bedrooms account for only approximately 6%. The five-bedroom apartment segment is especially striking: only two such transactions have been registered in the whole of Ventspils over the past five and a half years.
“If a family wants a modern layout, good energy efficiency and a home that does not immediately require extensive renovation, the available choice becomes extremely limited,” Austere said.
Apartment prices in Ventspils have increased by almost one-third in less than six years, reaching EUR 760 per square metre in standard apartment buildings and EUR 730 per square metre in pre-war buildings. Although the number of transactions remains relatively stable at approximately 86–119 per quarter, with only modest seasonal variation that is less pronounced than in Liepāja, the shortage of high-quality homes is pushing up the market average. Asking prices for apartments in standard buildings have already reached EUR 880 per square metre in 2026.
According to Austere, rising prices are also being driven by high construction costs and changing buyer expectations. Local families, professionals and newcomers from other cities or countries appreciate Ventspils’ well-maintained urban environment and good infrastructure. They are therefore prepared to pay more, but only for homes in excellent condition.
A new standard for family housing
The major renovation of the residential building at 3A Talsu Street demonstrates the changes taking place in the housing market. A total of 15 fully finished three- to five-bedroom apartments, ranging from 53 to 90 square metres, will be available for purchase in the building. The homes feature individually adjustable underfloor heating and heat-recovery ventilation systems, providing Class A energy efficiency and predictable utility costs.
“I vividly remember the moment about a year ago when I first entered this building. There was construction dust everywhere, but the builders were carrying out their work with exceptional care. The internal walls were being built from masonry rather than plasterboard. Even then, I understood that buyers would not need to worry about the quality of construction in this building,” Austere said.
Apartment prices range from EUR 93,100 to EUR 143,200, or EUR 1,591–1,757 per square metre. As the final interior works are still being completed, reservation agreements are currently being concluded, and some of the apartments have already been reserved. Once the building is fully completed, deposit and purchase agreements will be signed with buyers.
Although it is not a new-build development in the traditional sense, following reconstruction the project will provide an alternative rarely seen in Ventspils in terms of its technical solutions, energy efficiency and level of finishing.
While a single project cannot by itself resolve the shortage of new housing in Ventspils, it can be regarded as an important market test. It will demonstrate whether buyers’ interest in high-quality housing matches the developer’s vision. The major renovation of the building at 3A Talsu Street is therefore a significant development not only for local residents, but for all participants in the property market.
Business and investment opportunities expand
A shortage of supply is also evident in the commercial property segment in Ventspils. The market consists primarily of existing properties, alongside facilities modernised by the municipality and the Freeport of Ventspils Authority. At the same time, several major investment properties have recently entered the market, signalling that conditions are beginning to change.
One of these is a building complex at 23 Ostas Street in the historic part of the city. Priced at EUR 1.85 million, it comprises five buildings with a total area exceeding 5,100 square metres. The complex includes offices, a conference hall, underground parking, a swimming pool, basement premises and a range of adaptable spaces, making it an ideal location for developing a hotel.
The availability of such a complex represents an exceptional opportunity for businesses and investors not only in Ventspils, but across the entire Kurzeme region.
“It is difficult to find an alternative comparable to the Ostas Street property. Its location beside the port and close to the historic centre offers the new owner enormous business potential. The functionality of the complex is another advantage. The premises can be adapted to a variety of uses, which is particularly important in the hospitality sector.”
Other properties available in the city centre include a masonry building dating from 1906 at 48 Lielais Prospekts, priced at EUR 225,000, and a development investment project at 3 Gaismas Street, priced at EUR 270,000.
Outside the city, in Zlēkas Parish, the historic Zlēkas Mill complex has been offered for sale together with its currently operating guesthouse. The property comprises 505 square metres of premises and nearly three hectares of land, as well as an events hall, bedrooms, a sauna and a swimming pool. Part of the legendary Latvian feature film The Devil’s Servants at the Devil’s Mill was filmed at the mill. The complex is available for EUR 425,000.
Overall, the commercial property market in Ventspils is not oversupplied. Energy-efficient premises in strategically attractive locations quickly find tenants, while outdated properties with high heating costs are rapidly losing their competitiveness.
Office rents in Ventspils range from EUR 5 to EUR 7 per square metre, while retail premises command EUR 8–10 per square metre and EUR 12–15 per square metre in the most desirable locations. Compact, energy-efficient premises and ground-floor retail space in the city centre are in the highest demand.

During the Carpathian Eight Summit on Friday 18 September, Ukrainian gas company Naftogaz Group and Poland's state-owned energy company Orlen signed two memorandums on supplying energy resources to Ukraine.
Source: Naftogaz on its website
Details: The first memorandum concerns the supply of three cargoes of liquefied natural gas in the first quarter of 2027.
The second memorandum with Orlen was signed by Ukrnafta, part of the Naftogaz Group; it provides for the supply of petroleum products for Ukraine worth US$500 million.
Serhii Fedorenko, acting Chairman of the Board of Naftogaz, added that the companies are working through options for supplying Ukrainian crude oil for processing at oil refineries in Central Europe.
Another area of co-operation is the transfer of used fuel tankers to Ukraine, which will help compensate for losses from Russian attacks and strengthen petroleum product logistics.
Background: The Naftogaz Group signed a memorandum with the Budapest-based oil and gas company MOL Group regarding the construction of facilities to store petroleum products for Ukraine's needs in Hungary near the Ukrainian-Hungarian border.

The NRL is reportedly set to axe top referee Ashley Klein for the preliminary finals after admitting the Warriors were wrongly denied a crucial late penalty in their 12-10 semifinal loss to Newcastle.
NRL officials today confirmed the Warriors should have been awarded a penalty for an escort infringement by the Knights' Tyson Frizell with a minute left in yesterday's Eden Park thriller.
Had the penalty been awarded, the Warriors would have had the chance to level at 12-12 via a penalty goal from just to the side of the posts and send the match to extra time.
But the call was instead missed on the field, with the bunker unable to review the play, despite a stoppage for an injury soon afterwards.
A comprehensive NRL review of Newcastle's 12-10 semifinal did, however, back the bunker over two other contentious calls.
First, it was deemed that bunker official Chris Butler was right to rule that Warriors centre Ali Leiataua got a thumb to a ball before it went to ground late in the match.
The NRL also supported the bunker's decision to stick with the on-field call of a strip against Warrior Te Maire Martin.
But it is the non-call on Frizell that will annoy the Warriors most.
The Newcastle veteran appeared to get in the way of Leka Halasima as he chased through on a kick in the Warriors' last attacking raid.
Given the seconds that would have come off the clock while the Warriors lined up the shot, there would probably not have been time for a restart.
"I thought they were trying to find ways to take it off us," Warriors coach Andrew Webster said after the game.
"The last one, two points would have drawn the game, he is going across Leka, pretending to try and catch the ball which they've told us you can't do."
AAP understands Klein will pay for the error by losing his spot in the preliminary finals, with Grant Atkins or Gerard Sutton likely to be called up.
Klein has overseen every game of the past five State of Origin series and two of the last four grand finals.
He had been expected to referee last year's decider, before losing out to Atkins following 18 penalties in a Melbourne-Cronulla preliminary final.
Meanwhile, the NRL have threatened bans for fans who threw projectiles at Klein as he walked off Eden Park on Sunday night.

zuckoff uses bluetooth to let you know when smart glasses are nearby
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:15:18 UTC
17:15:18 KST

ZUCKOFF RECOGNIZES CAMERA GLASSES THROUGH BLUETOOTH
Created by Polish developer Paweł Szydłowski, ZuckOff is an independent app that makes the otherwise invisible presence of camera-equipped glasses more legible through Bluetooth. The app listens for signals emitted by devices including Ray-Ban Meta, Oakley Meta, and Snap Spectacles, alerting users when compatible hardware is nearby while showing the evidence behind each detection.
As cameras and other sensors appear disguised as objects that resemble ordinary eyewear, their technological capabilities can become difficult for people nearby to recognize. ZuckOff approaches that problem at the level of the device’s wireless communication, turning Bluetooth advertisements into information that can be inspected on a phone, watch, or computer.
image by Sadjad Frogh
Paweł Szydłowski’s APP SHOWS USERS WHY A DEVICE is FLAGGED
ZuckOff exposes the wireless signals that can indicate the presence of a potentially recording device, responding to a particular ambiguity created by camera glasses. Paweł Szydłowski’s app currently identifies Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta through their manufacturer signature, as well as Snap Spectacles. It can also record other Bluetooth devices it encounters, including display glasses and headsets such as Quest and Vision Pro, but does not flag those devices as camera glasses.
The app assigns confidence levels, including possible, likely, and strong. A Ray-Ban Meta detection, for example, can show its manufacturer ID, the advertised service, signal strength, approximate distance, and other identifying information. Users can therefore inspect the reasoning rather than receiving an unexplained notification, making ZuckOff an interface for interpreting an increasingly dense wireless environment.
image courtesy of Meta
seeing why a device was flagged
The app’s Sightings interface keeps a record of every Bluetooth device heard nearby, whether or not it is identified as camera glasses. Individual devices can be followed through a signal timeline, creating a record of when they appeared and how their signal changed. Users who own compatible glasses can also mark their own devices, preventing them from repeatedly generating alerts.
The interface deliberately communicates uncertainty. Signal strength can suggest proximity but cannot establish direction, while Bluetooth advertising cannot reveal whether a camera is actively being used.
ZuckOff also has limitations. Camera glasses are easiest to detect when they power on, pair, or leave their case, and most continue broadcasting while they are being worn. Some standalone models can remain silent, however. This means that not detecting a pair does not necessarily mean there are no camera glasses nearby, while detecting one does not mean that its camera is being used.
The app does not require an account, and users can export the full Bluetooth log as a CSV. Its detection rules are based on real device captures. ZuckOff is asking people to share short scans from camera glasses that are not yet supported, or to lend hardware for testing. The team is also open to working with privacy groups. This means the list of detectable devices can grow as new camera glasses appear. Each new device adds another Bluetooth signature that the app can learn to recognize.

The US deported more than 25,000 migrants to third countries under secret agreements - investigation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

11:14:22 EEST

The US deported more than 25,000 migrants to third countries under secret agreements - investigation
Kyiv • UNN
An investigation by Forbidden Stories uncovered secret US agreements with 35 countries on the deportation of more than 25,000 migrants. $410 million was allocated for the program.
The United States deported more than 25,000 people under secret agreements with 35 countries that agreed to accept migrants who have no ties whatsoever to those states, according to an investigation by Forbidden Stories. Agence France-Presse (AFP) reports this, writes UNN.
Details
As the publication notes, after U.S. President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, Washington began concluding agreements with developing countries to accept migrants who cannot legally be sent back to their countries of origin.
The Forbidden Stories investigation found that the U.S. administration had allocated $410 million to be paid directly to countries accepting deportees or to UN agencies to facilitate their relocation.
According to data collected by Forbidden Stories together with a consortium of international journalists, as of August 31, 2026, at least 25,447 people had already been deported to third countries.
The vast majority—about 20,000 people—were sent to Mexico. The rest were distributed among 27 other countries in Latin America, Africa, and the Pacific region, while agreements had already been finalized with seven more countries.
The terms of these agreements vary, including regarding citizens of which countries may be deported and whether people with criminal convictions may be accepted.
An AFP investigation conducted earlier this year found that Washington was using visa bans and restrictions against African countries to pressure them into agreeing to accept deportees.
Lawyers told the publication that deportees end up in a "legal black hole": they are held without being charged in countries with which they have no ties whatsoever and where they have very few or no rights at all.
Forbidden Stories reported that as many as 49 of the 54 African countries had been approached with an offer to accept deportees from third countries.
According to Forbidden Stories, most of the negotiations and payments were handled by a little-known unit of the U.S. Department of State—the Office of Remigration, established in May 2025.

Germany's auto crisis: Can the 35-hour workweek survive?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:13:00 UTC
17:13:00 KST

Germany's car crisis: Will the 35-hour workweek survive?
September 21, 2026
Germany's famed automotive sector is facing a deep crisis, squeezed by high manufacturing costs, punitive US tariffs, intensifying competition from China and a difficult transition to electric vehicles.
Industry heavyweights such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.
The branch is shedding jobs faster than any other industrial sector in the country.
Volkswagen, for instance, is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW announced it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.
Auto suppliers such as Bosch and ZF Friedrichshafen have also announced thousands of job reductions amid tough market conditions and global competition.
Germany's automotive industry is losing competitiveness as costs rise and production shifts abroad, said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, director of the Center for Automotive Research (CAR) in the German city of Bochum.
"In 2018, the industry employed around 830,000 people. Currently, that number is below 700,000," he told DW. "We project that by around 2030, it will be 500,000."
Regaining competitiveness and securing jobs in the future will require an array of measures including lower production and energy costs, better logistics infrastructure and favorable tax conditions, he added.
Labor costs too high in Germany?
Auto industry executives agree that labor costs in Germany are too high compared to international rivals.
Labor costs in the country average $3,307 (€2,882) per vehicle, compared to $769 in Japan and $597 in China, according to a reportpublished by the consulting firm Oliver Wyman.
To trim labor costs, carmakers want employees in Germany to work 40 hours a week instead of the current 35 hours, without any increase in pay.
The 35-hour workweek has long been standard across much of Germany's automotive industry, having emerged from collective bargaining agreements negotiated in the 1980s and 1990s.
It reflects an era when Germany was highly competitive, said Dudenhöffer, adding: "That time is over."
Workers' unions, however, vehemently oppose longer working hours.
Christiane Benner, the head of the influential IG Metall trade union, said workers had already accepted wage cuts and other concessions worth several billion euros, yet were now being told that this was still not enough.
The union argues that German automakers are struggling with weak demand and underutilized factories, not a shortage of labor hours. "Not a single additional car will be sold just because the workforce works longer hours," the union announced.
IG Metall is holding demonstrations at more than 200 locations nationwide on September 21 to oppose job cuts and other measures affecting working conditions in the automotive sector.
Can longer working hours save jobs?
The union is "fighting for relics from 20 years ago, forgetting today's reality," Dudenhöffer said.
The expert estimated that if carmakers were to move from a 35-hour week to a 40-hour week, personnel costs would decrease by 13%.
"We wouldn't be taking money away from employees, but we would be creating conditions that would make jobs possible in Germany, in the automotive industry, in the future," he underlined.
Stefan Bratzel, head of the Center of Automotive Management (CAM) in Bergisch Gladbach, said the 35-hour week represents a key achievement for trade unions in their collective bargaining history, so "conflict is inevitable" between management and unions.
On the other hand, more working hours for the same pay would mathematically lower labor costs per hour, he added.
"Ultimately, this raises the question of how the burdens of the current transformation are to be distributed between companies and employees," said Bratzel.
How can Germany's auto industry recover?
Experts say improving labor costs at German production sites is necessary, but it alone will not solve the industry's deeper structural problems.
"Working five hours more per week alone will not win the technological race against China," said Bratzel.
He stressed that, to restore their competitive edge, German carmakers need to deliver attractive and affordable electric vehicles, invest heavily in software and AI, and improve the efficiency of their development and manufacturing processes.
"German manufacturers must be at least as innovative and high-performing in technological terms as they are expensive by international standards," said Bratzel.
At the same time, he explained, Germany requires competitive framework conditions regarding energy, taxes, bureaucracy and infrastructure.
Dudenhöffer echoed this view, saying that Germany must pursue difficult but necessary reforms.
"Germany can only be considered a viable option for its automotive industry and jobs if we regain our competitiveness," he said.
And for that, action is required on multiple fronts, including lowering labor and energy costs, adjusting taxes, and creating better logistics infrastructure, he added.
"But the coming years will be very tough," Dudenhöffer warned. "And they will become even tougher if we stick to the status quo and believe we can simply rest on the prosperity we enjoyed 20 years ago."
