Meta’s Facebook, Instagram recover after brief outage
SAN FRANCISCO - Meta’s social media platforms Facebook and Instagram recovered after a brief outage disrupted service for thousands of users in the US on Sept 20, according to Downdetector.com.
The disruption began around 8.55pm ET (8.55am on Sept 21 Singapore time) and peaked at more than 17,000 reports of outages on Facebook and more than 5,000 reports on Instagram, according to Downdetector, which tracks outages by collating status reports from multiple sources.
Reports of outages had fallen sharply by about 10pm ET, indicating the services had largely recovered.
Meta did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on the outage.
Since the numbers on Downdetector are based on user-submitted reports, the actual number of affected users may vary.
Facebook and Instagram experienced a similar outage in July, when Downdetector logged as many as 4,808 reports of issues on Facebook and 2,829 on Instagram.
In Singapore, reports on Downdetector for Facebook spiked at 9.26am with 229 complaints, while there were 109 reports for Instagram at 9.25am.
More than half of the complaints for each platform were for problems with their websites. REUTERS

If Washington expands its tech blockade to include cloud networks, China’s AI sector will face its most severe choke point since the chip bans
When Chinese artificial intelligence developers want to train their next-generation frontier models, they all face the same daunting wall: they cannot legally buy the world’s most powerful AI chips.

====================================================================================================

Why the far right lost: 11 lessons for Europe from Sweden’s election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Why the far right lost: 11 lessons for Europe from Sweden’s election
POLITICO spoke to party leaders Magdalena Andersson and Ulf Kristersson — and leading analysts — to understand the far-right Sweden Democrats’ fall in support, and what it means.
Jimmie Akesson and Social Democratic Party leader Magdalena Andersson take part in a televised election debate hosted by TV4 in Stockholm, Sweden, on September 10, 2026, three days ahead of the country's general election. | Jonathan Nackstrand / AFP via Getty Images
STOCKHOLM — As far-right leader Jimmie Åkesson danced beside the pink balaclava-wearing singer Miss Smut at his final campaign rally, he hoped a late surge in the polls would carry his Sweden Democrats into power.
But the following day’s election instead delivered a rude shock to Sweden’s anti-immigration vanguard: A loss of vote share, support and influence for the first time since the SD was founded by neo-Nazis in the 1980s.
The left bloc narrowly won the contest and will now seek to form a government that doesn’t include any right-wing parties.
Advertisement
Amid reports of recriminations within the SD, Åkesson may take time away from frontline politics, but insists he won’t resign.
Jimmie Åkesson’s final rally takes place in Stockholm on Sept. 12, 2026. | Tim Ross/POLITICO
The disappointing outcome for the SD is a rarity these days in European politics: A far-right populist party making a name for itself campaigning against immigration, but then falling back instead of grasping power.
POLITICO spoke to experts and key players, including outgoing center-right Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson and his likely Social Democrat replacement Magdalena Andersson, to draw some lessons from the campaign.
The far right allied with the center — and lost
The SD’s vote share fell from 20.5% in 2022 to 17.5% this year, even though it had supported Kristersson’s center-right coalition within the parliament for four years. Although Åkesson’s party succeeded in pushing Kristersson’s administration to adopt tougher policies on crime and immigration, their electoral result was ultimately worse.
Kristersson’s Moderates party, meanwhile, increased its support and overtook the SD to become the second-largest force in the parliament. That outcome will have drawn the notice of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats and the far-right Alternative for Germany, for example, as well as of Britain’s Conservative Party and Reform UK.
It’s OK to blame voters, if it fits your story
Åkesson’s explanation for the SD’s disappointing result was bang on brand for an anti-migrant populist. At a Friday press conference he claimed the Social Democrats and their allies on the left had been “very good at mobilizing the Islamist voters who previously had other parties to vote for.”
Advertisement
At the same time, he said, some right-wing supporters had voted for tiny parties that didn’t make it over the 4% vote threshold required for representation in parliament.
Åkesson wasn’t alone in flagging voter behavior. Social Democrat leader Andersson spent much of the campaign warning voters not to put Åkesson and his team in power, casting it as a central election issue. She told POLITICO on election day that voters who supported Kristersson and other right-wing parties, knowing that support would put far-right ministers in government for the first time, were “in denial.”
“They don’t really want to see that they actually vote for a government dominated by Sweden Democrats,” she said.
Swedish firewall held, but more by chance than design
Mainstream European parties have for decades pursued a “firewall” policy against the far right to block it from power, determined to prevent a return of the fascism that so scarred Europe in the 20th century.
In reality, Sweden formerly stout firewall has developed many holes over the past four years. Kristersson broke the taboo against working with the SD back in 2022 when, in a coalition with two other right-wing parties, he signed a deal to implement key SD priorities in exchange for their support in parliament.
The pact gave Åkesson significant influence over Kristersson’s government, allowing the SD to drive a hardline crackdown on immigration and an agenda to tackle violent crime.
Advertisement
Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, leader of the conservative Moderates, speaks to the press during the Moderates’ election night party in Stockholm in the early hours of September 14, 2026. | Christine Olsson/AFP via Getty Images
Kristersson dismissed criticism that he was opening the door to extremists who would end Sweden as a tolerant country. Billing himself as a pragmatist, he asked voters to judge him on his government’s success at bringing down crime and immigration.
“For me, it’s the result that counts,” Kristersson told POLITICO in the final week of the campaign. In order to solve problems, he said, you need a majority in the parliament — which under Sweden’s proportional representation system meant working with the SD.
Don’t take normalization too far
Ahead of the election Kristersson went a step further, for the first time promising Åkesson seats in his Cabinet if their rightwing alliance retained power.
“That probably was beyond the pale for a small number of people who would otherwise have voted for one of the right-wing parties, particularly the Liberals,” said Nicholas Aylott, associate professor of politics at Södertörn University. In a close election, he said, such small things can make a big difference.
Overall, Aylott said, the firewall wasn’t central to this year’s election, despite attempts by left-wing parties to make it so.
Whatever the impact of Kristersson’s gambit, this election was almost a tie and nearly went the other way. If two seats had flipped to the right bloc, Åkesson’s team would be preparing to take over key ministries in the government. And if Andersson can’t persuade other parties to back her in coalition talks, that could still happen.
Advertisement
Firewalls don’t work forever
The Sweden Democrats entered parliament for the first time in 2010 — and mainstream center and left-wing parties refused to cooperate with them. According to Aylott, that “very strong” firewall allowed the SD to build support in the country.
“That created a huge space in the Swedish political context in which anyone with any sort of cautious or skeptical view toward immigration at the time really had only the Sweden Democrats to choose,” he said.
By 2022, with gang crime rife, the SD’s tough stance on law and order and migration drove it to its best-ever result. Its second-place finish put in a powerful position to influence Kristersson’s government.
It’s not a coincidence, Aylott said, that the far right fell back again after the firewall was partly set aside to allow it to join the government, for all that it didn’t have ministers in Kristersson’s Cabinet.
The firewall “is not holding anymore” in much of Europe, according to Grégoire Roos, Europe program director at the Chatham House think tank in London. “The citizens who cast their ballots for these parties are increasingly young. So referring to the darkest times of history does not appeal to them at all,” Roos said.
“To some extent, the more you bash these parties, the more popular they get,” he added, noting it was true of Trump and others in Europe. “I think in this regard we can see a pattern.”
Advertisement
Normal for Nordics
It’s not unusual for the far right to be integrated into governments in Nordic countries such as Norway and Finland. The center left in Denmark has also adopted particularly tough policies against migration, in part to mitigate the appeal of far-right populists.
These recent developments contrast sharply with the situation in Southern and Western European countries like Germany, Spain and France.
Pro-Russian policies cost you votes
While some European far-right parties have maintained pro-Russia attitudes without incurring major electoral costs, that’s not the case in countries like Sweden.
Sweden’s authorities regard Russia as the country’s No. 1 security threat, while Moscow has menaced Swedish airspace and interests in the Baltic Sea in recent years. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 prompted Sweden to end decades of military neutrality and join NATO — a decision that has enjoyed wide public and political support.
In the final days of the election campaign, the SD was hit by a scandal over alleged Russian infiltration — an inevitable voter repellent in Swedish politics.
Immigration isn’t the issue it used to be
After Sweden’s record 2015 intake of asylum seekers, the political backlash saw governments of both persuasions introduce harsh restrictions — reducing migrant numbers by 96% a decade later.
Advertisement
Andersson, who also favors limits on immigration, said some of the governing coalition’s policies had gone too far for average Swedes, such as deporting the teenage children of migrants who had grown up in Sweden. “These are young people that are part of the club and now they have to leave,” she said. “People don’t like it.”
Far right a victim of its own success
Two big issues that had driven support for the SD in previous elections — gang shootings and immigration — were lower on the agenda in this election, Aylott said. Perhaps because Kristersson’s coalition, with the SD’s support, had succeeded in reducing gun crime and throttling immigration.
Four years ago, the headlines were all about “gang violence, daily shootings, kids being killed,” Kristersson told POLITICO. “Now we have brought that down by some 80%.”
On immigration, Kristersson’s government began paying some foreign-born people €30,000 to leave the country.
“For me, results matter,” Kristersson said. His Moderates party won more seats this time around — perhaps a sign of voter gratitude — but the SD, which was so closely identified with anti-immigration policies, fell back.
“The paradox is that when the situation begins to feel less acute, it falls down the list of voters’ priorities,” said Aylott. When that happens, “probably the party that was favored is not going to be favored again.”
Advertisement
Healthcare, education and the economy topped the list of voter concerns, according to exit polls.
Centrist governments should just do their jobs
Andersson believes the SD can be fought on their traditional right-wing economic positions as well as on “the hate they have spread” and would propagate further if they won office.
Above all, she said, the lesson for centrists is that they have to deliver on voters’ concerns when they have the chance.
Magdalena Andersson and her husband Richard Friberg greet elderly people as they arrive to cast their vote at a polling station in a school during Sweden’s general election, in Nacka on September 13, 2026. | Jonathan Nackstrand/ AFP via Getty Images
“If you have governments that actually do deliver better living standards, better schools, better healthcare, build a society where people can feel hope for the future, then the room for right-wing populist parties will be smaller,” she said. “It’s clear that after the financial crisis of 2008- 2009, traditional parties haven’t really been able to deliver.”
Even Kristersson, although his bloc lost power, saw his center-right Moderates increase their share of the vote after a campaign in which he highlighted his government’s successes.
Far right not dead yet
Andersson said support for the far right “is not something you stop in a four-year period.” Voters across Europe choose populist nationalist parties “because politics is not delivering,” she told POLITICO.
Advertisement
“If traditional political parties aren’t delivering a better hope for a better future, then you vote for something else. So it’s really up to us to do our homework: Deliver when we are in power, and in opposition have good and realistic programs that we can deliver on once we are in power again.”
Aylott agreed that while the election was “certainly a setback” for the SD, it wasn’t a “total collapse.”
There has been speculation that Åkesson could walk away from the SD in the weeks ahead. If that happens, a new leader could revive the party with a return to a more radical posture, Aylott said. The freedom to speak out that comes with being in opposition will also likely help.
“It’s not inconceivable that we might see some re-radicalization of the party and an attempt to fire up the activists again,” Aylott said. “This could be a critical moment for the party. It could lead to infighting and very damaging disputes, but it could equally lead to a sort of renewal of the party’s appeal, perhaps with a younger leader.”

Endangered black robin wins 2026 Bird of the Year in New Zealand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
09:34:44 CST
10:34:44 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Karure black robin, a critically endangered bird native to New Zealand's Chatham Islands, has won the 2026 Bird of the Year competition after receiving 25,610 votes, Forest & Bird said on Monday.
The closely contested election attracted a record 105,000 voters, with about 88 percent of votes cast from within New Zealand, according to the New Zealand's conservation organization.
Kakapo, a flightless, nocturnal parrot native to New Zealand, finished second with 19,445 votes, followed by karearea, or New Zealand falcon, with 17,423 votes, according to the results.
Karure black robins are a conservation success story. In 1980, only five birds remained, including the only fertile female. A recovery effort by the Chatham Islands community and the Wildlife Service, now the Department of Conservation, began with a single breeding pair, Forest & Bird said in a statement.
There are now about 350 adult black robins living on two pest-free nature reserve islands. However, the suitable habitat on the islands is nearly at capacity, with all suitable territories occupied, it said, adding that a third population on another island is needed for the species to continue growing.
Forest & Bird said that conservation work on Pitt Island, which sits right between the two nature reserves, could provide safer habitat for the black robin and benefit the wider biodiversity of the Chatham Islands, which supports 20 percent of New Zealand's threatened bird species. ■

====================================================================================================

Malaysian King Approves Imprisoned Former PM Najib’s House Arrest Bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
01:29:00 UTC
10:29:00 KST

On Friday, Malaysia’s king granted imprisoned former Prime Minister Najib Razak a royal pardon, allowing him to serve the remainder of his prison term under house arrest, prompting an outcry and creating another potential political headache for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
Najib, 73, has been imprisoned since August 2022, when Malaysia’s top court upheld a conviction in a case linked to the multi-billion-dollar looting of the state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
In a statement, the government confirmed that Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar had granted Najib a “conditional pardon.” This will allow him to serve the remainder of his prison term under house arrest if he pays a 50 million ringgit fine ($12 million) imposed by the courts. Najib’s sentence expires on August 23, 2028.
The 1MDB state investment fund was established shortly after Najib’s election in 2009. In the ensuing years, Malaysian investigators claim, at least $4.5 billion was drained from the fund and laundered by Najib’s associates through a labyrinth of dummy corporations and bank accounts across the globe. The 1MDB scandal helped bring down Najib’s government at the general election of 2018, and has since led to criminal investigations in a number of other countries, including the United States, Switzerland, and Singapore.
Najib’s original conviction was handed down in 2020, when a court sentenced him to 12 years in prison and fined him 210 million ringgit ($51.5 million) for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust, and money laundering. The charges related to Najib’s illegal receipt of around $10 million from SRC International, a former unit of 1MDB.
Since then, Najib has pursued a range of legal and political tactics in order to reduce his sentence. In early 2024, he succeeded in gaining a royal pardon from Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah of Pahang, the country’s previous king, which halved his prison sentence and reduced his fine to 50 million ringgit. He has also mounted a legal bid to serve his sentence under house arrest, claiming that the royal pardon contained a royal “addendum order” that entitled him to serve the remainder of his sentence at home. Accusing the authorities of deliberately ignoring or concealing the order, he initiated legal action aiming to compel them to confirm its existence and to execute it. His legal bid was shot down by the Kuala Lumpur High Court in December 2025.
This royal pardon, based on the sweeping powers granted to the king under Malaysia’s constitution, effectively overrides that decision. As the Associated Press noted, the king’s decision “marked an unprecedented use of house arrest as a form of royal clemency in Malaysia and could renew debate over the rule of law and the treatment of Malaysia’s most prominent corruption convict.”
Indeed, much Malaysian social media commentary about the decision has been shot through with a resigned and weary acceptance that the rich and powerful will always manage to evade accountability.
G25, a prominent civil society coalition, said in a statement that it was “deeply shocked and dismayed” by the decision.
“This does nothing to strengthen public confidence in our criminal justice system. It is a travesty of justice,” the group said, adding that it was difficult to reconcile with the government’s stated commitment to strengthening the rule of law and combating corruption.”
Indeed, the decision has placed Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in a tricky position. While he has spent much of his career crusading against corruption, he is currently governing in a marriage-of-convenience coalition with Najib’s party, the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), the primary component of the Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition.
Given the various corruption scandals that have swirled around UMNO and its key figures, this has been a source of growing discontent within Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) and among its supporters, who argue that the Malaysian leader has been forced to compromise his principles in order to mollify his coalition partner.
This has reached a tipping point over the past year due to a string of corruption scandals, including the dismissal in January of 47 corruption charges against UMNO head Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, a key Anwar ally, and subsequent reports of widespread misconduct at the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission. This disillusionment arguably contributed to PH’s defeat in a string of important state-level elections over the past year.
In the wake of Najib’s pardon, Transport Minister Anthony Loke announced that he would tender his resignation, stating that the king’s decision, while legitimate, was “difficult to accept” for his Democratic Action Party (DAP), an important member of the PH coalition. The DAP, a party associated with Malaysia’s ethnic Chinese population, has performed poorly in the recent state elections due in part to the growing disillusionment with Anwar’s administration. In the wake of the recent state election results, some within the party have called for it to withdraw from the unity government in order to maintain its credibility as a liberal and reformist party. Last month, the DAP called a special congress to vote on the question. While the party’s members chose to stick with Anwar for now, it remains to be seen whether it will do so over the longer term.
At the same time, Najib’s release into house arrest would be a boon for UMNO and BN, which, while remaining in coalition with PH at the federal level, have competed with it in the recent state elections. In Negeri Sembilan, UMNO cooperated closely with the Islamist party PAS, a key member of the opposition Perikatan Nasional coalition, on a joint Malay unity platform, and won a significant majority in the state assembly. This offered a possible preview of the next general election, which is due by February 2028 – unless the growing PH-BN tensions prompt Anwar to call an earlier snap election.
On Friday, Anwar urged the public to accept the king’s decision, which he said would not weaken the government’s fight against graft and abuse of power.
“I want to stress that the principle of the rule of law remains intact,” he said, according to the AP. “Our commitment to taking action against all cases of corruption is not affected, and this does not mean the country should bow to practices of embezzlement and corruption.”
It remains unclear for now whether Najib will be able to fulfill the conditions necessary to secure his release from prison. A statement issued by Najib’s legal team yesterday said that the former leader was “profoundly grateful” to those who had offered their support and assistance. However, the question of whether he will be able to pay the required fine “does not lie in his own hands” given that many of his assets have been frozen due to the ongoing court cases.
“In those circumstances, our client is presently taking advice and considering his options as to how best to give effect to the condition,” the statement added.
After the royal clemency was announced, UMNO launched a “solidarity fund” in order to help, which had raised more than 1 million ringgit as of Saturday.
In the statement, Najib’s lawyers said that their client “does not wish the party, its members and supporters, or members of the public to feel burdened or obliged on his account.” He nonetheless remained “profoundly grateful” to all those who had “chosen to offer their support and assistance.”
As things stand, a lot of uncertainties surround Najib’s house arrest situation. Legal experts say that Malaysia does not have rules governing house arrest, and even if these are hastily put in place, it remains unclear how any potential breaches would be monitored or enforced.
However, there is a broad consensus that the pardon is unlikely to apply to the separate 15-year prison sentence handed down to Najib in a larger 1MDB-related trial late last year. In this case, judges found Najib guilty of 25 charges, including four counts of abuse of power and 21 counts of money laundering relating to 1MDB funds worth 2.27 billion ringgit ($574 million). Najib was also hit with a massive fine of 11.38 billion ringgit ($2.9 billion).
That prison term is due to begin after he completes his current sentence. Najib has appealed the verdict.

Trump administration readies sweeping sanctions against ICC, reports say
Measures targeting the court itself could disrupt payments, IT services and investigations.
The Trump administration is reportedly preparing sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) that could disrupt the tribunal’s finances and day-to-day operations.
The US sanctions would prohibit most transactions with the ICC after a grace period of six to seven months, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.

- list 2 of 2Duterte in person at ICC for first time over ‘war on drugs’ killings
The move would mark a sharp escalation in Washington’s campaign against the Hague-based court by targeting the institution itself rather than individual judges and prosecutors.
The Trump administration plans to announce the sanctions soon, according to the Reuters news agency, quoting two sources familiar with the matter.
The Journal, citing anonymous officials, said a decision could be finalised during this week’s United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York or soon afterwards.
If imposed, the measures would generally bar US citizens and companies from providing the ICC with money, goods or services without a licence from the US Treasury.
Banks and other companies often take an especially cautious approach to US sanctions because they rely on access to the American financial system.
The ICC president and registrar have previously warned that sanctions on the organisation as a whole could interfere with its ability to buy information technology and insurance services, hire investigators and make routine payments, including salaries for American employees.
The ICC was created in 2002 to prosecute individuals accused of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity when national authorities are unable or unwilling to do so.
Washington has already sanctioned more than a dozen ICC judges and prosecutors under an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in February 2025.
In August, it added the court’s President Tomoko Akane and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye to the list, with restrictions on them taking effect on September 17.
The United States has never joined the court.
The Trump administration says the court has exceeded its authority by pursuing officials from countries that are not ICC members.
Relations deteriorated sharply after the court issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Israel, like the US, is not an ICC member and rejects the court’s jurisdiction.
Washington has also objected to an earlier ICC investigation into alleged abuses in Afghanistan involving US personnel.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a campaign in July to further isolate the court and urged other countries to withdraw from it.
Trump’s move adds to growing opposition to the ICC in recent months.
Chad and Venezuela moved in July to withdraw from the court, following Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.
Four US-based rights groups sued the Trump administration in August, arguing that existing sanctions obstruct their legal and human rights work.

Egypt calls Ethiopian Renaissance Dam ‘illegitimate,’ reserves right to act to protect water security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
01:19:30 UTC
10:19:30 KST

Amer Solyman and Mohammad Sio
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
Egypt considers the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) “illegitimate” and reserves the right to take any measures it deems necessary to protect its water security, Irrigation and Water Resources Minister Hani Sewilam said Sunday.
Sewilam made the remarks during a briefing in Cairo with representatives of foreign media in Egypt organized by the State Information Service.
Egypt and Ethiopia have been at odds for years over the GERD, which Addis Ababa began building on the Blue Nile in 2011. Cairo has repeatedly demanded a legally binding agreement regulating the dam’s operation to safeguard its water security.
Sewilam said the completion of the dam and the passage of time did not mean that Egypt had accepted the situation or relinquished its rights.
He said the 2015 Declaration of Principles signed by Egypt, Ethiopia and Sudan was intended as a roadmap that established commitments on cooperation, reaching an agreement on the dam’s initial filling and annual operation as well as coordination and data sharing.
The declaration does not give Ethiopia the right to take unilateral measures concerning the dam, Sewilam said, adding that Egypt considers continued filling and operation without an agreement a breach of those commitments.
“The dam is illegitimate and will remain so. Egypt has the right to take appropriate action to remove the harm caused to it,” he said.
“We gave Ethiopia more than one opportunity and tried every possible way to reach understandings, but it did not respond and also violated the Declaration of Principles,” he added.
Potential risks
Sewilam warned that uncoordinated operation of the dam can lead to sudden increases or sharp declines in water flows, potentially affecting dams in both Egypt and Sudan.
He said Egypt’s main concern is the timing and quantity of water releases and the rules governing them, rather than simply Ethiopia’s use of the dam to generate electricity.
“Ethiopia’s actions and statements by its officials indicate that the primary purpose of building the dam is not electricity generation,” he said.
Sewilam stressed the need for a legally binding agreement setting out procedures for periods of prolonged drought or repeated flooding.
He also rejected Ethiopia’s claim that Egypt receives the “lion’s share” of the Nile's water.
Egypt’s annual allocation of 55.5 billion cubic meters represents about 2.7% of the roughly 2 trillion cubic meters of rainfall across the Nile Basin, he said.
Ethiopia received more than 1 trillion cubic meters of rainfall in 2023, including about 467 billion cubic meters over the Ethiopian portion of the Nile Basin, while its renewable water resources amount to around 122 billion cubic meters annually, according to Sewilam.
He said estimates of groundwater recharge in Ethiopia range from 51 billion to 81 billion cubic meters annually and are linked to rainfall, unlike Egypt’s deep groundwater reserves, which he described as non-renewable.
Sewilam said Ethiopia has more than 18 million hectares of agricultural land compared with about 4.03 million hectares in Egypt.
Rain-fed agriculture in Ethiopia uses around 148 billion cubic meters of what is known as “green water” annually, in addition to around 9.68 billion cubic meters of “blue water,” he said.
Green water refers to rainfall, while blue water refers to water from rivers and groundwater sources.
Sewilam said Ethiopia’s total agricultural water use reaches around 158 billion cubic meters annually, while the water footprint of its livestock sector amounts to around 85.5 billion cubic meters, most of it green water.
He called for greater cooperation on rainwater harvesting, groundwater and improving agricultural water-use efficiency.
He also pointed to Ethiopia’s potential in solar and wind power, arguing that diversifying its energy mix could ease water-related pressures.
Cairo and Khartoum have called for a legally binding trilateral agreement between Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia governing the filling and operation of the GERD to ensure their water rights and interests are not harmed.
Ethiopia, however, says operating the dam does not require a binding agreement and maintains that it does not intend to harm the interests of other countries.
The dispute led to negotiations among Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia being suspended for three years in 2020 before resuming in 2023 and stalling again in 2024.

High number of SIR notices result of rule change after Bihar experience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
01:19:18 UTC
10:19:18 KST

EC revised the rules in Phase 2 covering 12 states/UTs, doing away with the requirement to submit documents
NEW DELHI: The large number of notices served to electors under the special intensive revision (SIR) largely stem from a key change made to SIR instructions by the Election Commission, based on its experience during SIR Phase I in Bihar. During SIR in Bihar, the rules required electors to attach documents proving their eligibility to be included in the roll, over a dozen documents were listed as acceptable proof of birth, citizenship and residence, at the enumeration stage itself.However following the uproar over the inconvenience caused to electors who may not have had these documents and thus faced exclusion, the EC revised the rules in Phase 2 covering 12 states/UTs, doing away with the requirement to submit documents with the enumeration form (EF) and instead decided to map the electors with the electoral roll from last SIR. The mapping works with inbuilt algorithms to flag logical discrepancies between the last roll and the enumeration forms, based on which notices are automatically issued.“The logical discrepancy detecting software is agnostic and does not distinguish between a VIP and a common man. The fact that election commissioner. S S Sandhu also got a notice due a discrepancy, where his name was mentioned as S S Sandhu in one place and as Sukhbir Singh Sandhu in another, proves this,” an EC functionary pointed out.
“The high number of notices seems to unique to urban centres like Delhi, where the electors may have been a little casual while filling up the EF. Also, the BLOs could have been more meticulous in checking forms at the enumeration stage, as this could have cut down the discrepancies that led to the notices,” said an EC official.“If anyone does not return the EF despite three visits of the booth level officer (BLO) to his address and checking by booth level agent (BLA) of political parties, he is either absent, shifted, dead or duplicate elector and his name is not there in draft roll. If the received EF are incomplete or gives incorrect information, notices are issued.The official added that notices rarely lead to electors’ exclusion and are resolved the moment the elector presents the proof correcting the discrepancy.
“No elector is excluded without a hearing, which must be followed by a speaking order, which can, after the final roll be published, be challenged first before the district election officer and then the chief electoral officer,” said an EC official.“Besides, the option of being added back to the electoral roll remains open in perpetuity. Anyone whose name is left out can always fill up Form 6, along with the declaration, on his mobile to get back into the electoral roll,” the official added.
Bharti Jain is senior editor with The Times of India, New Delhi. She has been writing on security matters since 1996. Having covered the Union home ministry, security agencies, Election Commission and the ‘prime’ political beat, the Congress, for The Economic Times all these years, she moved to TOI in August 2012. Her repertoire of news stories delves into the whole gamut of issues related to terrorism and internal strife, besides probing strategic affairs in India’s neighbourhood.

US Treasury chief says meeting with China on trade, AI ‘very successful’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
01:06:37 UTC
10:06:37 KST

AI alert system over national security concerns being discussed between US, China
- The US and China discussed setting up an AI safety notification system to address national security concerns ahead of a meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese PresidentXi Jinping.
- The talks included plans for tariff cuts on non-sensitive goods and emphasised maintaining stable trade relations without immediate progress on critical minerals or export controls.
- US officials stress the need for an international AI safety agreement banning self-improving AI and preventing misuse, while China plans business consultations and potential auto investments in the US.
AI generated
NEW YORK – US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng concluded talks in New York on Sept 20 with the American side proposing a new AI safety-notification mechanism for US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to consider at their summit this week.
Bessent told reporters the two sides discussed setting up a new US-China dialogue on artificial intelligence, emphasising national security concerns with a notification system for common goals and common threats that would cover AI-related incidents that rise to a national security level.
“We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the No. 1 and the No. 2 AI powers in the world is very important,” Bessent said at the conclusion of the talks.
Trump and Xi first discussed potential consultations on AI development in May in Beijing, but that forum was never formalised.
Chinese state media said China and the US had “frank, in-depth, and constructive exchanges” on important economic and trade matters, including dialogue on issues related to AI.
“One or two meetings cannot resolve every issue, but the fact that both sides agreed to continue the dialogue is significant,” said George Chen, a partner and chair in digital practice at The Asia Group consultancy in Hong Kong.
“The US-China AI talks will move forward, with future sessions expected to tackle more sensitive topics such as the weaponisation of AI, principles for AI safety, protection of critical infrastructure and cyberattack prevention,” he said.
Chen added that prospects for cooperation on AI remain limited due to the low level of trust between both countries, and Beijing’s perception that Washington seeks to contain China’s AI development.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said US export controls on sophisticated AI chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment were not on the agenda for the AI mechanism talks.
Greer added that the discussions would prepare the groundwork for a “successful summit” between Trump and Xi on Sept 24 and 25 in Washington.
“These are the two most powerful countries on earth, whether it’s in trade or AI, and it’s imperative that they’re able to work together. It doesn’t mean there aren’t challenges in the relationship. A lot of these are obvious,” Greer said.
The meeting covered other key topics, including plans to “operationalise” a process agreed in May for each side to identify potential tariff cuts on non-strategic goods, called the “Board of Trade”.
Greer did not identify a specific list of products that could see such reductions, but he repeated his desire for a “relatively small subset of American and Chinese goods that can be traded in a balanced way, that are non-sensitive”.
These would be considered as “a class unto themselves”.
Potential candidates among Chinese exports include “consumer goods, low-tech items”, he said, while US exports for this treatment could include energy, agricultural goods and medical devices.
Greer and Bessent did not mention any progress on improving the flow of critical minerals to US companies, which US officials have said are insufficient despite Beijing’s prior commitments to ease restrictions under 2025’s US-China trade truce.
The discussions point to more incremental progress in avoiding an escalation of tensions in a delicate trade relationship that has major consequences for the global economy.
“I think status quo is probably both sides’ general best expectation,” Anna Ashton, a China trade analyst and founder of Ashton Intelligence, said before the meeting.
Unresolved issues
Bessent and Greer did not provide updates on other issues that are still unresolved after the May meeting in Beijing between Trump and Xi, including Chinese pledges to increase purchases of US agricultural goods by US$17 billion (S$22 billion) a year and to purchase more than 200 Boeing aircraft.
Trump and Xi must reach a deal that covers AI safety, said US Representative Ro Khanna, the ranking Democrat on the US House select committee on strategic competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party.
“The first ask is of Trump and Xi Jinping to come up with an international agreement, and two of the core principles should be one banning any self-improving AI, recursive self-improving AI. The second is to have safeguards so that AI can’t be misused by people for biological nuclear weapons,” Khanna said on Sept 21.
China’s Ministry of Commerce said on Sept 9 that He would also lead a delegation of Chinese companies to the US that would participate in economic and trade consultations ahead of the summit.
The business delegation, which mirrors a group of US CEOs that Trump brought to Beijing in May, was announced as Trump expressed openness to Chinese automakers building US factories.
US auto industry groups on Friday urged Trump to maintain an effective ban on Chinese vehicle sales in the US on national security grounds. REUTERS

DRC: M23 fighters abused miners and trafficked gold and coltan to Rwanda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
01:01:00 UTC
10:01:00 KST

- The plunder by M23 and Rwanda of DRC’s gold and coltan may amount to war crime of pillage
- M23’s multiple violations that also involve Rwandans may amount to war crimes
- “Rwanda has continued to illegally profit from DRC’s mineral wealth,” Agnès Callamard
- Minerals linked to abuses by M23 are prevalent in electronic devices owned by millions across the world
Rwanda-backed March 23 Movement (M23) fighters have committed horrific human rights abuses against artisanal miners in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) while facilitating the trafficking of gold and coltan to neighbouring Rwanda with the help of Rwandan authorities, Amnesty International said in a new briefing.
“DRC: We didn’t come to play: M23 abuses at artisanal mines and the trafficking of gold and coltan to Rwanda”, documents M23 violations including summary killings, torture and ill-treatment, arbitrary detention, forced labour and forced recruitment. It shows how M23 fighters forced miners to dig minerals, often making them work underground for more than a week at a time in coltan mines near Rubaya in North Kivu province, and Lomera, a gold mining site in South Kivu province. The violations may amount to war crimes, which are crimes under international law.
“Rwanda-backed M23 is committing horrific human rights abuses, which may amount to war crimes, against artisanal miners in eastern DRC. These are meant to punish and instill fear among miners and others living and working near the mines, as minerals are trafficked across the border into Rwanda, which has continued to profit from the exploitation of DRC’s mineral wealth,” said Agnes Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
Rwanda-backed M23 is committing horrific human rights abuses, which may amount to war crimes, against artisanal miners in eastern DRC. These are meant to punish and instil fear among miners and others living and working near the mines, as minerals are trafficked across the border into Rwanda, which has continued to profit from the exploitation of DRC’s mineral wealth,
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General
“The African Union and its Member States must take far bolder steps than they have done thus far to put an end to the likely pillage driven by an endless international appetite for African critical minerals. Failure to stand united against such pillage and the horrific abuses that comes in its wake will only encourage others to follow suit.”
“International actors must end their silence about M23’s atrocities, the smuggling of minerals from conflict affected areas, and Rwanda’s responsibility. They need to hold perpetrators, including Rwandan government officials, accountable.”
Amnesty International is calling for all countries and companies to cease the purchase of coltan and gold from Rwanda – or processors and refineries from third countries that buy these minerals from suppliers in Rwanda – until the Rwandan government provides concrete evidence that it has ended the receipt of coltan and gold trafficked from DRC. Rwanda’s authorities must also ensure that armed or other Rwandans are not present at and play no role in abuses at the Lomera and Rubaya mining sites.
The African Union and its Member States must take far bolder steps than they have done thus far to put an end to the likely pillage driven by an endless international appetite for African critical minerals. Failure to stand united against such pillage and the horrific abuses that comes in its wake will only encourage others to follow suit.
Agnès Callamard
Amnesty International is also calling on the US and EU member states not to establish any mining agreements involving the Rubaya mine or other M23-controlled mines in the DRC unless international human rights observers and independent international oversight organizations have full and unfettered access.
M23 controls dozens of artisanal mines in North and South Kivu, where tens of thousands of people rely on them for income. The group tightly controls access to these mines, which have no independent international oversight.
Amnesty International interviewed 26 people, including artisanal miners, mining experts, mine shaft owners and family members of victims. Researchers also analysed photos and video evidence from mining sites.
Testimonies indicate that Rwandans are present at Rubaya and Lomera. In Rubaya, miners said Rwandans play a dual role as civilian miners or mineshaft managers but also take part in hostilities when needed alongside M23 fighters. In Lomera and Rubaya, security guards, some of whom have identified as Rwandan and spoke Kinyarwanda, the language of Rwanda, collaborate with M23 and have beaten and ill-treated miners.
Neither M23 nor Rwandan government officials responded to Amnesty International’s request for comment.
Human rights abuses at the mines
The organization documented the summary killing of 18 artisanal miners at the Rubaya and Lomera mines. Witnesses and family members reported that 10 were beaten to death, two were shot dead and six abducted miners were later found dead.
Among those killed was Evariste*, a 22-year-old husband and father of a one-year-old daughter.
An eyewitness said:
“When we saw Evariste* he was in so much pain. He didn’t have the strength to speak. He couldn’t lift his feet. His entire body was bloody.”
Another miner who witnessed his brother beaten to death said:
“He was beaten on his chest with a pickaxe, when I denounced the man who beat him to death, [M23 fighters] put me in prison. They gave me a punishment of two weeks without salary in the mine shaft. I told people I wanted to take [his body] to our family. He was buried like an animal [in the mineshaft].”
He was beaten on his chest with a pickaxe, when I denounced the man who beat him to death, [M23 fighters] put me in prison.
Evaritse*, miner
Sixteen miners or civilians who lived near the mines recounted how they had been tortured or ill-treated by M23 fighters or security guards working with them. Some miners were beaten so badly that they lost consciousness. Miners described to Amnesty International how they were beaten if they requested breaks, refused to hand over minerals, or for minor transgressions.
A mining supervisor recounted how M23 fighters attacked one of his employees, “When we got out of the mine shaft with the mineralized sand, there were five well-armed [M23 fighters] and three who were not armed. They said: “We didn’t come to play. If you resist [giving us the mineralized sand], we will kill you.”
Near the Rubaya mine, M23 uses three shipping containers as detention cells. One interviewee said he could hear the screams of detainees as they are being tortured inside the containers. “It’s better to die than being detained there,” he said.
In Lomera, M23 detained four men and accused them of communicating with authorities in Kinshasa and suspected them of having links to the Wazalendo armed group.
One victim told Amnesty International that the supervisor of the detention site told him:
“I will kill you and then give you a weapon and say you were Wazalendo.”
Amnesty International also documented the use of underground detention cells known as ndake. More than 20 miners who worked at the Rubaya mine were kept in a ndake and beaten three times a day by M23 fighters.
The briefing also details how M23 uses the mines as forced recruitment sites. Seven miners recounted how M23 detained miners and threatened to send them to M23 military training centres if they failed to pay ransoms for their release.
Trafficking of minerals to Rwanda
Amnesty International found evidence that gold was trafficked out of M23-controlled areas into Rwanda through well-established smuggling routes.
Testimonies from miners, mining representatives, and others who worked at Lomera, as well as evidence gathered by Amnesty International’s Evidence Lab, confirmed that soil containing gold from Lomera was loaded onto boats at the Port of Lomera. Sacks of soil containing gold from DRC arrived via boat at a “sand port”, a collection site for sand used in construction, in Kamembe, a town in Rwanda’s Western province.
One Congolese miner who worked at Lomera said: “I was there at night. I hid and saw that [M23] sent three groups … to different mineshafts. They took the mineralized sand [soil containing gold] and took it near the lake…When they arrived, they put it in small boats and sent it to Rwanda.”
Another miner from Lomera said:
“We saw [boats being loaded]. Loaded with robotas [sacks of soil containing gold]. They did this very early in the morning. Each morning, they came with traders from Rwanda. And the same boats came at night.”
Amnesty International believes that M23’s plunder of gold and coltan likely amount to the war crime of pillage.
We saw [boats being loaded]. Loaded with robotas [sacks of soil containing gold]. They did this very early in the morning. Each morning, they came with traders from Rwanda. And the same boats came at night.
Miner, Lomera
Given the significant amounts of gold and coltan trafficked to Rwanda – often with the complicity of Rwandan and M23 leaders – it is likely that Rwanda is directly engaged in pillaging the resources of the DRC.
“This investigation should serve as a wake-up call to Rwanda that Rwandans may bear international criminal responsibility for facilitating the trafficking of pillaged minerals to Rwanda,” said Agnes Callamard. “Rwanda may also bear state responsibility for the horrific abuses against miners if Rwandans in the mines are acting under the direction or control of Rwanda, even if they are not employees of the government.”
Corporate responsibility
International standards establish clear expectations for states and companies to prevent and address human rights harms linked to mining activities. The corporate responsibility to respect human rights extends beyond those involved in the extraction of minerals, to all those along the supply chain.
The brutality of the crimes detailed in this report should be a warning for all corporations buying minerals from Rwanda. These minerals are likely to be trafficked into Rwanda from eastern DRC, where miners are the victims of horrific abuses at the hands of Rwanda-backed M23.
Agnès Callamard
“The brutality of the crimes detailed in this report should be a warning for all corporations buying minerals from Rwanda. These minerals are likely to be trafficked into Rwanda from eastern DRC, where miners are the victims of horrific abuses at the hands of Rwanda-backed M23,” said Agnes Callamard.
“The weight of evidence from Amnesty International and others means that corporations cannot claim ignorance. Their purchase of minerals out of Rwanda – and from the smelters that buy from Rwanda – is likely to contribute to human rights abuses by M23 in Rubaya and Lomera. Corporations could be held criminally responsible for complicity in war crimes.”
*Names have been changed to protect the identity of the interviewees

United Russia dominates wartime parliamentary election in early returns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
01:01:00 UTC
10:01:00 KST

Russia's ruling party, United Russia, has dominated early returns in the country's first wartime parliamentary election, according to figures released by the Central Election Commission.
With approximately 58 percent of precincts counted, United Russia holds nearly 58 percent of the vote for the 225 seats allocated through federal party lists.
The party is also positioned to sweep the remaining 225 single-seat races.
Turnout stood at just under 57 percent when polls closed late on Sunday.
The three-day ballot included voters across four occupied Ukrainian regions that Moscow unilaterally annexed after 2022, as well as the Crimean Peninsula, annexed in 2014—actions condemned by the European Union as a "blatant violation of international law".
Some parties excluded
Some anti-war opposition parties were excluded from the campaign.
The liberal Yabloko party, a group openly critical of the conflict, was barred from party-list balloting by Russia's Supreme Court.
Some parties reported electoral violations, including unsecure polling stations, and voters forced onto electronic terminals after being denied paper ballots.
Russia refused to invite observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
The vote concluded amid major military fallout.
Russia's Defence Ministry stated that air defences downed 1,110 Ukrainian drones across Russia, Crimea, and the Black Sea over the weekend.
Drone strikes across the Moscow region left two dead and 20 injured, damaging infrastructure following months of attacks on domestic refineries.

Mainland China’s stock exchanges mount charm offensive amid Hong Kong IPO boom
Domestic bourses are lobbying mainland firms to reconsider Hong Kong listing plans, sources say
Mainland China’s stock exchanges have stepped up lobbying of companies and regulators to prioritise their boards for listings after Hong Kong stole their thunder in fundraising activities in recent years, according to two sources familiar with the matter.
Figures from the exchanges recently met representatives of some mainland companies planning Hong Kong listings, especially first-time issuers and firms in sectors supported by national policies, a source said.
“Exchanges emphasised the benefits of listing on the mainland, including valuations that are generally higher than in Hong Kong, a clearer and more controllable timetable, and more policy resources for sectors that fit Beijing’s priorities,” the person said.
Another source, an intermediary who helps companies with Hong Kong initial public offerings (IPOs), said such lobbying efforts, while routine, had intensified as exchanges operated as businesses “competing for market rankings”.

The Sahel and the UN: a smaller footprint, a different role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
00:53:15 UTC
09:53:15 KST

The Sahel and the UN: a smaller footprint, a different role
As UNGA 81 begins, the UN faces a changing Sahel demanding greater sovereignty.
For a decade, the United Nations’s most visible role in the Sahel was its peacekeeping mission in Mali.
The United Nations Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in Mali (MINUSMA) was established by the Security Council in 2013. Its mandate was terminated in June 2023 at the request of Mali’s transitional government, and the mission completed its withdrawal by the end of that year.
But the end of MINUSMA did not end the UN’s engagement with the region.
Its political work continues through the UN Office for West Africa and the Sahel (UNOWAS), while the wider UN system remains involved in humanitarian and development work.
What has changed is the space in which that engagement takes place.
Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger formally left the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) on January 29, 2025. The three countries have also deepened cooperation through the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), putting sovereignty and strategic autonomy at the centre of their political message.
The humanitarian pressures, meanwhile, have not eased.
Displacement, insecurity, food insecurity and other pressures continue to cross borders, even as governments increasingly insist on handling their security and political affairs on their own terms.
The question is what influence the UN can exercise after the departure of the peacekeeping force that once represented its most substantial presence in the region.
What does the UN’s presence look like now?
The UN’s role today is less about troops and more about diplomacy, mediation, humanitarian assistance and development.
UNOWAS is a special political mission rather than a peacekeeping operation. Its work includes preventive diplomacy, good offices, political mediation, conflict prevention and support for political dialogue.
“The influence the UN can actually exercise is narrow. The AES states have stripped away the mechanisms that once gave outside institutions leverage, leaving ECOWAS and the Rome Statute, and building their own confederation and joint force instead,” said Mubarak Aliyu, a political and security analyst in Nigeria.
In February 2026, the Security Council extended UNOWAS’s mandate until January 31, 2029, while requesting an independent strategic review of its mandate and activities, to be finalised by September 30, 2026.
The review comes as West Africa’s political landscape is being reshaped by military governments, new regional alliances and a stronger emphasis on sovereignty.
Russia has also become an important part of that changing security picture.
“What has actually shaped events this year is Russia’s Africa Corps, which helped Mali’s and Niger’s military governments survive shocks the UN was never positioned to influence, functioning mainly as regime protection rather than counterinsurgency,” Aliyu said.
“Moscow’s leverage extends into the Security Council chamber too, since its veto shapes what collective action the Council can attempt on Mali in the first place.”
Kabir Adamu, founder and managing director of Beacon Security and Innovations Limited, an Abuja-based firm that provides security solutions in Nigeria, the Lake Chad Basin and the Sahel, said the UN should shift its approach away from large deployments of UN troops to diplomatic and towards diplomatic and development solutions.
“Looking ahead, the UN’s priorities in the Sahel should promote effective security sector governance and security sector reform. This will mean pivoting from traditional, large-scale peacekeeping to deep-rooted and core preventive strategies and diplomacy that addresses the root causes of fragility, conflict and violence, as well as instability,” Adamu said.
For the United Nations, diplomacy has become more important as governments turn to other security partnerships and regional arrangements.
How has sovereignty changed the political space?
Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have made sovereignty and strategic autonomy central to their political outlook and built the AES as a framework for closer cooperation.
Their departure from ECOWAS has changed the regional architecture through which West African governments have traditionally dealt with political and security crises.
The UN still works with regional organisations, including ECOWAS and the African Union, but governments no longer share one political framework or the same approach to external engagement.
Consequently, for the UN, maintaining vital political channels has become potentially more difficult.
Adamu said the fragmented security architecture means the UN should seek to work with and through regional organisations and groups, rather than establishing its own large-scale forces.
“As national security structures remain weak and extractive, and regional security architecture fragments, marked by the rise of the Alliance of Sahel States and shifting ECOWAS dynamics, the UN should prioritise pragmatic, inclusive mediation to bridge divides between Sahelian and coastal states, while actively bolstering alternative, functioning frameworks like MNJTF [Multinational Joint Task] and the Accra Initiative,” he said.
Have the problems in the Sahel gone away?
The retreat of peacekeepers has not removed the pressures that brought international organisations into the region in the first place.
Displacement, armed violence, organised crime, food insecurity and climate pressures continue to overlap across the Sahel.
Climate change is perhaps not the root cause of the instability, but environmental and economic pressures can add to existing vulnerabilities, particularly where state institutions are weak and communities are already dealing with conflict and displacement.
For the UN, humanitarian work remains one of the areas where engagement can continue, even when governments reject large-scale military intervention.
Humanitarian work also places greater emphasis on local and regional capacity.
“Crucially, the UN must double down on the core UNISS pillars of governance, resilience, and security by integrating climate-peace initiatives and empowering local capacities, ensuring that international engagement remains flexible, locally owned, and focused on sustainable, multidimensional stability rather than solely militarised responses,” Adamu said.
While the UN cannot determine the security partnerships of sovereign governments or force political processes on authorities that reject them, it can still facilitate dialogue, support humanitarian operations and raise regional crises before the wider international community.
What does UNGA 81 mean for the Sahel?
The 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly opened on September 8, 2026, with its General Debate due to begin on September 22.
The UNGA meets with no UN peacekeeping mission in Mali and with Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger outside ECOWAS, while the AES has become a separate framework for their political and security cooperation.
“That leaves the UN closer to an advocate and service provider than a shaper of outcomes,” Aliyu said. “It can report, brief, fund aid operations and press for access, but it cannot compel it or offer the regime security that has made Russia indispensable to the military governments.”
Yet for the Sahel, insecurity, displacement, humanitarian needs and economic and climate pressures remain.
In the changed regional environment, the UN’s influence is more likely to come through diplomacy than force, through access rather than authority, and through regional relationships rather than a large international security presence.

Bangladesh reports 87 dengue deaths in September, highest monthly toll this year
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
08:48:44 CST
09:48:44 KST

DHAKA, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Bangladesh has logged 87 dengue-related deaths so far in September, representing the highest monthly death toll due to dengue this year.
Six more dengue deaths were confirmed in the 24 hours ending at 8:00 a.m. local time on Sunday in Bangladesh, bringing the total number of fatalities in the country so far this year to 184, said the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
With 1,593 new cases reported in the last 24 hours, confirmed dengue cases have risen to 61,972 since January, according to DGHS figures from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Deaths this year include 87 so far in September, 43 in August, 36 in July and 13 in June.
During the first 20 days in September, 26,126 more dengue cases were recorded after 20,536 people were infected with the mosquito-borne disease last month, according to DGHS data.
The Bangladeshi government rolled out a three-month campaign earlier this month to prevent the disease.
Dengue fever, a viral disease transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, causes an acute illness that usually develops symptoms such as headache, high fever, exhaustion, severe muscle and joint pain, swollen glands, vomiting, and rash. ■

MELBOURNE, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Organized crime police in the Australian state of Tasmania have charged two men after seizing 17 kg of methamphetamine.
The Tasmanian police force said in a statement on Monday that organized crime officers intercepted two vehicles in the state's northwest on Friday.
During a subsequent search, police located and seized 17 kg of methamphetamine with an estimated street value of 8.5 million Australian dollars (6.1 million U.S. dollars).
Police said it was believed to be the single largest seizure of methamphetamine in Tasmania.
About 100,000 AUD (71,217 USD) in cash was also located during a search of the vehicles and other locations.

If convicted, they face maximum penalties of 21 years' imprisonment.

The head of Poland's Interior Ministry announced the measure on Saturday during a briefing in Lublin, amid increasingly frequent Russian strikes on targets near the Polish-Ukrainian border.
According to Kierwiński, Russia has changed its tactics: border crossings and other infrastructure facilities near the border are increasingly becoming targets of attacks involving strike drones and missiles.
"We are increasingly turning to tools designed to counter these threats," Kierwiński said.
The minister noted that at the beginning of 2024, the region had only around 30 operational sirens that could be activated remotely, whereas today their number is nearly 350.
The article says that the strengthening of protective measures followed a series of attacks that disrupted civilians' daily lives and exposed the vulnerability of infrastructure near Poland's border.
As Ukrinform reported, on the night of September 13, a Russian attack damaged a gas station near the Yahodyn border crossing in Volyn, on the border with Poland. A locomotive near the Polish border was also damaged.

Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as the strongest party in Sunday's state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while the Left Party finished first in Berlin's state election, according to preliminary results.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the AfD won 38.2% of the vote, ahead of the governing Social Democratic Party (SPD) with 35.5%, according to the state election commission.
The Left Party received 6.5% and the Greens 5.7%, giving them five seats each in the 71-seat parliament. The AfD is set to hold 32 seats and the SPD 29.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) fell below the 5% threshold with 4.9%, preventing it from entering the state parliament for the first time since the founding of the Federal Republic. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) also narrowly missed the threshold with 4.8%.
The result leaves the existing SPD-Left coalition without a majority, while an SPD-Left-Greens alliance would have enough seats to govern. All three parties have ruled out forming a coalition with the AfD.
In Berlin, the Left Party won the state election with about 25.3% of the vote, ahead of the CDU at 19%, according to preliminary results. The AfD received about 16% and the SPD 12.1%.
The elections, held on Sept. 20, were the first state polls in both regions in which 16- and 17-year-olds were eligible to vote.
The results are expected to intensify pressure on Merz, whose CDU suffered significant losses in both states.

Ethiopian armed groups forge alliance against government
Former adversaries say they will settle differences as fears grow of expanding war in Ethiopia.
Seven Ethiopian armed groups have formed an alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
The groups announced the alliance on Sunday, saying that they would work together to set up an inclusive transitional government.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items

- list 2 of 2US lifts sanctions on Eritrea ‘to advance US regional interests’ in Red Sea
“We have established a joint alliance called the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, known in short as the Alliance for Survival,” the groups said in a joint statement.
The alliance includes the Amhara Fano National Movement, a coalition of Fano factions that has fought federal forces in the Amhara region since 2023; the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office; and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), which has fought federal forces in Oromia since 2018.
Four smaller groups – the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), the Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (Ugugumo), the Benishangul Peoples’ Liberation Movement and the Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement – make up the rest.
The groups’ leaders had been talking to form the alliance for about a year, a source close to Fano told Al Jazeera on Sunday.
The announcement comes weeks after clashes in the northern region of Tigray, one of the most serious breaches yet of a 2022 peace deal, deepened fears of a return to full-scale war.
Fighting has gripped parts of Oromia since 2018 and Amhara since 2023.
Abiy came to power in 2018 promising sweeping reforms. He freed journalists, activists and other political prisoners and revoked bans on many political parties after taking power.
But his opponents and human rights activists accuse his government of reversing those gains in recent years.
In the statement, the alliance accuses the government of imposing “dictatorial rule” that has pushed the country towards break-up.
It also says a transitional government guided by a charter would work to end the wars, protect rights and open a national dialogue.
Jaal Marroo, the OLA’s military leader, told a local broadcaster earlier this month that they had met several times before settling on the final announcement.
Zemene Kassie, the Fano leader, first publicly indicated that deals had been reached in an interview with the Swiss newspaper Le Temps, published on August 16.
The government has not publicly commented on Sunday’s announcement.
Fano fought alongside federal forces against Tigray’s fighters in the Tigray war of 2020 to 2022, which killed hundreds of thousands.
Amhara and Tigray also both claim Western Tigray, which Amhara nationalists have administered since the war ended.
Ethiopian academic Eyob Tilahun told Al Jazeera on Sunday that the competing groups had agreed to have a dialogue and form an alliance “in the best interests of the public”.
“Those allied forces believe that they all face a survival threat from the government,” Eyob said.
The 2022 peace agreement, signed in Pretoria, South Africa, ended the war between the federal government and Tigray’s forces but left disputes over disarmament and the TPLF’s legal status unresolved.
In mid-July, the TPLF declared the 2022 Pretoria peace deal “effectively dead”.

What is celebrated on September 21 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
03:24:01 EEST
09:24:01 KST

What is celebrated on September 21 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On September 21, the International Day of Peace, World Alzheimer's Day, and World Gratitude Day are observed. Armenia and Malta celebrate their independence.
On September 21, Ukraine and the world observe the International Day of Peace and World Alzheimer's Day, while Armenia and Malta celebrate their Independence Days. According to the church calendar under the new style, the Feast of Saint Quadratus, Apostle of the Seventy, and the Finding of the Relics of Saint Demetrius of Rostov are commemorated, UNN writes.
Peace Day in Ukraine and the International Day of Peace
An official holiday in Ukraine, established by a presidential decree in 2002, which coincides annually with the International Day of Peace under the auspices of the UN (established in 1981 by a decision of the General Assembly). The event is dedicated to strengthening the ideals of peace, ceasefires, rejecting violence, and resolving armed conflicts. For Ukraine, amid Russia's full-scale aggression, this day is of exceptional importance, symbolizing the Ukrainian people's aspiration to restore justice, de-occupy their territory, and establish lasting and secure peace.
World Alzheimer's Day
A global medical and social observance established in 1994 at the initiative of Alzheimer's Disease International (ADI) and with the support of the World Health Organization. The event aims to expand public knowledge about neurodegenerative diseases, overcome the stigmatization of people with dementia, promote preventive factors, and support families and caregivers who look after seriously ill patients.
World Gratitude Day
An unofficial international holiday established in 1965 in Hawaii during an international meeting of spiritual leaders and endorsed under the patronage of a UN meditation group. The day encourages people to express sincere gratitude to relatives, colleagues, service members, medical professionals, and everyone who contributes to society's well-being, promoting emotional well-being and psychological resilience.
International Zero Emissions Day
An environmental initiative launched in 2008 by environmental activist Ken Wallace in Canada. The day aims to give the planet a "pause" from burning fossil fuels, encouraging people to minimize the use of electricity generated by coal- and gas-fired power plants, limit the use of cars with internal combustion engines, and draw governments' attention to accelerating the transition to renewable energy sources.
Independence Day of Armenia
The country's main national holiday commemorating the results of the nationwide referendum held on September 21, 1991, when more than 99% of citizens voted to leave the Soviet Union and restore the sovereign Armenian state. The day is marked by official flag-raising ceremonies, formal award ceremonies honoring prominent figures, and festive concerts.
Independence Day of Malta
An official state holiday commemorating the proclamation of the island nation's sovereignty and its withdrawal from the British Empire on September 21, 1964, while retaining membership in the British Commonwealth. The event is accompanied by ceremonial events in Valletta, military parades, and performances by national orchestras.
The Commemoration Day of Saint Quadratus, Apostle of the Seventy, of Athens
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Saint Quadratus, Apostle of the Seventy, of Athens, who preached the Apostolic teaching in Athens and Magnesia in the 2nd century and was consequently stoned and starved to death in prison under Emperor Hadrian. On this day, they also commemorate the finding of the relics of Saint Demetrius, Metropolitan of Rostov—a native of the Kyiv region, a prominent Ukrainian church figure, writer, and theologian of the 17th–18th centuries, and author of the fundamental work "Chet'i-Minei" (The Lives of the Saints).
According to the old calendar, believers celebrate one of the Twelve Great Feasts—the Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos (the Lesser Purification). The feast was established in honor of the birth of the Virgin Mary to the righteous Joachim and Anna in Jerusalem. In Ukrainian folk tradition, this day was considered a harvest festival, a women's day, and the beginning of autumn weddings, when people gave thanks to God for the grain harvested and prayed for the protection of their families.

Macron, Carney agree to deepen transatlantic ties at historic summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
00:23:53 UTC
09:23:53 KST

French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney have agreed to deepen transatlantic ties and advance cooperation across defence, energy and strategic sectors during a historic working summit in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon.
"Today, to be sovereign goes beyond being able to feed, fuel and defend ourselves," Carney said, adding that contemporary sovereignty "requires secure access to artificial intelligence, to space, semiconductors, critical minerals (and) clean energy."
The bilateral meeting in the French overseas archipelago, located 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) off the coast of Newfoundland, marked the first official visit by a Canadian prime minister to the territory.
Macron called for opening a new chapter following a "difficult page" written in 1992 that "traumatised Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon," referring to a June 10, 1992 international arbitration decision that drastically restricted the French territory's maritime borders.
He welcomed Carney's presence as repairing an "aberration of history" due to no Canadian prime minister having previously set foot on the archipelago, emphasising that both nations are united by shared democratic values, international law, and a commitment to strategic autonomy.
On defence and aerospace, Macron welcomed a contract signed on Friday between French space-tracking firm Aldoria and Public Services and Procurement Canada to supply space surveillance data to the Canadian Armed Forces Space Division.
Carney said the two countries had tasked their defence ministries and national space agencies to develop and share common infrastructure, including launch systems and reception facilities. Macron also highlighted Canada's place in the international coalition of the willing supporting Ukraine.
Addressing fuel prices and energy supply concerns driven by Middle Eastern tensions, the French president said that Canadian liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects could contribute to European energy security, noting that bilateral discussions on concrete projects have begun.
Forging closer ties
The leaders agreed to address short-term energy challenges at an upcoming G7 meeting dedicated to energy topics under French leadership while affirming their dedication to the medium-term energy transition.
In parallel, they welcomed a strategic partnership between CCI France and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce to bring their business communities closer together, while they separately discussed cooperation in critical minerals, rare earths, quantum technologies and artificial intelligence.
To advance regional integration, Macron announced that he asked France's higher education minister to cover the tuition fee differential for Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon students attending Canadian universities.
The leaders also tasked the Regional Joint Cooperation Commission between Atlantic Canada and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon to expand work in priority areas, including greenhouse gas emissions, economic growth, energy transition, climate resilience and telecommunications cables.
Looking ahead to the UN General Assembly in New York, Macron noted that France and Canada stand side by side on international priorities, including Palestine, child protection on social networks, and artificial intelligence regulation.
