Why is the blockade of the Black Sea being compared to the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz, and what threat does this pose to the world?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
03:21:19 EEST
09:21:19 KST

Why is the blockade of the Black Sea being compared to the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz, and what threat does this pose to the world?
Kyiv • UNN
The attacks have reduced grain supplies from Ukraine and Russia, pushing wheat prices to a three-year high. The EU warns of a global crisis.
The blockade of shipping in the Black Sea is increasingly disrupting global grain supplies and forcing the largest importers to seek alternative suppliers. Russia and Ukraine account for more than a quarter of global wheat trade, so further escalation could trigger another surge in food prices, Bloomberg reports, writes UNN.
Details
Supplies through the Black Sea have sharply declined following intensified attacks on ports, grain terminals, elevators, and vessels. According to SovEcon, combined wheat exports from Ukraine and Russia in July–September may amount to approximately half of last year’s volume.
Egypt—the world’s largest wheat buyer—has not received grain from the Black Sea for about a month. Meanwhile, wheat prices have risen to their highest level in three years.
The Black Sea is being compared with the Strait of Hormuz
The region’s role in the global food market is being compared with the Strait of Hormuz’s role in the oil market. In addition to more than a quarter of global wheat trade, Ukraine and Russia account for about two-thirds of sunflower oil trade and approximately 10% of corn supplies.
Buyers are already shifting to France, the Baltic states, Romania, Argentina, India, Australia, and the United States. However, it is difficult to quickly make up for the lost Black Sea volumes because of limited harvests, more expensive logistics, and a shortage of transport capacity.
The situation remains particularly difficult for Ukraine. The ports of the Odesa region usually handle about 90% of Ukraine’s grain exports, while alternative routes are unable to fully replace maritime transport.
In August, Ukraine’s agricultural exports fell to their lowest level since April 2022. Due to the accumulation of the new harvest, grain storage facilities in Ukraine could be filled as early as the beginning of November.
The EU warns that further disruptions in the Black Sea could trigger a new global food security shock, particularly for countries in Africa and the Middle East that depend heavily on Ukrainian and Russian grain.

Does a low resting heart rate actually cause antisocial behavior?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
00:00:38 UTC
09:00:38 KST

A new study has discovered that a desire for exciting and risky experiences is associated with higher levels of antisocial behavior, with little evidence that resting heart rate itself causes antisocial behavior. Published in Aggression and Violent Behavior, these findings suggest that sensation seeking may be a more useful focus for future prevention research.
Antisocial behavior refers to actions that break social rules or disregard other people’s rights and feelings. It can include aggression, deceit, rule-breaking, vandalism and violence. High levels of antisocial behavior during childhood can persist into adulthood and are associated with later criminal behavior and other harmful outcomes.
For decades, researchers have also observed a relationship between antisocial behavior and resting heart rate — the number of heartbeats per minute when a person is calm. People with lower resting heart rates have often been found to show more antisocial behavior. One explanation is that a low heart rate may create an uncomfortable feeling of under-stimulation, leading some people to seek intense experiences. Another possibility is that a low heart rate reflects lower fear or inhibition, making risky or harmful behavior less difficult.
Sensation seeking describes a strong preference for varied, novel and intense experiences, along with a willingness to take risks to obtain them. Previous studies have linked sensation seeking with aggression and rule-breaking, but most were observational. A major goal of this new study was to determine if sensation seeking mediates — or acts as a bridging mechanism for — the established relationship between resting heart rate and antisocial behavior.
Led by Timon G. Udo of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, researchers analyzed data from the Netherlands Twin Register. The broad sample included 8,422 adults (66.4% female, average age of 41.9 years). The researchers also examined 1,927 fraternal twins (67.1% female, average age 32.45 years) and a separate group of 2,599 identical twins (74.3% female, average age 34.73 years).
Participants completed questionnaires measuring antisocial behavior and sensation seeking. Because the researchers did not have direct resting heart rate measurements, they used polygenic scores — an estimate of genetic predisposition based on multiple genes — associated with resting heart rate as an indirect substitute. They then used statistical models to compare differences between families and differences between twins within the same family.
In the broad sample, people with higher sensation-seeking scores also tended to report more antisocial behavior. This relationship remained when the researchers analyzed fraternal twins and identical twins. A significant within-family relationship remained even among identical twins, who share 100% of their DNA and much of their early environment. This pattern is consistent with a possible causal contribution from sensation seeking, although it does not establish one.
The evidence for resting heart rate was less convincing. The genetic proxy for resting heart rate predicted antisocial behavior in the broad sample, but in an unexpected direction: a genetic tendency toward a higher resting heart rate was linked to more antisocial behavior. The relationship disappeared in the fraternal-twin analysis, and the proxy did not predict sensation seeking. The researchers therefore found no evidence that sensation seeking mediated a resting heart rate relationship.
Udo and colleagues concluded that “[sensation seeking] could therefore be an effective target for [antisocial behavior] interventions, regardless of [resting heart rate].” This does not mean that sensation seeking should simply be suppressed. The researchers suggested that safer activities could potentially provide stimulation without involving antisocial behavior.
The study had several important limitations. Resting heart rate was not measured directly, and the genetic proxy captured only part of the factors influencing it. Also, antisocial behavior and sensation seeking were assessed using self-report questionnaires. Furthermore, the participants generally scored very low on antisocial behavior, meaning the findings might not apply to severely antisocial populations, and the study could not definitively confirm the direction of cause and effect.
The study, “Adventurous and antisocial hearts: Investigating the causality of associations between antisocial behaviour, resting heart rate and sensation seeking,” was authored by Timon G. Udo, Susanne Bruins, René Pool and Camiel M. van der Laan.

Nearly 50% rise in drug seizures by Hong Kong customs in first half of year
About 60 per cent of 5,704kg of narcotics seized in six-month period was cannabis and ketamine, with notable increases in smuggling via air and sea
The Customs and Excise Department confiscated 5,704kg (12,575lbs) of illegal narcotics in the first half, a 49 per cent increase year on year, according to figures seen by the South China Morning Post.

Cannabis and ketamine accounted for about 60 per cent of the drugs seized in the first six months, marking a rise of 40 per cent and 78.8 per cent of those substances, respectively. The number of drug cases detected by customs and the number of arrestees also recorded a slight increase.

ICE officer shoots and wounds man in Austin, Texas, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
23:59:28 UTC
08:59:28 KST

ICE officer shoots and wounds man in Austin, Texas, officials say
An immigration attorney representing the man’s family identifies him as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan.
A man has been hospitalised after being shot in the torso by a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in the Texas capital, Austin, local authorities said.
The man was in a serious but stable condition at a hospital after being shot once in the torso on the city’s north side on Sunday afternoon, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said at a news conference with the local mayor and other city officials.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US judge declines Minnesota’s effort to force Texas to extradite ICE agent
- list 2 of 3Mother and daughter detained by ICE in hospital after car crash
- list 3 of 3US immigration agents arrested more than 49,500 people in July
An immigration attorney representing the man’s family identified him as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan.
Lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch said in a video posted to her Instagram account that she believed he had no criminal history and no final order of removal from the US, but she later told the Associated Press news agency that she did not know his current immigration status.
The man’s family has struggled to get any information from the hospital about his status or location, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.
Austin police officers were not involved in the operation or the shooting, which occurred after a traffic stop, Davis told reporters.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not participate in the news conference and didn’t immediately respond to requests for details.
Austin Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said he wants the city’s police department to be involved in the investigation so it can provide “clear, third-party eyes” in the process. Watson said he does not think it would be appropriate for ICE to conduct an investigation on its own.
Austin residents have “a right to feel safe in their city”, Watson said. A proper investigation will only enhance credibility, he added.
Asked if Austin authorities knew where the involved federal agent is, given that agents have left states after previous shootings nationwide, the mayor said: “We do not know that. But my hope would be that an agent that’s involved in an officer-involved shooting would not leave the city. Certainly not leave the state.”
Davis said she did not yet know the nationality of the person who was shot. The police chief said there were not many facts she could provide so soon after the incident, but added that her department’s special investigation unit was at the scene.
Protesters gather at shooting site
A large law enforcement presence was at the location of the shooting, along with a crowd of about 100 protesters. Some demonstrators cursed at police officers holding riot shields, while others yelled out as passing cars honked in support of the protest. One man held a sign saying “Nobody is safe” and, on the other side, “ICE Nazi”.
US Representative Greg Casar, a Democrat representing parts of Austin, called for transparency as the shooting is investigated.
“It is awful that this horror has come to our doorstep,” Casar told reporters. “For Austin to be safe, ICE should end its surge here.”
The shooting comes as ICE surged enforcement across the US this summer, producing more than 50,000 arrests a month for the first time in its history in July and August.
In July, an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, of Houston, after federal agents driving unmarked vehicles pursued him while he was taking his construction crew to a job site.

Israel places West Bank Muslim shrine under control of antiquities authority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
23:53:47 UTC
08:53:47 KST

Awad Rajoob and Mohammad Sio
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
Israeli forces raided several areas of Tulkarm in the northern occupied West Bank on Sunday and posted notices placing a Muslim shrine under the authority of the Israeli Antiquities Authority, according to official Palestinian media.
The Bint Yaqub shrine was among the sites declared subject to the antiquities authority, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
The two-story structure has a lower floor dating to the Roman period and an upper floor dating to the Mamluk era, Wafa said.
The site features domes, a prayer room and a passage leading to the ground floor. Two stone-built pools and two structures dating to the Roman period stand in front of the building.
An adjacent modern building known as Al-Fakhara is associated with pottery production and contains a kiln, according to the agency.
The Palestinian Tourism and Antiquities Ministry, in cooperation with Tulkarm Municipality, restored and rehabilitated the site between 2002 and 2004.
Responding to the Israeli move, the Palestinian Endowments Ministry condemned the move by Israeli authorities to designate the shrine as an archaeological area under the authority of the Israeli Antiquities Authority.
The ministry said the shrine stands on Islamic endowment, or waqf, land.
It described the measure as part of an Israeli policy aimed at “seizing and confiscating endowment lands to serve its settlement and expansion plans.”
The ministry called on international and human rights organizations to intervene urgently to halt the violation and protect religious endowment lands and properties from confiscation and seizure.
Sunday’s Israeli raids also targeted Izbat Abu Yasin in the village of Iktaba, the village of Al-Hafasi and other locations, where similar notices were posted concerning large tracts of land on the grounds that they contain archaeological sites.
The measures come amid Israel’s moves to expand its authority over archaeological sites in the occupied West Bank.
In February this year, the Israeli government expanded the powers of the Civil Administration’s archaeology officer to include measures involving archaeological sites in areas partly administered by the Palestinian Authority, according to Israeli organization Emek Shaveh.
In May, the Israeli Knesset approved in a first reading a bill to establish a civilian “Heritage Authority” under the Israeli Heritage Ministry to administer archaeological and heritage sites in the occupied West Bank instead of the Civil Administration’s archaeology unit.
Further advancement of the bill later stalled, according to Emek Shaveh.

It has become known how many &quot;Bars&quot; cruise missiles Ukraine produces — the figure is impressive
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

02:34:12 EEST
08:34:12 KST

It has become known how many "Bars" cruise missiles Ukraine produces — the figure is impressive
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine has announced the production of about 2,000 “Bars” missiles per month and 200 long-range missions. The warhead is planned to be increased to 60 kg.
Ukraine produces around 2,000 small Bars cruise missiles per month and actively uses them for long-range strikes against Russian territory. Defense Express reports this, citing a representative of an unnamed manufacturing company, writes UNN.
Details
As of spring 2026, Ukrainian forces have already carried out around 200 long-range missions using Bars missiles. At the same time, Defense Express emphasizes that the published production figures come from an unnamed manufacturer and have not been independently verified.
The stated production rate is approaching Russia’s output of strike drones powered by jet engines, which the publication estimates at approximately 3,500 units per month.
The Bars continues to be improved
The manufacturer plans to increase the missile’s effectiveness to a level at which approximately 75% of launched Bars missiles will be able to reach and hit their designated targets.
It is also reported that the warhead’s weight will be increased from 22 to 60 kg. At the same time, Defense Express draws attention to the limited capacity for producing small jet engines in Ukraine and partner countries.
Because of this, the further development of the Bars may involve gradually bringing its characteristics closer to those of full-fledged cruise missiles with greater striking power.

Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones have received new electronic intelligence and warfare systems that allow them to detect and suppress enemy radars and air defense systems. Such equipment could theoretically expand the capabilities of Ukrainian drones, Defense Express reports, writes UNN.
Details
Turkey’s Aselsan has integrated three external pods onto the Bayraktar TB2: the Antidot 2ES 100, Antidot 2EA 200, and Fulmar 200.
The Antidot 2ES 100 is designed for electronic intelligence. The system can detect, identify, and determine the coordinates of radio-emission sources, including radar stations.
Bayraktar receives air defense countermeasure systems
The second pod, the Antidot 2EA 200, is designed for electronic warfare. It can jam radar operations and increase the drone’s protection against missiles with radar homing seekers.
The simultaneous use of the two systems gives the Bayraktar TB2 the ability to detect air defense elements and counter their radars. In Aselsan’s promotional materials, the Russian Pantsir-S1 air defense gun-missile system is shown among the potential targets.
Another pod, the Fulmar 200, makes it possible to obtain SAR images at a distance of up to 40 km and from an altitude of up to 9 km.
Defense Express notes that, due to dense Russian air defenses, the strike use of Bayraktar TB2 drones in Ukraine is currently limited. The new equipment could theoretically give these drones a different role: reconnaissance, locating Russian radars and surface-to-air missile systems, and participating in the suppression of air defenses.

Archaeologists have found evidence that the Soviet Gulag in Kazakhstan may have operated longer than previously thought
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
02:22:30 EEST
08:22:30 KST

Archaeologists have found evidence that the Soviet Gulag in Kazakhstan may have operated longer than previously thought
Kyiv • UNN
Czech archaeologists discovered bottles dating from 1959–1960 at the site of the Steplag in Kazakhstan. This may indicate that the camp continued operating after its closure in 1956.
Czech archaeologists have found evidence that the Soviet StepLag camp in Kazakhstan may have continued operating after its official closure in 1956. Radio Prague International reports on the findings of researchers from the University of West Bohemia and the Gulag.cz organization, writes UNN.
Details
The researchers worked near the city of Zhezkazgan, where StepLag—a special camp for political prisoners—operated from 1948 to 1956. More than 20,000 people passed through it in total.
According to archival documents, the Soviet authorities closed the camp in 1956. However, a local witness told archaeologists that women continued to be held there until at least 1959.
The finds have cast doubt on the archival records.
During the excavations, the researchers discovered fragments of bottles dated to 1959 and 1960. In the archaeologists' view, the finds confirm that official Soviet archives alone cannot be relied upon when studying the history of the camps.
The site of StepLag also preserves traces of at least three rows of massive barbed-wire fences, guard towers, and solitary cells.
The Czech team is also studying other sites associated with the Gulag system. Previously, the archaeologists worked in Siberia and documented the first material evidence of the existence of Soviet camps in Uzbekistan.

Macron and Carney agree to deepen transatlantic cooperation during historic summit in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
23:09:26 UTC
08:09:26 KST

Yasin Gungor
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney agreed Sunday to deepen transatlantic ties and advance cooperation across defense, energy and strategic sectors during a historic working summit in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon.
"Today, to be sovereign goes beyond being able to feed, fuel and defend ourselves," Carney said, adding that contemporary sovereignty "requires secure access to artificial intelligence, to space, semiconductors, critical minerals (and) clean energy."
The bilateral meeting in the French overseas archipelago, located 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) off the coast of Newfoundland, marked the first official visit by a Canadian prime minister to the territory.
Macron called for opening a new chapter following a "difficult page" written in 1992 that "traumatized Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon," referring to a June 10, 1992 international arbitration decision that drastically restricted the French territory's maritime borders.
He welcomed Carney's presence as repairing an "aberration of history" due to no Canadian prime minister having previously set foot on the archipelago, emphasizing that both nations are united by shared democratic values, international law, and a commitment to strategic autonomy.
On defense and aerospace, Macron welcomed a contract signed Friday between French space-tracking firm Aldoria and Public Services and Procurement Canada to supply space surveillance data to the Canadian Armed Forces Space Division.
Carney said the two countries had tasked their defense ministries and national space agencies to develop and share common infrastructure, including launch systems and reception facilities. Macron also highlighted Canada's place in the international coalition of the willing supporting Ukraine.
Addressing fuel prices and energy supply concerns driven by Middle Eastern tensions, the French president said that Canadian liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects could contribute to European energy security, noting that bilateral discussions on concrete projects have begun.
The leaders agreed to address short-term energy challenges at an upcoming G7 meeting dedicated to energy topics under French leadership while affirming their dedication to the medium-term energy transition.
In parallel, they welcomed a strategic partnership between CCI France and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce to bring their business communities closer together, while they separately discussed cooperation in critical minerals, rare earths, quantum technologies and artificial intelligence.
To advance regional integration, Macron announced that he asked France's higher education minister to cover the tuition fee differential for Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon students attending Canadian universities.
The leaders also tasked the Regional Joint Cooperation Commission between Atlantic Canada and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon to expand work in priority areas, including greenhouse gas emissions, economic growth, energy transition, climate resilience and telecommunications cables. Macron also proposed working with Canada to provide new vocational training opportunities, particularly in fisheries.
The leaders also announced the creation of the Canada-France Polar Research Forum, which will alternate between both countries after its inaugural edition in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, while agreeing to enhance cooperation between national meteorological services and deepen early-warning systems under the CREWS initiative.
Looking ahead to the UN General Assembly in New York, Macron noted that France and Canada stand side by side on international priorities, including Palestine, child protection on social networks, and artificial intelligence regulation.

IMF chief says world economy faces multiple risks despite resilience
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
06:58:17 CST
07:58:17 KST

Kristalina Georgieva (R), managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), speaks in a dialogue at a special edition of the Qatar Economic Forum in New York City, the United States, Sept. 20, 2026. The world economy faces risks from stubborn inflation, higher debt service cost and artificial intelligence (AI) investment though it has proven to be more resilient than many feared, according to Kristalina Georgieva. (Xinhua/Liu Yanan)
NEW YORK, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- The world economy faces risks from stubborn inflation, higher debt service cost and artificial intelligence (AI) investment though it has proven to be more resilient than many feared, according to Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Speaking in a dialogue at a special edition of the Qatar Economic Forum in New York City on Sunday, Georgieva said, "Inflation is stubborn. We are not anticipating a quick resolution. And that means that many central banks have to tighten."
Georgieva noted that the fight to secure price stability also increased the cost and difficulty of debt service. There is a lot of understanding of the necessity of fiscal consolidation, but not enough action, she added.
Moreover, Georgieva highlighted the potential risks from leverage and circular financing in AI investment, saying this is "something that we have to be mindful of."
"If AI disappoints, because we have these high expectations, if they don't materialize, disappointment may lead to potentially a shock to the system," warned Georgieva.
Risk in AI financing is "primarily concentrated in the United States" while many other players in Asia and Europe are included in the supply chain of AI, added Georgieva.
The IMF's new projection on the world economy to be released in October will reflect the fact that the risks will remain high, according to Georgieva.
"Having growth that would be hovering around 3 percent is a massive achievement, given all the shocks we have been experiencing," said Georgieva.
Georgieva said she saw optimism from remarkable, fast action when it's necessary to counter the energy supply shock.
"While there is a lot of talk about a fragmented world. And indeed, it is less unified. It is still a world in which we are interdependent and we cooperate," said Georgieva.
"We have to be careful and cautious. The risks are high and uncertainty is the new normal," she added. ■

The Kremlin wants the elections to showcase popular support for the war in Ukraine and legitimise its action.
The ruling United Russia party is on course to win the country’s first wartime parliamentary elections, according to early returns from the tightly controlled vote, which was marked by cyberattacks and a barrage of Ukrainian drone attacks.
The Kremlin wants the elections, the first parliamentary vote since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, to showcase popular support for the war and legitimise its action.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3The view from Russia: ‘No party can be antiwar’ in parliamentary election
- list 2 of 3Do elections in Russia make a difference?
- list 3 of 3Russia’s elections are more than political theatre
Russian government officials accused Ukraine of trying to disrupt voting after Kyiv launched hundreds of drones at Moscow and other regions in what the TASS state news agency said was the biggest attack of its kind since the war began.
The drone strikes on Sunday killed at least three people in the Moscow region and two more in the Russian-held part of Ukraine’s Kherson region, including an election official, according to the region’s governor and the election commission.
Russian authorities also reported attacks on the country’s electronic voting systems and communication lines during the polls, but said the electoral process was mostly smooth.
With some 58 percent of the precincts counted, United Russia had nearly 58 percent of the vote for the 225 deputies apportioned by party lists, according to Russia’s Central Election Commission. Another 225 lawmakers will be chosen in single-seat races, and United Russia was also poised to win most of those.
Authorities said turnout at the close of polls stood at 56.66 percent.
Voting in Russian-held Ukrainian areas
The vote, which began on Friday for 111 million eligible voters, included residents of four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed after the war began, but still doesn’t fully control, as well as those in Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula that was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014.
Authorities in Kyiv denounced the voting in the Russian-held areas as illegal and urged foreign governments not to recognise the result. The European Union on Friday called the action a “blatant violation of international law”.
Voters cast two separate ballots, filling half of the lower house’s 450 seats by selecting political parties listed on the ballot. The rest are contested in single-seat constituencies, with voters choosing individual candidates.
The main Kremlin party, United Russia, is widely expected to retain its overwhelming control of the State Duma. Several smaller parties of the “systemic opposition” that vote in sync with Putin’s views on all key issues are also expected to maintain their presence.
A massive state media campaign and tight control over the elections in the absence of genuine opposition all but assure the Kremlin will keep tight control of Russian politics amid mounting economic costs and increasing Ukrainian drone attacks deep inside the country.
The liberal Yabloko party, the only registered political entity that dared to publicly criticise the war, was removed from the ballot last month by Russia’s Supreme Court. It only has a few dozen candidates in the single-constituency races.
Additionally, some anti-war politicians were imprisoned or forced to flee abroad ahead of the campaign.
Russia didn’t invite election observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe. The Russian Foreign Ministry has accused the body of “double standards” for its criticism of Russia.

2026-09-20

IN BRIEF
- Australia's overincarceration of Indigenous children could hinder its chances of joining the UN's Security Council.
- Indigenous young people between 10 and 17 years old made up 60 per cent of the youth detention population.
Australia is seeking international backing for a seat at the United Nations' highest table, but the federal government has recently been the subject of an urgent UN plea to address the overrepresentation of Indigenous children behind bars.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese launched the campaign for a two-year stint on the UN Security Council overnight in New York with a promotional video that begins with Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy speaking in her traditional Yanyuwa language.
She goes on to appeal for support for Australia's bid, saying: "We are home to the oldest continuous culture on the planet."
But the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination issued an "early warning and urgent action procedure” earlier this year, expressing grave concerns about racial discrimination against Indigenous children through education, healthcare and housing conditions — a "key factor contributing to their heightened vulnerability to arrest, incarceration and re-offending".
The committee criticised the states and territories where the age of criminal responsibility is 10 years of age and where children face adult penalties for their crimes, including life in prison.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
It also raised a red flag about the "limited progress" on the Closing the Gap measures which are at the heart of the federal government's Indigenous Affairs policy.
It followed an investigation by the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention into Indigenous youth incarceration in Australia.
Last year the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare found Indigenous young people between 10 and 17 years old made up 60 per cent of the youth detention population across the country — despite making up only 6.6 per cent of the general population.
Indigenous young people were 21 times more likely than non-Indigenous youth to be in detention, and the numbers were increasing.
When pressed by SBS News in New York to explain how he would address concerns that the federal government is not showing enough leadership, the prime minister said he would discuss the issues with Indigenous leaders when he returns to Australia.
"Indigenous disadvantage is a fact in Australia," Albanese said.
"My government continues to work on Closing the Gap in a range of areas in Australia."
The prime minister also responded to questions about an investigation by The Australian newspaper into the Indigenous child protection system in Western Australia, despite yesterday dodging similar questions by saying he would not address domestic issues while abroad.
"We're not about to intervene against the Western Australian government," he said.
"This is a Western Australian issue, and, you know, I will refer you once again to Malarndirri McCarthy, our minister in Australia. It is impossible to follow, on an hour-by-hour basis, what is happening in Australia from New York."
Albanese said it was right to highlight the importance of Australia's Indigenous culture in the United Nations Security Council bid, to secure a non-permanent seat for two years in 2029 and 2030.
"Indigenous disadvantage is something that, of course, I’m always concerned with ... we have in having the oldest continuous culture on Earth, and that needs to be a source of pride. It certainly is for myself as Australia's prime minister."
Albanese went on to outline the government’s efforts to address a chronic housing shortage in remote Indigenous communities.
"That is a multi-billion-dollar program being rolled out."
He also said the government's public education funding deal was helping young Indigenous students access school, and the federal government was assisting in healthcare, including providing financial support for dialysis treatment in remote communities.
He defended the measures the government has taken to support more job opportunities and said the Indigenous ranger program was raised during his trip to Apple headquarters in Silicon Valley, being partly funded by the company.
"You don't overcome intergenerational disadvantage in a year, or indeed in a term," he said.
"If there were easy answers, someone would have done it. The truth is, it hasn't happened. The truth is, all governments in Australia need to do better, and that is one of the priorities that my government has."
Australia and Finland are the only countries that have so far nominated for the two seats allocated for their geographic area; if no other countries nominate and they are accepted, they would be assured of securing the coveted positions.
Albanese said elevation to the council would ensure Australia has a voice on the future of Artificial Intelligence, climate action and dealing with international conflicts, arguing that would also mean being able to make a difference to domestic cost of living issues like inflation and fuel prices.
He said it would be a "modest" campaign in terms of the cost to taxpayers.

Qatar has said that its mediation team has been discussing proposals for nearly two weeks aimed at restarting talks between the United States and Iran.
“We have been exchanging various ideas for nearly two weeks on resuming talks between Washington and Tehran,” said Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari, according to Qatari media.
Qatar, alongside Pakistan, has been mediating between the two sides.
“We are working through our mediation team with Tehran and Washington to see whether talks can resume, and our mediators are currently moving between different capitals in the hope of making progress on this track,” al-Ansari said.
He added that Qatar had heard assurances from officials in the US administration that Washington wanted to reach an agreement.
Al-Ansari said there is a need for “a regional solution that achieves stability and an international understanding that protects waterways such as the Strait of Hormuz.”
“Subjecting waterways to the sovereignty of a single state and using them as a weapon will set a dangerous precedent for all of us,” he added.
The US has recently carried out military attacks on sites in Iran amid a deadlock in negotiations over disagreements concerning navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important routes for energy supplies and global trade, despite a memorandum of understanding signed by the two sides in mid-June.
Iran responded with attacks on what it said were US military facilities and equipment in Arab countries, including Saudi Arabia.
Some of the attacks caused civilian casualties and damage to civilian infrastructure, drawing condemnation from the affected countries and calls for them to stop.
“Unforeseen escalation”
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28, leaving more than 3,000 people dead, according to Tehran.
Iran responded with attacks that it said killed Americans and Israelis.
The remarks from Qatar came after the US State Department issued a security alert Sunday saying that “due to tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex, with the potential for unforeseen escalation.”
It urged US citizens in the region to exercise caution and those outside it to reconsider travel to or through the area.
Several US embassies in the region, including those in the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Jordan, issued similar warnings Sunday.
Earlier in the day, detailing his approach to the war, US President Donald Trump told US network Fox News, “My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up? They had better behave.”
Trump described his current options as wiping the country out, allowing it to “rot” economically, or negotiating a deal, adding that “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future.”

Unknown Publisher

Russia expands Alabuga-Volokno plant: jet-powered drone production could rise by 78% – Politico
Russian state-owned company Alabuga-Volokno is expanding its plant in Tatarstan, potentially increasing the production of jet-powered attack drones by 78%.
Source: Brussels-based politics and policy news organisation Politico, citing internal documents from Russian state-owned corporation Rosatom
Details: According to the documents, by 2029 Alabuga-Volokno plans to produce an additional 500 tonnes of military-grade aerospace carbon fibre every year.
Experts estimate that expanding this capacity could enable the production of an additional 28,000 jet-powered drones each year for attacks on Ukrainian cities. Russia is currently capable of producing more than 36,000 Shahed/Geran kamikaze drones per year.
Alabuga-Volokno is a key link in Russia's defence industry supply chain and the country's only producer of carbon fibre, which provides high strength with minimal weight for manufacturing fuselages for long-range drones.
Alabuga-Volokno and its parent company, Rosatom's advanced materials division KhimPromEngineering (Umatex Group), are under sanctions imposed by the UK, the US and many other Western countries.
Rosatom's business plans and project documents have been gathered by the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre (USCC). According to the documents, the company is building a state-of-the-art plant whose main product will be UMT42S-3K carbon fibre for the aerospace industry.
Satellite images from May to July show that land next to the existing plant is already being cleared for new construction.
The US House Select Committee on China and the Ukrainian government examined the internal documents and fully confirmed their authenticity.
Background:
- In September 2025, Alexander Tyunin, the director of KhimPromEngineering (Umatex Group), was found dead in Moscow Oblast. Early reports suggested that he had taken his own life.
- In early September 2026, evidence emerged of secret supplies of raw materials to the Alabuga-Volokno plant from Chinese company Jilin Chemical Fiber Group. Shipments of chemical precursors for carbon fibre were disguised as civilian materials.
- In late September, it became known that underground production facilities for Shahed attack drones were being built in Russia's Alabuga Special Economic Zone. According to an analysis of satellite images, Russia has already built around 42,000 sq m of underground production space.

Bengal SIR tribunals may take 12 years to decide on appeals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
22:13:55 UTC
07:13:55 KST

SIR appeals pile up in WB, EC says hike number of tribunals
NEW DELHI: The innumerable voters in West Bengal who were removed from the electoral rolls after special intensive revision (SIR) may not be able to vote for more than a decade as appellate tribunals set up by Supreme Court could take more than 12 years to decide on their appeals for inclusion, going by the present pace of adjudication.An affidavit filed by Election Commission before Supreme Court says 1,26,194 applications have been decided by tribunals in the last five months since they started functioning in mid-April. So, on average, 25,238 cases are being decided by the tribunals in a month when even Saturdays and Sundays are included as working days. The total number of pending cases as of Sept 16, when the affidavit was filed, was 37,05,235. At current speed, if the tribunals work seven days a week, it would take 146 months to decide all cases.
Excessive backlog
Admitting that the present infrastructure and number of tribunals are insufficient to handle the Herculean task of adjudicating 37 lakh cases, the poll panel pleaded with the court to increase the number of tribunals in the state from 24 to 42, almost double the present strength, and allow judicial officers to work from home.
"With a view to further streamlining and expediting the disposal of the pending appeals, it is proposed that the number of appellate tribunals in the state of West Bengal may be considered for increase to correspond with the number of parliamentary constituencies in the state, so as to facilitate expeditious disposal of the pending appeals," said the affidavit, filed in response to a petition from TMC MP Derek O' Brien. Allowing judicial workers to conduct hearings and undertake other proceedings from home "would assist in expediting the disposal of pending appeals by minimising the time lost in conveyance", it said.In another affidavit filed in response to a petition on the functioning of the tribunals, the commission said they were constituted pursuant to the directives of the apex court and the standard operating procedure (SOP) governing their functioning has been formulated by the committee constituted for this purpose, comprising, inter alia, former judges of the high court at Calcutta.
"It is humbly submitted that the reliefs sought by the petitioner pertain primarily to the functioning, procedure and accessibility of the appellate mechanism and, therefore, fall within the domain of the SOP governing the functioning of the appellate tribunals and the authorities entrusted with the administration thereof. The feasibility, modalities and implementation... are matters best left to the consideration of the concerned appellate tribunal..." the affidavit said.

21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
Qatar said Sunday that its mediation team has been discussing proposals for nearly two weeks aimed at restarting talks between the United States and Iran.
“We have been exchanging various ideas for nearly two weeks on resuming talks between Washington and Tehran,” said Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari, according to Qatari media.
Qatar, alongside Pakistan, has been mediating between the two sides.
“We are working through our mediation team with Tehran and Washington to see whether talks can resume, and our mediators are currently moving between different capitals in the hope of making progress on this track,” al-Ansari said.
He added that Qatar had heard assurances from officials in the US administration that Washington wanted to reach an agreement.
Al-Ansari said there is a need for “a regional solution that achieves stability and an international understanding that protects waterways such as the Strait of Hormuz.”
“Subjecting waterways to the sovereignty of a single state and using them as a weapon will set a dangerous precedent for all of us,” he added.
The US has recently carried out military attacks on sites in Iran amid a deadlock in negotiations over disagreements concerning navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important routes for energy supplies and global trade, despite a memorandum of understanding signed by the two sides in mid-June.
Iran responded with attacks on what it said were US military facilities and equipment in Arab countries, including Saudi Arabia. Some of the attacks caused civilian casualties and damage to civilian infrastructure, drawing condemnation from the affected countries and calls for them to stop.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28, leaving more than 3,000 people dead, according to Tehran. Iran responded with attacks that it said killed Americans and Israelis.
The remarks from Qatar came after the US State Department issued a security alert Sunday saying that “due to tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex, with the potential for unforeseen escalation.”
It urged US citizens in the region to exercise caution and those outside it to reconsider travel to or through the area.
Several US embassies in the region, including those in the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Jordan, issued similar warnings Sunday.
Earlier in the day, detailing his approach to the war, US President Donald Trump told US network Fox News “my question is if and when do I blow the entire nation up? They had better behave.”
Trump described his current options as wiping the country out, allowing it to “rot” economically, or negotiating a deal, adding that “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future.”

According to data from the European Drought Observatory (EDO), whose records date back to 2012, BiH was among nine European countries that experienced their driest August since the records began.

Under the legal framework of BiH, declaring drought a natural disaster would allow the authorities to legally and rapidly mobilize emergency reserve funds to directly compensate farmers for their economic losses. ■

Israel also imposed a general closure on the occupied West Bank for the holiday, restricting Palestinian movement into Israel and temporarily closing all crossings between the territory and Israel. ■

====================================================================================================

Motor neurone disease rates are rising. This new clinic hopes to stop it at the start
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
22:04:30 UTC
07:04:30 KST

In Brief
- The Brain Institute and Clinic will bring together researchers and clinicians who specialise in motor neurone disease.
- MND impacts the brain and neurons that control muscles, leading to progressive weakness and eventual paralysis.
As the rates of a once-rare neurological disease rise, it is hoped that Australia's first combined institute and clinic focused on brain diseases will help find an effective treatment.
On Monday, Macquarie University will launch its Brain Institute and Clinic to bring together researchers and clinicians who specialise in motor neurone disease (MND) to understand its origins and how to treat it.
MND impacts parts of a person's brain and neurons that control their muscles, leading to progressive weakness and eventual paralysis.
It can affect adults of any age and most cases are not genetic.
Macquarie University deputy vice-chancellor Patrick McNeil noted there was still no effective cure for the deadly disease, despite it becoming increasingly common.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The purpose of the institute was to find treatments and deliver them to patients more quickly, he said.
"It typically takes an average of 17 years between when an important research discovery is made ... and when that is implemented in the clinic," McNeill told the Australian Associated Press.
"When you have integrated research and clinical institutions, that journey is shortened."
Earlier this month, NSW became the first jurisdiction in the world to make MND notifiable, meaning medical professionals are now legally required to report cases to the government.
McNeil said he hoped the decision would help researchers better understand the cause.
"It would be good if the other states follow because that is the way that you can find if there is an environmental agent," he said.
"Because what we have been seeing anecdotally is these clusters of cases that seem to be more frequent in a particular town or region than you would expect."
Dominic Rowe, who heads up Macquarie's Neurology Clinic, said 800 Australians would die from the disease this year.
"But I actually disagree with using the term die; motor neuron disease kills you," he said.
"We need to redouble our efforts into working out why so we can fix it."
The facility will also do research and treatment around Parkinson's disease and dementia, including Alzheimer's disease.
Macquarie University professor James Burrell said he was hopeful experts could build on recent breakthroughs in dementia treatment.
He said there were therapies available that slowed the physical progression of dementia caused by Alzheimer's.
"We now have disease-modifying therapies for this disease, and this gives me tremendous hope that we can identify disease-modifying therapies for other neurodegenerative diseases as well," Burrell said.

People with low implicit self-worth are quicker to notice subtle facial cues of anger and disgust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
22:00:09 UTC
07:00:09 KST

People who harbor unconscious doubts about their self-worth, or who have a large gap between their conscious and unconscious self-esteem, tend to detect subtle facial expressions of disgust and anger earlier than others. This heightened sensitivity to potential social rejection is also linked to poorer interpersonal wellbeing, according to new research published in Personality and Individual Differences.
Self-esteem is generally understood as how much a person values themselves. But psychologists separate this concept into two distinct layers. Explicit self-esteem refers to conscious feelings of self-worth that a person can easily describe, such as agreeing with the statement that they have a number of good qualities. Implicit self-esteem refers to automatic, unconscious evaluations of the self that operate beneath the surface of awareness.
Sometimes, these two layers do not match. A person might report high self-esteem on a questionnaire but harbor deep unconscious doubts about their worth, or they might report low self-worth despite having positive automatic associations with themselves. This mismatch is known as self-esteem discrepancy.
The research was led by Patrycja Korzeniowska, a lecturer in psychology at the School of Psychology, Sport Science & Wellbeing at the University of Lincoln in the UK. She and her colleagues aimed to understand how these different layers of self-evaluation shape the way people perceive the social world around them.
“We were interested in why people differ in their sensitivity to subtle social signals of acceptance and rejection, because detecting and interpreting these cues is an important part of navigating social interactions,” Korzeniowska told PsyPost.
Previous research has explored how self-evaluation alters social perception. For instance, a 2021 study demonstrated that people with lower conscious self-esteem can detect emerging expressions of anger and disgust at earlier, more subtle stages than people with high self-esteem. Building on related concepts, a 2025 study indicated that having low unconscious self-worth, or a mismatch between conscious and unconscious self-esteem, predicts a tendency to interpret ambiguous facial expressions as rejecting.
“Our aim was therefore to examine these components together, rather than treating self-esteem as a single, purely self-reported construct,” Korzeniowska explained. This led the team to test whether unconscious self-worth and self-esteem clashes directly heighten perceptual sensitivity to emerging rejection cues, and how that heightened sensitivity might affect psychological wellbeing.
To investigate this, the scientists recruited 225 adults to complete an emotion detection task. In this task, participants watched short videos of faces that slowly morphed from a completely neutral expression into a full-intensity emotional expression. The possible emotions were anger, disgust, fear, and happiness. The faces increased in emotional intensity in two percent increments, starting from a neutral state and ending at a complete display of emotion.
Participants were instructed to press a key the exact moment they recognized an emotion taking shape on the face, and then they selected which emotion they had seen. This setup allowed the researchers to measure perceptual sensitivity, or the minimum intensity level of the facial expression required for the participant to accurately detect it.
Before the computer task, participants completed several psychological assessments. They filled out a standard questionnaire to measure their explicit self-esteem and a psychological wellbeing scale to assess aspects of their life like personal growth, positive relations with others, and autonomy. To measure implicit self-esteem, the participants completed an Implicit Association Test.
This computer-based task requires people to quickly categorize words related to the self or others alongside positive and negative words. Faster reaction times when pairing self-related words with positive concepts indicate higher implicit self-esteem. By comparing the explicit and implicit scores, the researchers calculated each participant’s self-esteem discrepancy.
The results indicate that unconscious self-evaluation plays a prominent role in reading social cues. Participants with lower implicit self-esteem were able to detect expressions of disgust and anger at much lower intensities than those with higher implicit self-esteem. They were also faster to detect expressions of fear.
The gap between conscious and unconscious self-esteem also played a role. Participants with a larger self-esteem discrepancy required less emotional intensity to spot anger and disgust. This held true regardless of the direction of the gap, meaning it applied both to people who consciously felt great but unconsciously felt poorly, and to people who consciously felt poorly but had high unconscious self-worth.
Interestingly, while conscious self-esteem initially appeared to predict how quickly people spotted anger, this relationship faded when the researchers accounted for unconscious self-esteem. This suggests that previous research attributing heightened rejection sensitivity to low conscious self-esteem might have actually been picking up on the effects of unconscious self-evaluation or the clash between the two layers.
“Wang and colleagues had previously found that lower explicit self-esteem was associated with greater sensitivity to anger and disgust using closely related stimuli, whereas in our models explicit self-esteem was not a significant predictor; instead, implicit self-esteem and self-esteem discrepancy emerged more consistently,” Korzeniowska noted.
“This does not mean that explicit self-esteem is unimportant, as it was strongly associated with psychological wellbeing in our data, but it suggests that different components of self-esteem may relate differently to rapid social-perceptual processes,” she added. “The main takeaway is that how we respond to subtle social cues may be associated with aspects of self-evaluation that are not fully captured by simply asking people how they feel about themselves.”
The researchers also explored how this sensitivity to facial expressions relates to mental health and social functioning. Being highly attuned to early signs of disgust and anger was not directly related to overall psychological wellbeing, but it was linked to specific social outcomes. Heightened sensitivity to disgust, driven by low implicit self-esteem and high discrepancy, predicted poorer positive relations with others.
On the other hand, heightened sensitivity to anger predicted higher self-reported autonomy. While autonomy is generally considered a positive trait, the authors note that in the context of low implicit self-esteem and a high self-esteem discrepancy, this might indicate a defensive posture. People who are hypersensitive to anger might distance themselves from others to avoid negative evaluation and social rejection.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The primary measure used for unconscious self-esteem is widely used, but its exact psychological interpretation remains a topic of debate. Some researchers argue that the sorting task measures automatic associations that a person has learned from their environment rather than a true, unified sense of self-worth.
“One important point is that ‘implicit self-esteem’ should not be understood as a hidden or unconscious ‘true’ self-esteem that the test somehow reveals,” Korzeniowska said. Because the test measures relatively automatic associations between the self and positive or negative evaluations, she noted that the findings “are best understood as evidence concerning automatic self-evaluative associations, and they should ideally be replicated using multiple methods.”
Additionally, while the study measured how quickly people can visually detect facial cues of rejection, this is not exactly the same as feeling rejected in daily life. Spotting a faint flicker of disgust on a computer screen is an automatic perceptual process, whereas real-world rejection sensitivity involves complex emotional and behavioral reactions to social events.
“We measured perceptual sensitivity to facial cues associated with social rejection, not rejection sensitivity as a personality or dispositional construct,” Korzeniowska clarified.
She also emphasized that the effects observed were relatively small, accounting for roughly 4 to 7 percent of the variance in sensitivity to anger and disgust. “These are modest, correlational effects, so the findings should not be interpreted as showing that a particular self-esteem profile causes someone to perceive rejection differently,” Korzeniowska explained. “I see the findings primarily as evidence for an association worth investigating further, rather than something that currently supports individual-level prediction or clinical application.” A larger sample size, she added, would help confirm some of the more subtle interactive effects observed in the data.
“An important next step is to test whether these associations replicate across different measures of automatic self-evaluation and different ways of assessing responses to social rejection,” Korzeniowska said. She hopes to explore whether the same pattern generalizes to more naturalistic social situations and to other behavioral or physiological measures of responses to rejection-related cues.
“I see this study as part of an emerging rather than settled picture,” she told PsyPost. “Together with our previous work showing that lower implicit self-esteem and greater self-esteem discrepancy were associated with interpreting ambiguous facial expressions more negatively, these findings suggest that automatic self-evaluations may be relevant both to how social expressions are interpreted and to how quickly subtle cues are detected.”
The study, “Implicit self-esteem and self-esteem discrepancy: Implications for dynamic facial expression sensitivity and psychological wellbeing,” was authored by Patrycja Korzeniowska, Kun Guo, and Petra M.J. Pollux.

Ukraine joins European framework for TV series co-production
As reported by Ukrinform, Deputy Prime Minister for Humanitarian Policy and Minister of Culture Tetiana Berezhna announced this in a Facebook post.
According to her, this marks an important step toward Ukraine’s integration into the European cultural and audiovisual space.
“For the first time, we are establishing a framework for the co-production of TV series. The document was signed during the Carpathian Integration Summit. For Ukraine’s industry, this creates new opportunities to produce series together with European partners, attract international funding, and enter new markets,” Berezhna said.
The Convention enables productions to obtain official co-production status and guarantees a share of the rights to the finished product, as well as revenue from its use. The document also establishes flexible conditions for financial participation: in multilateral co-productions, a partner’s minimum contribution may be relatively small, opening up more opportunities for Ukrainian teams to participate in major international projects.
“We are working to ensure that Ukrainian stories reach wider audiences around the world, while our producers and creative teams have more opportunities to develop international projects and reach new audiences,” the Deputy Prime Minister stressed.

Gaza launches emergency plan to evacuate and demolish 255 war-damaged buildings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20

Ramzi Mahmud and Mohammad Sio
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
Gaza’s Government Media Office on Sunday announced the launch of an “urgent emergency plan” led by the Ministry of Public Works and Housing in cooperation with various government ministries, institutions and international and UN bodies to evacuate and demolish 255 buildings damaged during Israel’s genocide on the enclave and considered at risk of collapse.
The move follows several partial and complete collapses of buildings previously damaged by Israeli strikes, including the collapse Wednesday of the Al-Saada building in Gaza City, which killed 21 Palestinians.
The plan is intended to eliminate the “imminent danger” posed by buildings at risk of total collapse and protect displaced people and other residents staying inside them, the media office said in a statement.
Authorities have been instructed to immediately begin field procedures under the evacuation plan, including placing warning signs around dangerous buildings and working to provide temporary shelter for affected families.
The media office said specialized government committees are continuing field assessments of damaged buildings and identifying families still living inside them.
It said the effort faces major challenges, including a lack of funding, shortages of heavy machinery and equipment needed for safe evacuations due to the Israeli blockade, and a lack of available land to accommodate displaced families.
On Wednesday, the Public Works and Housing Ministry said around 3,000 buildings had been classified as dangerous or at risk of collapse because of damage sustained during the Israeli war.
Widespread destruction of residential buildings has forced thousands of Palestinians to remain in damaged and unstable structures because of severe shortages of adequate shelter.
According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, 61 Palestinians have been killed in collapses of buildings damaged during the war.
Since a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, dozens of war-damaged buildings have collapsed on residents who had no alternative shelter amid shortages of suitable tents and Israel’s restrictions on the entry of temporary prefabricated homes into Gaza.
Palestinian government bodies as well as international and UN organizations have repeatedly called for shelter materials to be allowed into the enclave to prevent further deaths from building collapses and exposure during winter, but those appeals have not led to an Israeli response.
Since Oct. 8, 2023, Israel’s genocide on Gaza has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000 others, according to Palestinian figures, while an estimated 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.

Opposition grows to Paramount-Warner Bros. merger settlement as deal enters critical week

Opposition grows to Paramount-Warner Bros. merger settlement as deal enters critical week
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Critics of the $111-billion Paramount acquisition of Warner Bros. urged California Atty. Gen. Bonta and other state attorneys general to disregard pressure to reach a settlement.
- Paramount has threatened to leave Hollywood if the antitrust battle isn’t resolved soon — a prospect that has rattled state and local politicians fearful of losing more entertainment industry jobs. 
Tensions flared on the eve of a critical week ahead for Paramount Skydance’s proposed $111-billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, amid new urgency for talks aimed at settling antitrust litigation brought by California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta and 11 other states.
Over the weekend, opposition intensified to a proposed settlement as details trickled out, including a proposal to establish a bipartisan editorial board to monitor cable news channel CNN, one of Warner’s premier properties that Paramount Chief Executive David Ellison would control along with CBS News.
It was unclear Sunday whether a proposed settlement would require Paramount to sell off assets — something Bonta repeatedly has insisted upon. Critics of the deal urged Bonta and other state attorneys general to resist pressure to reach a settlement that would allow Ellison’s deal to move forward.
“State Attorneys General, please hang tough against the giant proposed Paramount-Warner Brothers merger,” Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) wrote on social media late Saturday.
“Paramount, run by the Ellisons, should not own both CBS and CNN. California must not cave and take a deal that leaves both under the same owner,” Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Fremont) wrote.
A resolution would allow David Ellison’s $111-billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery to finalize
Bonta and Ellison have made progress in the talks in recent days, according to four people familiar with the matter not authorized to speak publicly.
However, New York’s Letitia James and at least two other attorneys general who joined Bonta’s lawsuit in July privately have expressed reservations about the proposed compromises, believing they don’t go far enough to mitigate concerns about the power Paramount-Warner Bros. would wield over the film and TV industries should the merger go through, according to the people familiar with the matter.
Neither James nor Connecticut’s William Tong is on board with Bonta’s proposed settlement, three knowledgeable people said. A potential split within Bonta’s coalition could be a setback because Bonta needs the other state attorneys general who joined his legal effort to sign off on any deal.
California’s top prosecutor blasts Paramount-Warner Bros. conduct as ‘amateur hour.’
 
Reached for comment Sunday, a spokesperson for Bonta reiterated a statement from last week.
“Potential settlement talks are confidential,” the statement said. “We cannot confirm or deny whether settlement talks are occurring or their alleged substance.”
Paramount maintains its deal to bring HBO, CNN, CBS, TBS, Comedy Central and two legendary film and television studios together would create a stronger company that could withstand the fierce competition from tech giants such as Apple, Netflix, Google (which owns YouTube) and Amazon. The two studios, on their own, would not be strong enough to remain viable in the streaming age, the company has said.
On Thursday, Paramount lawyers plan to demand that U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín in Oakland require the states and the Writers Guild of America to post a $1.88-billion bond that would cover some of Paramount’s delay-related deal costs should the company eventually prevail.
The states and the WGA, which also sued to block the merger, have balked at the request, which was designed by Paramount to create fissures within the coalition of states, which also include Minnesota, Oregon, Colorado, Connecticut, New Jersey and Massachusetts.
Los Angeles’ identity and workers’ livelihoods are at stake, say worried residents who fear that Paramount will leave the state.
Ellison wants the merger finalized by Oct. 1, when his company will be obligated to make a higher payout to Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders. The company has threatened to move its Hollywood base from its historic Melrose Avenue lot to Tennessee or Texas should the antitrust battle stretch into October.
The prospective loss of an iconic California business — a century-old film studio that helped establish Hollywood — has rattled state and local politicians, who are fearful of losing more jobs at a time when Los Angeles film production levels already are at alarming lows.
Gov. Gavin Newsom, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for California governor, have publicly called on Bonta to settle the suit rather than prepare for a trial next spring. City Councilmember Nithya Raman, Bass’ opponent in the L.A. mayor race, has been one of few California politicians in support of Bonta’s fight.
Paramount’s board has approved David Ellison’s contingency plan to move headquarters from Hollywood as early as this fall, according to people familiar with the situation.
In an opinion essay Sunday, a trio of 1st Amendment and antitrust experts dismissed Paramount’s threat to leave Los Angeles as a ploy that doesn’t make business sense.
“Ellison’s threat is empty, and the AG should call that out — not give into it,” the experts — Fiona Scott Morton, Gene Kimmelman and Norm Eisen — wrote in the Contrarian.
Both Morton, an economics professor at the Yale School of Management, and Kimmelman formerly served in the U.S. Justice Department during Democratic administrations. Eisen, founder of the group Democracy Defenders Action, is helping lead the Block the Merger campaign.
“Paramount [would be] sinking the cost of moving before it knows what businesses it owns and how best to combine and organize them — which makes expensive strategic mistakes inevitable,” the trio wrote. “A company that raises its own costs while leaving behind the most valuable labor in the industry does not threaten California; it threatens itself.”
The group noted Paramount, in its regulatory filings, still lists its Times Square offices in New York as its corporate headquarters — not its Melrose Avenue campus in Hollywood.
“There is also the possibility that Ellison is planning to move Paramount to Tennessee regardless of how the lawsuit resolves,” the group wrote.
Bonta and Paramount have discussed including in any settlement a condition that Paramount would keep its operations in California for a set period, according to people familiar with the proposal but not authorized to comment.
Merger opponents planned a Sunday evening rally outside Bonta’s offices in Oakland to encourage him to stand tough. The group plans subsequent demonstrations this week outside James’ office in New York City and the Paramount lot in Hollywood.
The jockeying comes as President Trump, who favors the Ellison takeover of CNN and Warner Bros., has barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds because of reporting he dislikes.
“Trump just locked CNN out of the White House. Now his billionaire allies want to own it,” Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) added in a Sunday post. “State attorneys general: Don’t settle. Hold the line. Block this merger.”

In early July, China fired a test missile from a nuclear submarine into the South Pacific for the first time, a weapon capable of carrying nuclear warheads. Washington and Canberra were livid. The Pacific has long been the exclusive testing ground for such long-range missiles from the United States. How dare China!

Finally, this month, a PIF statement that “registered concern on the recent intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) test” was issued. China was not named, and Nauru disassociated itself.
Kiribati previously said singling out China was unfair when the US regularly tested such missiles near the Marshall Islands. In March, the US launched a Minuteman III ICBM from California, landing near the Marshall Islands 6,700km away; it followed a similar test in November last year. The US has test-fired at least 15 ballistic missiles into the Pacific since 2021.

Tropical Storm Fay has formed in the northern Atlantic Ocean, while in the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Odalis is gaining strength and could become a hurricane in the near future. Neither storm currently poses an immediate threat to land, the Associated Press reports, citing the U.S. National Hurricane Center, according to UNN.
Details
The maximum sustained wind speed of Tropical Storm Fay reached 100 km/h. It was located approximately 650 km southwest of the Azores.
No warnings have so far been issued for coastal areas because of Fay. According to forecasts, the storm is expected to weaken by the end of the week.
Odalis could become a hurricane
Tropical Storm Odalis has formed in the Pacific Ocean southwest of Mexico’s western coast. Meteorologists expect it could strengthen into a hurricane within approximately a day.
The storm is located approximately 2,160 km west-southwest of the southern tip of Baja California. Its maximum sustained wind speed is 85 km/h, and Odalis is moving west-northwest at about 17 km/h.
No warnings have so far been issued for coastal areas because of Odalis either.

Ex-Fatah official: Israel and Hamas were close to reaching deal before October 7
Former senior Fatah official Sufian Abu Zaida, who mediated between Israel and Hamas before the attacks on October 7, 2023, said on Monday morning that the sides had been close to signing an agreement before the massacre.
In a Facebook post, Abu Zaida, a confidant of exiled Palestinian politician Mohammed Dahlan, stressed that the talks had nothing to do with the surprise attack. "We have no connection whatsoever to what happened on October 7, nor does it have anything to do with the role I played," he wrote. "Everything I did was aimed at preventing Gaza from reaching the situation it is in today."
Abu Zaida added that in an interview set to air on Egypt's Alghad TV channel later this week, he will reveal a message that Hamas' then-leader in Gaza Yahya Sinwar asked him to convey to Israel about three weeks before the massacre, as well as Israel's response.
Abu Zaida said in an interview with Egypt's Alghad TV that Sinwar twice warned him in September 2023 that he was preparing a major operation and instructed him to pass the warning to Israeli officials.
The contacts, first reported by Haaretz earlier this month, involved Hamas political bureau member Ghazi Hamad and Abu Zaida, who was recruited by Israel as an intermediary in the talks and referred to as "Coal Eyes."
Two crew members lightly wounded after tanker attacked in Strait of Hormuz
Two crew members were lightly wounded after a tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said Monday.
