The tanker continued on to its destination after the attack, according to the agency.
Gaza medical sources: Palestinian child dies after Israeli gunfire in southern Gaza
A Palestinian child died Monday from wounds sustained in Israeli gunfire in southern Gaza, while several other Palestinians were reported wounded by Israeli fire and shelling across the Gaza Strip, according to medical sources and Palestinian news agency WAFA.
Ismail al-Bardawil died from wounds sustained after being shot by Israeli forces in the Al-Mawasi area of Rafah, according to WAFA.
Medical sources said his death brings the number of Palestinians killed since the cease-fire took effect on October 11 to 1,394, with more than 4,830 others wounded. WAFA reported that 831 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.
In northern Khan Yunis, three Palestinians were woundedby Israeli gunfire, WAFA reported. Two were wounded by fire from Israeli military vehicles near Hamad City, while another was wounded by Israeli forces' gunfire in the same area.
In central Gaza, a woman was critically wounded by Israeli gunfire directed at tents housing displaced Palestinians between the Bureij and Maghazi refugee camps, according to medical sources. A girl was also wounded.
Several other Palestinians were wounded by Israeli artillery shelling that struck tents for displaced people in the Al-Amal neighborhood west of Khan Yunis and a home in the Block 12 area east of Bureij, while another woman was wounded by Israeli gunfire in Halawa camp in northern Gaza.
WAFA also reported that Israeli gunboats fired heavily toward fishermen off the Gaza coast, forcing them to leave the water.
Iranian president to travel to New York for UN General Assembly Tuesday
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will travel to New York on Tuesday to attend the United Nations General Assembly, Iran's state news agency IRNA reported Monday, citing a spokesman for the president's office.
Pezeshkian is expected to address the General Assembly amid the ongoing war between Iran and the United States and Israel.
Washington has approved visas for a scaled-down Iranian delegation to attend the UN gathering.
Iran warns new attack would change scope of war, Revolutionary Guards say
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned Monday that any new attack on Iran would prompt Tehran to change the "geography" of the war and the means it uses to fight, according to a statement carried by Iranian state media.
The warning came amid heightened tensions after Iran said it had information that the United States and its allies were preparing a major new attack. Iran's military central command said Sunday that any such attack would trigger sustained retaliation against U.S. bases and interests, and that Washington's regional allies would be considered parties to the conflict.
World leaders gather at UN amid wars in Iran, Gaza and Ukraine
World leaders are gathering at the United Nations this week as wars and deepening geopolitical divisions dominate the agenda, with the conflicts in Iran, Gaza and Ukraine among the most pressing issues.
About 130 heads of state and government are expected to address the General Assembly, beginning Tuesday, with U.S. President Donald Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are scheduled on Wednesday. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is due to speak Thursday.
The gathering comes as the Middle East remains at the center of global diplomacy, with the U.S.-Iran war continuing to disrupt regional security, shipping and energy markets.
Washington approved visas for Pezeshkian and other senior Iranian officials despite the ongoing war, allowing Iran's delegation to attend the meeting. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas will address the assembly by video after the U.S. denied him a visa for the second consecutive year.
The gathering comes as the UN faces questions over its ability to influence major conflicts, amid a broader crisis of multilateral cooperation. UN Secretary-General António Guterres, serving his final year in office, warned that power is shifting in what he described as an "era of deep uncertainty."
The future of the UN itself will be a major issue. Member states have agreed on a broad reform package that includes changes to institutions such as the Security Council, where the U.S., Russia, China, Britain and France hold veto power. The race to replace Guterres will also feature in behind-the-scenes diplomacy.
The gathering is also notable for who is absent: Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are skipping the meeting.
Guterres has said international cooperation is more necessary than ever as the world confronts what he called "three existential threats."
Oil prices hit over 1-week low on hopes of boost to diplomacy in Iran war
Oil prices slid to their lowest in more than a week on Monday on hopes that diplomacy in the Iran war will get a chance this week amid a UN meeting, and as investors eyed a partial recovery in shipments from Saudi Arabia despite ongoing attacks by Yemen's Houthis.
Brent crude futures and U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude touched their lowest since September 10 earlier on Monday, with Brent at $101.71 a barrel by 02:13 GMT (05:13 Israel time), down $2.16, or 2.08 percent, after settling 0.91 percent lower on Friday.
US West Texas Intermediate crude lost $2.15, or 2.14 percent, to $98.15 a barrel following a 1.58 percent drop in the previous session.
"It seems that a degree of risk premium is being removed from oil prices on hopes that a diplomatic path to de-escalate the US-Iran war may arrive this week," Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade, said. "Whether that hope proves to be warranted or not is another question. Time will tell."
The WTI broke a key psychological support at $100 a barrel while some investors may have rolled over their positions in the October contract a day ahead of expiry to November, a Singapore-based broker said.
Number of vessels transiting Hormuz drops to 12 this weekend, down from 35 last weekend
A dozen commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on the weekend, down from 35 the prior weekend, shipping data showed on Monday, as tension in the Gulf persisted with the U.S. and Iran in a stalemate.
Visible traffic through the strait, the conduit for a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas before the war, has dwindled to a trickle. However, Middle Eastern producers continue to export oil on tankers travelling with their transponders off.
Among trackable ships, four vessels – two tankers carrying refined oil products and two empty carriers for bulk goods and gas – exited the strait on Sunday, while another two small-sized oil tankers entered the Gulf, provisional data from analytics firm Kpler showed.
On Saturday, five vessels left the Gulf carrying agricultural products, liquefied petroleum gas and fertiliser while an empty very large gas carrier entered, the data showed.
Before the US-Israeli war with Iran started on February 28, the strait typically handled about 125 large, commercial vessels per day, including tankers, gas carriers, bulkers and container vessels.

Trump administration prepares sanctions against International Criminal Court, say sources
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:23:53 UTC
06:23:53 KST

Trump administration prepares sanctions against International Criminal Court, say sources
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump’s administration has prepared sanctions against the entire International Criminal Court (ICC) and plans to announce them soon, two sources familiar with the matter said. The move would step up its attack on the global tribunal that prosecutes war crimes and genocide worldwide.
The Trump administration has made no secret of its disdain for the court and has worked to undermine it.
US officials want the court to drop its arrest warrants against Israeli leaders as well as a past probe into American troops in Afghanistan.
In July, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a campaign to isolate the court, calling on other countries to withdraw from the tribunal.
Washington has imposed sanctions on a number of ICC judges and prosecutors but has so far held off from imposing sanctions on the court itself, although the move has long been considered one of the options.
The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Sanctions against the court have been prepared, the sources said, even though the exact timing of an announcement remains unclear.
The Wall Street Journal cited officials who said the decision could be finalised as soon as this week during the UN General Assembly meeting.
Targeting the entire organisation directly, as well as entities that cooperate with it, could severely undermine the court’s work.
Any entity-wide sanctions imposed by the US Treasury would prohibit US citizens and companies from providing funds, goods or services to the court without a licence from the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control.
Banks often overcomply with such US sanctions because they depend on access to the American financial system.
Among the court’s operations that could be affected by sanctions against the entire organisation are purchasing information technology services and insurance, hiring investigators and conducting everyday financial transactions, such as paying dozens of American employees, the ICC’s registrar and president have warned.
Trump’s opposition to the court goes back to his first term. It surfaced again with a plan to penalise ICC officials, an idea developed in November 2024, when Trump was re-elected and the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza conflict.
The ICC was established in 2002 by the international community to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. It asserts jurisdiction only if a member state is unable or unwilling to prosecute atrocities itself.
The US has never been a member. REUTERS

Far-left party wins Berlin election, pledging to nationalise housing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:18:54 UTC
06:18:54 KST

Far-left party wins Berlin election, pledging to nationalise housing
BERLIN – The far-left Left Party’s victory in the Berlin state election on Sept 20 was overshadowed by the continuing advance of the far right in eastern Germany, but it marked another defeat for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s ruling coalition.
Lead candidate Elif Eralp campaigned on the soaring cost of housing in the German capital and immediately promised to follow through on a pledge to nationalise private housing associations that account for a large share of the city’s housing stock.
The result, which roughly doubled the party’s previous score, could see her become the first mayor of Berlin from the Left Party – which grew out of the former East German communist party following the reunification of the country 36 years ago.
With counting still under way late on Sept 20, it was already clear that her party was set to displace Merz’s conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) from the mayor’s office.
“From today, we’re changing Berlin together,” she told celebrating party members in Berlin.
The Left Party took 25.3 per cent, ahead of the CDU on 19 per cent and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) on 16 per cent. It also far outstripped the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) on 12.1 per cent.
In her first remarks after the polls closed, the 45-year-old daughter of left-wing Turkish parents who fled a coup in 1980 said the increasingly difficult rental situation was “the biggest social problem” in the capital.
She promised to proceed with nationalising the housing associations and “drive speculation from Berlin”, in accordance with a referendum from 2021 in which 58 per cent backed proposals to legislate for nationalisation.
Whether the policy, which would see about 220,000 housing units transferred to state ownership, is ever adopted remains unclear. SPD general secretary Tim Kluessendorf said nationalising the housing associations would cost about €20 billion (S$29.3 billion).
An Infratest Dimap poll also found that only 37 per cent of those surveyed were in favour.
The Sept 20 election in Berlin came the same day the AfD followed up on its success in the Sept 6 Saxony-Anhalt election by taking first place in the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state election. It also recorded its best-ever result in Berlin.
But while the AfD has attracted the most attention, the Left Party has also benefited from a general turn against the mainstream parties of the centre-left and centre-right.
As in the four other state elections held in 2026, the dire state of the German economy and uncertainty about the way ahead weighed on the election in Berlin, with the main focus fixed on rental costs.
But significant obstacles remain for Eralp.
Both the SPD and the environmental Greens signalled a willingness to join a coalition with the Left Party. But Greens leader Felix Banaszak said accusations of anti-Semitism that have been levelled against parts of the Left Party in Berlin had to be addressed for a partnership to work.
“We need a clear commitment to combating anti-Semitism; otherwise, things won’t work with us,” he said.
The Left Party rejects accusations of systematic anti-Semitism, saying it is against all forms of “group-focused hostility”, including anti-Semitism, racism and sexism. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Banaszak’s demand. REUTERS

Israeli army shells southern Lebanon, setting fields ablaze with phosphorus munitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:16:37 UTC
06:16:37 KST

Emre Demiral and Mohammad Sio
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
The Israeli army set olive groves and citrus orchards in southern Lebanon ablaze with phosphorus munitions Sunday amid artillery shelling and a ground incursion involving three tanks, according to Lebanese state media.
Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA) said the attacks affected towns and areas across Tyre, Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil and Marjayoun districts.
In Tyre district, Israeli forces fired phosphorus munitions that sparked fires in olive groves and citrus orchards around the towns of Majdal Zoun and Buyout al-Sayyad.
Majdal Zoun was also hit by a series of Israeli bombings and explosions as Israeli forces carried out a sweep of the area, with a large blast later reported in the town.
Israeli artillery also struck the town of Al-Mansouri, where repeated explosions had been reported since midnight, as well as the outskirts of Buyout al-Sayyad. Israeli shelling also targeted Wadi Zibqin.
Separately, a child was injured when an unidentified object left from the war detonated in the town of Debaal. The child was taken to a nearby hospital for treatment, while authorities launched an investigation into the incident.
In Nabatieh district, Israeli artillery targeted the outskirts of Zawtar al-Sharqiyah toward Mayfadoun, while an Israeli drone dropped a stun grenade on the town.
Heavy Israeli artillery fire was also reported in Yahmar al-Shaqif.
In Bint Jbeil district, Israeli artillery struck a wooded area in Aita al-Jabal.
Four 240mm artillery shells also landed on the outskirts of Haddatha toward the town of Haris, according to the agency.
In Marjayoun district, an Israeli force comprising three Merkava tanks advanced toward Deir Mimas and blocked its entrance, disrupting residents’ movement in and out of the town.
The force searched several homes during the incursion and damaged telephone poles along the road before continuing its movements in the area.
Israeli forces also fired four artillery shells at the town of Khiam and shelled Wadi al-Salouqi and Wadi al-Hujeir.
The developments came a day after the Israeli army targeted paramedics in an airstrike and set more homes ablaze while carrying out demolitions, explosions and shelling across several areas of southern Lebanon.
During the latest war, the Israeli army advanced about 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) into Lebanese territory and established a security zone, or the “Yellow Line.”
On June 26, Lebanon and Israel signed a US-sponsored Framework Agreement in Washington providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory and the deployment of the Lebanese army to areas vacated by Israeli forces.
Despite the agreement, Israel has continued to carry out attacks in southern Lebanon and maintains a military presence in parts of the south, including territory it has occupied for decades and other areas seized during more recent wars and military operations.

European intelligence services expect Russian provocations to intensify
Representatives of the intelligence services of Czechia, Latvia and Sweden expect an increase in Russian sabotage operations in Europe, whilst assessing the likelihood of an invasion of NATO countries differently.
Source: representatives from European intelligence services in an interview with The Guardian
Details: In separate interviews conducted over the past week in various locations, three heads of European intelligence services shared their perspectives on the potential threat posed by Moscow.
Michal Koudelka, Head of the Czech Security Information Service (BIS), believes that Russia could resort to a small-scale invasion of NATO countries or false-flag provocations within the coming months, rather than years.
Koudelka noted that, in addition to increased drone activity, small-scale invasions into the territory of NATO countries bordering Russia could form part of the Kremlin's plans.
"It's possible. It could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign," he said in an interview at the BIS headquarters in Prague.
Koudelka noted that this scenario could play out within "months, not years", but added that "a lot of people are doing everything they can to make sure this doesn't happen".
"We don't see indications of an imminent attack," stated Normunds Mežviets, Head of the Latvian State Security Service (VDD), in an interview at the agency's headquarters in Riga. He acknowledged that there are indications Moscow is preparing for more decisive actions in Europe but noted it remains unclear whether these plans are simply part of a destabilisation strategy.
"It's still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it's just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society," he said.
As reported by The Guardian, Baltic politicians, who for many years have criticised western Europe for its soft stance on Russia, now find themselves in the unusual position of having to urge some western leaders to show restraint in their public statements, fearing that talk of an imminent invasion could harm their societies and economies.
Mežviets noted that, overall, it is positive that western Europe has woken up to the threat posed by Russia.
Koudelka said the Kremlin seeks to exploit vulnerabilities in western societies in order to undermine their support for Ukraine's war effort.
Thomas Nilsson, Head of the Swedish Military Intelligence and Security Service, noted that he sees no signs of Moscow's readiness for genuine negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
All three intelligence chiefs stated that, regardless of how events unfold, Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe is likely to intensify in the coming months.
Nilsson called the recent incident involving an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig Airport, which German authorities have linked to Russian intelligence, a "gamechanger". According to Nilsson, behind the recent escalation in Russian sabotage activity lie several goals: to diminish support for Ukraine, sow division within NATO and intimidate the European populace.
Mežviets noted that Russia is transitioning from chaotic acts of sabotage and arson aimed at spreading panic to targeted attacks on specific facilities linked to western support for Ukraine.
Koudelka noted that another consequence of the sabotage campaign is the overstretching of intelligence services' resources, as doubts frequently remain even when incidents are caused by other factors.

Christine Taylor revealed how she was robbed at gunpoint in the '90s

American actress Christine Taylor revealed that in the early 1990s in Los Angeles, an armed man carjacked her at gunpoint. The star spoke about the attack and its aftermath on the podcast "We're Still Here, Honey," E! News reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to the 55-year-old actress, she was with her friend and neighbor David Pressman. The attack took place at around 3 p.m. near their apartment.
It was three in the afternoon. Detroit Street, near Beverly Boulevard—we lived in an apartment there, and we were robbed at gunpoint
The attack lasted only a few minutes
The actress said that she parked the car and got out with her friend. Another car stopped nearby, and an armed man got out. He ordered Pressman to stay where he was and Taylor to hand over the keys.
Because of the anti-theft steering-wheel lock, the attackers had to call her back so that she could remove it. After that, they also took the actress's bag.
It probably all happened within a minute and a half to two minutes, but it felt as though time had stopped. It was so frightening
Taylor admitted that she did not see a psychotherapist at the time, and that friends and family helped her cope with what had happened. A few days after the attack, the actress landed a role in the 1994 horror film "Night of the Demons 2."
According to her, filming unexpectedly became a kind of therapy for her. At the same time, the effects of what she had experienced stayed with her for years: whenever Taylor saw someone approaching a car, she could freeze out of fear that the attack might happen again.

China cultivates 14 plant species aboard space station
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
05:10:48 CST
06:10:48 KST

TIANJIN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China has now cultivated more than 20 varieties spanning 14 plant species in orbit -- a milestone that lays the groundwork for large-scale crop production aboard the space station, according to the Astronaut Center of China.
The breakthrough was highlighted at an aerospace medical engineering conference in Tianjin Municipality in north China, where Zhang Hongzhang, an astronaut from the Shenzhou-21 crewed mission, shared photos and videos of a flourishing "space garden" aboard China's Tiangong space station, featuring crops such as lettuce, carrot, sunflower, potato and wheat.
China's era of long-term crewed spaceflight began in October 2021, when Shenzhou-13 crew members Zhai Zhigang, Wang Yaping and Ye Guangfu moved into China's space station core module Tianhe.
"Long-term stays in space require us to reduce the reliance on Earth resupply. Our controlled ecological life support experiments aim to build an ecosystem in space that can regenerate water, air and food in situ -- cutting dependence on Earth and eventually achieving self-sufficiency," said Bian Qiang, an expert at the Astronaut Center of China.
Controlled ecological life support technology uses an artificially built, closed and controlled ecosystem to efficiently recycle and regenerate the air, water and food astronauts in orbit need to survive, establishing a life-and-health support system suited to long-term human habitation.
According to Bian, right now, two types of plant-growing units aboard the space station -- one using substrate culture and the other aeroponics -- are running continuously. Together, they are giving researchers valuable experience in building a basic life support system that leans mainly on physical and chemical recycling, with biological regeneration playing a supporting role.
"A more efficient aeroponics unit was sent up in 2025. Wheat has since completed a full growing cycle in orbit, and a second round cultivation using seeds from that harvest is growing well and close to reaping," Bian said.
Looking further ahead, Bian said China intends to establish a "lunar vegetable garden" as its lunar exploration program advances.
China's space station, Tiangong, which means Heavenly Palace, has now entered an era of long-term human habitation. One member of the Shenzhou-23 crew will conduct a one-year in-orbit stay, while the country's 2030 crewed moon landing mission is advancing steadily. ■

China Focus: Global mayors explore sustainable development prospects at China's Wuhan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
05:10:32 CST
06:10:32 KST

This photo taken on Sept. 20, 2026 shows a scene of the 2026 Global Mayors Dialogue - Wuhan in Wuhan, central China's Hubei Province. (Photo by Ni Na/Xinhua)
WUHAN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- More than 80 city leaders and representatives from over 20 countries, along with heads of international organizations, have gathered in Wuhan, Hubei Province, central China, to discuss shared urban challenges and explore pathways to sustainable development at the 2026 World Mayors Dialogue.
Held from Sept. 18 to 21 under the theme "River City: Shared Resonance, Shared Growth," the event focuses on how technological innovation, industrial cooperation and cultural exchanges can advance urban development and improve people's lives.
Shaukat Ali, Lord Mayor of Manchester, said he was impressed by Wuhan's efforts in developing low-carbon industries and advanced manufacturing, noting that Manchester and Wuhan have jointly established the UK-China Clean Energy Forum to harness the two cities' shared industrial and technological strengths for eco-friendly development.
Manchester and Wuhan became sister cities in 1986 because of shared industrial origins, leading educational institutions, and a shared appetite for economic transformation. As the cities have grown and evolved, the partnership continues to pioneer multi-level exchanges and developmental cooperation between the UK and China, Ali said.
The dialogue comes as Wuhan continues to pursue greener urban development while transforming its traditional industrial base.
Located at the confluence of the Yangtze and Hanjiang rivers, Wuhan is home to 166 lakes and 165 rivers. Once a major industrial center known for steel and automobile manufacturing, the city has in recent years stepped up efforts to improve its environment and promote greener industrial development.
As part of its urban renewal efforts, Wuhan has transformed small plots of unused or underused land into "pocket parks," bringing green space closer to residents. By the end of May, the city had built 788 such parks.
Water quality in Wuhan's sections of the Yangtze and Hanjiang rivers has remained at Grade II, the second-highest level in China's five-tier system, for six consecutive years.
The city also showcased its experience to international participants through visits to its suspended rail transit system, a smart home appliance factory, and a Yangtze finless porpoise breeding and conservation center, offering a closer look at its infrastructure, technological innovation, and ecological protection efforts.
"Our visits have given us different perspectives on how technological innovation and industrial development are reshaping cities and their economies," said Jordi Vaquer, secretary general of Metropolis. "We have also been reminded that innovation and development must coexist with the protection of natural systems."
Vaquer said cities play an important role in keeping international cooperation channels open, as urban challenges transcend national borders.
"None of us can address them entirely alone," he said.
Beyond Wuhan's transformation experiences, the dialogue also comes as China places greater emphasis on sustainable urban development.
This year marks the start of China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The outline calls for a shift in the approach to urban development and for building cities that are more innovative, livable, beautiful, resilient, culturally vibrant and smart. ■

Jim Chalmers says Australians will have to navigate a more dangerous and unpredictable world
Treasurer Jim Chalmers spoke at the Australian National University (ANU) a little earlier about the latest intergenerational report (IGR), which was released today.
The first IGR was released in 2002 by Treasurer Peter Costello, and they have been released every five years (roughly) since then in 2007, 2010, 2015, 2021, 2023, and 2026.
IGRs look deep into the future, with forecasts of major trends that stretch out for 40 years. They are an intellectual exercise, designed to focus everyone's attention on the path that Australia's economy is currently travelling and where we're likely to end up if we don't course-correct at some point.
Near the beginning of his speech, Chalmers said this:
"The world is becoming more dangerous, more unpredictable, more unequal, and more divided [...]
"Accelerating change is putting more pressure on people. It’s eroding trust in the institutions of our democracy. It’s exacerbating the strain felt by younger generations in particular. The division in politics now is not between those who accept this and those who don’t. But between those who prey on it and pick at it and politicise it and catastrophise it – and those who seek to alleviate it."
And then he spoke of the ways in which he's hoping that Australia can benefit from the major changes that are occurring in the global economy.
He said the future will depend on how we respond to five accelerating shifts in AI, energy, demography, industry and geopolitics.
And he said the "AI revolution" was "the most consequential new emphasis since the 2023 report, and the biggest economic transformation of our lifetime."
"The productivity, investment and labour market impacts of AI will be dramatic," he said,
AI will play a pivotal role in reaching long-term productivity growth of 1.2 per cent, and higher if productivity gains accelerate over time."

Why interest rates affect share prices
G'day ABC, can you help me understand how higher bond yields are bad for equities, ai keep hearing it but can't make the connection much. It seems like its bad for valuations due to the risk free bond. But how do equities actually get affected? Is it just higher borrowing costs, seems thats more a central bank mechanic. Any help please would be great.
- Bond Fan
Good question Bond Fan.
Most fundamentally, it comes down to the way analysts and fund managers value shares in the present based on their discounted future cash flows.
Meghan Shue, the chief investment strategist at US financial services firm Wilmington Trust, explained it well in this note written in 2019.
"First, the current price of a stock is simply the present value of the sum of all future cash flows (earnings plus buybacks plus dividends)," she wrote.
"Interest rates are directly linked to the cost of capital, or the rate used to discount those future cash flows (earnings plus buybacks plus dividends) of a stock or index.
"The lower that discount rate (in the denominator), all else being equal, the higher the present value of any future payouts (those payouts are in the numerator) and the higher the stock price."
Relatedly, lower interest rates also reduce the "opportunity cost" of owning more speculative stocks that don't currently generate an income stream.
"Second, as interest rates move lower, the relative appeal of other income-generating assets—including stocks—increases, even if they carry extra risk over a traditional bond," she explains.
"As interest rates fall, it lowers the 'income opportunity cost' of investing in stocks over bonds."
Meghan Shue goes on to note that, historically, rising interest rates have generally coincided with rising share prices.
Why?
"Most of the time rising rates are good for stocks because the increase in earnings growth expectations—which typically goes along with that increase in rates—tends to overwhelm the higher discount rate (with one exception being a stagflationary scenario of rising inflation and slowing growth)."
Unfortunately, the latter is the scenario many economists are concerned about for Australia and many other advanced economies.

Key Event
ASIC sues former Super Cheap Retail boss
ASIC is suing former Super Cheap Retail CEO Anthony Heraghty over allegations he failed to disclose and manage conflicts of interest arising from an alleged undisclosed relationship he had with a senior executive at the company.
The legal action centres on allegations that Mr Heraghty;
- continued to supervise the senior executive and participated in decisions affecting their employment, remuneration, incentives, rewards and redundancy package;
- participated in board and committee discussions of complaints and anticipated legal proceedings concerning the alleged undisclosed relationship; and
- provided or authorised information to be released to SRG's board and the market that omitted information concerning the alleged undisclosed relationship and was therefore misleading.
Mr Heraghty was fired from Super Cheap Retail in September last year after news of an alleged relationship with the company's former head of human resources emerged.
He has since taken up a post leading kitchen appliance outfit Winning Group ahead of a potential ASX float next year.
ASIC Chair Sarah Court said governance and directors' duties failures and misconduct damaging market integrity are enduring enforcement priorities for ASIC.
"ASIC alleges Mr Heraghty put himself in a position where his personal interests conflicted with his duties to Super Retail Group and that he failed to properly disclose and manage that conflict," Ms Court said.
"The allegations in this matter raise important issues about governance, transparency and trust in the information provided to boards and the market.
"This case is not about private relationships, but whether a director properly disclosed and managed conflicts of interest and met their duties to the company and shareholders.
ASIC alleges Mr Heraghty alleged actions exposed Super Retail Group to foreseeable risks of harm, including risks to its corporate reputation, complaints and litigation, regulatory action, costs, and harm to its share price and shareholders.
Super Retail Group houses a number of high-profile retail outlets including Supercheap Auto, BCF, Rebel and Macpac.
Breaches of directors' duties can attract penalties of up to $1,565,000 per breach, while providing misleading information to a company board also attracts a maximum penalty of $1,565,000 per breach.

"Australians have one of the longest life expectancies in the world. Life expectancy is projected to reach 89.5 years for women and 86.1 years for men by 2065–66," the IG report noted.

European intelligence services have warned of possible Russian actions against NATO within the next few months

European intelligence agencies are warning of possible provocations, acts of sabotage, or a limited Russian incursion into NATO countries. The Baltic states do not see an imminent attack.
The heads of European intelligence services warn that Russia may be preparing more decisive actions against NATO countries, including provocations, sabotage, or a limited invasion. One intelligence chief suggested that such a scenario could materialize within "months, not years," The Guardian reports, writes UNN.
Details
The head of the Czech Security Information Service, Michal Koudelka, said that possible Kremlin scenarios could include a limited invasion of NATO territory, false-flag operations, and large-scale influence campaigns.
It is possible. This could include a limited invasion, false-flag provocations, and a large-scale influence campaign
No signs of an imminent attack seen in the Baltics

We see no signs of an imminent attack

BIG builds a temporary city for shakira in madrid with reusable structures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:07:28 UTC
06:07:28 KST

Why settle for a stadium when you can build a town? For her Madrid residency, Shakira has taken over the 185,000-square-meter Iberdrola Music venue in Villaverde, transforming it into Macondo Park, a temporary cultural landscape designed by Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG). Conceived as an alternative to the conventional concert arena, the site combines a stadium for more than 50,000 spectators with colorful pavilions, markets, food, art, fashion, cinema, and children’s spaces — an entire world constructed around the shows rather than merely behind the stage.
Unlike an existing stadium, where attention converges on a single performance, the purpose-built environment allowed the architects to choreograph the audience’s full journey. ‘The architecture is designed to not only accommodate large crowds, but also to guide people, create moments of discovery, and offer places to gather, celebrate, and find shade throughout the day,’Stefani Fachini de Araujo, Associate at BIG and Design Lead on the project, tells designboom. Shakira may remain the main attraction, but the celebration is deliberately set in motion well before she appears.
colorful paths unfold across the temporary venue | all images courtesy of BIG
COLOR-CODED PATHS LEAD THROUGH A TEMPORARY TOWN
Visitors enter through a sequence of Es Latina welcoming arches, each assigned its own color and connected to a matching route across the site. The paths lead toward 12 temporary pavilions and complementary fan, VIP, and children’s areas, with eight of the main structures dedicated to pillars of Latin American culture. ‘Each path leads visitors to a different pavilion containing a unique experience,’explains Fachini de Araujo from BIG. At the center stands the Macondo Tree, a shared landmark that gives this otherwise vast event ground something resembling a town square.
More than 500 trees and planted islands draw from Mediterranean, Spanish, and Latin American landscapes, reducing the scale of the open venue and adding pockets of shade. ‘Along the way, more than 500 trees bring human scale to the site, turning a vast event ground into a park,’ the Design Lead continues. The fictional town of Macondo, borrowed from Gabriel García Márquez’s One Hundred Years of Solitude, becomes less a literal reconstruction than a spatial framework for mixing storytelling, popular culture, and collective celebration — with a little stadium logistics tucked underneath.
BIG designs macondo park for shakira’s madrid residency
BIG DESIGNS EVERY ELEMENT FOR A SECOND LIFE
Building this temporary universe meant working against both scale and time. According to Fachini de Araujo, the design process took around six months, while some of the pavilions were assembled in roughly ten days. ‘This led us to work with the components found at any large event, such as trusses, scaffolding, containers, and stage ground support systems, and to rethink how they come together,’ she shares. Wrapped in brightly colored fabric, the familiar event infrastructure becomes a family of shaded structures, each with a distinct identity but a deliberately pragmatic skeleton.
The temporary nature of Macondo Park also informed what happens after the final concert. ‘Knowing from the start that it would be dismantled, we chose every element with its next life in mind,’Fachini de Araujo tells designboom. The structures and fabrics are intended for reuse, the artificial grass can be relocated to schools and playgrounds, and the trees will return to the nursery. For a project designed around spectacle, its disappearing act has been considered surprisingly carefully.

Live: Australians to live longer and have fewer children by 2066

Federal politics: Australia's fertility rates expected to fall 'further and faster', treasurer says — as it happened
The population will reach almost 40 million people by 2066 as Australians live longer but have fewer children, according to the latest intergenerational report.
But there is no appetite from either the government or the opposition to revisit a Howard-era "baby bonus" in a bid to encourage people to have more children.

Marles meets with French counterpart at Geelong Art Gallery
Defence Minister Richard Marles held a quiet meeting and dinner with his French counterpart Catherine Vautrin at the Geelong Art Gallery last night.
There would have been plenty to discuss. France is a major military power, and it’s also got a very substantial security presence in the Pacific through its territories– including New Caledonia and French Polynesia.
The ministers discussed how the two countries could do more to cooperate on disaster responses, as well as tackling transnational crime in the region, as the Pacific continues to grapple with a surging illegal drug trade.
They also talked about how Australia and France could expand space cooperation and their joint support for Ukraine, as well as the ongoing crisis in the Middle East and the push by Paris for a multinational mission in the Strait of Hormuz.
There’s a bit of a curious echo here – the Geelong Art Gallery, where the two ministers dined, was also the venue used by Australia and the United Kingdom last year when they signed the Geelong Treaty – which is key to their joint effort to build nuclear powered submarines under AUKUS.
But perhaps the choice of venue shows that, five years on from Scott Morrison’s shock AUKUS announcement and his decision to ditch a massive contract to buy French made submarines, the two countries have now well and truly moved on from that particular dispute.
'We expect fertility rates to fall further and faster'
We've canvassed Australia's falling fertility rates a bit on the blog today. As Jim Chalmers says, it's one of the key conclusions of the intergenerational report.
But he's conscious about weighing in too much: "I do not and will not give free advice about these very personal decisions that [people] make about whether to start a family and when to start a family".
Chalmers says more people are having kids later and that means that families are smaller.
"If you look at the decline in the fertility rate, I think almost half of it is because of fewer families where there are three or more kids," he says.
Chalmers says it's up to the government to make it easier to make the choice to have children and points to things like childcare and extending paid parental leave.
Chalmers hopes IGR will eventually 'vindicate' housing tax changes
The intergenerational report only justifies the government's housing tax changes in the last budget, Treasurer Jim Chalmers says.
"In all the 20 or so budgets that I've worked on or responded to in my time in politics, there hasn't been a budget that has been more serious about meeting our intergenerational obligations," he says.
"And I think the pointiest part of that, the defining part of that, is really the housing market, which has locked young people out for too long."
Chalmers says he hopes that "every page" of the IGR in "justifies, validates and I hope one day vindicate" the decision to scale back the capital gains tax and negative gearing.
So is there a percentage of coming generations Chalmers would like to see on the home ownership ladder? The treasurer doesn't want to put a figure on it.
Chalmers not considering changes to GST
It's a pretty quick "no" from Jim Chalmers when asked if there's any circumstance in which he'd consider raising the goods and services tax.
The intergenerational report predicted indirect taxes such as the fuel excise will decline over the next 40 years.
"That's not something that we've contemplated really at any point," Chalmers says.
Australia to spend less on pensions than peers
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has outlined the budget will be "strained by still stronger" than was previously forecast.
He says spending is expected to increase by less and the budget bottom line has improved too. Gross debt will be lower too.
The treasurer flags the potential for future tax cuts down the line, through the Working Australians Tax Offset. The WATO was established in the budget and will, from next July, return $250 to people who earn a wage at tax time.
Chalmers says by the mid-2060s the aged pension is expected to cost $31b less due to the support of superannuation balances.
"We’ll spend less on pensions than any OECD economy by the 2060s even as retirement incomes go up not down," he says.
"While average spending on public pensions in those countries will rise to over 10 per cent of GDP – Ours will fall to just 1.8 per cent."
A quick look under the hood of the intergenerational report
Younger Australians face a future of working longer and struggling more to buy a home, without the same early gains in income and wealth experienced by the generations before them.
That’s according to the latest Intergenerational Report released today by Treasurer Jim Chalmers.
It lays out how an ageing population and falling birth rate are expected to reshape Australia's economy over the next 40 years.
Fertility is expected to fall to just 1.34 children per woman by 2065. The number of Australians over 85 will triple by 2066.
An older growing population, weaker productivity growth and rising costs in areas like defence and health will put increasing pressure on government finances.
But Chalmers says Australia is better placed than many other countries to face the challenges ahead.
Read more about the Intergenerational Report from Clare Armstrong at the link below.
One-third of new healthcare spending over next 40 years linked to ageing population
As we've been discussing all morning on the blog, Australia's population is changing in shape and size and it's different to previous forecasts.
More Australians are living longer and having fewer children, but this is the first IGR that deaths are projected to outnumber births by the 2060s.
That's part of the reason why Australia's population growth is expected to slow.
But with the number of people over 65 set to triple that will place further pressures on health and aged care services.
"This means one-third of new healthcare spending over the next 40 years will be because of ageing," Treasurer Jim Chalmers says.
AI the big change since the last intergenerational report
So what's the biggest change from the last intergenerational report handed down three years ago?
Basically, AI. Jim Chalmers describes it as the "biggest economic transformation of our lifetime".
"The productivity, investment and labour market impacts of AI will be dramatic," he says.
The report forecasts AI will play a pivotal role in Australia's' productivity growth. Australia, he says has positioned itself "early and well" for AI infrastructure projects such as data centres.
But he adds that, for all the upsides. there are "very serious risks to minimise and manage".
"We already see dangerous proliferation of misinformation, scams and malicious cyber operations. We are vigilant about managing the infrastructure build’s impacts on our resources and communities – And risks of market concentration, social harm and economic disruption," he says.
Chalmers kicks off address
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has just kicked off his address. It's his second time handing down the intergenerational report.
He says no previous version of the report has had to contend with "global challenges this great, with politics this fraught, or a future less certain".
But he says the report has Australia better placed than our peers.
However, the rapid pace of change is eroding trust in institutions. And to tackle this the "pace of opportunity" must also be accelerated.
"If people are unmoored economically, generationally, they feel disconnected from, and disregarded in, our politics. At worst that’s what we’re seeing now, at best it’s what’s at stake," he says.
Chalmers to release intergenerational report shortly
Are you excited? It's almost time for the release of the intergenerational report. Here's how the next hour or so will go on the blog.
The report will be released at 12.30pm. At the same time, Treasurer Jim Chalmers will stand up and deliver a speech to accompany it.
That'll be followed with by a Q&A session.
Don't worry, I'll bring you all the highlights on the blog, as always.
Wong speaks to Palestinian foreign minister
Foreign Minister Penny Wong has confirmed she spoke with her Palestinian counterpart, Varsen Aghabekian last week.
The pair spoke about the progress against the Palestinian Authority's reform commitments.
In a statement on social media, Wong said:
"Australia is committed to a two-state solution.
"I spoke with Palestinian Foreign Minister, Dr Varsen Aghabekian, about the PA's reform agenda and our joint efforts to strengthen Palestine's institutional foundations.
"We also discussed the devastating situation in Gaza. I reiterated that Hamas must play no role in the State of Palestine."
It's understood the pair agreed that senior officials from Australia and Palestine should meet in the coming months to discuss areas of mutual interest, including Palestinian reform efforts.
Students being taught negatives in schools: Canavan
A concern that not enough Australians would be willing to fight for the country if needed has been credited as the reason why the Nationals leader wants to reform the school curriculum.
The opposition unveiled its plan to overhaul the education system that would include subjects on Western values and less time spent on Indigenous history.
Matt Canavan is concerned students are being taught too many "negatives" and wouldn't be willing to defend the country as a result.
"We certainly do face the risk of conflict in our region. Some people put it higher than others in terms of risk. But it's a risk.
"And if only half of us would pick up a rifle and defend our country we're in a bit of a poor shape.
"I think we've got to get back to teaching children about how great Australia is. How lucky we are.
"We're not perfect and no one's asking us to teach ... students that Australia is perfect in any way, shape or form. But it is better than most places."
Canavan not open to 'baby bonus' in bid to lift Australia's fertility rates
Matt Canavan doesn't think a revival of a "baby bonus" is the right way to encourage more Australians to have children. 
The latest intergenerational report released today predicts Australia's fertility rate is expected to drop faster over the next 40 years than previously forecast.
Canavan says he wants greater support for families but a one-off bonus to parents isn't the best way to do it.
"I think anything that we should do should be more ... designed around the idea that if you ... work for yourself, if you're helping yourself, we'll help you some more. The baby bonus, it was just 'Here's some cash', without you having to put in the effort as well," he says.
He says the Coalition is working on a proposal and says it's something he's been pushing for a long time. He references his maiden speech in which he argued for income splitting for parents.
UN Security Council seat shouldn't be PM priority: Canavan
Nationals leader Matt Canavan is all for Australia having a bigger influence on world affairs but doesn't think a bid for a seat on the UN Security Council is the right move at the moment.
"But look, right now, I think the prime minister should be prioritising the cost of living here at home, not spending time to get a seat on some international board overseas," he says.
The prime minister launched Australia's push to hold one of the non-permanent spots on the powerful body overnight.
A secret ballot will take place in mid-2028. To succeed, a country must secure a two-thirds majority of UN General Assembly members, or at least 128 votes if all 193 members vote.
'All of it adds up': Canavan on promise for fuel excise cut
Nationals leader Matt Canavan has also been out and about this morning, spruiking the Coalition's pledge to cut the fuel excise.
The Coalition has proposed halving the tax paid on petrol every time the two-week average global oil price hits $US100 a barrel.
Canavan says if it was in place right now, a recent uptick in prices would have triggered an automatic cut.
"All of it adds up. All of it is meaningful. And this relief would could off if and when prices fell back down to average levels," he told reporters in Rockhampton.
He also argued the encouragement of exploration of oil in Australia to shore up fuel supplies.
"This remains Australia's greatest industrial weak point. When it comes to national security, we import about ... half our .. in liquid fuels. That's a lot. We need to do better to reduce that amount so we can protect our shipping lanes if things get really bad in our region," he says.
If Australia wants to lower migration it needs more productivity
Everyone now understands that growing the economy only by increasing the number of people, while individuals feel worse off, is a recipe for unhappiness and dissent.
Aggregate growth is a statistic, but individual decline is a vote. The political solution? Fewer people.
That's because those in focus groups and answering polling questions complain about how many people they can see, rather than the reason they are worse off: weak productivity, which they can't see.
As a result, we now have three significant political parties instead of the usual two.
The third newcomer, One Nation, is an anti-immigration party harvesting unhappiness and dissent. The other two have put on some anti-immigration clothes and have got on the grievance catwalk as well.
Read more of Alan Kohler's analysis at the link below.
The economy needs migration and data centres. Voters hate both
The two things holding up the economy are fast becoming the two most potent and dangerous political issues confronting the federal government.
Data centres and migration are the twin issues the government needs to keep pumping to keep the country in positive economic territory, but they are also the two issues voters have the most complex and hostile relationship with.
It presents a dilemma for the government: it can't live with it, but it also can't live without it.
Migration has long been a key contributor to the economy, with international students, workers and their spending helping tip dollars into treasury coffers.
One Nation and the Coalition want to drastically cut immigration and are smashing the government on the idea that they have allowed a "mass migration" program. Labor, stung by months of relentless campaigning on this issue, finally unveiled a plan to try to cut it back too.
But figures out from today's Intergenerational Report (IGR) show just how much we need migrants for the economy to keep growing, albeit slowly.
Read more of PK's analysis at the link below.
Tehan defends opposition's fuel price proposal
Dan Tehan has rejected claims the opposition's promise to cut the fuel excise when oil prices are high would be inflationary.
The Coalition has proposed halving the tax paid on petrol every time the two-week average global oil price hits $US100 a barrel.
Speaking to ABC's Radio National Breakfast, the shadow energy minister described it as a "sensible measure" that was completely offset by the Coalition's proposed change to the tobacco excise.
"There is no inflationary pressures put on. We have the discipline to be able to do the policy work, to make sure we can offset policies like this so it won't be inflationary," he says.
Tehan also accused the government of "deliberately" creating a scarcity of fuel flowing into the nation. He says the Coalition would encourage the exploration of oil in Australia in a bid to shore up fuel supplies.

Family violence at 'unacceptable levels'
Minister for Women Katy Gallagher has said the level of family violence in the Australian community is "unacceptable" after a spate of incidents in NSW over the weekend.
Three women, including a 90-year-old grandmother, were killed over the weekend in NSW in separate alleged domestic-violence incidents.
Separately, a 5-year-old child died and two younger children and a 42-year-old woman are in a critical condition after suffering stab wounds yesterday in the Blue Mountains. Police said the matter was being treated as a domestic violence incident and the woman is a suspect.
Gallagher said her thoughts were with the loved ones impacted by the "horrible" events.
"It's hard to get your head around the level of violence across — particularly aimed towards women and children — but in families across Australia," she said.
"This is something that is on our desk every single day … it's not just something that we look at when there are terribly sad, awful, horrific stories in the media."
She said the government was making domestic violence a priority at national cabinet and through the development of a second action plan (under their broader plan to end violence against women and children), but said governments alone couldn't deal with the issue.
"There is no easy solution, if there was one, we would have already put it in place," she said.
"More money is part of it, we're doing that, but again it's a whole of community response that's needed to end violence and to stand up and talk about the level of violence in our community right now, which is at unacceptable levels."

Germany's Central Council of Jews opposes Left Party-led government in state of Berlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:04:00 UTC
06:04:00 KST

Anadolu staff
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
The head of Germany’s Central Council of Jews on Sunday voiced opposition to a Left Party-led government in Berlin and urged other parties not to open state government coalition talks with the socialist election winner.
Josef Schuster said he was concerned about the Left Party’s solidarity with pro-Palestinian demonstrators protesting the Israeli government. He accused the party of antisemitic statements—claims its officials have repeatedly and firmly denied.
“During the election campaign, the Left Party repeatedly crossed the line with antisemitic remarks,” Schuster claimed. Entering a Left Party-led coalition, he argued, would mean promoting the “ongoing normalization of hatred against Jews.”
Left Party lead candidate Elif Eralp voiced support during the campaign for Berlin’s Palestinian community and sharply condemned the war crimes in Gaza of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government. She pledged that a Left Party-led state government would end repressive police measures against peaceful pro-Palestinian protests in the capital.
In the face of the accusations, Eralp said party leaders had distanced themselves from a handful of isolated incidents. She added that the Left Party opposes all forms of racism and noted that during her career she has been involved in projects combating antisemitism.
“It is absolutely clear that we stand for the protection of Jewish life,” she said in a recent TV debate with her rival. “Just as we stand for the protection of Muslim and Palestinian life.”
Germany’s socialist Left Party looked on track Sunday for a historic first-place finish in Berlin’s state election, with Eralp hailing a result that could make her the capital’s first governing mayor from a migrant background.
German public broadcaster ARD’s latest projection put the Left Party at 25.3% — more than double its 12.2% result in the 2023 election — and more than six points ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative CDU at 19%.
The anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) followed at 16.3%, the Greens at 14.4% and the SPD at 12.1%.
Despite its clear lead, the Left Party remained far from an absolute majority and would need at least two partners to govern. After a campaign that called for a change of course and rejected CDU policy, the most viable path was a three-party coalition with the SPD and the Greens.
Coalition math remained fluid before preliminary official results. Whether the left-populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) stays above the 5% threshold would still reshape the seat distribution. In the latest projection, it stood at 4.8%.
If the Left Party cannot reach an agreement with the SPD and the Greens, the second-place CDU could try a coalition with those two parties. The three would have enough seats if the BSW fails to enter the Berlin state parliament.

Italy to ban burqas in schools, limit foreign students per class
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:02:45 UTC
06:02:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Italy to ban burqas in schools, limit foreign students per class, PM Meloni says
Italy will ban burqas and niqabs in schools and limit the number of foreign students per class, far-right Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said Sunday.
Italy is a frontline country for migration, and integration is a major campaign issue ahead of next year's general election.
"A measure will soon be presented to a cabinet meeting to legally establish a maximum number of foreign students per class," Meloni told a gathering of the youth wing of her Brothers of Italy (FdI) party.
"It also requires parents of foreign students facing serious difficulties integrating into the school system to learn Italian, and bans burqas and niqabs in schools," she said.
A crackdown on the use of burqas in schools was called for in July by the National Future (FN) party.
The FN, not part of the governing coalition, is further to the right than Meloni's party and has emerged as a major challenger, rising sharply in the polls since launching in February.
While Italy has no law that expressly bans burqas in schools or public places, a 1975 law prohibits helmets or garments that make identification difficult without a justified reason.
In 2008, Italy's highest administrative court clarified that full-face veils may be worn for religious or cultural reasons provided that the face is revealed when identity verification is required.
The anti-immigrant League party, which is part of Meloni's coalition, submitted a bill to the Senate earlier this year that would ban helmets or garments except in certain circumstances, such as sporting events or places of worship.
Italian law already limits the number of foreign students per class, and Meloni did not spell out how that would change.
Foreign students account for just under 12 percent of those enrolled in Italian schools, according to the National Statistics Institute (ISTAT).
Since 2010, the number of foreign students has been limited to 30 per cent of a class and of a school's enrolment.
The limit can be raised in cases involving foreign students with adequate language skills, such as foreign students born in Italy, or lowered when foreign students have a poor command of Italian.

We confirmed that we are not attacking the United States or any other country in the strait, except for the Saudi enemy. This remains the case

Winless Bombers, Saints and Magpies AFLW coaches under pressure

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:01:59 UTC
06:01:59 KST

The AFLW has passed the midway point of this year's home-and-away season, with some expected storylines and some surprises.
With all the twists and turns, here's what fans are talking about the most.
Will pressure come on coaches without a win?
It's the question fans could be heard right around the boundary fence asking on Sunday afternoon: "Will Essendon win a game this year?"
The Bombers recorded their sixth straight loss, this time against Gold Coast by 41 points, which raised some doubts about the future of head coach Natalie Wood.
Last year, Essendon finished 14th with four wins and eight losses, but escaped a lot of scrutiny due to a high injury toll taking the blame.
This year, fans expected better. Against the Suns, the only goal came off the boot of Emily Gough.
But they're not the only ones. St Kilda remains without a victory and with a percentage of just 36.5.
It's the sixth season head coach Nick Dal Santo has been at the helm, over which time he's taken the team to one finals campaign (last year, in which it lost an elimination final to Adelaide by 44 points).
This year, they lost to Geelong by 85 points in round two, North Melbourne by 92 points in round five, and managed just one goal against Sydney in round three.
Then at Collingwood, the inaugural AFLW side continue to struggle for success, with another year down the bottom end of the ladder.
Sam Wright took over as head coach ahead of the 2024 season and quietly re-signed until the end of 2027 last week. It came amid media reports of player concern about the lack of direction in the club's AFLW program.
Wood and Dal Santo are both out of contract at season's end.
In 2022, Carlton launched an independent review into its AFLW program after managing just six wins across two seasons. The club then signed Mathew Buck as coach and rose to become a genuine finals contender.
Many are now starting to ask whether it's time Collingwood, Essendon and St Kilda do the same.
North are no longer a top of the ladder
Hawthorn's Friday night win over two-time reigning premiers North Melbourne sent shock waves through the AFLW competition.
The Kangaroos were on a 32-match winning streak — the longest in AFL/VFL/AFLW history — and had gone undefeated since 2023, a total of 1,020 days.
Carlton had got close to them the week before, going down by just 10 points, and many thought Melbourne might be the ones to break the run in round seven.
But then came along the Hawks in humid Cairns, where a clutch Lucy Wales goal in the dying minutes of a hard-fought four quarters changed the narrative of the season.
The unbeatable Kangaroos were beaten and the premiership race was blown wide open.
Less than 24 hours later, Melbourne put its foot down against Carlton to remain the only team undefeated this season and take the top spot on the ladder.
Umpiring an issue
One consistency across all leagues and codes, no matter the gender or sport, is fans having a gripe with umpiring or refereeing decisions.
But AFLW fans may have a better leg to stand on than most.
Loading Twitter content
This season, Ray Chamberlain, who retired from the AFL at the end of 2024 after 389 games, returned to help officiate and mentor the next generation of umpires in the AFLW.
He wasn't alone, with the AFL putting a call out to retired umpires to make a return in the women's game, which former AFL-listed umpires such as Jordan Bannister and Chris Donlon answered.
Ahead of the season, Chamberlain said he was happy to help because there was "a need there".
"You want to do it well and you want to support what they're doing," Chamberlain told SEN.com.au.
The state leagues are still the primary pathway for umpires wanting to make into the AFL, which has its finals campaigns running concurrently to the AFLW's start of the season.
With a lot of umpires prioritising the state leagues, there was a dearth of experienced umpires to officiate the AFLW and there was a desperate need for mentoring and development.
Who saw this coming from the Dogs and Suns?
While many of the top eight were predicted by pundits at the start of the season to be finals contenders — Melbourne, North Melbourne, Geelong, Sydney, Carlton and Hawthorn — two teams on the rise that have surprised fans have been the Gold Coast Suns and the Western Bulldogs.
The Suns have lured some big-name recruits in recent years, including premiership players Anne Hatchard and Lily Mithen.
But much of their rise this year has come off the back of teenagers.
The teams has enjoyed the fruits of the Suns Academy, with graduates Ava Usher, Alannah Welsh, Sunny Lappin, Georgia Davies, Mikayla Nurse, Dakota Baron and Bronte Parker all catching the eyes of the competition. And they've helped steer their side to four wins and two losses.
Meanwhile, things have started to click at the Kennel under Tamara Hyett, with the Dogs also sitting at 4-2.
The Dogs have struggled in recent years, and they finished in 12th place last season. But, buoyed by an extremely strong pre-season, they launched into this year with gusto.
Credit to them, they stuck to the plan even when external scrutiny came. Now they pose a serious threat to the teams coming up against them. All this work has been led by captain Isabelle Pritchard, forward Emma McDonald and midfielder Jess Fitzgerald.
There is still a lot to play out in the remaining half of the home-and-away season, particularly with Richmond and Fremantle knocking on the door of the top eight.
But one thing is for sure: It's got an ending a lot less clear than when the year started out.

US prepares sweeping sanctions on International Criminal Court — report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:00:19 UTC
06:00:19 KST

The Trump administration is preparing to implement expansive economic sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), The Wall Street Journal reported.
The upcoming US penalties would prohibit most financial and commercial transactions with the international tribunal following a grace period of six to seven months, according to the newspaper.
The planned sanctions mark a significant escalation in the Trump administration’s punitive actions, shifting from targeting individual court personnel to imposing broad restrictions across the entire organisation.
Sources cited in the report indicated that Washington could finalise the executive measures as soon as this week during the UN General Assembly session or shortly thereafter.
Washington has already penalised numerous tribunal personnel, including ICC President Tomoko Akane, under an executive order issued in February 2025 that declared a national emergency over court proceedings.
The sustained campaign follows the ICC issuing arrest warrants in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
A State Department spokesman declined to preview any sanctions decisions, the Journal said.
Last month, the ICC strongly rejected new US sanctions targeting the court’s president and a senior lawyer in its prosecutor’s office, describing the measures as a “flagrant attack” on judicial independence.
The Trump administration has imposed the sanctions in retaliation for ICC investigations into US personnel in Afghanistan and for warrants the court issued against top Israeli officials.
The latest designations target ICC President Tomoko Akane of Japan and Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, a senior trial lawyer at the Office of the Prosecutor, the Hague-based court said in a statement.
