Hacking this BYD was too easy. It didn't even have a password
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
19:00:56 UTC
04:00:56 KST

On a narrow country road outside Canberra, I'm driving a BYD Shark 6, the hybrid ute loved by tradies and even a cabinet minister.
But while I'm at the wheel, I'm not the only one in control; a hacker has access to the car.
As the 2.6 tonne ute rounds a bend, he gets to work.
Loading...
With the stroke of a key, he kills the headlights, plunging me into darkness.
The attack is not a total surprise. The Shark has spent the past two weeks with Dan Hreszczuk, a cybersecurity expert who specialises in cars.
His task was to hack the vehicle and find out what could be seen and done remotely by the Shark's Chinese manufacturer.
"It was easier than we were expecting," Hreszczuk says.
Modern connected cars, particularly EVs and hybrids, are increasingly run by software, giving manufacturers the power to change, update and control vehicles, like never before.
In the case of BYD and others, that software is controlled from China.
With fuel prices on the rise, EVs and plug-in hybrids like the Shark have gone mainstream this year, making up almost a third of new cars sales to date. More than half of these are from Chinese brands.
EVs, with all their sensors, cameras and microphones, hoover up and spit out vast amounts of data. Experts say that data poses a greater risk in the hands of Chinese EV makers because they can be compelled by the country's national security laws to co-operate with authorities.
To put this potential access to the test, it made sense to pick a model from China's top EV brand, BYD.
Hreszczuk, the co-founder of Fortify Labs in Canberra, was stunned by the BYD Shark's lack of cybersecurity.
"The access we took advantage of didn't even have a password," he says.
"It's a little bit scary how open … the BYD Shark is to a hacker."
This lack of a password allowed Hreszczuk to access the car's digital arteries.
From there it was a matter of unpicking the software programs which controlled different functions in the car.
After two weeks, Hreszczuk was ready.
Sitting by the side of the country road, he demonstrates what can be done with remote access to a vehicle.
First, he locks the doors while I'm inside, blasts music over the speakers and plays images on the BYD's giant infotainment screen.
Then, as I drive, he remotely switches the wipers on at top speed, sprays the windscreen with water and turns the lights on and off.
Loading...
The combination is unsettling and highly distracting.
Adding to the distraction, Hreszczuk has the speaker telling me repeatedly: "For safety, use low beam."
Fortunately, I was only travelling 30 kilometres per hour and the road was pretty straight.
Then, Hreszczuk kills the lights altogether.
Hreszczuk says he wasn't able to access more critical functions like brakes and cameras as these were well protected.
But it doesn't take much imagination to understand how dangerous, even this kind of access could be in the hands of a malicious actor, with a vehicle travelling at high speed on a winding road.
Surveillance
While sabotage is one worry, the concern most often cited is surveillance due to the array of cameras and microphones on an EV.
Last year, the UK military banned Chinese EVs, even those made with Chinese components, from parking within 3 kilometres of some of its most sensitive locations.
China itself has previously banned foreign EVs from military sites and political enclaves, aware of their surveillance potential.
In Australia, there's no blanket ban on Chinese marques by Defence, but ASIO has warned ministers and public servants not to have sensitive conversations in their cars or connect work devices.
But there's nothing to stop them owning a Chinese EV.
Trade Minister Don Farrell has a BYD Shark 6, the same vehicle that Hreszczuk hacked.
Farrell recently told a newspaper it's the "best ute I've ever owned".
ASIO's surveillance fears appear well founded, based on what else Hreszczuk is able to do to with the Shark even at a low level of access.
We devise a demonstration: I'll take the BYD for a drive around Canberra, and give my mother a call to talk her through some internet banking.
As I drive past the war memorial and down Anzac Parade, Hreszczuk has already remotely accessed the vehicle and is tracking my progress.
Then he gets to work.
"How about we turn on the microphone?" he suggests to the crew back at his lab.
At that point Hreszczuk can hear everything.
"Hey Siri," I say to my iPhone.
"Call 'mum mobile'."
When she picks up, I'm straight into the details of how I had set up her internet banking.
"I'm going to use as a temporary password, my initials, the number of my house, and then my full date of birth. And then you can go in later and change it if you want," I tell her.
Back at the lab Hreszczuk records the whole conversation.
The key is he's now got a recording of me saying, "Hey Siri".
When I pull into a service station and leave my phone unlocked in the car, Hreszczuk seizes his opportunity.
He's done a simple audio edit, stitching together me saying "Hey Siri" and his voice asking a few questions to get the personal details he needs.
Using the car's speaker system, Hreszczuk plays the voice command from his computer into the car.
"Hey, Siri, what is my home address?" the edited audio asks.
Siri replies, without questioning why I don't know where I live.
Hreszczuk repeats this process and quickly extracts my date of birth and age.
Within minutes, he's obtained the internet banking password.
Hreszczuk keeps fishing.
"Let's try and grab a few of his contacts. Let's see if he knows a prime minister.
"Hey Siri, tell me the phone number from my contacts for Malcolm Turnbull."
Once again, Siri dutifully delivers.
Hreszczuk's hacking challenge was made easier because Australia has no minimum cybersecurity standards for cars. That means BYD is not compelled to keep its software up to date or have a system for managing cybersecurity risks to its vehicles.
"I didn't need to pick the lock as BYD left the front door open," he says.
"I think people overlook a lot of these concerns for the convenience. It is a beautiful car to drive. It looks beautiful inside, but there are real security concerns."
Surprisingly, Australia has more cybersecurity regulation around connected washing machines or vacuum cleaners than cars.
Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke defends this, saying the government has started by putting regulations around connected devices in the household.
"You want to first regulate where you will get the fastest uplift and … you also want to focus first on where the cyber attacks have principally been," he says.
The government has just started consultations with industry to introduce new cybersecurity and software rules for cars in Australia, but they likely won't be in force for years.
Alastair MacGibbon, Australia's former national cyber security adviser, says there needs to be greater protections for the data collected by all connected cars, and clearer rules about what data can be sent overseas.
MacGibbon says a cabinet minister should not be able to own a Chinese EV.
"China has always shown its strong desire to steal things, to surveil," he says.
"No-one should be in any doubt that [Chinese EVs] are used in the same manner.
"The real question would come down [to]: Could they cause harm with these vehicles? The capability is definitely there.
"Is the intent? I don't know."
Opposition Defence spokesman James Paterson says Australians' data needs to be better protected.
"A connected EV vehicle from China is the highest-risk product in the marketplace. And right now, there's nothing that says to that brand what data you can collect on Australians, how it can be stored, when it can be transmitted."
BYD says the data it collects is stored in Australia. It says it has not and would not hand over the data of Australians to Chinese authorities.
Watch Four Corners' full investigation, Asleep at the Wheel, tonight from 8:30 on ABC TV and ABC iview.

====================================================================================================

SCG madness and Plugger's point: The Swans-Bombers prelim, 30 years on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:52:44 UTC
03:52:44 KST

Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72
SCG madness, Lloyd taken to hospital and Lockett's point: The Swans-Bombers prelim, 30 years on
When Dale Lewis recalls being at the Sydney Swans in the 1990s, it certainly was not all about big games and big crowds.
"We're training, doing preseason out of the showgrounds next door [to the SCG] and one of the days, the Big Day Out was on at these showgrounds. We had to walk the oval, arms linked like we're in a search party checking for needles and shit in the grass before we trained," he says.
"The Swans weren't popular. We were having crowds of 5,000 people. I jumped the fence one day to get the footy for a boundary umpire.
"I've got a great mate … his brother used to come, and he used to love it because he could sit anywhere, and he cracked the shits when we started getting good because he had to go buy a ticket and couldn't get a decent seat and sit where he wanted to."
It all changed in the mid 1990s, when the Swans went from the basement to the penthouse.
With three straight wooden spoons between 1992 and 1994, they went from winning one game in 1993 to four wins in 1994 and eight wins in 1995, then a surge to 16 wins and top of the ladder in '96.
A finals win over Hawthorn put them in a home preliminary final against Essendon at a heaving SCG, 30 years ago today.
Swans utility Troy Luff had gotten his opportunity that season. Originally from Traralgon in Victoria, he grew up attached to a footy like most kids, then he and his family moved to Nelson Bay near Newcastle.
He was spotted while kicking goals for fun in the Hunter, but struggled to make a mark with the Swans under Ron Barassi.
Then new coach Rodney Eade changed everything as Luff became a permanent fixture in the side.
"It was more excitement rather than pressure," Luff says.
"If we lose, we lose. We got this far, but everyone just went out there and enjoyed themselves, and the results came our way."
Lewis agrees.
"None of us saw it coming, but by Christ it was addictive once you started to win, especially at home," he says.
"Because I think that was the year we started. We ended up winning 22 or three in a row at the SCG as the run got going. You started to get a feeling about it.
"And once we'd beaten Hawthorn in that first qualifying [final], the expectation was why not?"
In 1992-93, the Swans lost 26 games in a row.
Lewis, drafted against his preferences in 1990 by Sydney, was out the week they broke the run against Melbourne and ended up playing in 33 consecutive losses. He tried to leave Sydney in 1994, but ended up staying.
In 1995, a series of important arrivals arrived, none bigger than the famous bookends, Paul Roos and Tony "Plugger" Lockett.
The former St Kilda superstar Lockett had won his third Coleman Medal (and first in Sydney) in 1996, booting 114 goals in the home-and-away season.
Former Fitzroy key position player Roos brought skill, leadership and experience.
Now they and the Swans were a win away from a grand final.
The game
It was fierce, frantic footy early doors. Not a heap of composure was shown, with lots of scrubby kicks under pressure, aiming for territory rather than accuracy.
Early in the game, Essendon was looking for James Hird, who - along with Michael Voss of the Brisbane Bears - would win the Brownlow Medal two days later. Hird kicked long from 60, and Steven Alessio marked before converting from 20 out.
Soon after, Lewis marked, then tripped over Hird and was crunched in a tackle. Hird grabbed the ball and scored. Swans fans were livid, but Essendon led by two goals.
The Swans tried kicking to Lockett, but Essendon cleared – their movement was better, and Hird earned a free on 50. He went long, Justin Blumfield came down with it and ran around to kick Essendon's third.
Sydney could not take a trick. Lewis grabbed the ball in the centre square and quickly went long again in Lockett's direction; in the end, Jason Mooney kicked a point to make it 3.1 to 0.1.
Hird came off the ground with blood streaming from his left cheek after he and Andrew Dunkley contested a ball, the Swans defender roughing the Bombers star as he lay on the ground with Dunkley on top of him.
A Barry Young point extended the lead, then Gary O'Donnell took possession and went long to Che Cockatoo-Collins, who marked and drilled it from inside 50. Seven minutes left, Bombers by 25.
The Bombers were dominating clearances, and Damien Hardwick set up Mick Symons for a contested mark, but his kicking radar was off. The Swans' forward forays were like chaos balls compared to the Dons.
Another series of points, then Wade Chapman marked a Stuart Maxfield kick near horizontal at half-forward. His kick came, and Lewis drifted in from the side for a great mark. He kicked it, and the Swans trailed by 19 at quarter time.
"Part of your job is to kick goals and everything else, but to take a big mark," Lewis says.
"That was in front of the Ladies Stand too, I think. A mad, mad Swans house there. Always nice to do that."
Luff says the Swans had built up confidence during the season.
"There was never an attitude of, 'Oh geez, they've got three goals on us, we're going to lose this.' We were like, 'No, no, we'll get that back.'''
Tough night for Essendon's Lloyd
On the Essendon side of things, forward Matthew Lloyd was playing a prelim in game 16 of his career, at just 18 years old.
Drafted at 16, thanks to a one-off change of the rules due to draft concessions for the new Fremantle side, Lloyd was highly touted.
He kicked three on debut against the Crows in 1995 before playing a couple of finals as a schoolboy.
In 1996 he kicked another seven against Adelaide, and then just before finals he booted three against the Swans at the MCG.
"I was playing local footy in 1993, Western Jets in '94, and then suddenly I'm playing as a 17-year-old in '95. So yeah, it all happened so fast, but I was very driven," Lloyd says.
"[The focus] was all footy, footy, footy. I was 78 kilos, and I actually ended my career at 92 to 94 kilos.
"So I was out of my depth physically. I did kick three on debut, and I kicked three in the first [1995] final, so I had some good moments."
Fast-forward to the prelim in 1996; it was a different story.
"I just felt like the SCG, where I hadn't played before, the crowd was on top of you, it was loud, and it was physical," Lloyd says.
"I was a very nervous type. I had a big fear of failure. I wasn't able to get my hands on the footy; it was more the atmosphere in that stadium and some big Sydney players too that I was playing on [that was intimidating]."
In the second quarter, Sydney was trying to hit back, and narrowed the gap through goals to skipper Paul Kelly and Daryn Cresswell. The lead was four points.
Lloyd was scrambling to make an impact. Nearly halfway through the quarter, a big Mark Harvey kick was bouncing towards the boundary at half-forward.
Mark Bayes and Hird were running one way, and Lloyd was racing out of forward 50. As Lloyd recalls, what happened next was "quite innocuous" as he tried to bump Bayes.
"You bump someone, and instead my elbow came back into my side. It took my breath away, and I felt winded. I played out the rest of the second quarter, but I felt like I was deteriorating health-wise," he says.
A review of the video does not suggest there was a huge problem – Lloyd kept launching himself into packs, although if you were keeping your eye on him rather than the ball, he was taking longer to get up each time.
"It's all a bit of a blur for me because I remember I couldn't concentrate; I couldn't really take in the half-time address [from Kevin Sheedy]," he says.
"I was losing colour in my face and body. I said to the club doctor, 'I'm not feeling very well', and they decided to have me start the third quarter and see how I was feeling after five minutes.
"I'm not sure how long I was in the third quarter where I eventually came off … but they knew to get me to hospital at that point."
Lloyd went to emergency at a Kings Cross hospital.
"I just remember lying there still in my full Essendon kit of the football jumper, the shorts, socks, and boots I presume, and just pain, just in so much pain," he says.
He was given morphine, and the pain subsided a little.
"They asked me to hop, and I hopped, and I said, 'I actually feel a bit better,'" he says.
"I can't remember what they thought it could have been, but they said, 'He's right to go back to the hotel.'"
Swans making a run
Back at the SCG, things were improving for Sydney.
After those two early goals, the Swans sensed an opportunity. Derek Kickett kicked from the right pocket to the square for Lockett to mark and goal. The crowd erupted and Sydney led by two with 9:26 left in the half.
Another scrambled ball was toed toward goal by Lockett, only for Sean Denham to palm it away like a goalkeeper.
Somehow Lockett got it out to Luff, who kicked the goal and Sydney led by eight. It was pandemonium at the SCG.
"From memory, he burst through and pushed someone out of the way, then handballed it to me at the top of the square and I snapped the goal," Luff recalls.
"And you just get pumped; it helps you keep building from moments, whether it's a good tackle or a good spoil [or a goal]."
Misses by Barry Young and Hird brought the margin back to six.
The play was getting faster and more chaotic, and the ball pinged in and out of 50 for Sydney. A kung-fu style kick from Luff found Greg Stafford, who ignored a furious Plugger before Cresswell snapped his second. Swans led by 12 at half-time.
Early in the third, a Lewis kick found Lockett near the point post – he marked then stumbled and fell over. His kick hit the post.
On the ABC Radio broadcast, commentator Peter Longman said: "He's done some good things, Lockett, but if he were a racehorse they'd be checking him out behind the barriers and declaring him a non-starter, I feel sure."
Teammates knew Lockett was in pain.
"An 80 per cent Plugger is better than not having him in the side at all, even 70 per cent Plugger. He was just that good," Luff says.
The back-and-forth continued, with a kind of stalemate.
Luff snapped over his shoulder, but it bounced out 15 metres wide of the posts. Luff then got the tap to Kelly, who took two steps and snapped for a Sydney goal. Cue huge chants from the red and white faithful.
"I started in defence when Paul Roos was injured. I'd play centre-half-back. Andrew Dunkley was injured, I'd play full-back. Plugger was out, I'd play full-forward. So I just played any role the team needed [including ruck]," Luff says.
There were 41,731 at the SCG that night – and they were totally fired up, making the noise of a much bigger crowd.
"David Murphy used to tell me before that year, 50,000 people, you can just hear your teammate. [With a] 75,000 crowd, you can barely hear your teammate," Lewis says.
"Anything over 85, 95,000, you can't hear your teammate, and you can't even feel yourself get hit. Such is the noise and the adrenaline; you don't even know what's happening.
"The messaging was always, [finals are] going to be quicker, it's going to be faster, it's going to be harder. And none of it's bullshit."
Just when Swans fans might have been feeling a little confident, the Bombers had a forward 50 stoppage; the tap went to Harvey, and then O'Donnell, who kicked from 35 and the lead was 13 points.
But Sydney went down the corridor, and Lewis marked. A huge roar greeted his goal, and a fan leapt the fence and ran next to the umpire to do a tandem goal signal. He then got out of there quick-smart.
At 19 points down, the Bombers were not done. Dean Wallis marked in the pocket, then Sydney gave away 50. Dunkley was in the umpire's face – Wallis goaled, then confronted the Sydney full-back.
The Bombers won the next clearance, and Alessio found Hird in the square to score. With 3:00 left in the term, it was a seven-point game.
In the final minute, Alessio marked around 50 – and converted. A quarter to go, Sydney led by a solitary point, 8.7 to 8.6.
"I remember Rocket (Rodney Eade) just saying that we needed to shut that down at the start of the last quarter, not go out and try and kick a goal," Luff says.
"If they got the first goal, they've kicked four in a row, and they may have gone on with it. But if we just shut that momentum down, play a bit defensive to start with, then once the game settles, then we [can] go out and attack."
Only three of the 16 goals kicked had been to the left-hand end. The Bombers would be kicking to that end in the final quarter.
Early on, O'Donnell fed Che Cockatoo-Collins, who burst down the right. His kick found Hird, and the Essendon champion slowed, then raced forward and snapped. The umpire scampered around. The Bombers had their early goal.
With 18:27 left, Essendon led by five. Everyone was tiring, and play was largely stuck between the arcs. Time ticked slowly; after a series of misses it was 9.9 to 8.9.
The tension was rising. Essendon's Denham might have cracked a rib; Sydney's Michael O'Loughlin hurt his knee. He came off and returned, still limping.
From a boundary throw 40m out, Harvey handballed to a running Symons.
ABC's Peter Longman was left incredulous:
"He's put it through! The Bombers lead by 12 points! Symons, a duffer from a standing start, has a checkside kick from 35m out and he's put it through – and he might have put the Bombers into the grand final next week!"
The Bombers led by 12, 4:09 on the clock.
The final minutes
Lewis had a sick feeling, wondering if this was how it would finish.
"Something you've wanted so bad as a kid, as a senior footballer, as an AFL player, it's within your grasp, but you can't touch it … It hits you in the gut real hard. I'm not going to lie to you, that was a shit feeling when he kicked that one," he says.
The runner told Lewis to drag Hird to full-forward because Sydney needed goals.
"So I hightailed it out of there," Lewis recalls.
Essendon hacked it forward; Adam Heuskes cleared to Kelly. He found Maxfield, who was chased through the middle, taking two bounces as the roar built. A kick from 60 to Hird and Lewis – and Lewis grabbed it and kicked the goal. Six points, 2:48 left.
It got even more frantic, the ball stuck in the middle. The Swans cleared, and it went to Simon Garlick, then Chapman, then Maxfield to Lockett, who played on but didn't go for goal, opting to kick inside to Cresswell. Cresswell marked then lay down, cramping.
He got up and kicked it, and with 89 seconds left, the scores were level.
Cresswell raised his arms skywards. The Sydney Airport curfew was still half an hour from kicking in, but the roar erupting would have matched a take-off from Mascot.
The clock ticked down, a ball-up with 1:02 left, no real progress.
The play was ferocious as players collided. The ball went inside 50; Swans couldn't mark. Blumfield cleared it desperately, and Chapman marked to the right of the centre square. He back-pedalled, then kicked high to the left side of 50.
From stage right came Tony Lockett to pluck it from the sky and draw every single decibel from surrounding suburbs with 17 seconds left.
He was 52 metres from goal, with an injured groin, and no other options. The clock ran down.
"The video shows me walking past him as he's about to line up to take the shot. I've just turned around to him and said, 'All you have to do is get it over the line. Doesn't matter what it is, just get it over the line,'" Luff recalls.
The siren's gone, the crowd's collective blood pressure had spiked into the stratosphere, but Plugger had it.
Loading...
Everyone watched the ball fly towards goal. Was it there? A point was enough; out on the full or short meant extra time.
The roar gathered. The umpire fired out one finger to signal a behind, and absolute bedlam ensued at the SCG. The Bombers were distraught. The Swans were ecstatic.
It was over. Two seasons removed from the wooden spoon, the Swans were in their first grand final since South Melbourne's infamous "Bloodbath" decider against Carlton in 1945.
Lewis recalls the feeling when Lockett took the grab.
"Call it presumptuous, but the moment he marked it, I knew we were going to play in a grand final," he says.
What about Plugger's groin, the distance, the pain, the effort required?
"None of it became relevant because he's Tony Lockett," Lewis says.
"We would pick him from anywhere, any angle, any distance. Because that's what he does. Not only was it his job, but the belief we had in him when he had the ball in hand, kick a goal or convert and finish was just amazing."
The aftermath
Luff was quick to the party.
"We're like, 'That's going to score.' And then the excitement hit us. And I was one of the first ones to jump on Plugger, and then everyone else just piled on top," Luff says.
"And what I do remember is Plugger on the bottom going, 'Get off me, get off me.' He was so sore from his groin that everyone jumping on didn't help his cause.
"Then [we] got up and we're like, 'We're in the grand final. We're in the grand final.' It was ecstatic. It was fantastic."
Lewis turned to Stafford in the square to find he was already off running.
"I get in a bit late on the pile on, and all I can do is pat a few blokes … because I was too busy celebrating down the goal square looking for a bit of love from teammates who'd already done the bolt," he says.
The euphoric crowd of Swans fans surged onto the ground.
"That's the precursor to the Buddy moment [Lance Franklin's 1,000 goals] in terms of the crowd getting on the ground at the SCG," Lewis says.
"You didn't want to get off [the ground], but you wanted to get off because you wanted to get into that little room downstairs and soak it all in with each other and just go, 'F***, how good is this. We're in one.'"
Lloyd's dream turns 'nightmare'
Back at the Bombers team hotel, Matthew Lloyd was in his room with his parents. Players were coming in, but the morphine was wearing off.
Once people had gone, Lloyd asked his parents to help him to the bathroom, where he passed blood.
Essendon's Dr Bruce Reid came, and Lloyd says he was "rolling around in bed, just the worst pain of my life." Reid asked him if he had shoulder pain.
"I stopped for a second, and I said, 'Yeah, really strong shoulder pain.' I remember him saying, 'Get him an ambulance. He's got a ruptured spleen,'" Lloyd recalls.
Scans showed a large tear in his spleen, and a litre and a half of blood. It could have been fatal if left longer. As scary as this was, Lloyd had to come to terms with what it meant for his footy career.
"I knew going into this game, the reserves had qualified for the grand final," he says.
"I thought, 'Well, I'm going to play in that because I qualify for that or I'm going to play in the AFL grand final,' and then it turned into my nightmare."
Lloyd lost eight kilos, was bedridden for a time and could not do anything physical for three months. But in 1997 he burst out with a 63-goal season.
"I lived and breathed footy, no interest in going to parties," Lloyd says.
"My dad played 29 games for Carlton, and from the moment I was three or four, I had a footy in my hand, and it's all I ever wanted to do … and I was no different with my rehab; I was willing to do anything to play AFL footy."
That determination saw Lloyd finish as Essendon's top goal-kicker and eighth in VFL/AFL history, with 926 majors.
While Lloyd was suffering through a ruptured spleen, the other Bombers were dealing with a season cut short.
He says the players filing through his hotel room that night let him know coach Kevin Sheedy had exploded like never before after the game.
Lloyd was told Sheedy was pointed in his criticism of the team and of individuals, not just for the loss but for the way they lost and a perceived lack of toughness.
Three years later, a dominant Bombers team came up against Carlton and lost in the prelim. Lloyd says it still hurts today.
"In 1999, [Sheedy] was very different. He [went], 'OK, how I'm going to go to sell to these boys the hurt and what we're going to do in 2000 and this should steel us for 2000.' But in '96, he wasn't like that."
Essendon, including Lloyd, had to wait until 2000 for the flag, as they tore through the AFL going 24-1, including three finals by a ridiculous combined margin of 230 points.
For the Swans, the euphoria became a magic grand final week and a dream first quarter and a half – but then the Kangaroos put their foot down, and North ran away with it to win by 43 points. Lockett kicked six, but it wasn't enough. Sydney had to wait until 2005 for the drought to break.
Luff, Lewis and Lockett never won a flag, although Plugger made history with an untouchable 1,360 goals.
It is now 30 years, but Dale Lewis, for one, has not forgotten that night.
"I can see it now. I get a little bit emotional about it," he says with a slight crack in his voice.
"I can see that [night]. I can see the looks in a couple of guys' eyes. I know who I turned to. You look at it, and you go, 'Unbelievable'."

Labor's dilemma is that Australia needs two things voters fear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:49:03 UTC
03:49:03 KST

analysis
The economy needs migration and data centres. Voters hate both
The two things holding up the economy are fast becoming the two most potent and dangerous political issues confronting the federal government.
Data centres and migration are the twin issues the government needs to keep pumping to keep the country in positive economic territory, but they are also the two issues voters have the most complex and hostile relationship with.
It presents a dilemma for the government: it can't live with it, but it also can't live without it.
Migration has long been a key contributor to the economy, with international students, workers and their spending helping tip dollars into treasury coffers.
One Nation and the Coalition want to drastically cut immigration and are smashing the government on the idea that they have allowed a "mass migration" program. Labor, stung by months of relentless campaigning on this issue, finally unveiled a plan to try to cut it back too.
But figures out from today's Intergenerational Report (IGR) show just how much we need migrants for the economy to keep growing, albeit slowly.
Australia's population growth is projected to slow from an average of 1.4 per cent a year over the past 40 years to 0.9 per cent a year over the next 40 years. This is 0.2 percentage points lower growth compared with the projection period of the 2023 IGR.
The population is projected to reach 39.3 million by 2065–66. In 2062–63, the projected population is 1.8 million lower than projected in the 2023 IGR (Chart 8.2).
So while politicians from all the major, minor and yet-to-be-determined sides launch into a debate around migration, the projections are blunt — we are failing to build our own population from our own numbers.
Migrants are the ones renewing us whether we like it or not.
The data centre conundrum
And while migration is the government's perennial political headache, data centres present the same bargain: an economic boost at an unknown political cost.
Touted as the next boom, with some figures indicating they could deliver around $150 billion by 2030. For a country that has relied on revenue from selling the things we dig up, data centres have looked like the next pot of gold.
With inflation still high and economists predicting the Reserve Bank will deliver another rate rise this month, the government will be desperately relying on investment returns from both.
That both issues are the subject of furious debate not just in Canberra but across the country is inconvenient, to put it lightly.
Huawei, the Chinese-owned tech giant banned in 2018 from being involved in Australia's 5G rollout, released a report a few days ago predicting data centres could consume up to 10 per cent of the world's electricity by 2035.
The figure is staggering.
Australia is trying to thread the needle: the government's proposed standards would force new centres to generate their own renewable energy and minimise water use to offset their demand. But those standards are not yet law.
Meanwhile, increasingly dystopian stories about the toll the centres are taking on power, water and the grid are emerging from the United States.
While migration is well-traversed political ground, the emergence of data centres and the community hostility is new territory.
The PM wants to build public consensus through national standards, but it is fanciful to think laws will contain voters' anger if people feel they are competing with global big tech firms for water and power.
Anthropic has signed an agreement to use part of a $32 billion data centre proposed for a site on Queensland's Western Downs. It will be the largest facility in Australia and would draw as much power as about 1.5 million average households.
AI questions won't disappear
Not afraid of calling a spade a spade, Labor MP Ed Husic says the government has so far had a "patronising" approach to people's concerns about artificial intelligence implementation.
"I'm still concerned that we don't have a uniform approach to dealing with the risks of AI," Husic told Afternoon Briefing.
"I've seen AI firms, in fact, some operating right here out of Canberra that are developing generative AI products that are way cheaper than what you're seeing out of US tech [companies]," he said.
But Husic said he did not think Australia would back itself to go local, pointing to leaked Treasury advice "that says we should just be the quickest at adapting someone else's technology".
"That massively undermines our ambition and capability and ability to scale up our own local solutions, and I've got to say, if you want to build confidence in AI, people knowing homegrown AI is available for them that can meet the job and give them a lot more confidence.
"I am concerned that we are dragging the chain. The best thing, if we want to have AI sorted out, is to get a national approach and get it done once, get it done right."
This is a wicked problem for Labor.
Anthony Albanese has urged the United States and China, the two leading powers in the AI race, to strike a deal that ensures "humans remain in control". He has also left the door open to changing copyright laws to attract AI investment in Australia.
Albanese will speak with like-minded leaders at the United Nations General Assembly about global rules to regulate AI development, and while significant, those discussions won't fix domestic concerns over AI.
The government needs to show voters it won't leave them footing the bill for these new futuristic centres and the cash that comes with them; otherwise, the public will keep getting angrier.
Without a reckoning not just on data centres, but also on migration, the two streams the government is banking on to sustain the economy will become two of the government's biggest liabilities.
Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4 pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

====================================================================================================

The politics of migration hides Australia's real problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:41:02 UTC
03:41:02 KST

analysis
Everyone now understands that growing the economy only by increasing the number of people, while individuals feel worse off, is a recipe for unhappiness and dissent.
Aggregate growth is a statistic, but individual decline is a vote. The political solution? Fewer people.
That's because those in focus groups and answering polling questions complain about how many people they can see, rather than the reason they are worse off: weak productivity, which they can't see.
As a result, we now have three significant political parties instead of the usual two.
The third newcomer, One Nation, is an anti-immigration party harvesting unhappiness and dissent. The other two have put on some anti-immigration clothes and have got on the grievance catwalk as well.
The starting number for the fashion parade is 300,000, roughly the current level of net overseas migration (NOM). We learnt on Thursday that population growth in the year to March was 392,700, of which 292,100 were migrants.
That is 100,000 a year more than between the global financial crisis and the COVID pandemic, and 200,000 more than in the decades before that. ABS data shows that over the past four years, population growth has averaged 400,000 a year, or 1,100 a day. The result is noticeable crowding in cities and a 23.5 per cent increase in the national median house price.
Population growth has produced average annual GDP growth since 2010 of 2.4 per cent, while GDP per capita has grown 0.5 per cent and real disposable income just 0.1 per cent and has often been negative, according to the ABS data.
Three offers to ease migration grievance
Here are the three competing bids for the migration grievance vote:
- One Nation: Negative NOM for three years followed by a cap of 130,000 a year.
- The Coalition: 170,000 a year, or roughly the number of houses being built (based on the idea that each migrant needs a house to themselves).
- Labor: 245,000 this financial year and 225,000 in 2027/28.
All agree that we need as much, if not more, skilled migration, preferably from those who can handle a nail gun or a trowel.
That means all three plans affect farmers and universities because the only flexibility to reduce NOM lies with unskilled visitors who pick fruit and vegetables. These workers are needed because Australians don't want to do this work. Students who pay higher tertiary education fees are needed because governments have cut university funding.
None of them is what you would call a promise.
One Nation is closest, offering a pledge and a commitment. The Coalition has an elastic target tied to housing. Labor has converted a forecast into a target.
In a media release to go with his National Press Club speech on Thursday, delayed six weeks while he presumably negotiated with agriculture and education ministers over the impact the changes would have on their constituents, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the plans were "designed to deliver the Net Overseas Migration forecasts in the budget of 245,000 in this financial year and 225,000 in 2027/28".
Treasury must forecast migration for the budget every year, and they are always wildly wrong because this is the first time the minister in charge of migration has taken any notice of them.
Does Canada have the answer?
Meanwhile, two days earlier, in an exquisitely uncomfortable coincidence, Canada announced a stunning set of policies designed to lift productivity.
It is a year since Canada announced a 23 per cent cut in temporary migration, that is, international students and temporary workers from 6.5 to 5 per cent of the population.
Australia's current stock of temporary residents is 10.5 per cent. Cutting that to 5 per cent would involve deporting 1.5 million people.
Maybe in a year's time the Australian government will also address productivity. If so, they could do worse than draw inspiration from Canada.
It's true that Canada is responding to an emergency: the collapse in its relationship with the United States and the imposition of a 50 per cent tariff on its exports to the US. Drastic reform is neither optional nor politically unpopular.
Australia is dealing with an emergency of a different kind: a rut of low growth and low productivity, with high inflation likely to prompt more interest rate increases starting next week.
This will make life harder for people already in such hardship that they're prepared to try Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce.
Canada has introduced what it calls a "Productivity Mega Deduction" (PM Mark Carney says they already used "super" last year) that expands the number of investments that businesses can fully write off for tax purposes in year one from 15 per cent to 65 per cent.
The qualifying investments include fibre-optic cable and data-network infrastructure, mining property, oil and gas pipelines and production-related capital, software, computer equipment and R&D-related assets, aircraft and vehicles, patents, rail track, bridges and roads and Canadian development expenses.
The Canadian government says this will reduce the overall effective business tax rate on new investment from 13 per cent to 6.4 per cent.
At the same time, Canada's Carney announced a broader plan to streamline approvals for major projects and supply chains, framed as: "One project. One review. One year."
The government's stated standard is that a project should face one coordinated assessment rather than overlapping federal processes and receive a decision within one year.
It sits alongside the new Build Canada Strong Act and extends the expedited approach beyond the projects already handled through the Major Projects Office.
So the tax package lowers the cost of investing, and "one project, one review, one year" is designed to reduce regulatory time and burden and uncertainty.
The key reason for Australia's low productivity is declining business investment.
Not only could the Albanese government copy Mark Carney's approach, but there are also many benefits to doing so.
Alan Kohler is a finance presenter and columnist on ABC News. He hosts the podcast That’s Business with Alan Kohler in the ABC Business Daily feed on Friday. He also writes for Intelligent Investor.

TRNC urges global community to reaffirm sovereign equality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:34:43 UTC
03:34:43 KST

The Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) has once again called on the international community to take steps toward reaffirming its inherent right to sovereign equality and equal international status.
In a written statement on Sunday, the TRNC foreign ministry noted that the TRNC and Türkiye’s official policy on the Cyprus issue are based on the principles of sovereign equality and equal international status.
The statement underlined that, for a lasting settlement to be reached on the island, the international community must recognise the TRNC's equal status.
"The fundamental reality is that there are two separate peoples and two independent and sovereign states living side by side on the island. Policies pursued in disregard of these realities will continue to be doomed to failure," the statement said.
On a proposed "rotating presidency" between Turkish and Greek Cypriots in a hypothetical state covering the whole island, the ministry said:
"Although this issue was an element of the model negotiated for decades, that model ultimately collapsed due to the maximalist and uncompromising stance of the Greek Cypriot Administration, which refused to recognise the TRNC's equal status and rejected the sharing of governance and resources. Moreover, the concept envisages a system of governance within a unitary state and represents a policy that is fundamentally incompatible with the TRNC's position based on sovereign equality and equal international status."
The statement once again called for the TRNC's sovereign equality and equal international status to be reaffirmed and urged the international community to take steps in this direction.
Similarly, referring in the European Parliament to "the right to two seats allocated to Turkish Cypriots" and attempting to claim those seats would mean accepting the status of the so-called 'Republic of Cyprus', in which Turkish Cypriots neither participate nor are represented and whose institutions were seized by force by the Greek Cypriot side in 1963, as well as accepting its EU membership based on that status.
"While such an approach cannot be accepted, the Turkish Cypriot people should also not be expected to support initiatives pursued in this direction."
The Greek Cypriot Administration has illicitly claimed to represent the whole island as a member of the European Union since 2004.
Decades-long issue
The island has been mired in a decades-long dispute between Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots despite a series of diplomatic efforts by the UN to achieve a comprehensive settlement.
Ethnic attacks starting in the early 1960s forced Turkish Cypriots to withdraw into enclaves for their safety.
In 1974, a Greek Cypriot coup aimed at Greece’s annexation of the island led to Türkiye’s military intervention as a guarantor power to protect Turkish Cypriots from persecution and violence.
As a result, the TRNC was founded in 1983.
It has seen an on-and-off peace process in recent years, including a failed 2017 initiative in Switzerland under the auspices of guarantor countries Türkiye, Greece, and the UK.
The Greek Cypriot Administration entered the EU in 2004, the same year that Greek Cypriots single-handedly blocked a UN plan to end the longstanding dispute.

United Russia projected to win over half the votes in State Duma "election"
Three days of voting in the elections for Russia's State Duma (lower chamber of the Russian parliament) election have ended. The ruling United Russia party is set to win around half of the vote, according to pro-Kremlin exit polls and early figures from Russia's Central Election Commission.
Source: Kremlin-aligned Russian news agency TASS, citing "exit polls" and early data from Russia's Central Election Commission
Details: Three days of voting to elect members of Russia's State Duma have ended. Polling stations closed at 21:00 in Russia's westernmost oblast, Kaliningrad Oblast.

TASS is also posting figures from pro-Kremlin exit polls conducted by the Russian Public Opinion Research Center (VCIOM) and the National Institute for Opinion Surveys and Marketing (INSOMAR) .
According to VCIOM, United Russia is on course to win 49.4% of the vote, the Communist Party of the Russian Federation 14.2%, the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia 10.7%, New People 9.7% and A Just Russia 6.6%.
According to INSOMAR, United Russia is set to win 52.8%, the Communist Party of the Russian Federation 14.8%, the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia 9.9%, New People 8.6% and A Just Russia 5.5%.
After processing 13.88% of the ballots, Russia's Central Election Commission said United Russia was winning 57.54% of the vote.
Background:
- It was reported that mobile networks and internet access could be shut down in Russia during the three days of voting for the State Duma and regional parliament elections on 18-20 September due to what authorities described as "security measures". Meanwhile, systematic pressure on election observers, coercion of public-sector employees and widespread electoral fraud have been reported across the country.
- Investigative journalists published leaked internal documents concerning the State Automated Vybory 2.0 (Elections 2.0) System, which was being used fully for the first time in the Russian federal elections in 2026. According to the developer's technical documentation, the updated system contains tools that allow final ballots to be directly tampered with, electoral rolls to be altered and unverified electronic voting results to be uploaded.

Liam McIntyre, the next Australian Wolverine, on playing 'gruff, angry loners'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Marvel's Wolverine has new Australian lead in Liam McIntyre
Before becoming an actor, Liam McIntyre was an assistant manager at EB Games whose duties included inspecting trade-ins and selling the latest releases.
Twenty years later, he's back selling games but there's one small difference behind his throwback return: it's his face on the cover of the PlayStation 5 game Marvel's Wolverine.
"I don't think I believed it for three years," McIntyre tells ABC Arts.
As an avid gamer (and recent Pro Jank Footy enthusiast) and X-Men fan who grew up watching the cartoons, this represented a dream role.
"I filmed three-quarters of the game going, 'You're sure I'm Wolverine?'"
When he was invited to audition for "Rough Guy John", an angry man with razor-sharp knives jutting out from his knuckles, he didn't need Wolverine's superhuman senses to sniff out that he was actually auditioning to star in Insomniac Games's latest superhero blockbuster.
Marvel's Wolverine promises a more grounded, violent and combat-driven experience than the developer's quippy, webspinning Spider-Man series. McIntyre's background in ferocious gladiatorial combat in the Spartacus: Vengeance TV series was an advantage for recording Wolverine's animalistic grunts, terse dialogue and ferocious roars in a Burbank motion-capture studio.
"I don't know why I keep being picked to be these gruff, angry loners who wield violence to help people," McIntyre says. "What's that say about me?"
Wolverine's world
McIntyre has moved into voice acting in recent years, but the relentless scrutiny of providing both a comic icon's face and voice reminds him of his early theatre career at venues like Melbourne's White Whale Theatre.
"This is the weirdest blend of stage and film, because you're always in the round, you're always in a close-up. And you never know which one they're going to pick," he says.
The experience reminds him of sparse and intimate "black box theatre" venues; he had to use his imagination while performing in a tight Lycra suit dotted with reflective balls.
As the line between Hollywood and big budget video games narrow, McIntyre faces the same unusual challenges as Marvel A-listers when he pretends to crawl through burning buildings, decapitate The Hand's crimson-cloaked ninjas, or jump out of a plane sticking two middle claws up at his feral rival Sabretooth.
"You've got this giant helmet on, so if you try to hug someone you try not to Velcro onto them, which ruins the sound, and try not to clank into each other, which ruins the footage," says McIntyre.
"But I always think about regular film and television; you're still pretending there isn't a wall of cameramen and lights."
"You're used to removing segments of the reality you're in so you can act."
Why Australians play Wolverine best
Fourteen years ago, when McIntyre was asked for his favourite actor he immediately replied "Hugh Jackman". Now he's the second Australian to play a starring role synonymous with the Sydneysider superstar.
McIntyre feels unfazed by the pressure that comes with following a beloved predecessor in a storied role; his American TV breakthrough followed the tragic death of original lead Andy Whitfield.
He carries the same lessons for Wolverine. He resists the temptation to imitate, to copy how Jackman clenches his jaw, furrows his brow, or holds his claws up like a boxer (Jackman's stance was inspired by watching Mike Tyson title fights).
"I can't ever be him. I wouldn't want to copy him," McIntyre says of Jackman.
Instead, he's drawing from beyond Hollywood, including Chris Claremont's famous run on the Marvel comics series and Cal Dodd's Clint Eastwood-influenced vocal delivery on X-Men: The Animated Series.
Despite the illustrious competition, between McIntyre and Jackman there's a strong argument that Australians make the best Wolverines.
"I don't think you have to be Australian to be Wolverine. But it helps!" McIntyre says. "The Australian ethos, gruff, earthy, don't seek the plaudits, tall poppy syndrome, all align with the way Wolverine is. He keeps his head down."
The cycle of violence
Wolverine's barely suppressed rage is one characteristic neither Australia or Canada would claim. Yet Wolverine's anger is a core element of the game, with an aggressive rage system where collecting kills is rewarded with increasingly powerful attacks and graphic slaughter.
This emphasis created an odd situation familiar to any video game voice actor: the need to record an extraordinary quantity of agonising screams, roars and grunts.
McIntyre hoped to space out these strenuous non-verbal sessions. That didn't happen.
"There was one day where it [the day's recording runsheet] was 'Grunts, angry.' 'Grunts, perturbed.' "Grunts, confused.'" remembers McIntyre, who made it through with herbal remedies and some surprisingly effective vocal exercises using a straw.
"This is the most acting I'll do in my life,' he says.
A longer, broader story than the movies
Once his voice was restored to its deep and sonorous pitch, McIntyre can be grateful for opportunities that come with the game's extended run time.
Players get 15 to 20 hours to uncover the core dichotomy of a character caught between two selves: an animal who can fall prey to his worst instincts, and a man who desperately hopes to be better than the lonely screw-up he so often is.
"I love this rare opportunity to tell this longer, broader story," McIntyre says.
"It's got so much detail and time with the character to really explore that. You don't always get that, even in a movie."
Moving from movies to games came with some surprises. Screen mediums usually give the final say to the director, but games share that autonomy with players with occasional interference from a few erratic glitches.
McIntyre was surprised to see his facial animations become the subject of numerous in-jokes in Insomniac's Slack channel, especially one glitch where his character's famous yellow outfit remained in one room, while his character progressed to the next entirely naked (a stunt double's body, he swiftly adds).
"Which was fine in theory until I realised that people would save this and then share it around. That's my face! Please be gentle," laughs McIntyre, fearing what millions of players will do with his likeness. "I didn't think that through when I signed away my rights."
Despite those misgivings, McIntyre still can't believe his career has taken him to a place where he needs to worry about such a vast global audience.
"I was a kid that got bullied at school. It just wasn't my worldview to imagine I could achieve such cool things," says McIntyre, who feels his past self had a lot to learn from Wolverine's resilience. The character's superpower isn't really his adamantium claws; it's his capacity to take a beating.
"Just keep pushing. That's what I like about Wolverine the most: No matter how many times he gets kicked down, he always finds a way to dust himself off and keep going. I want to have more of that in my life."
Marvel's Wolverine is out now on PlayStation.

Striking a balance between living for the present and future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Readers on striking a balance between living for the present and future
How much time do you spend living in the future?
Jack Waters recently wrote about how a drive to "set himself up" and optimise every part of his life made it hard to enjoy the present.
This is what readers had to say about finding the balance (and joy) in their own lives.
Striving for perfection
"My whole life has been about optimisation. In my 20s, I started exercising fanatically … in my mind I had to exercise every single day, and I remember 'having to go' for a run at midnight on a family holiday in Merimbula in the 90s instead of relaxing and going to bed.
I started journalling at 17 and still do it. It's like hoarding memories. It has spread to using my phone to video things instead of just enjoying the moment during concerts and on bushwalks.
I've always been a workaholic, a habit my parents instilled in me, and I dislike taking time off. I work hard, not smart.
Five years ago, I started learning guitar and piano to fulfil a lifelong dream. That now consumes all my spare time, probably to no avail, as I'm too self-conscious to play for anyone.
But I have missed hours of watching [TV] with my wife. I'm 60 now, and I am struggling with the thought of impending retirement, and I have serious trouble just enjoying experiences. It's got to the point where I'm wondering when the life I've been setting myself up for will start."
- Marc
"I was intensely focused on optimisation in my 20s.
I turned vegan and only ate whole foods; I stopped drinking; I tracked habits and had a rigid exercise routine. It all came tumbling down and ended in an actual mental breakdown.
I've recovered, but it wasn't without [professional] help.
Optimisation is at an all-time high, and I see articles about hacks, self-help books and the like daily. But I've never been more miserable than when I was trying to track my life.
Life is messy and beautiful and uncertain, and it would be great if we could lean into that more, which is why I ocean swim and started playing rugby union to recover."
-Kathleen
Discovering balance
"Jack's story really resonates with me as I am the same; unable to enjoy the present and rushing through, always thinking about the future. I would love to learn and understand what it means to live in the present rather than rush through my life."
- Christine
"I have recently been tossing up changing electricity providers and found myself thinking, 'This plan has a lower off-peak rate than I am currently on. If I shower at five, my hot water system should have reheated before seven and I will pay less electricity.' I knew that would put more pressure on me, so I didn't switch to that one.
I particularly struggle with exercise and food; it's all in or nothing. Balance is what I am trying to learn now."
- Sally
"I received my first cancer diagnosis at 30 and second diagnosis at 52.
I'm now 55, and while I thought for many years I would die early, I'm now faced with dying of old age.
For me, I try to make sure there's something joyful in each day, do things that help the present and future like exercise and eating well, prioritise activities that require health and mobility like trekking, and don't invest a lot in activities that might need 25 years to return the investment. It's a balance."
- Tanya
Living in the moment
"I spent my 20s living life in the moment and telling myself I'll let the future me worry about it.
I have had plenty of good experiences. I'm 32 now and have spent the last two years on personal development and optimisation. I'm feeling like I'm trying to make up for lost time.
There are so many things that I'm looking back on and feel like I could have done better, but hindsight is a beautiful thing.
Finding a happy medium is hard to accomplish.
At the moment, I'm at a place where I have left my old life behind, but I haven't fully achieved my life yet."
- Joshua
"I slogged through school and four years of a mathematics degree and programming, only to find no employment with it 10 years in.
I've stopped saving and investing and learning, sick of the constant scheming to improve my future life. I went car-free, share-housed, brewed beer, avoided ticketed events, saved $200,000 while house prices went up.
Now I spend my whole pay cheque enjoying my life, going to music festivals again, and earning less than I did in 2012. If I were a teenager again, I would consider myself reckless, but I had a go at doing the right things, tried and failed the 'getting ahead' thing. Feel like I wasted 15 years of my life."
- Phillip

Houthis warn against joining Saudi Arabia in Yemen's civil war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:29:18 UTC
03:29:18 KST

Breadcrumb
Houthis warn against joining Saudi Arabia in Yemen's growing civil war
A senior official with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels is warning countries against joining Saudi Arabia in Yemen's revived civil war, telling The Associated Press on Sunday that his group has assured the Trump administration that it won't attack US vessels in the Red Sea.
Mohamed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis' political bureau, said Washington reached out to the rebels after their rapid advance down Yemen's western coast to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait earlier this month.
"We confirmed that we are not targeting the United States, or any other nation, in the strait, with the sole exception of the Saudi enemy," he told the AP in a Zoom interview from the rebel-held Yemeni capital, Sanaa. "That remains the case."
US President Donald Trump last weekend said his administration has "had discussions" with the Houthis, but did not say when. "The Houthis called us, and they don't want to fight with us," he said. "They would much prefer not having us involved, and they're letting most ships go through."
The AP later reported that Oman hosted a meeting between US and Houthi representatives last weekend, citing a Houthi official and another individual familiar with the talks. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.
However, al-Bukhaiti only confirmed indirect contacts with US officials through longtime mediator Oman, which brokered a 2025 ceasefire between the Houthis and the Trump administration. That ended a weeks-long US bombing campaign against the rebels in return for them ceasing attacks on US vessels in the Red Sea.
"The goal of our military operations is not to close the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, but rather to ensure freedom of navigation through it for everyone, including Yemen," he said.
Al-Bukhaiti said the rebels have the capacity to fight a war on multiple fronts "should any nation become implicated in the aggression against Yemen alongside Saudi Arabia."
"Today, Yemen is capable of waging battle, not merely an internal conflict, but an international one as well," he said.
He said the Houthi attacks against neighbouring Saudi Arabia will persist until Riyadh ends its decade-long blockade on rebel-held areas in Yemen and allows vessels to reach Houthi-controlled ports on the Red Sea. Then they will be ready to negotiate, he said.
Al-Bukhaiti blamed Saudi Arabia for the latest escalation of violence in Yemen, which he said erupted after an airstrike blamed on the Saudi-led coalition fighting the rebels hit the Sanaa international airport.
The strike prevented an Iranian flight carrying a Houthi delegation to land. The flight was a Houthi attempt to challenge the coalition's air and naval blockade.
The Houthis responded with missile and drone strikes on Saudi Arabia, including one that targeted Riyadh on Saturday before being intercepted. Saudi officials said debris from a Houthi drone also killed one civilian and injured others.
The Houthis also declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea, attacking Saudi-linked vessels and oil facilities inside the kingdom, the world's top oil exporter.
The Saudis and their allies have long struggled to contain the Houthis, and may be tempted to seek a diplomatic solution to halt attacks. That might ultimately require US concessions to Iran, the only country with leverage over the Houthis. But Washington's negotiations with Tehran over their own war fell apart weeks ago.
The US, which bombed Yemen under the Biden and Trump administrations, has shown no interest in getting involved militarily this time around.
The rebels' advance inside Yemen seized the crucial port city of Mokha and key Red Sea islands that allow them to better monitor shipping traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb, through which some 12 percent of world trade normally passes.
The Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, long divided into factions, withdrew but have vowed to regroup.
The escalation ended a 2022 ceasefire that largely ended fighting in Yemen's civil war, which started when the Houthis swept in from their mountainous heartland and seized much of northern and central Yemen, including Sanaa, 12 years ago.
The Saudi-led coalition entered the war the following year on behalf of the internationally recognised government. The civil war killed at least 150,000 people, according to UN estimates, and pushed the country to the brink of famine.
Now, with Houthis in control of Yemen's western coast overlooking the Red Sea shipping corridor, "the balance of power has shifted in favour of the Sanaa government," al-Bukhaiti said, referring to the rebels' de facto authorities there.
"Ultimately, (Saudi Arabia) lost its most critical card: the west coast," he said.

Germany's Merz remains defiant after historic state elections defeat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:26:21 UTC
03:26:21 KST

Germany's Merz defiant after historic state elections defeat, vows to press ahead with reforms
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz remained defiant on Sunday, vowing to press ahead with potentially painful reforms to Europe's biggest economy, after suffering a bruising electoral setback in two state elections.
Exit polls by public broadcaster ARD indicated that Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union, or CDU, came in with just 5% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania – the lowest result ever since World War II for the party in any state. Meanwhile, the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany, or AfD, party made significant gains.
Merz acknowledged that the result was a "disaster" but said he would still move ahead with his government's reform agenda. He argued that Germany's economic and political problems made difficult and potentially unpopular reforms more urgent, not less so, and pledged to press ahead.
"What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness, and patience," Merz said in a statement shortly after the exit polls were announced on public television. "I will demonstrate these qualities as chairman of the CDU and, above all, as chancellor of our country."
In Berlin, the CDU was projected to come in second with 20%, behind Die Linke (The Left Party) at 24.5%, according to ARD's exit poll.
"In our city, love and justice have triumphed over hatred," said Die Linke's lead candidate Elif Eralp, the daughter of Turkish migrants, celebrating her party's triumph over AfD.
Merz's authority was already damaged by the CDU's stinging defeat to AfD in the Sept. 6 election in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. That result shocked many Germans who had believed their country had developed an immunity to nationalism and assertions of racial superiority after confronting the horrors of its Nazi past through education and laws to outlaw persecution.
On Sunday, AfD was projected to make big gains in both states. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, it garnered 37% of the vote, and in Berlin it achieved 15.7%, according to ARD. But it was nowhere close to being able to form a regional government.
AfD's national co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, told ZDF television that "the chancellor's statement today really was more than feeble — he announced that he'd carry on as before, instead of finally drawing the consequences and resigning."
However, in an apparent reference to the far-right party, Merz said that his government's reforms would be "the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism, which is penetrating ever deeper into our society as the fascination with authoritarianism grows."
The CDU has run Germany's government off and on for the vast majority of its post-World War II history.
Merz, 70, became Germany's leader 16 months ago with promises to turn around an economy that has barely grown in years. But his government is grappling with a weak economy, and many voters who had hoped the former corporate executive would fix that have become disillusioned with delays in implementing financial and tax reforms.
While Germany is again seeing moderate growth, the labor market deteriorated last year. In August, more than 3 million people were unemployed, an increase of 36,000 from the previous year. Demand for labor remains weak, according to the Federal Employment Agency.
The strong showing of AfD in the Saxony-Anhalt election, where it has the best chance yet of forming the country's first far-right regional government since World War II, has further weakened the chancellor's standing on the national level as well.
In the past two weeks, there have been calls, even from within his own party, for him to be replaced as chancellor, although no top-level allies have called publicly for his departure, and many have warned against "personnel debates."
Apparently anticipating a tough post-election period, Merz abandoned a planned trip to New York next week to attend the U.N. General Assembly. Despite the strong headwinds, he has repeatedly said that he's determined to stay on and finish his term as chancellor.

Manchester City beat Sunderland 5-3 on Sunday in an eight-goal thriller to move three points clear at the top of the Premier League.
Enzo Fernandez put City ahead in the ninth minute, catching goalkeeper Robin Roefs off guard with a near-post free-kick from a tight angle.
Sunderland equalized three minutes later through Brian Brobbey, who lifted the ball over Gianluigi Donnarumma after receiving Enzo Le Fee's pass behind the City defense.
Rayan Cherki restored City's lead in the 29th minute with a low finish through a crowded penalty area, but Brobbey struck again four minutes later to make it 2-2.

Semenyo doubled City's advantage in the 57th minute with a low finish, but Brobbey completed his hat trick just two minutes later to reduce the deficit to 4-3.
Erling Haaland sealed the victory in the 81st minute, sliding in to convert Josko Gvardiol's cross after the VAR referee overturned an initial offside decision.
The result extended City's perfect start to the Premier League season and moved them three points clear at the top of the table.

US indicts 30 suspects in assassination of Haitian president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:24:35 UTC
03:24:35 KST

Yasin Gungor
20 September 2026•Update: 20 September 2026
Federal prosecutors in the US indicted 30 individuals Sunday for their alleged participation in the 2021 assassination of Haiti’s president.
"Today marks the next major phase in our pursuit of accountability for the assassination of President Jovenel Moise," US Attorney for the Southern District of Florida Reding Quinones said, adding that authorities transferred 18 defendants to the US state of Florida from Haiti via military aircraft to face charges in federal court.
Quinones stressed that investigators will continue pursuing those who financed, facilitated, or committed crimes to enable the killing. "Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished," he said.
Brett Skiles, the FBI special agent in charge, said the individuals carried out the assassination to secure "illicit" business opportunities and contracts, emphasizing that multinational arrests demonstrate sustained efforts to hold all conspirators accountable.
Moise was killed on July 7, 2021, by an armed commando at his private residence in a suburb of the capital Port-au-Prince.
After the assassination, Haiti slid into a worse crisis, including gang coalitions seizing most of the capital, the collapse of political institutions, and humanitarian conditions deteriorating to near failed-state levels.

Suspects in 2021 killing of Haitian president flown to US to face trial

Suspects in 2021 killing of Haitian president flown to US to face trial
PORT-AU-PRINCE, Sept 20 - A military plane whisked 18 suspects in the 2021 killing of Haitian President Jovenel Moise out of Haiti and flew them to the United States on Sunday, according to Jason Reding Quiñones, the US Attorney for the Southern District of Florida.
"Today marks the next major phase in our pursuit of accountability for the assassination," Quiñones said in a statement posted on social media.
The 53-year-old president was shot dead in July 2021 at his private residence in the hills above Port-au-Prince, a killing that left a gaping political vacuum in the Caribbean nation and emboldened powerful armed groups in the country.
The killing has prompted multiple investigations and indictments in Haiti and the United States.
On Sunday, Haitian Justice Minister Patrick Pelissier confirmed in a statement that suspects had been transferred from Haiti to the US, adding that Haitian judicial proceedings had been delayed.
"While the American procedure has recorded significant progress, notably arrests, prosecutions, and convictions, the Haitian procedure remains confronted with major difficulties and has not, to date, resulted in a trial being held, after five years of proceedings."
US prosecutors have argued that suspects in the case used South Florida as a "staging ground for a deadly foreign plot." Thirty people have been indicted in the US in relation to the crime, according to Quiñones' statement on Sunday.
In May, four South Florida men were convicted of plotting to kill the Haitian president by hiring mercenaries to assassinate him at his Port-au-Prince home.
Prosecutors argued during the nine-week trial in a Miami federal court that the men assembled two dozen former Colombian soldiers and supplied them with money, guns, ammunition and tactical vests in a conspiracy to kill Moise.
In Haiti, prominent human rights activist Pierre Espérance said that the slow pace of the Haitian case and the transfer of the 18 suspects to the US was a "disgrace for the Haitian justice system."
He argued for strengthening the country's justice system to allow for such complex cases to be tried inside Haiti, rather than sending them to the US for prosecution. REUTERS

AI, data center alarms dominate Congressional Black Caucus week in Washington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
18:05:02 UTC
03:05:02 KST

This year's Congressional Black Caucus Annual Legislative Conference, which wraps Sunday, has taken on a different feel than its usual college homecoming vibe. The event, which has drawn thousands of attendees to Washington, took on a more serious tone with briefings and conversations focused on artificial intelligence opportunities and regulation amid escalating concern about threats posed by the technology.
"I stand 100%, and so does the CBC on regulation," CBC Vice Chair Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., told CNBC. "I think we need guardrails, I think we need transparency, I think we need to prepare and protect the community from the potential ills that come with it."
Carter said at least 60 of the 62 members of the CBC would vote for a bill to regulate artificial intelligence, creating guardrails and placing guidelines on human safety. He added that competition with China should not be a factor in any legislation.
"I'm not going to run and race with China, they're not doing it the right way. They are not protecting communities," he said. "Our race should be enhanced innovation, advanced technology, while we simultaneously protect the rights of the American people."
The CBC is an influential group whose members include 29% of Democrats in the U.S. House. As Democrats aim to take control of the House in November's midterm election, the caucus's standing could rise.
The CBC's tackling of AI came amid the backdrop of Open AI becoming the latest company to report an incident where AI agents conducted what they call 'concerning model behavior,' It's one of a growing number of so called 'jailbreaks,' the slang term for when models bypass guidelines and perform unauthorized actions.
"The message they wanted me to bring is how we can do this in a way that protects our communities but do not put us in a position to lose in a national security race," said X. Eyee, an AI expert and Army veteran, who spoke with CBC members about striking a balance between putting boundaries on the technology without inhibiting innovation. "To do that, it does require addressing some of these areas where algorithms are being used with little boundaries around them."
Carter said he is talking with voters about how important the upcoming midterm elections are for AI regulation. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., this month asked that the House stay in session to find a way to legislate AI safeguards. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., after President Donald Trump called AI-safety concerns a "hoax," countered that "It's time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people."
"They're not bringing it to the floor because I'm not sure that they want the regulation that we want," Carter said of Republican House leadership. "I've heard them say pump the breaks. I've heard them say let's let innovation handle it on its own, but we can't afford to do that."
With AI skepticism high in the caucus, the AI and tech industries also showed up for the CBC's Washington gathering.
Meta President and Vice Chair Dina Powell McCormick touted the economic benefits of data centers and the AI buildout they power. Meta is building the Hyperion data center project in Louisiana, and its hyperscaler rivals, including Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft, are all also in the data center expansion race.
"Technology and AI are the economic revolution of our generation," Rep. Steven Horsford, D-Nev., a former CBC chair who now leads its technology committee, told CNBC. "That means that as Black Americans, we cannot allow this innovation to pass us by."
Horsford spoke about the importance of helping shape the energy-intensive AI buildout on a panel with Exelon CEO Calvin Butler.
Exelon provides power and grid services for the Philadelphia, Chicago, Baltimore, and Washington areas, and Butler said he is having continuing conversations with lawmakers about the potential impact on energy prices and residents' quality of life.
"AI is a real conversation because people are trying to figure out where they fit in and can have a voice," Butler told CNBC. "What they are saying is we can't sit on the sidelines and let our constituents be impacted, and you as energy companies have a role in helping us solve this problem."
Data centers, the CBC and redistricting
The debate over AI regulation and data centers took on greater urgency because congressional redistricting could affect CBC members. The Supreme Court's ruling in Louisiana v. Callais will make creating "minority-majority" districts difficult and have major ramifications for the 2028 election and 2030 census, according to the Harvard Kennedy School.
CBC Chair Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-N.Y., estimated earlier this year that as many as 19 seats held by CBC members are at risk due to redistricting.
Carter said that while that number is lower now after court challenges to redistricting plans, the impact on the Black community remains.
"This is not just about congressmen," he said. "This is about school boards. This is about legislative seats."
Horsford echoed concerns about threats to minority representation in Congress.
"This has never been about protecting any one district, and it is absolutely not about protecting one party or another," he said. "It's about protecting the voters' right to pick their representatives, and not the representatives being able to pick which voters they serve. And as long as we keep that at the center of the work, then we're honoring what our democracy is supposed to be about."
