Hong Kong holds state funeral for 1st postcolonial leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:24 UTC
01:36:24 KST

Hong Kong yesterday held a state funeral for its first postcolonial leader, Tung Chee-hwa (董建華), who led the territory through the initial years of its transition from British rule after it was returned to China in 1997.
Chinese officials from Beijing joined Hong Kong political leaders for the service in what was the third state funeral in the territory since the handover.
Tung, a shipping magnate handpicked by Beijing to serve as the territory’s chief executive from 1997 to 2005, died on Sept. 8 at the age of 89. The staunch conservative oversaw a rocky eight-year tenure, grappling with the Asian financial crisis and the SARS epidemic until he resigned in 2005, following widespread protests.
Photo: Reuters
Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference Vice Chairman Shi Taifeng (石泰峰), the former head of the Chinese United Front Work Department, referred to Tung in a eulogy as a close friend of the party and a renowned patriot, the state-run Xinhua news agency reported.
He said Tung was an outstanding contributor to the “one country, two systems” framework that governs Hong Kong and Macau.
Flower wreaths lined the wall outside the Hong Kong Funeral Home and Tung’s casket was draped in a Chinese flag when it was brought out after the service. The media were not allowed inside.
Other visiting officials included Chinese Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office Director Xia Baolong (夏寶龍).
About 200 people were invited to the service, the South China Morning Post reported.
Members of the public paid condolences at three venues set up around Hong Kong.
Cheung Kwok-lik, an 89-year-old retired renovation worker, said he had traveled an hour by bus to pay his condolences to the former leader.
During his tenure, Tung weathered the Asian financial crisis and the SARS epidemic in 2003 that killed nearly 300 people and dealt another blow to the economy, which “was by no means easy,” Cheung said.
Tung’s leadership also coincided with record unemployment and the 1997 avian flu outbreak.
In 2003, an estimated 500,000 people took to the streets to protest the government’s plan to enact an anti-treason law that was seen as a threat to civil liberties. The government shelved the plan, and Tung resigned in 2005, citing health reasons.
That protest marked the start of years of pro-democracy protests that came to a head in 2019 and were followed by a crackdown and the Beijing-imposed National Security Law in 2020.
Tung was later elected to the post of vice chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference. He was among 42 people who received national medals and honors in 2019 for their contributions to the country.

Photos: Nepal flood survivors find little trace of former lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:36:03 UTC
01:36:03 KST

In Pictures
Photos: Nepal flood survivors find little trace of former lives
Nepal’s floods displace thousands, with survivors mourning loved ones and searching for belongings amidst the debris.
When Anusa Thapa Magar rushed home from her job in the Maldives after hearing of Nepal’s devastating floods, she clung to the hope that her grandmother had somehow survived.
Instead, when she reached Betrawati, the small riverside town where her family lived, she found only a flat expanse of hardened grey silt.
There was no house, and no Betrawati.
“If my house is buried underneath, that means my Aama is still here underneath too, right?” the 23-year-old said quietly, standing where the family’s two-storey home once stood. Her grandmother, who could barely walk, was last seen resting on her bed.
Last month’s torrent of mud, rock and water, triggered by a glacial collapse in the mountains along the Nepal-China border, tore through settlements along the Trishuli River, killing at least 1,386 people on the Nepal side. Authorities say 5,130 are still missing, and while searches continue, it has been days since anyone was found alive.
To reach what used to be Betrawati, survivors now climb a steep hillside, cross a narrow ridge and descend into a wasteland. Along the route lie scattered shoes, school ties and children’s backpacks – “silent evidence”, residents say, of the panic as people scrambled to flee the surging floodwaters.
Garment business owner Kalpana Thapa Magar, 43, recalled the moment a friend phoned from upstream. “Run! Run!” she was told. “I just ran. When I looked back, everything was gone, even the people who had been running behind me,” she said.
Downstream in Devighat, shattered shells of houses still stand. Some residents pick through the rubble for belongings, but many say there is no reason to return; the land itself has vanished beneath debris.
For many here, the disaster reopens wounds from Nepal’s 2015 earthquake, which killed nearly 9,000 people. Teacher Sita Thapa Magar, 45, Kalpana’s older sister, said that after the quake, families were at least able to rebuild on their plots. “This time, we have lost everything,” she said. “Our houses, our land, our future.”
On a single broken floor tile – the last visible trace of her home – 61-year-old Shanti Dangol clutched a photograph of the three-storey lodge she once ran for pilgrims and trekkers.
“Economically, people here had started doing well,” she said. “Now, nothing remains.”

Meloni pushes for burka ban in Italy’s schools, cap on foreign students
Italian prime minister tells party rally that foreigners must ‘respect our rules’ under proposed integration package
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Sunday she will soon introduce a measure to her government that would cap the number of foreign pupils in classrooms and ban the wearing of burkas and niqabs in schools.
Meloni told the youth wing of her nationalist conservative Brothers of Italy party that the measure would also make Italian language lessons compulsory for parents of foreign pupils having “serious difficulties integrating into the school system”.
“For us, anyone who comes to Italy and wants to build their future here must learn our language, understand our culture, and respect our rules,” she said to a standing ovation at the Gioventu Nazionale national festival in Rome. “It is the only serious way to welcome them.”
Meloni specifically referred to a ban on the burka, an all-covering dress worn by some Muslim women, and the niqab, the veil worn by the most conservative Muslim women, in which, at most, only the eyes show. But Meloni did not mention the hijab, the headscarf worn by some Muslim women.

Statement on missing ICIJ journalist Micah Reddy

Update, 4.30pm ET / 11.30pm Djibouti: ICIJ has been informed that Reddy is believed to be in custody for failing to obtain media accreditation. It is understood Ismael is also being held in custody by Djiboutian authorities.
The International Consortium of Investigative Journalists is gravely concerned for the safety of our colleague Micah Reddy, ICIJ’s Africa coordinator, and local journalist Mohamed Willo Ismael (“Kooki Mahmoud”).
Contact with the pair was lost in Djibouti City on Saturday, September 19, at approximately 1 p.m. local time, and neither has been in contact or reachable since.
Reddy was not reporting on Djiboutian affairs when he went missing. He was staying at the Escale International Hotel in Djibouti City.
ICIJ does not yet know the circumstances behind Reddy’s sudden loss of contact.
The Committee to Protect Journalists said Sunday it is “deeply concerned” by reports that the pair can no longer be reached, and has called on Djiboutian authorities to urgently establish their whereabouts and confirm their safety.
ICIJ echoes that statement without reservation.
We are calling on the government of Djibouti to:
- Immediately clarify Reddy and Ismael’s whereabouts and confirm their well-being;
- Launch a prompt, transparent investigation into their disappearance;
- Keep their families, colleagues and employers fully and promptly informed.
Reddy is both a citizen of the U.K. and South Africa. ICIJ alerted both London and Pretoria shortly after the pair went missing.
Authorities in Djibouti have not responded so far to ICIJ requests for information.
Before joining ICIJ, Reddy was an investigative reporter at South Africa’s amaBhungane Centre for Investigative Journalism, known for his reporting on governance, corruption and regional affairs across the continent.
Journalists must be able to travel without fear of disappearance or obstruction.

Former Kremlin political prisoner Mykola Karpiuk killed at the front
Kyiv • UNN
Mykola Karpiuk was killed at the age of 62 in a Russian drone strike. He was a co-founder of UNA-UNSO and returned from Russian captivity in 2019.
At the front, former Kremlin political prisoner and one of the founders of UNA-UNSO Mykola Karpiuk was killed in a Russian drone strike: he was 62. The death was reported by another well-known UNSO member, Armed Forces of Ukraine serviceman Ihor Mazur, known by the call sign "Topol", reports UNN.
Details
As Mazur noted, Karpiuk was killed on the birthday of another well-known member of UNA-UNSO, Oleksandr Muzychko, better known as "Sashko Bilyi." He was killed in March 2014 while being detained by officers of the Sokol special unit of Ukraine's Interior Ministry.
Yesterday (September 19 — ed.), on Sashko "Bilyi's" birthday, Mykola Karpiuk was killed by an enemy drone. Two men from Rivne, both had been members of the UNA-UNSO Leadership since the 1990s
Who was Mykola Karpiuk
Mykola Karpiuk was one of the leaders of Ukraine's nationalist movement in the early 1990s. He stood at the origins of the Ukrainian National Assembly — Ukrainian People's Self-Defense (UNA-UNSO), as part of which he took part in hostilities in Transnistria (against Moldova — ed.) and Abkhazia (on Georgia's side — ed.).
He was also one of the leaders of UNA-UNSO and headed its Rivne branch. He actively participated in the "Ukraine without Kuchma" campaign (for which he served 4.5 years in prison), the Orange Revolution, and the Revolution of Dignity.
In March 2014, he was abducted by Russian special services and taken to the russian federation. He was charged with a completely fabricated allegation of supposedly participating in the First Russian-Chechen War of 1994–1996.
In 2016, he was sentenced to 22.5 years in prison. According to human rights activists, confessions were extracted from Karpiuk and another defendant, Stanislav Klykh, through brutal torture.
In September 2019, as part of a major prisoner exchange, Karpiuk returned to Ukraine.

Germany’s far right secures another win in key regional election, exit poll says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:11:44 UTC
01:11:44 KST

Merz vows to stay on as chancellor despite ‘disaster’ in another German regional vote
The embattled chancellor’s conservative party suffered its worst result in postwar German history as the far-right AfD won its second regional election in two weeks.
AfD party co-leader Tino Chrupalla reacts to preliminary results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state elections following the closure of polling stations on September 20, 2026 in Schwerin, Germany. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
BERLIN — Germany’s embattled Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his conservatives suffered a second major defeat to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in a regional vote Sunday — a result Merz conceded was a “disaster.”
But the chancellor moved to quickly quell a rising storm of speculation that he would move to step aside following the loss, which comes only two weeks after another historic defeat to the AfD in a regional contest. He appeared before cameras just minutes after the polls closed Sunday to say he would continue to push through his reform agenda and act as an anchor of stability in turbulent times.
“These reforms are the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism,” he said. “What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness, and patience. I will demonstrate these qualities as chairman of the CDU and, above all, as chancellor of our country.”
The AfD won around 38% of the vote in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — the second-best result in its history, just ahead of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) on 35%, according to preliminary results.
Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) suffered its worst result in a state or national election since the end of World War II, by the end of election night coming in at 4.9%, according to a preliminary count, just below the vote threshold required to make it into the state parliament.
The failure to meet that threshold deals an even more painful blow to the chancellor, who is already struggling to maintain support among his party’s rank and file.
Advertisement
AfD leaders hailed their victory — party national co-leader Tino Chrupalla called the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result a “sensation” — while also putting the pressure on a profoundly weakened Merz to step aside and abandon his party’s policy of maintaining a “firewall” around the far right.
“Friedrich Merz is the wrong chancellor for the CDU and is dragging the CDU down with him,” national co-leader Alice Weidel told German public television. “So the CDU must ask itself, above all else, does it want to continue with this chancellor and with these left-wing policies?”
Merz took the unusual step of convening CDU leaders at the party’s Berlin headquarters on Sunday night in an effort to rally their support ahead of what he knew would be another humiliating election defeat. Merz’s approval ratings are among the lowest ever recorded for a German chancellor at this point in their tenure, prompting internal CDU discussions about a possible change at the top—Kanzlertausch.
“Of course, the mood isn’t exactly lighthearted,” Ines Claus, a CDU politician who took part in the leadership meeting, told ARD. “If you ask me now whether one might prefer to just pull the covers over one’s head, well, that might be the case. But that’s not what responsibility is about; stability is what’s required now.”
Just 1% of voters — and 1% of CDU supporters — said Chancellor Merz had helped his party’s election performance in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, according to a poll by public broadcaster ZDF.
“We can’t sugarcoat the results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania,” Merz said after the polls closed Sunday. “It’s a disaster.”
The CDU also saw its support decline in a separate regional vote in Berlin, finishing second with around 19%, according to a preliminary count, behind the Left party, a far-left force which won 25.5% and is now poised to take over the capital’s mayoralty from Merz’s conservatives in coalition with center-left parties.
But as Germany’s export-oriented growth model continues to suffer amid increased competition from China and U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariff wars, German voters don’t appear to be giving him the benefit of the doubt.
The chancellor’s agenda includes raising the retirement age to shore up the pension system, cutting some health-insurance benefits to curb rising premiums and making it harder for workers to take sick leave in an effort to boost growth.
Many of those reforms impose clear costs on ordinary voters, giving the far right and far left ample opportunity to exploit public discontent.
Schwesig is now likely to lead a new coalition government in the state with a coalition of left-wing parties.
CDU leaders blamed Schwesig’s approach for effectively turning the election in her state into a two-party race that has greatly weakened Merz’s conservatives. “The CDU fought hard, but in the end, it was crushed in the escalating confrontation between the SPD and the AfD,” Merz said.
But Schwesig blamed Merz and the CDU for failing to connect with voters and was able to gain on the AfD late in the race in great part because she attacked Merz as out of touch with ordinary people and his reform drive as punishing some of the most vulnerable.
“The issue of the cost of living is a very significant one, and it’s important for the federal government to take a stand in favor of greater economic development to create jobs, but also to provide relief,” she told a public television broadcaster after the vote.
Still, trying to stabilize the situation, Philipp Amthor, a CDU politician from Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the chancellery’s federal-state affairs chief, said it was time to end the Kanzlertausch discussion.
“We have seen that what we have experienced over the past two weeks since the state election in Saxony-Anhalt has done more harm than good — namely, ongoing discussions about personnel that have completely overshadowed the discussion of the issues at hand,” he said.
“In that regard, it is right to put an end to these personnel discussions now and refocus on the issues.”

Transcript: Rep. Ro Khanna on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Sept. 20, 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20

Transcript: Rep. Ro Khanna on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Sept. 20, 2026
The following is the transcript of the interview with Rep. Ro Khanna, Democrat of California, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sept. 20, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We begin today with California Congressman Ro Khanna, who is the top Democrat on the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and he joins us from Fremont. Good morning to you, Congressman.
REPRESENTATIVE RO KHANNA: Good morning, Margaret.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So China and the U.S. are in an arms race. You've proposed this idea that Chinese AI firms should cooperate with American companies. You sent letters to DeepSeek, Alibaba, other firms, urging them to follow the lead of the American firms like OpenAI and Anthropic to slow the rate of AI advancement until society develops guardrails, as you put it. Have any of these Chinese firms responded to your proposal?
REP. RO KHANNA: They have not. Winning an AI war is like winning a nuclear war. It is catastrophic for civilization. And what we have asked is that they agree to some basic terms. Look, there are two dangers to AI: either the loss of control or misuse, and the Chinese firms have taken no actions on either of them.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, I'm looking at what the FBI, the NSA, and Homeland Security, their division CISA, they have all warned that China-based AI companies are targeting and copying American artificial intelligence at what they describe as an industrial scale. So, how can you ask competitors to collaborate? Isn't it inherently at odds if they're stealing technology?
REP. RO KHANNA: Well, they're right that they are engaging in distillation. Basically, they are copying American models. That's one reason, frankly, to regulate American models because they're copying them. Some of the safeguards would protect the world, but at the same time, we also need an international agreement with Xi Jinping to have basic standards. That should include international monitoring, it should include checks through the data centers where you can tell whether a model is being used for inference or training, and it should use enforceable and verifiable tools. Now, obviously, you can't just trust the Chinese, but like any agreement, like an arms control agreement, as Reagan said, you need to trust and verify. And the world has done this before. There's no reason we can't do it when it comes to AI.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, I'm looking at Bloomberg's figures. They report China is preparing to spend about $300 billion over the next five years to build data centers across that country, which will be operated by state-owned firms. As you know, there's really no wall between the state and industry in China. So, when you are acknowledging they commit human rights abuses and their AI firms help the state to commit those abuses, aren't you asking the CEOs to- to do something that's at odds with what Xi Jinping is- is seeking to do?
REP. RO KHANNA: Well, the first ask is of Trump and Xi Jinping to come up with an international agreement, and two of the core principles should be one: banning any self-improving AI, recursive self-improving AI. That's basically AI that continues to improve itself, and where we could lose control. The second is to have safeguards so that AI can't be misused by people for biological nuclear weapons. The letters to the Chinese companies were simply seeking information about what they're doing. It wasn't intended as a solution. What it was intended to do was highlight the need for the Chinese government and the U.S. government to come to an agreement, and that needs to be the first agenda item on the Trump-Xi Jinping summit.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, we know it's going to come up. We just don't know the details of exactly what it is the U.S. is proposing at all. We're going to watch for that in this next week-long set of meetings with China. You sit on the Armed Services Committee. Yesterday, President Trump posted on social media that his plan is to create an AI czar and form the "AI Force, much like I did the Space Force." I'm not exactly sure where he's going with that, but you yourself have called for a new government agency to be set up to deal with AI. So you both seem to agree that the existing infrastructure isn't enough. Why can't you just have Cyber Command handle all of this? What does the executive branch or Congress actually have to do?
REP. RO KHANNA: Well, we need to set up an AI agency like the FDA. I mean, I don't know what Trump- President Trump's vision is. I don't know if he's using AI in an offensive capability, which would give me a lot of pause, especially because when you have things like the shooting of the Iranian school, where you had AI information basically feed something into a- into a general, and then you had pro-forma sign off. That gives me concern. What I'm talking about is what Geoffrey Hinton, the godfather of AI, has said, which is that this can be regulated like we regulate nuclear energy, electricity, aviation, have independent technical experts make sure AI is safe. And Margaret, one of the things that really annoys me is when you have these tech CEOs out there saying, "Oh, this is too complicated. People in Washington don't understand this." Give me a break. We have regulated very complex things. We know we can appoint independent, smart people from universities. This is not complicated. We need to have an independent federal agency.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, respectfully, Congressman, Congress hasn't regulated a lot of things or come forward with much legislation of late. But to put that aside, I take your broader point. I want to ask you about another important topic at this meeting with Xi Jinping and President Trump, and that is the fate of Americans who do business or travel to China. Secretary Rubio has designated 2 U.S. citizens as wrongfully detained by China, and one of them is your constituent, scholar Min Zin. He has been held for 100 days now by the Ministry of State Security without access to a lawyer, he has no court date, and I spoke with his wife on Friday. Take a listen.
[SOUND ON TAPE]
SYLVIA ZIN: He's been charged with endangering national security, and that's all we know.
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's a big charge.
SYLVIA ZIN: It's a huge charge. It's a, you know my daughter looked it up, and she, I think that really freaked her out. That's when she was like, "What is going to happen to Dad?" You know, and yeah, it's- it's a shock, right? I mean, he's a scholar, he's an academic, he's not a spy.
MARGARET BRENNAN: What did you think when the U.S. government explained to you this charge?
SYLVIA ZIN: That was what I asked. Like, what does that mean? You know, and they like we don't have more information. This is all we've been told.
MARGARET BRENNAN: When the U.S. government says that the safety of Americans is their highest priority, do you believe that?
SYLVIA ZIN: Well, President has brought home over 100 wrongfully detained Americans home, right? So, I'm hoping my husband is the next one.
[END SOUND ON TAPE]
MARGARET BRENNAN: Now, this scholar was disappeared shortly after he landed to a conference he was invited to. A lot of Americans go to China to conduct business. What are you and others in the government doing to help those who are detained when they're doing work there?
REP. RO KHANNA: Well, it's appalling, and while I have my disagreements with Secretary Rubio, in this I stand in complete solidarity with him, as does the China Committee. We cannot have American citizens or scholars in America be detained or disappeared because of what they say. And when I was in China about a year ago, we raised this issue not on this specific case, but we had heard cases of Chinese students in the United States who were not being allowed to continue because they may have engaged in some protest or had an errant social media tweet. We had heard cases of people who were detained, business leaders or people doing business because they disagreed with the Chinese government, and that is unacceptable to the United States. And then, of course, there's the whole situation with the Uyghurs. We just had a hearing last week on the Uyghurs situation, extraordinary human rights abuses, and we need that to be front and center in this meeting as well.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Congressman Khanna, we thank you for your time today.

UN chief calls for global financial reform, permanent Security Council seats for Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:03:46 UTC
01:03:46 KST

Yasin Gungor
20 September 2026•Update: 20 September 2026
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Sunday called for sweeping reforms to global governance structures, urging permanent African representation on the UN Security Council and an overhaul of multilateral financial institutions.
"We must reform the international financial architecture that was created by the rich for the rich, and we must make it more representative of the needs of developing countries, especially in Africa," Guterres told attendees at the Unstoppable Africa 2026 forum, held on the margins of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York.
The UN chief emphasized that the continent was a "double victim of colonialism," explaining that historic subjugation prevented African nations from having a seat at the table when post-World War II international institutions were established.
Guterres argued that both the UN Security Council and international financial institutions fail to reflect Africa's demographic presence and interests, asserting that the continent must be granted permanent seats to participate directly in global decision-making.
Addressing economic transformation, Guterres noted that global markets are undergoing a fundamental structural transition from simply doing business in Africa to "doing business with Africa."
Despite global disruptions stemming from wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, Guterres said Africa's economy expanded 4.4% last year, with trade under the African Continental Free Trade Area on track to reach $230 billion this year, creating an opportunity to retain economic value domestically rather than relying on raw exports.
Critical minerals, renewable transition
Turning to natural resources, Guterres warned against ongoing exploitation amid intensifying geopolitical competition. "We must ensure that Africa's vast natural resources, particularly critical minerals, create local value and decent jobs, rather than simply being shipped overseas."
He highlighted significant advances in renewable energy and digital technology across the continent, pointing to Kenya generating more than 90% of its electricity from renewable sources, Morocco advancing plans for a submarine power cable to Europe, Tunisia competing internationally in artificial intelligence, and Rwanda developing nationwide drone logistics.
Guterres urged multilateral development banks to scale up concessional lending, match climate pledges with concrete adaptation financing, and direct capital to female entrepreneurs, who represent more than half of the continent's business owners.
Linking economic progress to sustainable peace, the UN chief praised African-led mediation efforts in regional conflicts, including in Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, reiterating that durable development cannot exist without political stability.

Women show greater willingness to interact with creative individuals experiencing schizophrenia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:00:27 UTC
01:00:27 KST

A study published in the EvoS Journal: Evolutionary Studies and Higher Education presented results of an online experiment that asked participants how much they would like to interact with a social media profile of a creative individual who also suffers from schizophrenia. Results showed that women were more interested in such interactions than men, particularly in the condition when the creative expression of the target person was unsuccessful. When it was successful, there were no differences between men and women.
Mental health stigma refers to negative stereotypes and prejudice directed toward people with mental health conditions. Individuals with mental illness are often perceived as dangerous, unpredictable, weak, or socially incompetent, even when these assumptions are unsupported. Such stigma can contribute to social rejection, difficulties in employment and relationships, and reluctance to seek professional help. It can also be internalized by affected individuals, reducing self-esteem and worsening social and psychological outcomes.
That said, psychological disorders often do involve characteristics that interfere with everyday functioning. On the other hand, there tend to also be positive traits associated with mental health conditions. From an evolutionary perspective, genetic properties that predispose individuals to certain mental health conditions persist in the population precisely because they come in combinations of traits that can sometimes provide situational advantages, particularly if the mental health condition manifests in milder, subclinical forms.
Anxiety, for example, may heighten vigilance toward threats, while social withdrawal may sometimes reduce exposure to harmful or overwhelming social situations. Psychotic traits (such as delusional thinking or disorganized behaviors) are associated with substantial cognitive difficulties and a strong social stigma, but are also linked to creativity, novel thinking, and heightened emotional sensitivity.
Lead author A. Hicks and colleagues wanted to explore how much the potential benefits of creativity protect individuals with psychotic traits from mental illness stigma. More specifically, they wanted to know how much learning that an individual is successful in creative work and/or that they suffer from schizophrenia would affect participants’ willingness to interact with such a person.
They conducted an online study. Participants were 308 individuals recruited through Prolific Academic. Of these, 167 were women. Their average age was 35 years. Study authors paid them $1.50 for their participation in the study.
Participants viewed a hypothetical Facebook post and were tasked to evaluate the person presented in the post. The posts differed in two ways: whether the person in the post spoke about suffering from schizophrenia or not, and whether the person was successful in their creative work or not (i.e., whether a poem they wrote was accepted for publication or not).
This was done in the form of a post to a writers group made by a person named Taylor Ross. In the post, Taylor Ross says that they want to give a life update and that they are working on their poetry. They also note (depending on the condition) that they are doing well or that they are struggling with schizophrenia, and that one of their poems was published or that it was denied publication. The study specifically utilized a gender-neutral silhouette for the profile picture to prevent gender bias from influencing the results.
Participants rated how much they would like to interact with Taylor Ross by liking or commenting on their post, considering them as a friend, or as a romantic partner. They also completed an assessment of stereotype endorsement by rating how much an individual with schizophrenia differs (in their view) from the general population on 11 positive and 11 negative traits.
Results indicated that women showed a greater interest in interacting with the target (Taylor Ross) than men, regardless of the study condition. Whether Taylor Ross was presented as successful in publishing the poem or not did not have an effect on how much participants wanted to interact with them overall.
When study authors looked only at the variant where Taylor Ross suffered from schizophrenia and was not successful in having their poem published, women showed a greater desire to interact with them than men. In the condition when Taylor Ross was successful, men and women did not differ in their desire to interact.
The average desire to interact with Taylor Ross was closer to the negative pole of the scale (not wanting to interact). Participants who reported having friends with mental illness were more interested in interacting with the Taylor Ross version that was creatively successful and not suffering from schizophrenia, than with the version that was both not successful and not suffering from schizophrenia.
The study contributes to scientific knowledge about the social desirability of people with mental health conditions. However, it should be noted that participants evaluated the target individual (Taylor Ross) only based on a short post, without any background information. This is unlike how people make social judgments in most real-world situations. Results of studies providing a more comprehensive set of information about an individual may differ.
The paper, “Salience of the Benefits of Psychotic Traits Buffers Against Mental Illness Stigma,” was authored by A. Hicks, D. F. Sacco, K. N. Boykin, O. Olabegi, Z. Buckner, and M. Brown.

Why have US prosecutors labelled China’s Huawei a criminal enterprise?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:57:48 UTC
00:57:48 KST

Why have US prosecutors labelled China’s Huawei a criminal enterprise?
Huawei faces a landmark US trial, accused of theft, fraud and sanctions violations in a high-stakes legal battle.
Chinese technology giant Huawei is facing a landmark criminal trial in the United States amid Washington’s long-running tech rivalry with Beijing.
The trial began in federal court in Brooklyn, New York, on September 9, with US prosecutors portraying Huawei as a criminal enterprise that spent two decades stealing technology from US companies, deceiving banks and circumventing sanctions on Iran.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump and Xi: The history of encounters between two superpower leaders
- list 2 of 3How Chinese, Iranian companies profit in Russia-occupied Ukrainian regions
- list 3 of 3China’s secret weapon in AI race with US? Lots of cheap energy
Huawei has pleaded not guilty and says the US government is attempting to turn ordinary business disputes and the actions of individual employees into evidence of a company-wide conspiracy.
The trial is expected to last about three months and overlaps with Chinese President Xi Jinping’s September 23-25 visit to Washington, where trade, artificial intelligence, tariffs and access to critical technologies are likely to be on the agenda.
Here is what you need to know:
What are the allegations against Huawei?
US prosecutors have accused the company of racketeering, money laundering, bank and wire fraud, sanctions violations, obstruction and conspiring to steal trade secrets from five US technology companies.
Prosecutors say the alleged wrongdoing stretched from about 1999 to 2020.
“Theft, lies, cover-up,” Justice Department lawyer Taylor Stout said in his opening remarks.
Prosecutors allege Huawei stole technology, including internet-router source code from Cisco and a robotic arm used by T-Mobile to test phones.
They also accuse Huawei of concealing the nature of its operations in Iran to move US dollars through the financial system despite US sanctions.
The government also alleges that Huawei supplied equipment that could help Iranian authorities monitor protesters during demonstrations in 2009.
How has Huawei responded?
Huawei, a major manufacturer of telecommunications equipment, denies any wrongdoing.
The tech giant’s lawyer Brian Heberlig told jurors the case was about “competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct.”
Heberlig accused prosecutors of “cherry-picking isolated events” to construct a conspiracy that did not exist. Huawei’s defence says some incidents involved individual employees whose actions were dealt with internally, rather than reflecting company policy.
He told jurors that prosecutors will describe routine activities by global tech companies “but will twist those ordinary activities to try to make them look criminal”.
Huawei separately described the broader prosecution as an attempt to undermine its competitiveness, saying the US government’s “overarching narrative is demonstrably false” and that it had “the utmost respect for intellectual property”.
The case originated during Donald Trump’s first presidency. His administration placed Huawei on a US trade blacklist in 2019 and pushed allies to exclude the company from 5G networks, arguing its equipment could present national security and espionage risks.
Huawei has repeatedly denied that its technology is used for spying.
What has China’s response been?
Beijing has strongly criticised the prosecution, which has come weeks ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US.
On Thursday, a Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson said “the Chinese government firmly opposes the US side’s suppression and containment of Chinese enterprises”, when asked about the case and the American prosecutor’s “criminal enterprise” description.
China “firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests”, the spokesperson said at a regular news conference.
What is Huawei, and has the tech giant faced investigations before?
Huawei is one of the world’s largest telecommunications equipment manufacturers. It also produces smartphones and has become increasingly important to China’s semiconductor and AI industries.
Its activities have drawn scrutiny well beyond the current US trial.
Belgian prosecutors launched an investigation in 2025 into suspected bribery involving the European Parliament allegedly for Huawei’s benefit.
The European Parliament subsequently suspended access for Huawei lobbyists. Huawei said it had “zero-tolerance” for corruption and would cooperate with authorities.
Huawei chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou made worldwide headlines in 2018 when she was arrested on a US warrant after landing in Vancouver, straining both US-China and China-Canada relations.
The warrant was filed after a sealed indictment accused her and the company of bank fraud for misleading HSBC and other banks about Huawei’s business in Iran.
She returned to China in 2021 under a deferred prosecution agreement, and the charges against her were later dismissed.
Admissions Meng made as part of that agreement can, however, be presented as evidence in Huawei’s current trial after a US judge ruled them admissible in June.
Are these issues related to the US-China trade war?
They are legally separate but form part of a much wider economic and technological competition between Washington and Beijing.
Huawei became one of the most prominent targets of US restrictions during Trump’s first term.
Since then, the rivalry has expanded from telecommunications and 5G into semiconductors and AI, with Washington restricting China’s access to advanced US chips and chipmaking technology.
Last week, Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, warned that a “Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world” and urged Washington to maintain restrictions on cutting-edge AI tech. He also called for action against alleged “distillation” of US models by Chinese AI laboratories.
China’s Foreign Ministry on September 14 accused the US tech giant of “fearmongering”.
“Fomenting various threats, engaging in confrontation and malicious competition will only disrupt the process of global governance of artificial intelligence and is not in the interests of any party,” said ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun.
The state-backed Global Times newspaper went further, describing Amodei’s proposal as a “Cold War playbook” whose real purpose was to curb Chinese AI development and preserve US technological dominance.
China and the US were engaged in a tit-for-tat tariff war at the beginning of Trump’s presidency in 2025. The trade war ended in a truce, but the world’s two largest economies have failed to strike a trade deal.
Beijing, meanwhile, has used its dominance of critical minerals as leverage and accelerated efforts to build domestic alternatives to American technology.
Currently, China controls most of the world’s rare earth minerals, including metals that are necessary for the manufacture of many technological items, from smartphones to fighter jets. The world’s second-largest economy has 60 percent of these minerals and processes 90 percent of the world’s supply.
In October, Beijing announced plans to require foreign companies to obtain permission to export Chinese rare earth equipment or material.
This meant companies anywhere in the world would need a licence to export rare earth magnets and certain semiconductor materials that contain even trace amounts of minerals sourced from China or produced using Chinese technology.
China’s Ministry of Commerce said its export controls on rare earths, which Trump had labelled “surprising” and “very hostile”, were introduced in response to a series of US measures.

Traditional Chinese medicine supports China's crewed space missions: experts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
23:54:27 CST
00:54:27 KST

TIANJIN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has played a significant role in supporting China's crewed space missions over the past decade and could offer comprehensive health protection for astronauts in the future, experts said at an aerospace medical engineering conference in Tianjin Municipality in north China.
The conference, held from Saturday to Sunday, brought together experts and scholars from fields including aerospace medicine, human factors engineering and life sciences to discuss the medical engineering challenges of future deep space exploration.
Zhang Boli, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering and a renowned TCM master, said the unique conditions of spaceflight -- where astronauts face altered breathing, digestion and mobility in microgravity -- make TCM's holistic approach particularly well-suited for maintaining crew health.
"TCM uses a comprehensive approach to regulate the body, such as adjusting qi, or vital energy, and blood imbalances with herbal medicine and using acupuncture to improve unstable heart rates, indigestion and poor sleep," Zhang said.
Wu Bin, an expert at the Astronaut Center of China, highlighted specific applications of TCM in space. Acupuncture can help regulate sleep and prevent muscle atrophy, while Chinese patent medicines can improve cardiovascular function and help astronauts adapt to microgravity.
"In the future, we will continue to use the national space laboratory as a unique platform to conduct TCM research -- not only to address health protection for low-Earth orbit flights, but also to seek TCM technologies and methods for medical challenges in crewed deep space exploration," Wu said.
Astronaut Zhang Lu, who has flown on both the Shenzhou-15 and Shenzhou-21 missions, said TCM has been closely linked to mission success. During the Shenzhou-21 mission, which lasted nearly seven months in orbit, the crew used TCM equipment to stimulate nerves and muscles in the mid-to-late stages of flight to counter muscle atrophy, he said.
The space station is stocked with TCM medicines, including the space heart-nourishing pills and functional drinks that help with radiation protection and immune support, Zhang Lu added.
Zhang Boli noted that research shows TCM approaches can also counter orthostatic intolerance, cardiovascular dysfunction and space motion sickness, enriching the toolkit for astronaut health protection from physical and mental conditioning to disease prevention.
China's space station, Tiangong, which means Heavenly Palace, has now entered an era of long-term human habitation. One member of the Shenzhou-23 crew will conduct a one-year in-orbit stay, while the country's 2030 crewed moon landing mission is advancing steadily. ■

Thousands march in France against ‘licence to kill’ draft law
PARIS – Thousands of people marched in Paris and other French cities on Sept 20 against a proposed law on the legitimate use of violence that critics say would be a “licence to kill” for police and gendarmes.
In July, deputies in the National Assembly approved the Bill, which says that any law-enforcement official who uses force is assumed to have acted legally in using their weapon. It now faces a vote in the Senate.
Politicians, rights groups and other activists joined others marching at the protest, among them Mathilde Panot of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party.
“The police kill already,” Panot told the crowd, calling for the Bill to be voted down in the Senate.
“In the Republic, there can be no organised police impunity,” she said. “In the Republic, there cannot be a category of citizens who have the right of life or death over other citizens.”
Amal Bentousi, the sister of Amine, a robber who was shot in the back by police in an incident in 2012 at Seine-Saint-Denis, just north of Paris, was among the marchers.
What she described as a “licence to execute” was intended to “reverse the burden of proof” in such incidents, she said.
Amnesty International, France’s magistrates’ union and the country’s League of Human Rights also took part in the protest.
Scores of other marches to protest against the Bill were organised in cities around France over the weekend.
A petition against the Bill on the National Assembly website gathered 730,000 signatures, but the Parliament’s law committee dismissed it in July.
Defenders of the Bill say it would avoid law enforcement officers automatically coming under suspicion or being detained when using armed force.
But in the Marseille protest, Cedric Picard, of Amnesty International, said that “we are afraid that police violence would only grow with this law”.
“In a country where police abuse is among the worst, this law risks worsening the situation,” said one protester, a high school student who gave his first name as Hugo.
On Sept 19, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez called on police to be “particularly vigilant” during the protests, fearing incidents.
In the city of Rennes, officials said eight people were arrested and three police officers injured after projectiles were thrown at them. AFP

Trump says monumental arch in Washington, DC will also be military complex
Plans for the arch had been met with opposition along with other projects by the US president to reshape capital city.
A planned “triumphal arch” near some of the most iconic landmarks in Washington, DC, will also be a military complex used to store drones and other military equipment, according to United States President Donald Trump.
The changes were made at the request of the military and for “National Security purposes,” Trump posted on his social media platform on Sunday.

list of 3 items

- list 2 of 3Trump’s threats to demolish Kennedy Center sparks protest

The project would now be used to “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage,” Trump said. “There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World.”
Trump first proposed building a monumental arch last year to mark 250 years of US independence, saying it would be akin to other famed arches like the Arc de Triomphe built in Paris after World War Two, but “the biggest one of all”.
On Sunday, the US president did not provide details on the new design, which was previously planned to be a lofty 76-metre-high (250-foot) arch that would tower above many other landmarks in the capital. By law, the height of new construction in the city is generally restricted.
Trump’s arch project has faced criticism ever since then for its size and location, and for potentially obscuring views of the Arlington National Cemetery, the country’s famed resting place for war veterans.
In February, three veterans of the Vietnam War filed a lawsuit against the plan, saying it would block the view between the cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial, erected to honour the US president who oversaw the Civil War. The view from the monument, the veterans said in a court filing, was “carefully designed to symbolise the unification of the country after the Civil War and the strength of a united nation”. Any major monument around the capital, the lawsuit also argued, would need approval from the US Congress. A judge ordered the Trump administration to provide notice of any work on the monument, but courts have not ruled on the larger challenge yet.
“The President’s belated efforts to manufacture a national security justification for this project do nothing to cure its fundamental illegality,” Nicolas Sansone, one of the attorneys representing the litigants, said Sunday. “Congress has not authorized the arch and unless and until Congress does so, the project should not be permitted to move forward.”
The Trump-appointed US Commission of Fine Arts, a key agency involved in the project, approved a design in April that featured statues of golden lions at the base of the arch, and golden eagles and a winged angel atop a baroque arch resembling the one in Paris.
The Federal Aviation Administration said last week the arch would not be a hazard to the nearby Reagan Washington National Airport, but would need a warning beacon on top.
Democratic Congressman Don Beyer of Virginia, who represents the area, noted a drone launching facility there would be directly in the flight landing path of the airport, which he called “a stupid, dangerous, and unworkable idea,” in a post on X. “Trump clearly expects to lose a lawsuit and therefore wants to set up a pretext to argue that the arch is tied to national security. Which is obviously idiotic.”
The monumental arch is one of several Trump projects in the capital to receive public pushback.
On Saturday, thousands rallied, and some protesters formed a human chain around the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, the landmark along the Potomac River waterfront built to honour the 35th US President John F Kennedy. Trump has threatened to demolish the venue if he is not allowed to add his name to it, saying that is the only way to ensure it gets enough funding to survive.
Trump is also overseeing a $400m controversial project at the White House, where the East Wing of the complex was demolished to make way for an 8,400sq m (90,000sq ft) ballroom with an impenetrable underground bunker. Historic preservation groups filed a lawsuit to stop that project, but last month the US Supreme Court allowed construction to continue.
Like the triumphal arch, Trump has also justified the need for the new ballroom on national security grounds and has referred to it as a “military complex”.

====================================================================================================

The Central Paradox of Stoicism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:07:50 UTC
00:07:50 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
Throughout our lives we live by the rubric of principles we’ve absorbed, inherited, or deliberately embraced. We consider these ideas foundational. We follow their direction in our plans and our actions, they guide us through our ups and downs.
But occasionally these foundational ideas come to a point where they collide. This leaves us flummoxed — do we disregard one idea and follow another? Do we reconsider all our beliefs altogether? It can lead to private crisis.
The central paradox within Stoicism is one that even Stoics struggle with. It’s ignored for the most part in modern Stoic literature. Embedded within the ancient Stoic texts, there’s a black hole that threatens to break Stoicism’s internal coherence.
On the one hand, we possess a faculty of choice. It is so fundamental that it cannot be touched by circumstance or coercion. And yet, there is another idea within Stoicism, an idea that is no less insistent and forceful. When somebody commits a wrong, they are not to blame. The Stoics tell us not to punish them.
The first idea is what Stoics call prohairesis, we can translate this into modern English as “will”. It is in our power to judge, to assent to the impressions that flood through our consciousness, and to set actions in motion with our intentions.
These three faculties are ours alone, and, according to Epictetus, this tripartite structure is both the core of our being and where our absolute freedom lies. You can choose. You have moral agency. Always. This is a central force in Stoic thinking.
The second idea is that moral evil has no essence. Just as darkness is absence of light, and error is the absence of knowledge, moral evil is simply a mistake.
Everybody wants what is beneficial to them, but they become confused about what exactly is beneficial. This is ultimately an idea the Stoics inherited from Socrates. For Socrates there is no human good and evil, there is wisdom and ignorance. The good is the lodestar for all of us. Those who commit evils are simply mistaken about what is good.
It’s hard to think of good and evil in this way because for two thousand years, Western thinking has largely defined good and evil as two sides of a cosmic conflict manned by human souls.
In the Socratic view, evil is simply the absence of good, not a self-standing existing thing with an essence.
Marcus even quotes Socrates in Book 7 of the Meditations:
“‘No soul’, [Socrates] said, ‘is willingly deprived of the truth’; and the same applies to justice too, and temperance, and benevolence, and everything of the kind. It is most necessary that you should constantly keep this in mind, for you will then be gentler towards everyone.”
This seems strange — people are, after all, cruel, deceitful, lazy and so on. But somebody being deceitful to get a promotion, for example, is taking their own well-being to be more important to them than the well-being of the community.
If that person understood that the well-being of the community is paramount to the good of everybody — including themselves, and that fulfilling self-centered desires doesn’t make you truly happy, then they wouldn’t use deceit to get a promotion.
In the Discourses of Epictetus, this is made clear:
“Philosophers say that people are all guided by a single standard […] If all this is true, then what grounds do we have for being angry with anyone? We use labels like ‘thief’ and ‘robber’ in connection with them, but what do those words mean? They merely signify that people are confused about what is good and what is bad. So should we be angry with them, or should we pity them instead?” (Discourses 1.18)
Marcus repeats the idea at the start of his famous first paragraph of Book 2 of his Meditations.
“Say to yourself at the start of the day, I shall meet with meddling, ungrateful, violent, treacherous, envious, and unsociable people. They are subject to all these defects because they have no knowledge of good and bad”. (Meditations 2.1)
Those people, Marcus implies, are innocent because their thought is defective. In the Gregory Hays translation, the middle part is rendered as, “They are like this because they can’t tell good from evil” (My emphasis).
So we have the collision of two ideas:
- 
You are in absolute control of your judgements, your desires, and your intentions.
- 
You are ignorant when you commit a wrong.
It’s easy to see the questions that would arise from this paradox.
If somebody has full control over their beliefs, desires, and intentions, then how could they not be responsible for a crime they commit? If virtue is a matter of dispelling ignorance, then doesn’t luck play a role in becoming virtuous? If you’re ignorant, how can you climb out of ignorance, if your ignorance is what pulls you away from virtue?
How do we unravel this knot? How do we reconcile those two ideas? How can a person possess full control over their will, and yet be blind to what is good? How can you be wholly responsible for your choices and yet at the same time be blameless for your actions?
How We Solve a Paradox
We’re trapped between two seemingly impossible positions. Either the sinner had the power to choose correctly and failed to make use of it — and therefore deserves condemnation — or they were unable to know the difference between good and evil, which robs them of the agency — the will / prohairesis — that Stoicism takes as real.
Condemning evil in other people is in itself evil in the Stoic view of the world. Theft, violence, and insults affect only what the Stoics call “indifferents” — the externals of our property, our bodies, and our reputation — things that are neither good nor bad in themselves. We have no moral right, as far as Epictetus was concerned, to be displeased with these transgressions, let alone punish them. He wrote, “As long as you honour material things, direct your anger at yourself rather than the thief or adulterer.” (Discourses 1.18).
Epictetus is suggesting that while we cannot blame others for moral failings, we can blame ourselves. It’s clear in his own words that self-directed condemnation is permissible.
We can therefore say that Stoicism isn’t a moral system for the world — it’s a moral system for you.
The focus is inward, and the Stoic must be always watchful of moral lapses and errors that arise from misunderstanding their place in the Cosmos, and what is good in respect to that.
Other people’s ignorance may impinge on our lives, but we must handle those wrongdoings as we’d handle other externals such as natural and social evils like sickness, injury, and misfortune: with the Stoic “indifference”, choosing to see them as neither good nor bad, since only our own actions in response to them can be good or bad.
It is not incumbent on you to judge others; it’s incumbent on you to set an example to others, and to teach those who are willing to learn.
But if good is a matter of knowledge, how do we know that we’ve correctly identified the good?
Epictetus explains in the Enchiridion that “just as targets are not set up in order to be missed, so neither does the nature of evil exists in the world.” (27)
This metaphor can be interpreted as either relating to cosmology or the human condition. In the cosmological sense, Epictetus could be saying that we live in a providential universe that’s oriented toward the good. When we act badly, when we fail to be morally excellent, we “miss” the goals intended for us.
This reading may well be the one that Epictetus intended, but we can read it in another, more secular, sense that is just as compelling. We could say that all life aspires to what is good for it, and avoids what is bad.
Natural targets such as abundance, the greater good, love, and happiness, are “set up” within all of us. We strive and aim for what is good, and we miss when we misunderstand the good.
Against this background, we can see that agency and blamelessness are not in tension. The fault at stake here is a correctable error of understanding.
We all aspire to the good, but an insufficient understanding of what good is leads to moral evil. If I were to think that my own gratification at the cost of somebody else’s well-being were a good, I would simply be wrong about what is good — I’d be deficient in my understanding of the good. I’d miss the target set up for me.
But the targets for good are supplied by nature. They are enduringly there as surely as the ground beneath our feet. Nature has given us reason, and guides us with happiness, contentment, compassion, and love. We err from good, but it insistently waits for us.
Thank you for reading.

Sudan gold mine collapse kills 10, injures 21, survivors say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:07:31 UTC
00:07:31 KST

Breadcrumb
Sudan gold mine collapse kills 10, injures 21, survivors reveal
A gold mine collapsed in northern Sudan, killing at least 10 people and injuring 21 others, two survivors told AFP on Sunday after overnight rescue efforts.
Since war erupted in April 2023 between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the war efforts of both sides have been largely funded by the country's billion-dollar gold trade, in addition to foreign backers.
Shafts of the Awny mining area near Sudan's border with Egypt collapsed on Saturday.
By Sunday morning, "10 bodies had been recovered, and 21 injured miners pulled out", said one of the survivors who was working at the mine when it collapsed, requesting anonymity for security reasons.
Another survivor, also requesting anonymity, told AFP the rescue operation was "being carried out by the miners themselves" with little equipment available.
More miners were feared dead under the rubble, and survivors said the search for the missing was ongoing.
Many young Sudanese have joined a dangerous gold rush, working in unregulated mines with their hands and rudimentary tools for meagre daily wages.
They face chemical poisoning and regular mine collapses.
Last week, at least 82 people were killed and dozens injured in a collapse in the southern Kordofan region.
Artisanal and small-scale mining, which takes place in unofficial zones or decommissioned mines, accounts for most of the gold extracted in Sudan.
According to Sudanese officials and mining industry sources, nearly all of the gold produced by both sides of the war flows to the United Arab Emirates, which denies reports that it arms the RSF.
Even before the war pushed nearly 20 million Sudanese into severe hunger, artisanal mining employed more than two million people, according to industry figures.
Africa's third-largest country is one of the continent's top gold producers, and recorded a "five-year high" of 70 tonnes of production last year, the government said.
But officials say most of the gold is smuggled across Sudan's borders, including through Chad, South Sudan and Egypt before reaching the UAE, the world's second-largest gold exporter.

Xinhua Headlines: China-Africa cooperation in vocational education builds skills, opens opportunities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
22:58:22 CST
23:58:22 KST

* The skills that carried African competitors to skills competitions like the World Vocational College Skills Competition are among the everyday subjects in classrooms that China and Africa run together. For some, success in competition has opened the door to employment.
* Young Africans across the continent are gaining practical skills as China-Africa cooperation in vocational education continues to grow. For many, mastering a skill is ultimately about finding a job, or even starting a business. The longer game is not training one class of students, but enabling African schools to train their own.
by Liu Jie and Lin Jing
WINDHOEK, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- In a workshop in Ongwediva, northern Namibia, fabric rustles as Wilhemina Amadhila measures, cuts and stitches.
"Each stitch comes together to form a stunning outfit," said the 22-year-old woman who will take the craft to the 48th WorldSkills Competition to be held on Sept. 22-27 in Shanghai, China.
Amadhila and 16 other young Namibians will compete in different categories of the competition. Besides Namibia, other African countries such as Kenya, Egypt, South Africa and Morocco are also taking part in the contest to showcase their technical and vocational skills.
This is not the first time African competitors have taken part in skills competitions in China. Their active participation offers a glimpse of growing China-Africa cooperation in vocational education, which has helped endow many Africans with practical skills and opportunities.
LEARNING THROUGH PRACTICE
At the 2025 World Vocational College Skills Competition held in north China's Tianjin, Angolan student Massak Ventura Noquena Eduardo took silver on the strength of industrial robotics and automated production-line skills learned from Chinese teachers. "I hope to apply what I have learned to Angola's industrialization," he said.
The skills that carried him to the podium are among the everyday subjects in classrooms that China and Africa run together. At the Angola-China Institute of Technology, students study mechatronics, industrial robotics and automation.
Guo Xiaoyu, a teacher from Baotou Vocational and Technical College in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, remembers students who were at first hesitant to even use a multimeter or an oscilloscope.
"Vocational education cannot be based on theory alone. Students have to do things with their own hands," Guo said. After a semester of practice in circuit assembly and fault diagnosis, more than 90 percent of them met the required standard.
At Ethiopia's Holeta Polytechnic College, Chinese instructor Ma Yujie demonstrated surgical suturing as animal science students gathered around the table, taking turns practicing on training pads.
"We are now participating in practical demonstrations," Lemi Abera, 22, said. "With our Chinese instructors linking classroom concepts to practical animal health practices."
Ma is one of 20 Chinese teachers working at six vocational colleges across Ethiopia. "The students really cherish the opportunities to practice on training models, to the extent that some are willing to spend extra time in the laboratory after class," she said.
In Cameroon, the classroom has moved onto the construction site.
In early August, China First Highway Engineering Co., Ltd. teamed up with Cameroon's Ministry of Higher Education and the National Advanced School of Public Works to run the country's first certification course for surveyors.
Cameroon's Minister of Higher Education Jacques Fame Ndongo said the program turns construction sites into "open-air classrooms" and builds a direct bridge between universities and major projects.
This cooperation is not just about building roads; it is about training people, and about the future of Cameroon's workforce, the minister added.
According to an action plan released at the 2024 Beijing Summit of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, China will continue vocational education with Africa, build with African countries schools of engineering technology, set up or upgrade 10 Luban Workshops, and offer 60,000 training opportunities aimed chiefly at African women and youth.
China has established 17 Luban Workshops in 15 African countries and trained tens of thousands of professionals.
FROM SKILLS TO LIVELIHOODS
For many young Africans, mastering a skill is ultimately about finding a job, or even starting a business.
At the end of 2025, 30 Rwandan students came home from a year of advanced training at Jinhua University of Vocational Technology in east China's Zhejiang Province.
Aimable Tuyishime, a 23-year-old e-commerce graduate who studied logistics, warehouse management and data analysis there, is now building an online shopping platform for Rwandan consumers.
"This is the right time to put all the skills and experience I gained into practice," he said.
In Tanzania, the Kilimanjaro Institute of Technology and Management launched a Chinese culinary program early this year, combining video lessons from chefs in China with practice in local kitchens.
"These are skills that make you different, and I can even start my own restaurant one day," said hospitality student Ruth Washima Seni.
For some, success in competition has opened the door to employment. At last year's Namibian national skills contest, the gold medalists in cooking and restaurant service also won three-month apprenticeships with a local hospitality group.
SEEDS THAT STAY
The longer game is not training one class of students, but enabling African schools to train their own.
In Cote d'Ivoire, seven modern vocational schools built by Chinese contractors opened last September. Spanning some 83,000 square meters, they can take about 5,600 students in 15 trades, from machining to auto repair and agro-processing.
Moreover, 184 Ivorian teachers and administrators from the schools spent four months in China learning to use and maintain equipment, while 15 school managers studied school management there. Two Chinese vocational institutions now help operate five of the schools.
In Kenya, China-supported vocational education cooperation is entering a new phase: 69 institutions will receive equipment for 70 training workshops, and 1,190 instructors and technicians will be trained in both countries.
"A trained instructor can train many generations of trainees; (and) a modern workshop can continuously produce skilled workers," said Esther Thaara Muoria, principal secretary of the State Department for Technical and Vocational Education and Training in Kenya's Ministry of Education.
Wu Jiashun, who heads the central Africa regional center of China First Highway Engineering, put it more plainly: a young person trained today will work for 30 years, and will bring up more young people along the way. "That is how a country learns to build its own roads."
For Amadhila and her teammates, Shanghai will be more than a place to compete. It will serve as a global classroom where they can test their skills, learn from their peers and bring new ideas home.
Behind these young Africans are more classrooms like these, where young people across the continent are gaining practical skills as China-Africa cooperation in vocational education continues to grow.■

Ukraine Launches Retaliatory Strikes on Moscow Refinery Supplying 40% of Region’s Petroleum Product Demand
In response to the Russian military aggression, Ukrainian strike drones and cruise missiles hit the Moscow Oil Refinery in Kapotnya overnight on September 20, sparking a large-scale fire at the plant.
Footage of the strike was published by the monitoring channel Exilenova+, which Militarnyi cited on September 20. The attack ignited a blaze on the refinery grounds, with further consequences still being assessed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Monitoring resources logged a drone-danger alert at 3:19 a.m. By 3:51, Russian channels reported air defenses engaging over the capital region, and interceptor activity continued past 5:27 a.m., according to Militarnyi.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed on social media that Russian air defenses had destroyed 151 drones overnight, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Emergency crews were working at sites where debris had fallen, he added.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the operation in a post on X. He wrote: "Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night. One of Russia's key oil industry facilities and the aggressor's logistics facility were hit. These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine."
Zelenskyy added that "the systems used included FP-1, RZ-100, MICH-2000, Palianytsia, Vendetta, Liutyi, Bars, Flamingo, Sichen, and Pelican." He did not tie individual systems to specific targets. The president also noted the strike affected a facility in the Voronezh region.
Geolocation of the footage indicated the strike damaged installations at the refinery:
- a combined crude-oil processing unit, known as the KUPN;
- the ELOU AVT-6 primary distillation installation.
A separate fire broke out at the "Sofyino" logistics technopark, matching the logistics facility Zelenskyy referenced.
Among the systems Zelenskyy listed was the FP-5 Flamingo, a Ukrainian long-range missile. Near the refinery, local residents recovered debris from an unidentified missile visually resembling the FP-5, and one video captured the sound of a jet engine, Militarnyi reported. Its use at the site remained unconfirmed.
The Kapotnya plant ranks among Russia's ten largest refineries and supplies roughly 40% of the Moscow region's petroleum products, per Militarnyi. It processes up to 11 million tons of crude annually across more than 30 technological units, including catalytic and thermal cracking and reforming lines.
The facility produces AI-80EK, AI-92EK, and AI-95EK gasolines, diesel, aviation kerosene, bitumen, sulfur, and polymers, the outlet noted.
The strike extends a sustained Ukrainian campaign against Russia's military aggression. On August 28, FP-1 drones set fires at the Slavneft-YANOS refinery in Yaroslavl, the largest oil-processing site in Russia's Central Federal District, in an attack that killed one person and injured 27. Weeks earlier, on August 5, a drone raid ignited a blaze at Rosneft's Bashneft-UNPZ refinery in Ufa, more than 1,400 kilometers from Ukraine.

Forced Deportation of Ukrainian Children Now Explicitly Triggers US Sanctions Under Law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:56:37 UTC
23:56:37 KST

- Category
- World
Forced Deportation of Ukrainian Children Now Explicitly Triggers US Sanctions Under Law
The US president, Donald Trump, signed H.R. 5334 into law on September 18, making the forced deportation of Ukrainian children an explicit statutory ground for sanctions against Russia. The measure covers knowing involvement in the removals, whether direct or indirect.
This was reported by Bring Kids Back UA on September 19, a day after the signing of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Among the grounds for sanctions, the law expressly names forcible transfers and the forced deportation of children as serious human rights abuses against citizens of Ukraine, the initiative noted. The list also includes enforced disappearances, unjust detainment, and torture, and is not exhaustive.
The measure reaches not only those who physically remove children but also the officials, institutions, and intermediaries who organize or enable the transfers, according to Bring Kids Back UA. Its threshold is knowing involvement, direct or indirect, and the law treats a person as liable if they should have known the consequences of their conduct.
Foreign persons—both individuals and legal entities such as guardianship structures, foundations, and transport operators—can be named, alongside senior Russian officials designated by virtue of their posts. The initiative reported that the designation carries two sets of restrictions.
The first is a full asset block, freezing all property and interests held in the United States or controlled by US persons, and barring transactions in such property and interests. The second is a visa bar that strips the right to enter the country and revokes any visas already issued.
The deportation of children now carries a price written into US law, not only into political statements
Maksym Maksymov
Head of Bring Kids Back UA
Because the law covers indirect involvement, it reaches those who processed and financed the removals—guardianship bodies, transport operators, and officials who signed the paperwork, Maksymov added. It places the deportation of children in the same statute as sanctions on Russian oil, banks, and the defense industry, he explained.
That turns the issue into a full instrument of pressure rather than a separate humanitarian track.
The bill was introduced in Congress in September 2025, with the sanctions text added in the summer of 2026, the initiative noted. It expands mechanisms targeting Russia's officials and its financial and energy sectors, as well as those who help Moscow evade existing restrictions, and extends the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 through 2031.
What sets the decision apart is its level, Bring Kids Back UA emphasized. The ground for sanctioning the deportation of Ukrainian children is now written into statute rather than an executive order, meaning it cannot be undone by a change of administrative policy.
The law designates no one automatically. It builds the mechanism, and decisions on which individuals and organizations are added to the lists rest with the US administration.
The statute lands amid a widening Western push to make the removal of Ukrainian children personally costly, for Russia, as the European Union had adopted an initial package in May, targeting 16 Russian officials and seven entities tied to the systematic deportation, indoctrination, and illegal adoption of Ukrainian children.

Israeli father killed in Slovenia while rescuing seven-year-old son from ravine fall

A 44-year-old Israeli, Gail Hillel, a member of Kibbutz Yizrael, was tragically killed in Slovenia on Saturday while trying to rescue his 7-year-old son, who had fallen into a ravine during a family trip.
The accident occurred near the Slap Savica waterfall, a popular natural site in the Bohinj area of northwestern Slovenia.
According to the Kranj District Police, the family had stopped at a nearby rest area with picnic tables and benches after visiting the waterfall. During this stop, the boy wandered away from his family. Soon after, they heard his cries for help.
Hillel immediately searched for his son and fell into the ravine while trying to reach him.
Rescue teams later found Hillel in the Savica River channel, suffering from fatal injuries, and pronounced him dead at the scene, while his son was also located by the rescue team.
The child received initial treatment at the scene for serious injuries before being evacuated by helicopter, operated by the police aviation unit, to the University Medical Center in Ljubljana.
Rescue teams locate Israeli Father and son
The Bohinj Mountain Rescue Service stated they had initially received reports indicating that only a child had fallen into the ravine but upon their arrival, they discovered that Hillel had also fallen.
Several members of the rescue unit were conducting a training exercise nearby at the time of the incident, which enabled them to reach the accident scene quickly. The team descended nearly 60 meters into the river channel below and was able to assist both Hillel and the child, preparing them for evacuation.
After the child was airlifted to the hospital, Hillel’s body was recovered from the steep terrain using ropes.
“We sincerely hope the child recovers quickly and in the best possible way, and that one day he and the rest of his family will be able to cope with this tragedy,” local rescuers expressed in their condolences to the family.
Slovenian police have stated that they are continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the accident. Once their findings are complete, a report will be submitted to the relevant district prosecutor’s office.
