Rail Tourism in Iran: Connecting Historic Cities, Landscapes and Cultural Heritage
Railways have always played an important role in connecting different parts of Iran. However, today, they can offer much more than transportation. With its rich cultural heritage, historic cities, and diverse natural landscapes, Iran has great potential to develop rail tourism. Traveling by train can provide tourists with an opportunity to discover the country in a different way, making the journey itself an important part of the travel experience.
The Growing Potential of Rail Tourism in Iran
The emergence of the railway industry first began and developed in the 19th century in Iran, when it had different uses. Today, this industry is trying to take a different path in the tourism industry. Iran is a country with wonderful nature and landscapes. The railway network in this country runs through these landscapes, crossing forests, rivers, mountains, and many other places. It is more than just transportation; it is a tourism experience itself. Local people and foreigners are aware of it, and it helps the growth of rail tourism in Iran.
Why Explore Iran by Train?
Like many other countries, there are different means of transportation for exploring Iran. Trains are one of those options, and several factors make them a good choice. First, the railway network in Iran can take tourists through very different environments, from intact parts of the northern forests and mountains of Iran to the southern coast of the Persian Gulf, which cannot be fully explored by other means of transportation. Second, rail travel is a more environmentally friendly form of transportation because of its reduced energy consumption and lower environmental pollution. Third, among other kinds of transportation, trains can be a safer choice for travelers. The next factor is price. Train tickets in Iran are cheaper than flights. They cover the same distance at a lower price, which is an attractive criterion for those who want to explore large parts of Iran. Lastly, rail tourism can bring many tourists to smaller towns and suburbs. It can provide some economic benefits and create employment for local people, especially in accommodation, restaurants, and handicrafts.
Historic Cities Connected by Iran’s Railway Network
One of the factors that make rail tourism an interesting choice for travelers is the connection between historic cities, which is achieved through Iran’s railway network. There are four main railway corridors for the tourism industry. The first one is the northwestern corridor, which connects Tehran, Qazvin, Zanjan, and Tabriz. All four cities played an important role in the history of Iran, and they are still considered significant cities in modern Iran, too. The second one is perhaps known as the best rail-tourism route in Iran, which connects Tehran, Kashan, Isfahan, Yazd, and Kerman. All those cities are major Persian heritage cities with great historical backgrounds from different eras of this country. Also, this route contains lots of unique desert landscapes.The third route passes through Tehran, Mashhad, and Neishabour. This route is mostly used for religious purposes. People who want to visit the holy shrine of Imam Reza can use this railway. Fadak Train is a well-known luxury train that takes travelers along this route. Although this route is famous for religious purposes, it can also be used to visit historical cities of Iran that were once connected to the Silk Road. Finally, the last route connects three cities: Tehran, Ahvaz, and Shush. This route has great potential to be considered the archaeological railway route of Iran. This part of Iran was home to early civilizations in this area, and now this region has a lot to say about archaeology, with ancient sites such as Susa, Chogha Zanbil, and Haft Tappeh.
From Deserts to Mountains: Landscapes Along the Way
As mentioned in the previous sections, the railway corridors of Iran connect different parts of Iran. This network offers an amazing journey from the northern part of Iran, which contains the Alborz mountain range and the forests that cover its slopes, to the southern part of Iran with its pristine desert landscapes. Buying train tickets in Iran offers travelers a fantastic opportunity to experience such wonderful geographical diversity at once.
Iran’s Railway Heritage and Cultural Tourism
The importance of railways in Iran multiplies when we understand that they do not act just as a means of transportation, but also as a means of cultural tourism. Buying train tickets in Iran gives travelers two different opportunities. First, they experience different kinds of landscapes during their journey. Second, they pass through different cities with great historical backgrounds. These historic cities offer travelers the opportunity to visit archaeological sites, traditional villages, museums, cultural landmarks, local and traditional markets, and ancient monuments. People can discover ancient Persian culture, architecture, and beliefs through these places. This process helps promote the development of cultural tourism through Iran’s railway heritage.
Planning a Rail Journey Across Iran
Planning a rail journey across Iran is a great option to combine the most necessary things for traveling: transportation, cultural tourism, and nature-based tourism. This planning doesn’t require much effort. First, travelers need to decide which route they want to choose. It depends on their personal interests and preferences regarding the experiences they want to have and the places they want to visit. The second one is buying tickets. Buying train tickets in Iran can be done through online booking on the Raja website, travel agencies, and authorized ticket offices at railway stations. Without a doubt, this rail journey will be an unforgettable experience for travelers.
Rail Tours and New Ways to Experience Iran
Unlike normal tourism around the world, rail tours in Iran not only prevent travelers from thinking only about the destination, but also make the journey itself a part of the experience. In recent years, many trains, like Fadak, have given passengers distinguished facilities during the journey and made them feel at home. Meanwhile, passengers can enjoy different and wonderful landscapes of this country along the route. These developments have transformed the role of the railway industry in Iran and are constantly contributing to the growth of railway tourism.
The Future of Rail Tourism in Iran
As mentioned before, there is great potential for rail tourism in Iran. This country has well-developed railway corridors, rich cultural heritage, and different landscapes, which are enough to change the future of this industry in Iran. In the future, train tickets in Iran will be more than just a means of transportation; they will serve as a gateway to the depths of history and hidden natural wonders.
Discovering Iran Beyond the Destination
Rail tourism allows travelers to discover Iran beyond the destination. The journey itself is an opportunity to experience different landscapes, cultural heritage, and historical cities and to interact with local people while traveling between destinations. It’s a chance to appreciate the stories and hidden treasures that lie between them. Moreover, traveling by train is a slower experience. Instead of rushing from one place to another, travelers have time to observe and interact.
In conclusion, railway industry in Iran has all factors to develop rail tourism in this country. Iran’s historic cities, special landscapes and cultural heritage can change a train journey to an unforgettable experience . By developing train facilities and planning attractive tours, Iran can attract many domestic and international tourists.

It comes after the US State Department warned Americans against travel to the region, as hostilities rage between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis.
This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly,” it warned.
The violence has already disrupted air and marine traffic, as well as energy exports, pushing global oil prices past $100 a barrel.
Ratcliffe’s visit comes days after de facto Saudi leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met Sisi in Cairo.
The pair urged safe and secure maritime navigation through Bab al-Mandab, after the Houthis seized the Yemeni coast in a lightning offensive.
U.S. media last week reported Washington refused a Saudi request to strike the Houthis.

Postponing the future: War and inflation redraw marriage terms in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:12:40 UTC
22:12:40 KST

Postponing the future: War and inflation redraw marriage terms in Iran
Iran’s cost of living crisis is affecting the dreams and everyday life choices of young Iranians.
Subhan Dashti had already picked a date for his wedding. He and his fiancee, Nadia Sabzi, together since 2016, had settled on Nowruz 1405, the Iranian New Year, which falls on March 20 to 21. They had already started buying items for their future home, but then last year, prices started to climb. Political and social unrest followed, and then the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran on February 28. Dashti’s family fled Tehran for the north of the country, and preparations for their wedding stalled.
When the fighting paused, the families returned to Tehran and the couple tried to resume their plans. But a television Dashti had budgeted at 70 million tomans ($302) now cost closer to 100 million tomans ($432). Despite earning about 100 million tomans a month ($432) – well above average for an Iranian worker – he concluded that marrying immediately no longer made sense.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iranians rally in biggest show of defiance against US since war began
- list 2 of 4Iran stages show of force during mobilisation campaign in Tehran
- list 3 of 4Iran says conditions to re-engage in talks, end war sent to US via Qatar
- list 4 of 4What are Iran’s latest conditions to end its war with the US?
“We decided to postpone the wedding for at least a few more months,” Dashti, 35, said.
The minimum wage for an Iranian worker is about 16 million tomans per month, which is less than $68 at current open market rates, while the average monthly wage for workers is around 25 million tomans, or roughly $105.
For Sabzi, 34, the maths are only part of the fear. She has made peace with a smaller ceremony – a simpler dress, a modest hall. What she cannot make peace with is safety.
A US strike in early September hit a house in Kuhestak, in southern Iran’s Sirik County, where a wedding celebration was taking place; Iranian authorities said several people were killed and dozens wounded, including women and children.
“For the past two weeks, I have been asking Subhan at night: what if the war starts again when we are getting married?” Sabzi said.
Their stalled wedding is one small sign of a larger crisis in Iran for young people. Across Iran, war, sanctions, inflation and shortages are shaping young couples’ marriage decisions amid a shifting focus on wedding costs, what a household requires and how far into the future anyone dares to plan.
Simin Nouri, a bridal makeup artist in Tehranpars, said that during the summer’s peak wedding season, her salon once saw two or three brides a day. Now it sees only two or three a week.
Prices are now even higher, she said. In Tehran, a regular bridal package costs about 70 million tomans ($302), while a VIP package can reach 150 million tomans ($648). In lower-income parts of the city, prices are usually around 50 million tomans ($216). Clients have not abandoned services entirely – they downgrade them. They skip skincare and hair extensions, and book only makeup and hairstyling for the wedding night itself.
“They still want to do these things,” she said, “but they go for the less expensive option.” She noted that two of her own friends postponed their weddings outright. One declined Nouri’s offer of free makeup paid later. “Because the makeup was never the real obstacle – the wedding itself was,” she said.
Newlyweds – and a bill that keeps growing
Pejman and Sanaz, who met studying electronic engineering and asked that their surnames and university be withheld, married in July just after last year’s 12-day war. Their rent tells the story: a deposit and monthly rent that totalled roughly 34 million tomans ($144) a year ago now cost about 58 million tomans ($246) – a 71 percent rise for the same Tehran apartment.
That includes a jump from a 300 million-toman ($1,296) deposit and 25 million tomans ($106) monthly rent, plus 1.5 to 2 million tomans ($6–$8) in building charges, to a demand from a new landlord of a 400 million-toman ($1,728) deposit and 46 million tomans a month ($198).
Pejman, 30, earns 56 million tomans a month ($242); the new rent alone would consume about 82 percent of it.
“Last year, just to cover the costs of starting our life together, we had to sell 13 grams of my wife’s gold,” he said. That gold is now far more expensive to replace: 18-carat gold has risen from roughly 6.48 million tomans a gram ($28) in June 2025 to more than 23 million tomans ($99) by mid-September 2026.
A mid-range Tehran wedding for about 100 guests – hall, bridal services, clothing, photography, music and modest gold – now runs close to 1.1 billion tomans ($4,752), versus roughly 480 million tomans ($2,074) before the 2025 war, though costs vary by neighbourhood and provider.
Economist Amir Hossein Mohaddes separates the crisis into two problems: the cost of starting a household and the cost of sustaining one.
“A couple can make the wedding smaller. They can remove parts of the ceremony. But they cannot remove housing,” Mohaddes said.
He argues the more serious damage is unpredictability itself – couples cannot plan a few months ahead due to rapidly rising prices. He warns that even a ceasefire or a full halt of the war would not reverse this trend: a refrigerator that has doubled in price does not fall back on its own. Landlords who increase rents rarely lower them again.
For Abbas Derafshi, 30, a bank employee who had been planning to marry his fiancee, Parastoo, even a state-backed marriage loan has not been enough to bridge that widening gap.
Under President Ebrahim Raisi’s government, Derafshi said, bank employees had been instructed to work closely with young couples applying for marriage loans, processing applications with minimal guarantees – often requiring just one guarantor.
The 2023 rules set the standard loan at 180 million tomans per person ($778), or 360 million tomans for a couple ($1,555). Derafshi calculated that the combined loan was worth more than $7,000, with a 10-year repayment period and a 4 percent service fee.
The standard loan has since risen to 300 million tomans per person ($1,296), or 600 million tomans for a couple ($2,592).
A couple receiving the full amount would now face monthly repayments of roughly 5.5 million tomans ($24), Derafshi said, about 2.2 million tomans ($9.50) more each month than a couple borrowing the standard amount in 2023. Despite the loan’s nominal value rising, Derafshi calculated its real purchasing power has fallen roughly 64 percent in dollar terms since 2023.
“When I applied for the loan under the [President Masoud] Pezeshkian government, even though I work at a bank myself, I faced so many obstacles – from branch assignment and credit checks to guarantor requirements and additional documents – that I eventually gave up,” he said.
His account reflects his own experience rather than the conditions set with every Iranian bank for every young person, he notes. But for him the result was concrete: with housing and wedding costs continuing to rise, he and Parastoo no longer enjoy the financial conditions to begin married life as planned.
“The plans we had for starting our life together have basically been put on hold until further notice,” Derafshi said.
What the numbers mean
Political science professor Jalil Dara, who also studies social and future-oriented trends, explained that prolonged inflation and uncertainty are “contributing to anxiety, lower optimism and delayed family formation among young Iranians”. That is alongside a countervailing rise in national solidarity that coexists uneasily with the economic strain. But Iran’s economic difficulties did not begin with the current war.
“Years of sanctions, chronic inflation, currency depreciation, weak investment and domestic policy failures had already made marriage and housing harder for young people,” he said.
“The war worked as an accelerating shock, not the sole cause. Even an end to hostilities would not automatically reverse the damage.”
For household purchasing power to recover, Mohaddes said, Iran would need more than peace. What is essential for ending the cost of living crisis is currency stability, real wage growth, productive employment, stronger investment and lower economic uncertainty.
“That is why the consequences of war can outlast the sound of explosions,” he concluded.
Facing costs they can no longer absorb, Pejman and Sanaz are now considering leaving Iran to study abroad.
“We both love Iran. We would like to return after finishing our doctorates and work for our country,” Sanaz said. “Hope the situation would be better by then”.

Ukraine signs memorandum on gas storage in Hungary – Naftogaz
The Naftogaz Group has signed a memorandum with the Budapest-based oil and gas company MOL Group regarding the construction of facilities to store petroleum products for Ukraine's needs in Hungary near the Ukrainian-Hungarian border.
Source: acting Naftogaz CEO Serhii Fedorenko on Facebook
Details: Fedorenko said the agreement was reached at the Carpathian Economic Forum as part of the Carpathian Eight Summit.
Quote: "Amid relentless Russian attacks on our fuel infrastructure, diversifying supply routes and building additional storage capacities outside the area of attacks is a matter of market-wide stability.

Background: More than 50 investment and trade projects worth a total of over €1 billion have been developed during the Carpathian Economic Forum.

Russian tanks take back seat as 20-km drone ‘kill zone’ limits assaults – military spox

Unknown Publisher

Russian tanks take back seat as 20-km drone ‘kill zone’ limits assaults – military spox
Victor Tregubov, Spokesperson for the Joint Forces Grouping, said this during a television broadcast, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“Heavy equipment is, in fact, no longer being used [by the Russians]. It exists, of course, but if we detect, say, one tank damaged somewhere in a day, that is a successful hunt, and it was most likely damaged somewhere deep in the rear. Possibly even by something like a mid-strike.
“But as for them directly advancing somewhere with tanks or heavy equipment – no. The kill zone extends 20 kilometers, and no ‘cope cage’ can protect against fiber-optic drones. So, under our current conditions, tanks have gradually moved not just to the back seat, but to the third row,” Tregubov said.
According to him, when several drones simultaneously hunt tanks within the kill zone, Russian forces can use heavy equipment only with mass drone support.
“And in addition to planning the entire operation, they also need to get the weather right so that drones are barely able to fly. In other words, if a storm with tornadoes were to hit somewhere here, the Russians would probably be able to deploy heavy equipment somewhat more extensively,” Tregubov said.
As reported by Ukrinform, in June, soldiers from the Lasar’s Group special unmanned aerial systems unit of the National Guard of Ukraine, working with artillery units from neighboring formations, destroyed 18 Russian tanks in a single special operation.

Trump says his planned arch to double as military base

WASHINGTON – A massive arch that US President Donald Trump wants to build on a historic location in Washington will double as a base for drones and snipers, he announced on Sept 20.
“I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch... into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social, “to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage”.
“There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World. Out of the 59 top cities and Capitals, Washington, DC, IS THE ONLY ONE IN THE WORLD THAT DOES NOT HAVE A TRIUMPHAL ARCH, but it will now and, by far, the greatest of them all!” the US leader added.
The proposed giant structure along the Potomac River near the Arlington National Cemetery is part of Trump’s drive to put his personal stamp on the capital.
The Trump administration has not sought congressional input for such a major change to the US capital.
Given its massive size, it would obscure the sight lines between the Lincoln Memorial, one of Washington’s iconic landmarks, and Arlington National Cemetery, the final resting place for hundreds of thousands of American service members.
Since returning to power in January 2025, Trump has launched a series of renovation projects, several of which have led to legal disputes.
They include a massive and costly ballroom that is being built at the White House, for which Trump had an entire wing of the presidential mansion demolished.
Another project is the laborious renovation of the Reflecting Pool, a massive rectangular water basin on the National Mall.
For a time, Trump also had his name placed on the walls of the Kennedy Center, the culture and arts institute named after assassinated president John F. Kennedy, before a judge reversed the move. AFP

China's prodigy Yu clinches first major title from Asian Games
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:07:58 CST
22:07:58 KST

Gold medalist Yu Zidi (C) of China, silver medalist Chang Mohan (L) of China and bronze medalist Okuzono Misa of Japan pose during the awarding ceremony for the women's 200m butterfly at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Tokyo, Japan, Sept. 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Zhizun)
TOKYO, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- 13-year-old Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi made a sound Asian Games debut on Sunday to secure her first title from major events, as China claimed six gold, one silver and two bronze medals on the opening day of swimming competition at the Games.
Yu dominated the women's 200m butterfly in two minutes and 5.08 seconds, setting a new Games record. Fellow Chinese Chang Mohan took silver in 2:08.44.
"I hope I can swim even faster," Yu said with a smile. "I believe I will perform better next time."
The teenager said she still had room for improvement, particularly in her technique. "I need to lower my head earlier and improve the movement of my legs," she said.
For Yu, the gold marked the beginning of her Asian Games journey. She became the youngest swimming world championships medalist in history last year at the age of 12, when she helped China win bronze in the women's 4x200m freestyle relay in Singapore. She is also one of the youngest athletes to be nominated for the Laureus World Sports Awards.
China also won the women's 4x100m freestyle relay in a Games record time of 3:33.10. Zhang Yufei said she was "very happy" with the result and felt she had produced a peak-level performance in her leg.
Returning to the Tokyo Aquatics Centre, where she had competed at the Tokyo Olympic Games, Zhang said she felt a rare sense of familiarity and comfort. "I really enjoyed it and felt completely immersed," she said.
Tang Qianting defended her women's 50m breaststroke title in 29.45 seconds, improving the Games record she set in the morning. "I think I can still do better," Tang said, setting her sights on breaking the 29-second barrier.
Olympic champion Pan Zhanle also defended his men's 100m freestyle title in 47.61 seconds. Although the result fell short of his expectations, Pan said he had regained some confidence after a difficult period. "I don't care as much about winning or losing as I used to. I just want to enjoy the competition and leave no regrets," he said.
The opening day also saw Xu Jiayu successfully defend his men's 100m backstroke title in an event record of 51.98 seconds, while Li Bingjie retained her women's 1,500m freestyle title in 15:53.52.
In the men's 200m individual medley, five-time Asian Games veteran Wang Shun took bronze as Japan's Tomoyuki Matsushita won gold.
For Wang, returning to the Tokyo venue brought back memories of his winning Olympic competition five years ago.
"It felt like I was making up for the regret of having no spectators five years ago," Wang said. "I really enjoyed it and was completely immersed in it."
For Yu, the first day of competition marked the beginning of what promises to be a busy Asian Games campaign, with two more individual events still to come. ■

A drone photo taken on Sept. 17, 2026 shows a view of Xingdong New Village of Dongming County in Heze, east China's Shandong Province. The Yellow River, dubbed the Mother River of China, has long nourished the land in Heze, east China's Shandong Province, but recurring floods once posed a persistent threat to residents living on its floodplain. To protect local residents from flooding, a large-scale relocation and reconstruction project was launched in 2017 and completed in 2020.
Some 600,000 residents from the floodplain moved into newly built communities with improved housing and access to kindergartens, community clinics, elderly care centers and public spaces. Some 600,000 residents from the floodplain moved into newly built communities with improved housing and access to kindergartens, community clinics, elderly care centers and public spaces. In recent years, local authorities have also developed agriculture, rural processing and tourism-related industries to create more income opportunities for residents. (Xinhua/Guo Xulei)

Economic Watch: China builds national computing network as key pillar of new infrastructure
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:07:52 CST
22:07:52 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- As artificial intelligence (AI) and large-scale data processing reshape the global tech landscape, China is accelerating the construction of a nationwide computing power network as a cornerstone of the country's future infrastructure.
The computing power network has been incorporated into the national "six networks" infrastructure framework as the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) enters its first year, marking the industry's shift toward high-quality development, said Wang Jinping, president of the China Association of Information, at an industry conference.
The Computing Power Network Industry Conference and AI Computational Power Industry Expo 2026, which concluded recently in Beijing, brought together academicians, researchers, industry leaders and other key stakeholders to explore pathways for building an integrated national computing power network, advancing technological innovation and fostering ecosystem collaboration.
Formalized by a top-level decision in April 2026, the computing power network -- alongside the networks of water, next-generation power grids, next-generation telecommunications, underground urban pipelines and logistics -- has become as indispensable to the digital age as water and electricity. It is expected to unlock a new wave of strategic development opportunities.
RAPID EXPANSION AND NATIONAL LAYOUT
Strong policy support and robust market demand are already propelling China's computing power industry into a new stage of high-quality, large-scale development.
As of June 2026, the country's intelligent computing capacity reached 2,185 EFLOPS -- each unit representing 1 quintillion floating-point operations per second -- up 177 percent year over year. More than 70 computing power transmission corridors linking major computing hubs and key regions have been built, and 17 national computing interconnection regional nodes have been approved.
Building on this momentum, China is now accelerating the construction of an integrated national computing power network, forming an "8+10+3" spatial layout centered on eight national computing hubs, 10 national computing clusters and three computing-electricity coordination zones.
To centrally pool the nation's computing resources, a national computing service platform is accelerating its expansion, steadily connecting platforms across 31 provincial-level regions. Its marketplace has attracted more than 10,000 enterprise users, over 200 service providers, more than 2,000 computing products and over 300 large models, while offering developers computing access services and accumulating billions of monitoring data records.
COMPUTING-ELECTRICITY COORDINATION
Beyond interconnecting existing facilities, the computing power network is matching supply in resource-rich regions with surging demand in the fast-growing east through "computing-electricity coordination."
Regions such as Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region and Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region are converting abundant wind and solar power into on-site computing capacity, supporting the east's growing needs for large-scale data processing and AI training.
Inner Mongolia offers a telling example. With green electricity priced at around 0.35 yuan (about 5 U.S. cents) per kilowatt-hour, a cool climate that allows natural cooling for nearly 10 months a year and network latency of no more than 5 milliseconds to Beijing, the region has emerged as a preferred destination for large-scale computing projects.
As of the first half of 2026, 20 of China's 30 leading private computing companies had established a presence in Inner Mongolia, with combined investment exceeding 200 billion yuan, and nine of the country's top 10 computing service providers had set up operations in the region.
GLOBAL REACH AND SERVICE INNOVATION
The network's benefits are also extending beyond China's borders. As of early August, Chinese large models had ranked first in call volume for 15 consecutive weeks on model aggregation platforms that mainly serve overseas users, according to data from OpenRouter. More overseas developers are choosing to train AI models in China or directly tap its mature computing resources.
Meanwhile, token export services -- providing overseas users with computing and AI services billed by tokens, the basic unit of AI information processing -- have emerged as a new form of services trade at this year's China International Fair for Trade in Services.
INTELLIGENT FOUNDATION FOR NEW GROWTH
According to Xiao Hongwei, a researcher at the State Information Center under the National Development and Reform Commission, the computing power network, functioning as an "intelligent foundation" for economic and social operations, can not only meet computing demands across diverse scenarios including large model training, film rendering, autonomous driving and smart finance, but also drive upgrades across the entire industrial chain encompassing AI, big data and industrial internet.
"The computing power network will fuel the development of new quality productive forces," Xiao said, adding that the six networks are now interwoven and mutually supportive, jointly forming the infrastructure foundation for this new growth paradigm. ■

China's tax revenue growth broadly in line with economic expansion
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:07:49 CST
22:07:49 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's tax revenue rose 5.9 percent year on year in the first eight months of 2026, data from the State Taxation Administration showed on Sunday.
The figures cover taxes collected by the tax authorities and exclude import value-added tax (VAT) and import consumption tax collected by customs, tariffs and tonnage tax.
"Tax revenue is calculated at current prices, and growth this year has generally kept pace with the economy," said Huang Lixin, an official with the administration.
China's gross domestic product grew 4.7 percent year on year at constant prices in the first half of 2026, while at current prices, it grew 5.4 percent -- slightly below the 5.9 percent tax revenue growth recorded for the first eight months.
Huang attributed the accelerated pace of tax growth to three main factors.
Prices are no longer a drag. China's producer price index, which measures costs for goods at the factory gate, ended 41 straight months of decline in March and turned positive. The index rose by 2 percent cumulatively over the first eight months of the year, helping to boost tax revenue recorded at current prices.
Capital market activity is boosting receipts. A more active stock market has driven up the securities transaction stamp tax by 82 percent, along with corporate income tax, personal income tax and domestic VAT tied to trading and investment gains.
Policy adjustments are also a key factor. As the country's VAT law and related regulations took effect this year, some tax policies were adjusted accordingly. At the same time, the country has tightened certain tax preferences that no longer align with high-quality development or current conditions, which contributed to higher tax revenue. Such policy adjustments, however, do not directly translate into GDP growth.
"Taken together, these factors lifted tax revenue growth slightly above GDP growth, but overall it remains broadly consistent with growth in the economy's tax source," Huang said. "That speaks to the resilience and vitality of China's economic development."
Chen Binkai, vice president of the Central University of Finance and Economics, said that in terms of who pays, tax revenue is mainly contributed by large enterprises, while small and micro businesses enjoy more tax and fee benefits.
Tax data show that in the first eight months, the top 10,000 taxpayers by amount paid accounted for nearly half of all tax revenue, and the top one million accounted for 90 percent, while the remaining enterprises, including small and micro businesses, made up only about 10 percent.
China has rolled out a series of preferential tax and fee policies for smaller firms in recent years. Small-scale VAT taxpayers with monthly sales below 100,000 yuan (about 14,810 U.S. dollars) are exempt from VAT, and eligible small low-profit enterprises face an effective corporate income tax rate of 5 percent.
"These policies have played an important role in reducing the tax burden on the vast number of small and micro enterprises," Chen added. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: China's tech strategy for preserving precious black soil farmland
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
21:07:41 CST
22:07:41 KST

Leng Jiantian, a researcher at the Northeast Institute of Geography and Agroecology (IGA) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), introduces a crop rotation model to protect the black soil in Dongliao County, northeast China's Jilin Province, Sept. 16, 2026.(Xinhua/Yu Fei)
CHANGCHUN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- When agricultural scientist Leng Jiantian arrived in the hilly area at the source of the Liaohe River in northeast China's Jilin Province about 10 years ago, he found that local farmers planted only corn year after year. Pests and diseases were frequent, pesticides and fertilizers were overused, and the soil and river were seriously polluted.
Through investigation and research, Leng and his team developed a crop rotation model involving soybeans, sorghum, wheat and rapeseed. As a result, the use of pesticides and fertilizers is greatly reduced, the ecological environment is better protected, and farmers have higher incomes.
From soil ecological restoration to innovation in farming models, and from sky-ground monitoring to molecular breeding chips, Chinese scientists are deploying an integrated strategy to protect the country's precious black soil and maximize its value.
The black soil in Heilongjiang, Jilin and Liaoning provinces, all located in China's northeast, and in some parts of north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, is hailed as the "giant panda of arable land." With high fertility and stable yields, it forms a vital foundation for China's food security. Yet high-intensity cultivation for decades has left this valuable land facing a crisis involving thinning, impoverishment and hardening.
The Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), together with authorities in the four provincial-level regions, launched the "Black Soil Granary" program in 2021 to provide sci-tech support for the fight against soil degradation.
Under this program, scientists have built a sky-ground integrated monitoring system for black soil, mapped a comprehensive multi-factor information atlas covering the entire black soil region, and conducted pioneering theoretical research on soil organic matter evolution and degradation control.
DISTINCTIVE ENDEAVORS
In the black soil area of eastern Jilin, the challenges were complex: severe soil erosion on sloping farmland, soil acidification, prominent non-point source pollution, and low benefits from traditional planting models.
Rather than imposing a one-size-fits-all solution, the researchers devised tailored models targeting different problems, according to Leng, a researcher at the Northeast Institute of Geography and Agroecology (IGA) of the CAS.
Short-stalk and dense-planting crops are adopted in grain-soybean rotation to reduce soil erosion. A technique integrating straw, organic fertilizer and biochar is applied to increase carbon, reduce acidity and build fertility. High-value specialty industries are developed to boost farmers' incomes. Some sloping farmland is returned to forest to develop understory economies featuring forest-grown vegetables and medicinal plants.
Among these, the grain-soybean rotation model centers on soybeans, wheat (followed by rapeseed after the wheat harvest), and short-stalk sorghum. The research endeavor defines key technical parameters for crop pairing, planting density and field management, forming a standardized technical framework.
"Short-stalked, densely planted crops reduce surface exposure and soil erosion, and their straw is also easier to return to the field. At the same time, we have developed an integrated technology model that combines organic fertilizer, straw and biochar to increase carbon and reduce acidity. Our goal is to restore the carbon content in the soil to the level 20 years ago," Leng explained.
This grain-soybean rotation technology has been promoted on a large scale in the source region of the Liaohe River, covering more than 453,000 hectares.
In core demonstration zones, farmland fertilizer use was reduced by 20 percent, pesticide use by 30 percent, non-point source pollution load by 22 percent, and soil erosion by more than 17 percent. Output value of sloping farmland increased 23 percent to 38 percent. The soil pH level in the demonstration zones rose from 5.12 in 2021 to 6.44 in 2025, which means acidification is effectively brought under control, Leng said.
In Nongan County of Jilin Province, researchers have improved a comprehensive conservation tillage technology, including the strip tillage technique with straw covered on the soil surface, and compatible agricultural machinery. The measures reduce soil wind erosion and water erosion in the core demonstration area by more than 80 percent, cut fertilizer use by 12.3 percent to 15 percent, and increase yields by an average of 10 percent.
The Institute of Applied Ecology of the CAS has, meanwhile, established a modern agriculture experimental station in Changtu, a major grain-producing county in the city of Tieling, Liaoning Province. In the process of protecting black soil, researchers have attached importance to fully integrating livestock and poultry manure resource utilization technology, straw return and conservation tillage technology, and modern planting technology.
By establishing a manure treatment network, they have achieved the collection and centralized treatment of livestock and poultry manure, and developed a new anaerobic fermentation process to realize an efficient and harmless manure treatment system, thereby achieving precise manure return to fields and soil fertility improvement. Its technical system has been promoted over a cumulative area of more than 330,000 hectares, with chemical fertilizer reduced by 15 percent to 30 percent and crop yields increased by 6 percent to 21 percent.
China has the potential to showcase and share its black soil protection knowledge and information with other countries. According to the Land and Water Division of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations, an FAO-China South-South cooperation program was launched last year to promote optimized black soil management practices, support the establishment of soil analysis laboratories, and develop national digital soil maps.
INNOVATIVE BREEDING
While protecting the black soil, researchers have advanced breeding innovation, which depends much on solid-phase breeding chips. These chips used to be largely monopolized by foreign companies, said Feng Xianzhong, director of the Key Laboratory of Soybean Molecular Design Breeding of the IGA.
Feng led his team in tackling the entire chain, from core reagents, chip substrates and DNA probe design to chip assembly and scanning instrument construction, and developed domestic soybean solid-phase breeding chips and detection equipment.
The researchers explained that some key sites in the soybean genome called SNP sites are highly associated with agronomic traits such as yield and disease resistance. Probes targeting these sites are pre-fixed on a chip. In processing, sample DNA hybridizes with the chip, fully matched fragments remain in corresponding positions, and fluorescent signals are scanned for genotypes to be read.
In 2025, the soybean breeding chip and detection equipment developed by the team were able to perform type detection of 20,000 SNP sites highly associated with agronomic traits, providing important support for the future development of an intelligent design breeding technology system for soybeans and other crops.
The chip's detection density reaches 100,000 probe sites per square centimeter, equivalent to packing 100,000 detection sites into an area the size of a fingernail. Technically, it has caught up with the indicators of related foreign products, according to Feng.
On the basis of the chips, the team further developed detection equipment that can accurately read the genetic information of 20,000 soybean SNPs within 10 minutes.
To address the high cost of existing solid-phase breeding chips, which can only be used once, the team is developing a new type of erasable and reusable solid-phase breeding chip. Its success will substantially reduce breeding detection costs and make large-scale breeding applications feasible.
Through gene chip screening, new salt- and alkaline-tolerant soybean varieties developed via molecular design, when planted in saline-alkaline land in western Jilin, produced roughly 40 percent higher yields than control varieties. It would take around 10 years to breed such varieties using traditional methods, but molecular breeding has shortened the time to approximately 5 years, Leng noted. ■
Feng Xianzhong, director of the Key Laboratory of Soybean Molecular Design Breeding of the Northeast Institute of Geography and Agroecology (IGA) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), introduces soybean molecular design breeding in Changchun, northeast China's Jilin Province, Sept. 17, 2026.(Xinhua/Yu Fei)

Asian Games | Athlete experience key to organizing major sporting events, says IOC chief

IOC President Kirsty Coventry speaks to the media after visiting the athletes' accommodation area at the Asian Games on Sept. 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Yin Jiajie)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry said Sunday that the experience of athletes should be a key consideration when organizing major sporting events.
Coventry made the remarks after visiting the athletes' accommodation area at Garden Pier in Nagoya Port, where she met with athletes competing at the Asian Games. She also acknowledged that organizers must take into account the costs and logistical complexities involved in delivering such an experience.
The 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games have accommodated athletes on a cruise ship, in container-style huts and at hotels in different locations as part of efforts to reduce costs. Such arrangements have drawn criticism from some athletes and delegations.
Accommodation has been a major focus in the run-up to the Games, with organizers opting not to provide a traditional athletes' village. Some teams have criticized the quality of their accommodation, including beds that were too short, while others have complained about a shortage of rooms.
Coventry defended the organizers' decision, saying she was "impressed" with the accommodation and describing the cabins as "really nice." At the same time, she stressed that athletes' basic needs should remain the priority.
IOC President Kirsty Coventry speaks during the 146th International Olympic Committee Session in Lausanne, Switzerland, June 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Lian Yi)
Drawing on her own experience as an athlete, Coventry said athletes were less concerned about how their accommodation looked than about whether it met their basic needs. For her, the priorities were "a really comfortable bed," "really good food" and transportation that "ran really well."
She said the IOC would place greater emphasis on the athlete experience and work with organizing committees and future hosts to establish minimum standards for accommodation and other services.
Olympic Council of Asia Director General Husain Al-Musallam said at a press conference on Friday that a traditional athletes' village remains the preferred option for organizers, but flexibility is also necessary.
"We wish that we have an athlete village, number one. But, number two, we also have to be flexible," Al-Musallam said.
Coventry said the issue extends beyond accommodation. The size and scale of a sporting event determine the number of venues required and have a direct impact on the costs of accommodation, transportation and food. The IOC is discussing venue use and scheduling with international sports federations, including ways to allow different sports to share venues and reduce the need to build additional facilities. ■

====================================================================================================

Ukraine’s history as part of world history: What 200 researchers led by Timothy Snyder are creating
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:06:00 EEST
22:06:00 KST

Ukraine’s history as part of world history: What 200 researchers led by Timothy Snyder are creating
What does it take to tell the history of Ukraine to the world? For three days in Kyiv, 80 scholars, researchers, and other contributors gathered to work on that question, and to bring three years of collaborative research closer to publication.
The third annual conference of the Ukrainian History Global Initiative (UHGI), held from 14 to 16 September 2026, marked an important transition for the project. With its research programme moving towards completion, the Initiative is now preparing to transform years of academic work into books and an ambitious digital platform designed to make Ukraine's history accessible to audiences around the world.
Founded by businessman and philanthropist Victor Pinchuk in 2023 and led academically by world renown historian Timothy Snyder, UHGI brings together an international community of about 200 researchers to develop a comprehensive history of Ukraine, from prehistory to the present, placing the lands and peoples of Ukraine within the broader history of the world.
As Snyder explained in his opening remarks, the ambition is to produce a comprehensive history of Ukraine through the history of the world, and a comprehensive history of the world through the history of Ukraine.
A different kind of academic conference
Unlike conventional academic conferences, the Kyiv gathering was organised around collaborative work without formal presentations.
Over three days, participants discussed 58 research papers in 58 dedicated workshops. Each session brought together authors and fellow scholars to examine drafts, challenge interpretations, explore connections between different periods of history, and consider how complex academic research could be communicated to readers beyond academia.
There were no slideshow presentations and no hybrid online participation. The emphasis was on being together in the same room, reading one another's work, exchanging ideas, and building the intellectual relationships that make a project of this scale possible.
For many participants, the conference was also an opportunity to reconnect with colleagues who have been working together since the Initiative began, while welcoming new contributors who joined the project this year.
The discussions reflected one of UHGI's central ambitions: to produce history that meets rigorous scholarly standards while remaining engaging and accessible to a broad public.
That requires more than simplifying academic language. It means developing narratives that help readers understand why historical events matter, how different periods and places are connected, and how Ukraine's past forms part of a much larger human story.
Building a scholarly community in wartime
The decision to gather in Kyiv carried particular significance as Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues.
For international participants, travelling to the conference meant experiencing some of the realities of wartime Ukraine firsthand. For Ukrainian researchers, it meant continuing their academic work amid the challenges and uncertainty of war.
Susan Bonner, a Canadian journalist and Senior Fellow at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, joined UHGI's Academic Council this year, bringing four decades of experience in journalism and public communication.
Her journey to Kyiv was disrupted by a Russian drone attack on railway infrastructure near the Ukrainian-Polish border. Travelling alongside other UHGI participants, she experienced lengthy delays and an evacuation to a railway station shelter before reaching the capital.
In an article published in Policy Magazine following the conference, Bonner reflected on the experience of travelling through a country at war to join an international project devoted to making Ukraine's past accessible to a global audience.
Her account illustrates a central idea behind the Initiative: understanding Ukraine's present requires a deeper understanding of its past and of the country's place in world history.
https://www.policymagazine.ca/letter-from-kyiv-riding-the-rails-in-putins-war/
For Timothy Snyder, the gathering also demonstrated the importance of scholarly collaboration at a time when isolation and intimidation threaten intellectual life.
In his closing remarks, he reflected on what participants had achieved together:
"We're certainly working against isolation. We're working against over-specialization. We're working against intimidation. We're working against demoralization and nihilism."
But the purpose of the gathering, he emphasised, was not simply to resist these pressures. It was also to build something together: a community founded on intellectual exchange, mutual support, and a shared commitment to historical truth.
"We're working towards community," he said, "but also affirmation of the principle that we can pursue scholarly truth and that you can do it together."
From academic research to books and a digital experience
The conference also marked the beginning of a new phase in UHGI's development.
Over the past three years, researchers have been investigating subjects spanning thousands of years of history. Their work encompasses archaeology, the movement of peoples, cultural and religious exchange, political developments, and the many connections between Ukraine and the wider world.
The discussions in Kyiv demonstrated the progress made in developing these individual studies into a coherent historical narrative.
Authors are now moving towards the next stage of their work: completing their research, responding to academic feedback, and preparing their texts for publication.
During the conference, researchers also met members of UHGI's editorial team led by Clive Priddle, which has begun working with authors to develop texts that combine academic rigour with clarity and accessibility.
The editorial process will be accompanied by the development of maps, illustrations, and other visual materials to help bring the research to life.
As Snyder explained in his closing remarks, the ambition extends beyond producing a conventional collection of academic publications.
"We're doing both scholarly and popular history," he said. "We're meant to be doing both written history and experienced history."
The Initiative plans to publish its research through books in English and Ukrainian, alongside an ambitious digital platform designed to bring Ukraine's history to a global audience.
The platform is intended to offer more than a digital library of academic texts. By combining historical narratives with visual materials and interactive ways of exploring the past, UHGI aims to create an experience that allows readers to discover Ukraine's history, understand its connections to world history, and explore subjects in greater depth according to their interests.
Snyder described the ambition as bringing scientific research to a very large audience in a way that respects readers' different backgrounds and empowers them to deepen their knowledge.
The next chapter: 2027 and 2028
Although the third annual conference has concluded, the work of the Initiative continues.
Further workshops are planned from October 2026 into 2027, allowing researchers to continue reviewing one another's work, strengthen connections between related subjects, and develop their manuscripts.
The coming year will focus on completing the remaining research and writing, alongside the continuing editorial process. Where necessary, additional focused studies will help address gaps in the research and strengthen connections across the broader historical narrative.
In parallel, UHGI will continue developing its publishing arrangements, visual materials, and digital platform.
The Initiative currently anticipates preparing its principal research outputs for public release in 2028, with the ambition of reaching audiences across Ukraine and internationally.
For Snyder, the opportunity offered to the researchers is an unusual one: to see their academic work become part of a much larger collective project, supported by extensive scholarly collaboration, professional editing, and new ways of reaching the public.
He encouraged participants to embrace that opportunity and to continue working together towards the project's completion.
The conference ended with a shared understanding that the work ahead extends beyond finishing individual manuscripts. It is about bringing together years of research into a history of Ukraine that can be read, explored, and experienced by people around the world.
And, as the gathering in Kyiv demonstrated, that work begins with the people willing to come together to make it possible.
Ruslan Kavatsiuk, Managing Director Ukrainian History Global Initiative

Psilocybin and standard antidepressants both shift the brain away from negative biases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
13:00:56 UTC
22:00:56 KST

Psilocybin and standard antidepressants both reduce the brain’s tendency to view the world through a negative lens. The findings suggest both drugs might relieve depression by shifting how the brain processes emotional information, though they may achieve this through different timelines. The research was published in Translational Psychiatry.
Depression involves more than just a persistently low mood. It affects how people perceive reality on a subconscious level. People with major depressive disorder often exhibit a negative affective bias, meaning they tend to interpret ambiguous or even positive social cues as negative. They might look at a neutral facial expression and perceive anger or sadness.
According to cognitive models of depression, this skewed perception plays a fundamental role in maintaining the illness. When people constantly interpret their social environment as hostile or rejecting, it reinforces their depressed mood. Breaking this cycle is a primary goal of psychiatric intervention.
Traditional treatments like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, known as SSRIs, aim to correct this imbalance. Medications such as escitalopram often take several weeks to produce noticeable improvements in a patient’s mood. Researchers believe this delay happens because the drugs first shift the brain’s emotional processing bias. Patients then need time to interact with their environment and experience positive social feedback before their overall mood lifts.
In recent years, psychiatric researchers have explored psychedelic compounds as alternative treatments for depression. Psilocybin is the active hallucinogenic ingredient in magic mushrooms. Clinical trials indicate that psilocybin can alleviate depressive symptoms much faster than traditional daily pills, but it remains unknown exactly how the compound changes cognitive functions to achieve this rapid relief.
A team led by Marieke A. G. Martens, a psychiatry researcher at the University of Oxford, designed a study to compare the cognitive effects of both drugs. The team included Robin Carhart-Harris and Catherine J. Harmer, among other researchers. They wanted to see if psilocybin works through the same emotional processing pathways as conventional antidepressants.
The study involved 59 patients diagnosed with long-standing, moderate-to-severe depression. The researchers randomly assigned these participants into two separate groups for a six-week trial. They conducted the study under double-blind conditions, meaning neither the patients nor the clinicians knew which full treatment protocol any individual received.
The first group received two 25-milligram doses of psilocybin spaced three weeks apart. These patients also took an inactive placebo pill every day for the six weeks. The second group received a daily dose of the SSRI escitalopram for the entire six-week period. To maintain the blind design, this second group also received two tiny one-milligram doses of psilocybin, which acted as a placebo during the dosing sessions.
Medication was only one component of the treatment protocol. Both groups received identical psychological support throughout the trial. This included preparatory sessions before receiving the psychedelic doses. Therapists also provided integration sessions afterward to help patients process their hallucinogenic experiences.
To measure emotional processing, the researchers used a computer-based assessment called the Facial Expression Recognition Task. Participants completed this task at the beginning of the trial and again at the six-week mark. During the test, patients viewed images of human faces flashing on a screen for half a second.
The faces displayed one of six basic emotions: anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, or surprise. The researchers morphed these images to display varying intensities of emotion, ranging from completely neutral to full intensity. Participants had to identify the emotion shown on each face as quickly and accurately as possible using a keyboard.
Before the treatments began, the participants displayed a measurable negative bias, accurately identifying negative emotions but struggling with positive ones. After six weeks, both treatment groups showed a reduction in this negative bias. The differences between the psilocybin and escitalopram groups were not statistically significant.
Across both groups, participants became less accurate at recognizing negative emotions compared to their baseline scores. They also made fewer errors misclassifying faces as negative. Reaction times for identifying negative and positive emotions improved after the treatments. The researchers noted that patients recognized positive emotions even faster than negative ones at the end of the trial.
Previous brain imaging studies on these same patients showed that the two drugs had different physical effects on the brain. Escitalopram reduced activity in the amygdala, an area involved in processing fear and emotion, when patients viewed faces. Psilocybin did not produce this same dampening effect on amygdala activity. Despite these neurological differences, the behavioral outcomes on the emotional recognition task were remarkably similar.
The researchers then looked for links between these cognitive changes and overall depression symptoms. They measured depression severity using a standard self-report questionnaire at the six-week mark. At this concurrent time point, the reduction in negative emotional bias did not correlate with a drop in depression scores for either group.
The team followed up with the patients one month after the trial ended, at the ten-week mark. For the patients who took escitalopram, a decrease in misclassifying positive faces as negative at six weeks predicted lower depression scores at ten weeks. This aligns with the theory that SSRIs slowly improve mood as patients experience the world through a less negative lens.
This longitudinal relationship did not appear in the psilocybin group. The reduction in negative bias at six weeks did not predict better depression scores at ten weeks for these patients. The lack of correlation suggests that while psilocybin does alter emotional processing, its fast-acting antidepressant effects might rely on other psychological or neurological mechanisms.
The researchers noted several limitations to their experimental design. The trial did not include a pure inactive placebo group that received no active medication at all. Without a strict control group, it is difficult to completely separate the chemical effects of the drugs from the psychological support provided during the trial.
There was likely an inadvertent sample bias among the volunteers. Patients who sign up for clinical trials involving psychedelics often hold a strong preference for receiving psilocybin over traditional daily medications. This preference could influence how they respond to the respective treatments and how they report their symptoms.
Future studies will need to incorporate active placebo groups to better manage the blinding process in psychedelic research. Researchers also plan to measure emotional processing much earlier in the treatment timeline. Assessing patients within days of taking psilocybin could reveal how quickly these cognitive shifts occur compared to traditional medications.
Both treatments successfully shifted how patients interpreted emotional information, highlighting a shared cognitive outcome. The exact pathway from altered perception to mood improvement remains an active area of investigation. The study, “Negative affective bias in depression following treatment with psilocybin or escitalopram – a secondary analysis from a randomized trial,” was authored by Marieke A. G. Martens, Bruna Giribaldi Cunha, David Erritzoe, David Nutt, Robin Carhart-Harris, and Catherine J. Harmer.

North Korea launches missiles as it dials up pressure against U.S.
North Korea launched two short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea on Sunday, South Korea's military said.
The launches came just days after Pyongyang reasserted its status as a nuclear-armed state and rejected a United Nations resolution demanding it halt its nuclear activities. They were also the latest in a series of weapons demonstrations even after President Trump scaled back a joint military exercise with South Korea last month in an apparent effort to revive diplomacy with the North's leader, Kim Jong Un.
The two missile launches — about three hours apart — were conducted from North Korea's eastern coastal Wonsan area. The first missile flew about 280 miles while the second one flew more than 370 miles, both toward the North's eastern waters, South Korea's military said.
"South Korean and U.S. authorities are conducting a detailed analysis to determine its exact specifications," South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said of the second missile.
The missiles eventually ended up in the sea.
U.S. Pacific Command said in a statement that it was aware of North Korea's missile launches and is "consulting closely with our allies and partners."
"Based on current assessments, these events do not pose an immediate threat to U.S. personnel or territory, or to our allies," it said in a post on X. "The United States remains committed to the defense of the U.S. homeland and our allies in the region."
South Korea's presidential office urged North Korea to immediately halt ballistic missile launches that are banned by U.N. Security Council resolutions. The South's military said it maintains readiness to repel any provocations by the North under a solid alliance with the U.S.
Japan's Defense Ministry said it detected a suspected North Korean missile earlier Sunday but that the weapon did not land in its territorial waters.
Kim's sister and senior official, Kim Yo Jong, earlier shrugged off Mr. Trump's overture, saying that shortening the drill wouldn't change its "provocative, aggressive nature." North Korea's military later launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea, apparently following through with a previous threat to respond to the U.S.-South Korean drill.
On Friday, Kim's sister slammed another recent U.S.-led multilateral maritime exercise in the region as a "frantic military move" by the Americans meant to prolong their hegemony in the Asia-Pacific area. The "Pacific Vanguard" exercise brought together the U.S., South Korea, Japan, Australia, New Zealand and Canada.
She claimed that "regular U.S.-led war rehearsals" are the main source of worsening tensions in the Korean Peninsula and the region.
"Our will to defend our sovereignty will be expressed in clearer action and there will be never ever change in the course of intensifying the nuclear war deterrence," she said.
Earlier this month, North Korea conducted what it called a joint live-fire drill involving missiles, artillery and drones, a day after the United States, South Korea and Japan wrapped their five-day trilateral military drill that North Korea described as a provocation. North Korea said its drill included firing different types of weapons simultaneously, likely aiming at developing the ability to overwhelm South Korean and U.S. air defenses.

Frederiksen says Greenland deal respects Denmark's 'red lines’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:52:06 UTC
21:52:06 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
20 September 2026•Update: 20 September 2026
The recent agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the US respects the kingdom's “red lines,” including its sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said on Sunday.
“It has been absolutely crucial for us, with a desire to strengthen security in the very troubled world we live in, that our red lines are respected,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.
Frederiksen said strengthening security in the Arctic and respecting Denmark and Greenland's core interests had been crucial during the negotiations.
“The Kingdom of Denmark is a sovereign state, and the Greenlanders' right to self-determination must be respected in the future. And what we call our territorial integrity. All of that is contained in this,” she added.
Frederiksen declined to discuss the specific content of the agreement before it is signed.
“I will not go into the substance of this, and there is a great deal of speculation, and I understand that there is huge interest in the specific content, but I will not go into the details until we have a signed agreement,” she said.
She said she understood particular interest among Greenlanders about what the agreement would mean for them, after what she described as a difficult period.
“But generally, I would not put my signature, and neither would Jens-Frederik Nielsen, on an agreement that was not good for Greenland and the kingdom,” Frederiksen said.
Frederiksen also confirmed that she would meet US President Donald Trump in New York, where the agreement is due to be signed.
Asked whether she expected Trump to honor the agreement, she said she assumed all sides would do so.
“We have spent a very, very long time on this, both politically and diplomatically,” she said.
Frederiksen said she had “a good relationship” with Trump and described the agreement as beneficial for security.
“I have a good relationship with the American president and in a troubled world, I believe that this agreement is good for our security,” she said.
She said the agreement was beneficial from both a European and NATO perspective, particularly regarding security in the Arctic and across the Atlantic.

Sheeran appeared to read from a teleprompter as he opened the concert with a statement, saying this is not how he usually opens his performances.

"But, this is a humanitarian issue, and i cannot hide how i feel about it any more," he continued. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic, and unjustifiable and disproportionate. My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians' lives - of children's lives. "Ed Sheeran just gave a speech at his concert tonight. He talks about the suffering on BOTH sides of this conflict. The fallout over Sheeran's Loop tour began after rapper Macklemore revealed earlier this month that he was dropped from the shows after stadium owner and business tycoon Robert Kraft applied pressure regarding the matter.
According to Macklemore, Kraft demanded that he be removed from the lineup, and called on other stadium owners to do the same.
Sheeran and Kraft issued their own statements, with Kraft appearing to respond to a pledge from Macklemore to donate $1 million to Palestinian humanitarian causes by saying he would also make a donation to "the region". Kraft added that he had spent "decades" supporting causes related to the Palestinians.
An investigation by The Intercept this week revealed that Kraft has been a long time supporter of the Friends of the Israel Defence Forces, "an organization that collects money on behalf of Israeli soldiers, and the United Democracy Project, the super PAC of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which lobbies to tilt American politics in favor of Israel".
The report added that the Kraft Family Foundation has donated $196,000 to Friends of the IDF since 2006, according to tax forms, and has given $123,000 to other organisations related to the Israeli army and former soldiers.

Caribbean nations considering legal strategies to bring UK to reparation negotiation table - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:44:20 UTC
21:44:20 KST

Caribbean officials are considering legal strategies in an effort to get the United Kingdom into a negotiation for a reparations deal, The Guardian reported on Saturday.
The recent push came during the CARICOM Regional Conference on Reparations, which took place from Thursday to Saturday, the Guardian reported.
The conference was hosted by Barbados, and, according to its website, featured between 150-20 representatives from numerous Caribbean nations, including governmental officials, academics, activists, and cultural leaders.
Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley compared slavery to the Holocaust during the conference, the Guardian cited, pointing out that the German government had repaid the Jewish community $95b.
She said that she did not want anybody to "diminish the fact that in this country here, which I have the honor to lead, that from settlement in 1627, 400 years ago next year, for 211 years, not six, people were treated as chattel.
“If they dared to speak or to do things that were displeasing, their lives and limbs were put at risk. The evidence is clear. What is absent is the will,” she said.
Repair Campaign adviser calls for multigenerational plan
“We need a concrete, multigenerational plan,” Ralph Gonsalves, former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines who now serves as an elder and adviser for the Repair Campaign, said.
According to the Guardian, Gonsalves challenged claims that Britain was not obligated to pay reparations due to it not having violated historical laws during the era of transatlantic slavery.
“The fact is that the consequences of slavery fall squarely under the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, which obliges states to help address the consequences of native genocide and slavery,” Gonsalves said.
Caribbean nations may go to ICJ for UK reparation negotiations
Among the legal strategies which may be employed by Caribbean nations is going to the International Court of Justice, David Comissiong, deputy chair of the Barbados National Task Force on Reparations, said.
Another option currently being employed by Jamaica, the Guardian cited Comissiong as saying, was "trying to engage with the national legal judicial system of the UK, the privy council."
The chair of the CARICOM Reparations Commission, Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, called reparations a matter of justice.
“When Jamaica took its petition to the UK, we had to surround that petition with the fact that when Jamaica became independent in 1962, 80% of the black people in Jamaica could not read or write," he said. "After 300 years of British colonization, they moved into independence with 80% illiteracy. How do you build a modern nation, not even a competitive economy, with 80% illiteracy?”

US House of Representatives passes act mandating free AM radio in every vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:44:18 UTC
21:44:18 KST

The US House of Representatives passed the bipartisan AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act by voice vote on September 15, 2026, moving forward legislation that would require automakers to provide AM broadcast radio at no additional cost in every new passenger vehicle manufactured or imported into the United States.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
H.R. 979 directs the Department of Transportation and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to establish a rule making AM radio standard equipment in new passenger vehicles. Automakers would be prohibited from charging additional fees or subscriptions for access to AM stations.
Supporters say preserving AM radio in vehicles is particularly important during emergencies when cellular networks, electricity, or internet services are unavailable. The technology also remains an important source of local news, weather, and agricultural information in rural communities.
“AM radio is a lifeline. When the power goes out, when the cell towers go down, and when the Internet cuts off during a storm or an emergency, AM radio is often the only way families can get the life-saving information they need,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5), who first announced and introduced the legislation in the 118th Congress.
National Religious Broadcasters (NRB), an international association of Christian communicators, welcomed the House vote.
“For Christian communicators, this vote stands as a major victory for radio and free broadcast distribution as a whole,” said Troy A. Miller, President and CEO of NRB.
Companion legislation, S.315, has more than 60 cosponsors and previously cleared the Senate Commerce Committee. The measure still requires approval by the full Senate before it can be sent to the president.
Trump tells NRB he supports AM radios in vehicles
US President Donald Trump has previously supported efforts to preserve AM radio in vehicles.
